The research addresses a critical gap in Scandinavian historical linguistics: while major sound changes (e.g., Old Norse breaking) are well-documented, the interplay of sociolinguistic, geographic, and contact-induced factors in shaping less systematic dialectal variations remains poorly understood. To analyze these complex patterns, we propose employing high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process and model two primary datasets: (1) a digitized corpus of 15,000+ dialectal transcriptions and manuscript fragments spanning 800–1600 CE, and (2) acoustic data from contemporary rural speech communities preserving archaic features. Computational methods will include phylogenetic algorithms adapted from biological sciences to reconstruct probabilistic language trees, coupled with neural transformer models fine-tuned for Old Norse orthography to detect subtle phonological variations across temporal and spatial parameters. The HPC infrastructure is essential for handling memory-intensive tasks such as training custom word embedding models on irregular historical orthographies and running Monte Carlo simulations to test competing hypotheses about contact phenomena between Norse, Sami, and Finnic languages. Expected outcomes include the first quantitative atlas of North Germanic sound change trajectories, a publicly accessible database linking manuscript evidence to phonological reconstructions, and methodological frameworks for computational historical dialectology. This work will significantly advance the theoretical understanding of language change in small-scale speech communities while demonstrating how HPC-enabled approaches can revitalize research on fragmentary historical language data in the humanities.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on one or more of the languages, literatures, and linguistics of the peoples of Scandinavia and associated Northern European island groups. Programs may involve multiple languages and language families, not be specific as to the name of the language(s) studied, or be otherwise undifferentiated.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the evidence-based understanding of somatic bodywork therapies by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model the biomechanical and physiological effects of manual touch interventions. While somatic practices such as Rolfing, lymphatic drainage, and Hellerwork are widely used to address pain, mobility, and stress, the mechanisms underlying their therapeutic outcomes remain understudied at a systemic level. Current clinical studies and basic biomechanical analyses lack the resolution to capture complex tissue interactions, dynamic fluid movements, or longitudinal neurophysiological responses. To address this gap, we propose a computational framework integrating multi-scale modeling of human soft tissues, circulatory systems, and neural feedback loops. Finite element analysis (FEA) will simulate tissue deformation and force propagation during manual interventions, while computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models will map pressure gradients in lymphatic and vascular systems. Machine learning algorithms, trained on anonymized clinical outcome data (e.g., pain scales, range-of-motion metrics), will identify patterns linking specific techniques to therapeutic effects. These models will be validated against motion capture data from practitioner-client sessions and wearable biosensor outputs (heart rate variability, EMG). The HPC environment is critical for managing the high-dimensional parameter space of anatomical variability, real-time feedback simulations, and large-scale data integration. Expected outcomes include optimized pressure-depth-duration profiles for structural integration techniques, predictive models for client-specific intervention planning, and mechanistic insights into the interplay between tactile stimuli and autonomic nervous system regulation. By establishing quantitative benchmarks for manual therapy efficacy, this work aims to strengthen clinical training protocols, inform safety guidelines, and support the integration of somatic bodywork into mainstream rehabilitative care pathways.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to promote physical and emotional balance and well-being through the application of skilled touch principles and techniques. Includes instruction in therapeutic massage and other hands-on touch methods, anatomy and physiology, structural/functional integration and various holistic health systems (Rolfing/Structural Integration, colon hydrotherapy, Breema, Hellerwork, lymphatic drainage, Rosen Method, hydrotherapy, and others), client counseling, practice management, and applicable regulations and professional standards.

abstract: Pediatric rehabilitation medicine addresses complex, multifactorial conditions where congenital and childhood-onset physical impairments intersect with medical, functional, and psychosocial challenges. Current clinical approaches often lack the capacity to model dynamic interactions between biological, behavioral, and environmental factors, limiting personalized intervention strategies. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop predictive, multiscale computational models that integrate heterogeneous datasets—including electronic health records, neuroimaging, wearable sensor data, and patient-reported outcomes—to optimize rehabilitation pathways for children and young adults with physical impairments. The computational approach employs machine learning (ML) algorithms to identify biomarkers of treatment response, coupled with agent-based simulations to map longitudinal interactions between rehabilitation interventions, functional gains, and psychosocial outcomes. Key technical challenges include managing high-dimensional data with temporal and spatial variability, scaling ML workflows across multimodal inputs, and simulating population-level outcomes under varying intervention scenarios. HPC resources are essential to address these challenges, enabling parallel processing of large datasets, training of deep neural networks on GPU clusters, and iterative simulation runs to test clinical hypotheses. Expected outcomes include (1) a framework for stratifying patients based on predicted responsiveness to specific therapies, (2) validated models linking early intervention patterns to long-term functional independence, and (3) open-source tools for simulating rehabilitation outcomes across diverse socioeconomic contexts. This work will directly inform clinical trials and practice guidelines by quantifying how interdisciplinary care models—spanning physiotherapy, cognitive-behavioral interventions, and assistive technologies—can be dynamically tailored to mitigate lifelong disability risks. By bridging clinical research with computational innovation, the project aims to establish a replicable paradigm for data-driven precision rehabilitation in pediatric populations.
cip_definition: Research on how to use an interdisciplinary approach to prevent, diagnose, treat, and manage congenital and childhood-onset physical impairments in children and young adults, including related medical, physical, functional, psychosocial, and vocational limitations or conditions.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of novel ceramic materials and glazes through predictive modeling and simulation, addressing a critical gap in the empirical trial-and-error methods that dominate ceramic arts. Traditional approaches to formulating glazes and optimizing kiln firing conditions are time-intensive, resource-heavy, and limited by the physical constraints of material experimentation. By integrating computational chemistry, thermodynamics, and machine learning, this research aims to simulate the molecular behavior of clay bodies and glaze components under varying thermal and atmospheric conditions. Key objectives include modeling phase transitions in crystalline glazes, predicting crack propagation in clay substrates during drying and firing, and optimizing kiln temperature profiles for energy efficiency and artistic outcomes. Finite element analysis (FEA) will be employed to simulate thermal stress distributions in ceramic structures, while molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will explore interactions between organic additives and inorganic glaze matrices. Additionally, generative adversarial networks (GANs) will be trained on datasets of historical and contemporary ceramic artworks to propose innovative texture and color combinations. The computational workflows will be validated through parallel physical experiments, with iterative feedback loops refining model accuracy. Expected outcomes include open-access databases of simulated glaze properties, predictive tools for reducing material waste in studio practice, and new methods for replicating historical ceramic techniques with modern sustainability standards. By bridging computational science and ceramic arts, this project aims to establish a framework for data-driven artistic innovation while preserving craft traditions, ultimately expanding the technical and expressive possibilities of the medium.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals creatively and technically to express emotions, ideas, or inner visions by producing art works out of clay and similar materials. Includes instruction in handbuilt and wheel thrown techniques; molding; slips and glazes; trimming and decorating; firing and kiln operation; oxidation; mixed media; ceramic murals; and personal style development.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a data-driven framework to optimize wine program management for the hospitality industry by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze complex, multidimensional datasets spanning enology, sensory science, and consumer behavior. Traditional approaches to wine selection, storage, and pairing rely heavily on heuristic expertise, which can limit scalability and adaptability in dynamic markets. The research problem centers on the lack of integrative computational tools capable of modeling the interactions between wine chemistry, environmental storage conditions, and evolving consumer preferences. By compiling datasets from spectral analysis of wine compounds, climate-controlled aging experiments, and aggregated sommelier service records, this project will employ machine learning models to predict optimal wine preservation parameters, identify underappreciated regional varietals, and generate dynamic pairing recommendations tailored to diverse culinary contexts. Computational challenges include processing high-resolution gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) data to map degradation pathways, simulating micro-oxygenation effects under varying storage conditions, and training natural language processing algorithms on sommelier tasting notes to refine predictive pairing systems. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallelized simulations of long-term aging processes across thousands of virtual wine profiles and real-time optimization of inventory decisions through reinforcement learning. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for quantifying preservation risks, a regional wine potential index to guide purchasing, and an adaptive pairing engine that integrates seasonal menu changes. By bridging enological science with computational analytics, this work aims to reduce waste in wine programs, enhance sommelier decision-making, and democratize access to advanced tools for small-scale hospitality businesses, thereby fostering sustainability and innovation in a traditionally expertise-driven field.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to manage wine selection, purchasing, storage, sales, and service for a variety of establishments in the hospitality industry. Includes instruction in wine production, wine regions of the world, wine tasting, food and wine matching, service techniques, and wine program management.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize decision-making for elementary and middle school administrators by modeling the complex dynamics of school operations. School principals face multifaceted challenges in resource allocation, including balancing staffing needs, facility utilization, budget constraints, and safety protocols while addressing diverse student needs. Traditional qualitative approaches often struggle to account for the interdependencies among these variables. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to create agent-based models (ABMs) simulating school environments. These models will integrate real-world data on student demographics, staff schedules, classroom capacities, and emergency response protocols to evaluate the impact of administrative decisions under varying scenarios. Machine learning techniques will be applied to historical datasets to identify patterns in resource utilization and predict outcomes of policy adjustments. The computational workflow requires parallel processing to manage large-scale simulations of school districts, enabling sensitivity analyses of factors such as redistricting proposals, budget reallocations, or pandemic-style disruptions. Expected outcomes include a decision-support toolkit that quantifies trade-offs between competing priorities (e.g., class size reductions vs. specialist staffing levels) and generates evidence-based recommendations for equitable resource distribution. This work will advance computational approaches in educational leadership by providing administrators with predictive analytics capabilities traditionally unavailable at the K-8 level. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling the combinatorial complexity of school systems, particularly when modeling longitudinal outcomes across multi-year budgetary cycles or assessing emergency preparedness scenarios requiring real-time simulation. Results will be disseminated through partnerships with statewide principal networks to bridge the gap between computational social science and practical school administration.
cip_title: Elementary and Middle School Administration/ Principalship
cip_definition: A program that focuses on educational administration at the elementary and middle school (K-7) levels and prepares individuals to serve as principals and masters of elementary and middle schools. Includes instruction in elementary and/or middle school education, program and facilities planning, budgeting and administration, public relations, human resources management, childhood and pre-adolescent growth and development, counseling skills, applicable law and regulations, school safety, policy studies, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze patterns in caregiver-child interaction dynamics and their relationship to developmental outcomes in home-based childcare settings. While early childhood development research has traditionally relied on observational coding and small-sample studies, this work addresses a critical gap: scalable, data-driven modeling of complex, real-world interactions to identify nuanced predictors of child well-being. The research integrates anonymized audio-visual datasets from childcare environments—capturing vocalizations, movement patterns, and environmental stimuli—with developmental assessment records. Using computational linguistics frameworks and computer vision pipelines, we will process multimodal interaction data to quantify caregiving behaviors (e.g., responsiveness, engagement strategies) and child responses. Deep learning architectures will be trained to detect micro-level patterns in these interactions, while agent-based modeling will simulate how variations in caregiving approaches propagate through developmental trajectories. The computational intensity arises from processing terabytes of unstructured sensory data, training transformer-based models for temporal sequence analysis, and running large-scale simulations of interaction-outcome relationships across diverse demographic profiles. Expected outcomes include: (1) predictive models linking specific caregiver interaction patterns to developmental benchmarks, (2) an open-source toolkit for automated interaction analysis in childcare settings, and (3) evidence-based guidelines for personalized caregiving strategies. By applying HPC methodologies to a domain typically constrained by manual coding and limited sample sizes, this work pioneers computational social science approaches in childcare research. The results aim to empower providers with data-driven insights while informing policy through statistically robust models of how caregiving practices impact early development.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to be primary providers of home, family, residential, or institutional-based child care services. Includes instruction in child growth and development, nutrition, recreation, planning and supervision of play and learning activities, child abuse and neglect prevention, parent-child relationships, and applicable legal and administrative requirements.

abstract: Acute care medicine faces critical challenges in predicting patient deterioration and optimizing time-sensitive interventions, particularly in high-stakes environments such as intensive care units (ICUs) and emergency departments. Current predictive models for sepsis, acute respiratory failure, and multi-organ dysfunction lack the precision and generalizability required for real-world clinical deployment, often due to insufficient integration of high-dimensional clinical data and inadequate computational scalability. This project proposes the development of a machine learning framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multimodal ICU data—including high-frequency vital sign streams, laboratory results, imaging metadata, and unstructured clinical notes—to predict acute decompensation events and guide personalized treatment protocols. The computational approach will involve training ensemble models and transformer-based architectures on retrospective datasets spanning 50,000+ ICU admissions from five academic medical centers. Parallelized preprocessing pipelines will harmonize heterogeneous data formats, while distributed computing will enable hyperparameter optimization and cross-validation at scale. A federated learning component will address data privacy constraints by training localized models across institutions without raw data transfer. The project will further simulate real-time prediction workflows using GPU-accelerated inference to quantify latency requirements for clinical integration. Expected outcomes include validated predictive algorithms for sepsis onset (target AUC ≥0.92) and respiratory failure (target AUC ≥0.89) with interpretable feature attribution maps, alongside benchmarks for computational efficiency in acute care settings. By overcoming existing limitations in processing speed and model complexity, this work aims to establish an HPC-supported infrastructure for rapid, granular clinical decision support, directly addressing the National Institutes of Health’s priorities for scalable AI in critical care. Resource allocation will specifically support GPU node utilization for deep learning workloads and high-memory nodes for large-scale cohort analyses.
cip_definition: Research focused on Acute Care Medicine

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance forensic nursing research by developing computational models that analyze complex patterns of violence-related injury and evidence dynamics. Forensic nursing practice requires integrating heterogeneous datasets—including medical imaging, wound documentation, toxicology reports, and crime scene evidence—to support victim care and legal proceedings. Current manual analysis methods struggle to synthesize these multidimensional data efficiently, limiting insights into injury mechanisms, perpetrator behavior, and long-term health outcomes for survivors. To address this gap, we propose a computational framework combining machine learning (ML) and agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate injury causation scenarios, predict evidence degradation patterns, and identify biomarkers of non-visible trauma. The ML component will train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on annotated photographic and radiographic datasets to classify injury types, estimate timelines of inflicted trauma, and correlate findings with contextual forensic data. Parallelized ABM simulations will model interactions between biological tissues and external forces (e.g., blunt impacts, chemical exposures) under variable environmental conditions to quantify evidence persistence in diverse crime scenes. HPC resources are essential to process high-resolution 3D medical images, optimize hyperparameters for ensemble ML models, and run large-scale simulations accounting for stochastic variables. Expected outcomes include validated predictive tools to guide forensic evidence collection, improve testimony accuracy regarding injury causation, and inform trauma-informed care protocols. By bridging computational science and forensic nursing practice, this work aims to establish scalable methodologies for analyzing violence-related health data, ultimately strengthening medicolegal investigations and victim advocacy efforts.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply the law and forensic science to nursing practice and collaborate with other professionals for the care of victims and the prosecution of criminals. Includes instruction in advanced physical assessment, evidence collection and preservation, forensic anthropology, legal testimony, medicolegal investigation, pathophysiology, pathohistology, pharmacology, and violence prevention.

abstract: Early childhood education is foundational to cognitive and socioemotional development, yet optimizing instructional strategies for diverse learners remains a challenge. This project seeks to develop a computational framework for modeling individualized learning trajectories in preschool settings, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multimodal educational data at scale. The research problem centers on the dynamic interplay between instructional methods, child-specific factors (e.g., attention span, language exposure), and learning outcomes—a complex system requiring fine-grained temporal analysis. Current approaches in teacher education often rely on aggregated classroom-level metrics, limiting personalization. To address this, we propose a machine learning pipeline integrating classroom video recordings (processed via computer vision), audio transcripts of teacher-student interactions (analyzed through NLP), and longitudinal assessments of skill acquisition. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of terabyte-scale datasets from 50+ classrooms, coupled with agent-based simulations to test how variations in pedagogical strategies propagate through heterogeneous learner populations. The computational models will quantify the efficacy of differentiated instruction patterns under varying resource constraints and student ability distributions. Expected outcomes include (1) probabilistic mappings between teachable moments and concept mastery rates, (2) generative AI tools to help educators anticipate individual needs during lesson planning, and (3) open-source code for simulating inclusive classroom environments. By bridging developmental theory with computational precision, this work aims to equip preschool teacher training programs with evidence-based, scalable strategies for addressing variability in early learning. The requested resources are critical for handling the temporal resolution required (sub-second behavioral coding across months of observation) and the combinatorial complexity of simulating thousands of plausible intervention scenarios. Results will directly inform competency frameworks in early childhood teacher education while maintaining strict privacy standards through on-premises HPC deployment.
detailed_field: Teacher education, specific levels and methods
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach students in formal settings prior to beginning regular elementary school, usually ranging in age from three to six years (or grade one), depending on the school system or state regulations. Includes preparation to teach all relevant subject matter.

abstract: Workforce education programs face increasing demand to deliver scalable, adaptive training that aligns with rapidly evolving industry needs. Traditional instructional design methods struggle to efficiently analyze large-scale learner performance data, model skill acquisition pathways, and optimize curriculum sequencing across diverse learner populations. This project seeks to develop computational models of workforce skill development using machine learning techniques applied to multimodal educational datasets, requiring high-performance computing resources to process complex interactions between instructional variables. The research will utilize anonymized learner records from vocational training platforms, including performance metrics, engagement patterns, and demographic variables, combined with natural language processing of curriculum materials and employer skill requirements. Deep neural networks will be trained to simulate skill mastery trajectories under different instructional conditions, while reinforcement learning algorithms will explore optimal intervention strategies for at-risk learners. Computational experiments will systematically vary training modalities, pacing, and competency thresholds across simulated cohorts representing different workforce demographics. The proposed HPC infrastructure is critical for processing terabytes of longitudinal training data and running parallel simulations to identify robust instructional patterns. Expected outcomes include predictive models of skill transfer efficiency, evidence-based frameworks for adaptive curriculum design, and decision-support tools for workforce educators. By computationally modeling the complex dynamics between instructional strategies, individual differences, and labor market needs, this research aims to advance data-driven approaches for workforce development that balance educational effectiveness with scalable delivery—a critical need in preparing workers for 21st-century employment challenges.
detailed_field: Adult, continuing, and workforce education and development
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach programs designed to develop or upgrade specific employment-related knowledge and skills in various settings, and to various age groups.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance large-scale computational analysis of diachronic and synchronic variations in the Japanese language, with a focus on philological evolution, dialectal diversity, and sociolinguistic applications. A central challenge in Japanese linguistics lies in systematically tracing linguistic shifts across historical periods (Ancient, Medieval, Modern) and geographically dispersed dialects, processes that require parsing complex, non-standardized textual and audio datasets. Traditional manual methods struggle to manage the scale of corpora needed to robustly analyze morphological, syntactic, and semantic changes or to model dialectal continua across Japan’s regional speech communities. This project will employ natural language processing (NLP) techniques, including transformer-based models and phonetic alignment algorithms, to process digitized classical texts, modern regional speech recordings, and mixed-mode corpora spanning pre-modern to contemporary sources. Computational workflows will be designed to identify patterns in language change, quantify dialect boundaries using phonological and lexical features, and simulate contact-induced shifts in specialized contexts (e.g., technology-related terminology adoption). HPC resources are critical for training custom tokenizers for historical Japanese orthography, running parallelized analyses across multi-century text corpora, and processing high-resolution audio data for dialect mapping. Expected outcomes include: (1) a publicly accessible diachronic corpus of annotated Japanese texts with computational linguistic metadata; (2) probabilistic models of regional dialect classification informed by sociogeographic variables; and (3) frameworks for predicting semantic drift in technical lexicon, with applications for cross-cultural communication and pedagogy. By integrating computational rigor with philological expertise, this research aims to establish scalable methods for preserving linguistic heritage and addressing contemporary challenges in Japanese language standardization, education, and technology-driven lexical innovation.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Japanese language. Includes instruction in philology; Ancient, Medieval, and Modern Japanese; dialects; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: This project seeks to develop and validate a computational framework for modeling the efficacy of adaptive pedagogical strategies in computer science teacher training programs. A critical challenge in computer teacher education is the lack of data-driven methods to optimize instructional approaches for diverse learner backgrounds, particularly as emerging technologies like AI and machine learning reshape computational literacy requirements. Current models of teacher competency development rely on generalized assessments that fail to account for dynamic interactions between instructional content, learner cognition, and evolving technological tools. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled study combining agent-based modeling, educational data mining, and machine learning. Large-scale simulations will reconstruct heterogeneous virtual classrooms, modeling trainee teachers’ skill acquisition trajectories under varying pedagogical conditions. Input datasets include historical performance metrics from accredited teacher preparation programs, cognitive task analysis results, and longitudinal technology integration surveys. Parallelized Monte Carlo methods will assess probabilistic outcomes of intervention strategies, while natural language processing pipelines will analyze reflective teaching journals for competency indicators. The computational workload necessitates HPC resources due to the combinatorial complexity of simulating 10,000+ agent interactions across multidimensional parameter spaces (e.g., prior knowledge levels, curriculum pacing, and tool exposure sequences). Expected outcomes include a validated predictive model for optimizing computer teacher training pathways and an open-access repository of simulated teaching scenarios aligned with CSTA standards. This work will directly inform the design of adaptive professional development systems, potentially reducing skill gaps in K-12 computer science instruction by 20-30% in pilot implementations. The resource request supports 18 months of computationally intensive experimentation, including GPU-accelerated neural architecture searches for personalized learning recommendation engines.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach computer education programs at various educational levels.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a scalable computational framework for optimizing hybrid renewable energy systems (HRES) that integrate solar, wind, and energy storage technologies. A critical challenge in HRES design lies in balancing intermittency, storage capacity, and demand variability across dynamic spatial and temporal scales, particularly in underserved regions with limited grid infrastructure. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled modeling approach combining multi-objective optimization, stochastic weather simulations, and machine learning-driven demand forecasting. The computational workflow will leverage parallelized Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate system reliability under thousands of weather and load scenarios, coupled with gradient-based optimization algorithms to minimize levelized energy costs while maximizing resilience. Key innovations include the integration of probabilistic climate projections into short-term operational models and the development of adaptive control strategies for distributed storage systems. The HPC resources will enable processing of high-resolution meteorological datasets (1 km² grid, 15-minute intervals) and concurrent evaluation of design parameters across heterogeneous geographic contexts. Expected outcomes include: (1) an open-source software toolkit for HRES optimization, validated against field data from microgrid deployments; (2) predictive metrics for storage sizing under climate uncertainty; and (3) policy-relevant insights into cost-reliability tradeoffs for off-grid energy access. This work directly supports the global transition to low-carbon energy systems by providing computationally robust tools to overcome planning barriers in complex, resource-constrained environments. The requested computing allocation will specifically enable large-scale parameter sweeps and sensitivity analyses that are infeasible on local clusters, reducing time-to-solution for regional energy scenarios from weeks to days.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in energy systems technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Nursing education faces a growing need to optimize pedagogical strategies that bridge theoretical knowledge, clinical competency, and adaptive teaching practices in diverse learning environments. However, the complexity of modeling educational outcomes—which depend on dynamic interactions between instructor methodologies, learner behaviors, and clinical context—exceeds the analytical capacity of traditional statistical tools. This project proposes the development of a computational framework to simulate and evaluate nursing education interventions using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The research will integrate multi-source data, including longitudinal student performance metrics, clinical simulation logs, and psychometric evaluations, to construct agent-based models (ABMs) that replicate classroom and clinical training scenarios. These models will test hypotheses about how variations in instructional pacing, feedback mechanisms, and clinical scenario sequencing influence learner proficiency and retention. A parallelized Monte Carlo approach will assess the robustness of simulated interventions across heterogeneous student cohorts and clinical contexts. Additionally, natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will analyze qualitative data from reflective practice journals to quantify correlations between self-reported learning experiences and competency development. The HPC infrastructure is critical for managing the high dimensionality of educational datasets, enabling real-time parameter optimization in ABMs, and supporting ensemble simulations across thousands of virtual learner profiles. Expected outcomes include identifying evidence-based thresholds for clinical instruction frequency, predicting at-risk learner trajectories, and generating actionable guidelines for personalized competency frameworks. By establishing a computational platform for nursing education research, this work aims to advance the scientific rigor of pedagogical design while addressing workforce demands for nurses prepared in evolving healthcare environments. The project will further enable nursing educators to adopt data-driven strategies for curriculum adaptation, clinical mentoring, and addressing equity gaps in skill acquisition. Resource allocation will directly support the scaling of models to incorporate multi-institutional datasets, fostering collaborative research across nursing education programs.
cip_definition: A program that prepares registered nurses to teach in academic and clinical settings, including staff development. Includes instruction in advanced nursing practice, nursing role development, curriculum and instruction, program and course design, clinical instruction, and evaluation of learning.

abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders in pediatric populations present unique challenges due to the dynamic nature of growing bones and tissues, necessitating tailored diagnostic and treatment strategies. Current clinical approaches often rely on generalized protocols derived from adult studies, which fail to account for developmental variability and the long-term biomechanical consequences of interventions. This project seeks to address this gap by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to develop patient-specific predictive models for surgical and non-surgical management of early-onset scoliosis (EOS) and developmental hip dysplasia (DDH). The research will integrate multimodal clinical data—including longitudinal imaging (MRI, CT), motion capture, and electronic health records—to analyze growth patterns, biomechanical stress distributions, and post-intervention outcomes across diverse pediatric cohorts. Computational workflows will employ finite element modeling (FEM) to simulate spinal and hip joint mechanics under varying treatment scenarios, coupled with machine learning algorithms to identify predictive biomarkers of progression or complications. A key innovation involves coupling these models with population-level registry data to quantify the impact of socioeconomic factors on treatment accessibility and outcomes. The HPC resources will enable large-scale parameter sweeps for sensitivity analysis, Bayesian optimization of treatment parameters, and real-time visualization of complex biomechanical interactions. Expected outcomes include validated computational tools to guide implant selection in EOS, optimize bracing protocols for DDH, and stratify patients by risk of secondary complications. By establishing open-source datasets and modular simulation pipelines, this work will provide a scalable framework for precision orthopedics in pediatric populations, reducing the need for iterative invasive procedures. Resource requests include GPU nodes for deep learning tasks, high-memory nodes for FEM simulations, and secure storage for sensitive patient data, with all workflows adhering to HIPAA and institutional ethics standards.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis, surgical and non-surgical treatment, and management of musculoskeletal diseases, abnormalities and trauma in infants, children, and adolescents.

abstract: The sustainable production of bioenergy from plant and microbial feedstocks requires resolving complex trade-offs between environmental impacts, resource efficiency, and economic viability. Current challenges include optimizing microbial consortia for lignocellulosic biomass conversion, predicting feedstock suitability under variable hydrological and soil conditions, and scaling bioprocess designs to minimize energy-intensive separations. This project seeks advanced computing resources to develop multi-scale models integrating genomic, metabolic, and ecosystem-level data for bioenergy systems. High-performance computing (HPC) will enable genome-resolved simulations of microbial community interactions during anaerobic digestion, dynamic flux balance analysis of engineered metabolic pathways for enhanced biofuel yields, and spatially explicit assessments of region-specific feedstock viability. Coupled machine learning approaches will identify optimal microbial strains, pretreatment strategies, and harvest cycles that maximize energy output while minimizing water and nutrient use. The computational framework will incorporate regional hydrology datasets, soil carbon dynamics, and life-cycle inventory data to evaluate trade-offs between bioenergy production and natural resource conservation. Expected outcomes include predictive models to guide the design of low-impact biorefineries, maps of optimal feedstock zones under climate uncertainty, and open-source tools for real-time bioprocess optimization. By quantifying linkages between microbial efficiency, ecosystem services, and supply-chain logistics, this work aims to advance scalable bioenergy solutions that align decarbonization goals with sustainable land and water management. Access to HPC resources is critical for resolving the high-dimensional parameter spaces and stochasticity inherent in biological and environmental systems, which cannot be feasibly addressed with conventional computing infrastructure. The results will directly inform policy frameworks and industrial practices aimed at achieving net-zero bioenergy systems within planetary boundaries.
detailed_field: Environmental/ natural resources management and policy
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the environmental and economic impact of using plants and microbes for the production of bio-based fuels such as ethanol and biodiesel. Includes instruction in biochemical engineering, bioprocessing, bioseparations, conversion, feedstock, economics, environmental sustainability, hydrology, and natural resource management.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the role of bioelectric signaling gradients in modulating collective cell migration during cancer metastasis, a phenomenon underexplored in conventional molecular medicine frameworks. While molecular mechanisms of metastasis are well-studied, emerging evidence suggests that endogenous electric fields (EFs) at wound or tumor margins guide cell migration via voltage-gated ion channel interactions. However, the computational tools to model these dynamic, multiscale bioelectric processes—spanning subcellular ion flux to tissue-scale EF patterns—are lacking. We propose to develop a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled hybrid model integrating stochastic lattice Boltzmann methods for extracellular ion dynamics with agent-based simulations of cellular electrophysiology. The model will simulate how tumor microenvironmental factors (e.g., pH, extracellular matrix conductivity) alter bioelectric gradients and subsequent metastatic cell behavior. Machine learning approaches will be applied to parameterize ion channel interactions from existing single-cell electrophysiology datasets. The computational framework will be validated against in vitro measurements of EF-directed migration in 3D cancer spheroid models. By bridging electrophysics and cell biology, this work aims to identify novel therapeutic targets that disrupt pro-metastatic bioelectric signaling without directly interfering with biochemical pathways. Successful implementation will provide the first open-source platform for simulating bioelectric microenvironments in cancer, enabling predictive modeling of non-invasive interventions such as applied EFs or ion channel modulators. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling the high-dimensional parameter space and real-time coupling of physicochemical processes across spatial scales. Outcomes will advance understanding of electrophysiological drivers in metastasis while establishing computational methodologies for bioelectricity research in molecular medicine.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the molecular and cellular basis of disease, and the application of this knowledge to the development of new clinical and diagnostic tools, medications, and therapies. Includes instruction in cell biology, molecular biology, physiology, pharmacology, biochemistry, genetics, pathology, molecular immunology, research and quantitative methods, and biomedical research computing.

abstract: This project addresses critical gaps in evaluating health policy interventions within complex, multi-level healthcare systems, where traditional analytical methods struggle to account for dynamic interactions between policy design, institutional capacities, and population health behaviors. The research will develop a computational framework to simulate the longitudinal impacts of health policies—such as insurance expansion, hospital funding models, and preventive care incentives—on health equity and system performance. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), the team will construct agent-based models integrating granular data from national health surveys, electronic medical records, and facility-level operational metrics. These models will capture heterogeneous patient decision-making, provider workflows, and resource constraints across urban-rural divides. Computational experiments will assess how policy variations influence care access, cost burdens, and chronic disease outcomes under demographic and epidemiological shifts. HPC resources are essential for calibrating models using Bayesian inference across high-dimensional parameter spaces, running multi-policy scenario ensembles, and conducting uncertainty quantification at scale. Results will identify leverage points for reducing disparities in care delivery and generate open-source policy simulation tools tailored for low-resource health systems. The work directly supports evidence-based decision-making by enabling rapid, data-rich comparisons of policy alternatives—a capability urgently needed to address evolving challenges in global health governance. By advancing computational methods for health policy analysis, this project aims to establish reproducible frameworks for evaluating systemic interventions while avoiding oversimplified assumptions common in conventional health services research.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic analysis of public policy issues related to domestic and international health and health care systems. Includes instruction in contemporary health issues and policies, politics and economics of health care delivery, epidemiology, public health, comparative and global health, medical law and ethics, statistical methods, and applications to specific public policy topics.

abstract: The development of advanced drug delivery systems is hindered by the complex interplay between nanoparticle carriers, active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), and biological environments. Traditional experimental approaches to optimize nanoparticle self-assembly, stability, and drug release kinetics are time-intensive and resource-limited, particularly when evaluating multifactorial variables such as polymer composition, surface functionalization, and physiological conditions. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to perform multi-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and machine learning (ML)-driven analysis to predict the behavior of polymeric nanoparticles in drug delivery applications. Coarse-grained MD simulations will model the self-assembly of block copolymer nanoparticles at physiologically relevant scales, while all-atom simulations will resolve API-polymer interactions critical to drug loading and release. Concurrently, ML algorithms will be trained on simulation outputs and experimental datasets to identify predictive relationships between polymer properties, nanoparticle morphology, and in vitro release profiles. The computational workflow demands HPC capabilities to manage the high-throughput execution of simulations across parameter spaces and the processing of terabyte-scale trajectory data. Expected outcomes include predictive design rules for nanoparticle formulations with enhanced targeting efficiency and controlled release, directly addressing challenges in oncology and chronic disease therapies. By integrating computational modeling with experimental validation, this project aims to accelerate the development of next-generation nanomedicines while reducing reliance on iterative trial-and-error approaches. The resource allocation will support advancements in pharmaceutical sciences by bridging molecular-level insights with translational drug delivery applications, aligning with priorities in dosage formulation, manufacturing innovation, and precision medicine.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the basic sciences that underlie drugs and drug therapy and that prepares individuals for further study and/or careers in pharmaceutical science and research, pharmaceutical administration and sales, biotechnology, drug manufacturing, regulatory affairs, and related fields. Includes instruction in mathematics, biology, chemistry, physics, statistics, pharmaceutics, pharmacology and toxicology, dosage formulation, manufacturing, quality assurance, and regulations.

abstract: The proposed research project seeks to address critical gaps in understanding the molecular mechanisms of neuropharmacological agents targeting neurotransmitter receptors implicated in neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders. Despite advances in identifying candidate drugs, predicting their dynamic interactions with neural receptors and downstream signaling pathways remains challenging due to the complexity of brain-specific pharmacokinetics and the limited resolution of traditional experimental models. This project aims to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop multiscale computational models that simulate drug-receptor binding dynamics, allosteric modulation, and functional outcomes in heterogeneous neural environments. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will be conducted using optimized force fields to capture atomic-level interactions of small molecules with G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and ion channels over biologically relevant timescales. Machine learning frameworks will integrate MD trajectories with experimental pharmacokinetic data to predict blood-brain barrier penetration, off-target effects, and dose-response relationships. The computational pipeline will further employ ensemble docking strategies to screen compound libraries against receptor conformations associated with disease states, such as hyperactive NMDA receptors in Alzheimer’s disease or dysregulated dopamine receptors in schizophrenia. By utilizing GPU-accelerated HPC clusters, these resource-intensive simulations will achieve the sampling depth required to resolve rare conformational states and stochastic binding events. Expected outcomes include the identification of novel lead compounds with improved selectivity, the characterization of drug-induced neural signaling cascades, and predictive models of neurotoxicity risk. This work will directly inform preclinical drug development, reduce reliance on low-throughput in vivo screening, and advance personalized therapeutic strategies for neurological conditions with high unmet clinical need. The requested computing resources are essential to overcome current limitations in processing power and data storage, enabling iterative modeling of complex neuropharmacological systems at unprecedented resolution.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of drugs that modify the function of the brain and central nervous system, the effects of such drugs on health, disease, perception, motor action, and behavior; and the development of countermeasures and treatment therapies. Includes instruction in neuroanatomy, neurophysiology, behavioral neuroscience, neurobiochemistry, neuropathology, the mechanisms of brain function, medicinal chemistry, pharmaceutics, and studies of specific drugs and drug therapies.

abstract: Dental biomechanics and the interplay between occlusal forces, temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dynamics, and long-term implant stability remain poorly understood, limiting personalized treatment strategies for complex craniofacial rehabilitation. This project proposes a multiscale computational framework to model the biomechanical behavior of dental implants and surrounding bone under dynamic functional loads, integrating patient-specific anatomical data, material fatigue properties, and real-world mastication patterns. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we will develop finite element analysis (FEA) models at unprecedented resolution (sub-10 µm mesh) to capture microstrain distributions in peri-implant bone, coupled with discrete element method (DEM) simulations to analyze particulate wear at implant-abutment interfaces. A machine learning pipeline will process clinical cone-beam CT (CBCT) datasets from 500+ reconstructed cases to establish statistical shape models of mandibular bone morphology, informing boundary conditions for biomechanical simulations. The computational workflow will be validated against in vitro models using digital image correlation (DIC) strain mapping and 6-degree-of-freedom force sensors during simulated chewing cycles. Expected outcomes include predictive algorithms for implant failure risk based on local bone density patterns, optimized occlusal contact schemes to minimize microdamage accumulation, and data-driven design principles for next-generation implant surfaces. This interdisciplinary approach bridges dental materials science, biomechanics, and computational modeling to address the critical gap in understanding how cumulative functional stresses drive late-stage implant complications—a leading cause of revision surgery. The generated models and simulation tools will be shared as open-source resources to advance precision dentistry research, potentially reducing the 15-34% ten-year failure rate observed in current implant systems while informing clinical guidelines for load-adapted prosthetic rehabilitation.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of dentistry/dental medicine, encompassing the evaluation, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of diseases, disorders, and conditions of the oral cavity, maxillofacial area, and adjacent structures and their impact on the human body and health. Includes instruction in the basic biomedical sciences, occlusion, dental health and prevention, oral pathology, cariology, operative dentistry, oral radiology, principles of the various dental specialties, pain management, oral medicine, clinic and health care management, patient counseling, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: Despite the widespread use of aromatherapy in complementary health practices, the biochemical mechanisms underlying its therapeutic efficacy remain poorly characterized at the molecular level. This project seeks to address this gap by employing high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model interactions between essential oil compounds and biological targets, enabling predictive analysis of therapeutic potential and safety. The primary challenge lies in the combinatorial complexity of essential oils, which contain hundreds of bioactive constituents whose synergistic effects cannot be comprehensively evaluated through conventional experimental methods alone. We propose a multi-scale computational approach integrating molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and machine learning to systematically investigate how terpenes, phenolics, and other volatile organic compounds interact with human physiological systems. Simulations will focus on key targets such as olfactory receptors, inflammatory mediators, and cell membrane dynamics, complemented by cheminformatic analysis of absorption, distribution, and metabolic transformation pathways. HPC resources will be critical for processing large datasets of phytochemical profiles, optimizing quantum chemical calculations for energy minimization, and training neural networks to predict blend synergies. Expected outcomes include the identification of novel bioactive compounds with validated molecular targets, quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models for efficacy and toxicity prediction, and evidence-based frameworks for optimizing extraction methods and application protocols. This research will advance the scientific rigor of aromatherapy practice by establishing mechanistic links between traditional applications and modern molecular pharmacology, while improving safety standards through computational toxicology screening. The resulting computational workflows will create new paradigms for studying plant-derived therapeutics, bridging traditional knowledge systems with contemporary computational biology.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide therapeutic care through the preparation and application of extracted essential oils from plants, including flowers (botanicals), roots, berries, and bark. Includes instruction in aromatherapy history and theory, basic physiology of absorption, aromachemistry, organic chemistry, botanical taxonomy, carrier oils, essential oils, extraction methods, blending techniques, application methods, safety, client consultation and treatment planning, business management, professional standards and ethics, and applicable regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to optimize patient intake and administrative workflows in medical reception settings by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model and simulate complex, dynamic interactions between patients, staff, and institutional constraints. Medical receptionists face challenges in balancing efficiency, regulatory compliance, and patient satisfaction, particularly in high-volume healthcare environments. Traditional methods for workflow analysis often fail to account for the multivariate, real-time nature of these systems, including variable patient arrival rates, diverse care pathways, staff availability, and evolving policies. To address this, we propose a computational framework combining agent-based modeling (ABM) and machine learning (ML) to simulate clinic operations under diverse scenarios. The ABM component will represent patients, receptionists, and providers as autonomous agents with behavior profiles derived from anonymized clinic data (e.g., check-in times, query types, documentation requirements). ML algorithms will analyze historical data to predict bottlenecks, optimize scheduling, and evaluate the impact of policy changes on throughput and wait times. Additionally, natural language processing (NLP) techniques will be applied to de-identified patient-receptionist interaction logs to identify communication patterns that correlate with service efficiency and patient satisfaction metrics. HPC resources are essential to process large datasets (spanning thousands of patient encounters), run parallelized simulations at scale, and train ML models with high-dimensional inputs (e.g., temporal, linguistic, and operational features). Expected outcomes include actionable insights for redesigning intake workflows, a predictive tool for staffing allocation, and evidence-based recommendations for improving receptionist training programs. By integrating computational modeling with healthcare administration principles, this work aims to advance data-driven decision-making in medical reception—a critical yet understudied component of patient care delivery.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of office managers, nurses, or physicians, to provide customer service, visitor reception, and patient intake and discharge services. Includes instruction in medical office and health care facility procedures, medical terminology, interpersonal skills, record-keeping, customer service, telephone skills, data entry, interpersonal communications skills, and applicable policies and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the spatial and temporal dynamics of informal settlement adaptation to climate stressors in coastal megacities, integrating cultural practices with environmental constraints. While informal settlements account for over 30% of urban populations globally, their adaptive strategies—shaped by localized knowledge, material improvisation, and social networks—remain poorly quantified at scale. Traditional ethnographic methods struggle to capture the multi-scalar interactions between micro-level decision-making and macro-level environmental shifts, necessitating computational approaches. We propose a hybrid agent-based modeling (ABM) framework coupled with high-resolution geospatial analysis to simulate how households in Manila, Lagos, and Mumbai negotiate flooding, heat stress, and resource scarcity. The ABM will parameterize cultural variables (e.g., kinship-based resource sharing, vernacular architecture) using field survey data from partner NGOs, while incorporating real-time satellite-derived flood maps, LiDAR-based elevation models, and climate projection datasets. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for three components: (1) running ensemble simulations across decadal time horizons at 10m spatial resolution, (2) processing petabytes of Sentinel-2 imagery to track settlement morphology changes, and (3) training transformer models on community-generated social media text to infer adaptive behavior patterns. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible digital twin platform visualizing resilience trade-offs under different warming scenarios, and a novel cultural adaptation index quantifying non-economic factors in urban climate vulnerability. By bridging computational social science with critical geography, this work advances methodologies for studying embodied environmental knowledge in underserved communities while providing actionable insights for equitable adaptation planning.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on human cultures and their adaptation to physical environments. Includes instruction in archaeology, biogeography, climatology, cultural anthropology, cultural geography, economic development, environmental geography, geomorphology, global environmental change, historical geography, mapping sciences, physical anthropology, political ecology, Quaternary studies, and urban geography.

abstract: This research project seeks to address the computational challenges inherent in modeling and optimizing adaptive urban soundscapes—a novel engineering domain integrating acoustic physics, real-time sensor networks, and psychoacoustic human responses to mitigate noise pollution while enhancing public well-being. Current approaches to urban sound management remain reactive and fragmented, lacking the dynamic, system-level frameworks required to balance competing priorities such as traffic efficiency, architectural design, and community health. To overcome these limitations, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled workflow combining finite element acoustic simulations, machine learning-driven noise source identification, and agent-based behavioral modeling. Large-scale parallelized simulations will resolve wave propagation phenomena across geometrically complex cityscapes at frequencies relevant to human perception (20 Hz–20 kHz), while reinforcement learning algorithms will iteratively optimize soundscape parameters using real-world noise data and psychoacoustic metrics. The computational pipeline will integrate heterogeneous datasets, including LiDAR-derived 3D urban topographies, IoT sensor streams, and psychometric surveys, to create closed-loop adaptive systems. Anticipated outcomes include a validated open-source framework for predictive soundscape engineering, quantitative guidelines for context-aware noise regulation, and novel metrics for evaluating auditory urban livability. The HPC resources are critical to achieving the required spatial-temporal resolution for acoustic predictions across kilometer-scale domains and enabling real-time optimization cycles. By bridging gaps between physical acoustics, data science, and human-centered design, this work aims to establish computational foundations for next-generation smart cities where engineered soundscapes actively contribute to environmental sustainability and quality of life. The methodologies developed may also find applications in therapeutic acoustic environments, augmented reality systems, and infrastructure resilience planning against noise-induced stressors.
cip_definition: A program with a general focus on the general application of various combinations of mathematical and scientific principles to the analysis and evaluation of engineering problems, including applied research in human behavior, statistics, biology, chemistry, the earth and planetary sciences, atmospherics and meteorology, and computer applications.

abstract: This project seeks to advance understanding of coupled geochemical and petrological processes governing magma crystallization and hydrothermal ore formation through high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled reactive transport modeling. A critical challenge in predicting the evolution of magmatic-hydrothermal systems lies in simulating multi-phase, multi-component interactions across scales—from micrometer-scale mineral reactions to kilometer-scale fluid flow—under dynamically changing pressure-temperature-composition regimes. Current models often simplify thermodynamic equilibria, kinetic barriers, or spatial resolution, limiting their predictive power. We propose to develop and apply a parallelized reactive transport code integrating high-fidelity thermodynamic databases (e.g., HCh, Deep Earth Water) with lattice Boltzmann methods to resolve pore-scale fluid-rock interactions, coupled with continuum-scale advection-diffusion models. This hybrid approach will leverage HPC resources to handle 3D simulations of ore-forming systems with >10^8 grid points, incorporating real mineral textures from micro-CT datasets. Key objectives include quantifying how subgrain-scale zoning in pyroxene and plagioclase affects magma chamber dynamics and evaluating the role of fracture network geometry in controlling metal transport in porphyry copper systems. Simulations will be validated against experimental data and natural samples from the Stillwater Complex and Bingham Canyon deposit. The computational workflow will utilize MPI-OpenMP hybrid parallelism on GPU-accelerated nodes to manage memory-intensive phase equilibria calculations and fluid flow solvers. Expected outcomes include new scaling laws linking microtextural data to reservoir-scale geochemical anomalies, reducing exploration uncertainty for critical minerals. This work will provide open-source tools to bridge atomic-scale geochemistry and system-scale petrology, addressing a persistent gap in interpreting ore-forming processes within evolving tectonic frameworks.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the igneous, metamorphic, and hydrothermal processes within the earth and the mineral, fluid, rock, and ore deposits resulting from them. Includes instruction in mineralogy, crystallography, petrology, volcanology, economic geology, meteoritics, geochemical reactions, deposition, compound transformation, core studies, theoretical geochemistry, computer applications, and laboratory studies.

abstract: This research project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing resource allocation in cloud-based information systems under dynamic demand fluctuations, a critical issue for organizations managing scalable digital services. Rapid shifts in user demand, coupled with the complexity of multi-cloud environments, often lead to inefficient resource utilization, inflated costs, and service latency. Traditional heuristic approaches fail to account for real-time variability and interdependencies between computational, storage, and network resources. To overcome these limitations, the project proposes the development of a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven simulation framework coupled with adaptive machine learning models. The HPC infrastructure will enable large-scale, parallelized simulations of diverse demand scenarios across hybrid cloud architectures, capturing nonlinear interactions between workload patterns, pricing models, and contractual constraints (e.g., service-level agreements). Concurrently, graph neural networks will be trained on synthetic and real-world workload traces to predict optimal resource scaling strategies while minimizing budgetary impacts. The computational workflow integrates discrete-event simulation, constrained optimization, and sensitivity analysis to evaluate trade-offs between performance, cost, and regulatory compliance factors such as data sovereignty requirements. Expected outcomes include an open-source decision support toolkit that enables organizations to dynamically optimize cloud resource portfolios, reducing operational costs by an estimated 15–25% while maintaining QoS targets. This interdisciplinary approach bridges computational systems theory with information resource management, offering novel methodologies for operationalizing cost-aware scalability in enterprise cloud ecosystems. The project’s HPC requirements center on GPU-accelerated nodes for neural network training and distributed memory clusters for massive scenario testing, with an initial allocation of 200,000 node-hours requested to establish baseline models and validate the framework against industry-standard benchmarks.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply principles of information technology, computer systems management, and business operations to the planning, management, and evaluation of information services in organizations. Includes instruction in telecommunications, systems planning and integration, information policy, information security, contracting and purchasing, budgeting, information technology, operations management, human resources, communications skills, and applicable law and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing persuasive communication strategies in dynamic, multi-platform digital environments through advanced computational modeling. As digital advertising and public relations campaigns increasingly rely on real-time, data-driven decision-making, traditional analytical methods struggle to process the scale and complexity of user interactions, sentiment patterns, and cross-platform content diffusion. Our research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop agent-based models simulating information cascades across social networks, paired with natural language processing (NLP) pipelines for analyzing multimodal campaign content (text, video, and audio) at scale. The computational framework will integrate real-world datasets spanning social media engagement metrics, demographic variables, and psychographic profiles to test hypotheses about message personalization, timing, and platform-specific resonance. Key technical challenges include parallel processing of heterogeneous data streams, training transformer-based models for cross-cultural sentiment analysis, and optimizing network diffusion algorithms for scenario testing. Expected outcomes include a predictive toolkit for evaluating campaign prototypes under diverse sociotechnical conditions, evidence-based guidelines for mitigating misinformation risks in crisis communication, and scalable metrics for measuring the ethical implications of AI-enhanced persuasion tactics. By enabling rapid iteration of complex communication scenarios that mirror real-world information ecosystems, this project aims to advance both theoretical frameworks in applied communication and practical strategies for industry practitioners. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling memory-intensive NLP tasks, large-scale network simulations, and the integration of generative AI tools for automated content variation testing—capabilities beyond the scope of standard departmental computing infrastructure.
detailed_field: Applied communication, advertising, and public relations
cip_title: Public Relations, Advertising, and Applied Communication
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on organizational communication, public relations, and advertising; and that prepares individuals to function in a wide range of public and private sector positions requiring the skills of persuasive communication. Includes instruction in communications, public relations, and advertising theory; principles and techniques of persuasion; message/image design; marketing strategy; professional writing; public speaking and multi-media presentation skills; digital communications; and applied research.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of predictive models for early detection and personalized treatment of complex ophthalmic diseases, including diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and glaucoma. Current diagnostic methods often rely on static clinical imaging and manual feature extraction, which lack the capacity to integrate dynamic, multimodal data or model disease progression at scale. To address this, we propose a computational framework combining deep learning with large-scale biomechanical simulations to analyze longitudinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus imaging, and patient-specific genetic datasets. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallel processing of high-resolution 3D retinal scans (>10,000 images) and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to identify novel biomarkers. Finite element modeling of intraocular pressure dynamics and retinal tissue stress will be optimized using GPU-accelerated solvers to simulate disease pathways under varying physiological conditions. Recurrent neural networks will then integrate these multimodal outputs to predict individual patient trajectories and optimize intervention strategies. The computational workload demands significant memory allocation (~1 TB RAM) and multi-node GPU clusters due to the scale of image processing and iterative model training. Expected outcomes include validated algorithms for early risk stratification, a generative model of disease progression for surgical planning, and open-source tools for automated analysis of ophthalmic imaging data. This work will directly enhance clinical decision-making in ocular pathology management and provide a template for computationally driven precision medicine in ophthalmology. By allocating these resources, the project aims to reduce diagnostic delays for sight-threatening conditions and improve the cost-effectiveness of vision-preserving therapies.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis, prevention treatment of ophthalmic diseases and disorders, and ocular pathology procedures. May included related research in eye surgery.

abstract: The dynamic behavior of silicate minerals under extreme pressure and temperature conditions governs critical geomorphological processes, including subduction zone dynamics, mantle convection, and metamorphic transformations. However, predictive models of silicate phase transitions and deformation mechanisms remain limited by insufficient resolution of atomic-scale kinetics over geological timescales. This project seeks to advance understanding of silicate mineral behavior by integrating quantum-mechanical simulations with large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) to model phase stability and defect propagation in olivine, pyroxene, and quartz systems under lithospheric conditions. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve the multi-scale nature of these processes, which span femtosecond-scale atomic interactions to millennial-scale tectonic deformation. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations will parameterize interatomic potentials for MD simulations, while enhanced sampling algorithms will accelerate rare-event analysis of phase transition pathways. Simulations will be validated against experimental data from high-pressure diamond anvil cell studies and synchrotron X-ray diffraction. The computational workflow requires massively parallel architectures to manage system sizes exceeding 10^6 atoms and simulation timescales up to microseconds, leveraging GPU-accelerated nodes for energy barrier calculations. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models of silicate plasticity in subducting slabs, (2) quantification of metastable phase persistence in exhumed metamorphic rocks, and (3) open-access datasets of strain-rate-dependent mineral properties. These results will directly inform field-based studies of mountain building processes and improve hazard assessments in seismogenic zones. The requested allocation of 500,000 node-hours on HPC clusters will enable unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution in coupled quantum/classical simulations, addressing a critical gap between atomistic mechanisms and plate-scale geodynamics.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the silicates and other substances formed by chemical and physical geomorphological processes.

abstract: Institutional researchers in higher education face growing demands to leverage complex, multi-source data for strategic decision-making, yet existing analytical approaches often struggle to integrate large-scale administrative records with emerging unstructured data streams. This project seeks to develop predictive models of student success and institutional effectiveness using advanced computational methods that require high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The research will analyze integrated datasets spanning 10 years of institutional records (enrollment, academic performance, and retention), instructor-generated text feedback, and facility utilization logs from a consortium of six public universities. Key challenges include processing natural language data at scale, managing temporal dependencies across longitudinal records, and resolving entity matches across decentralized systems. The computational approach employs distributed data processing with Apache Spark for initial feature engineering, followed by GPU-accelerated training of ensemble machine learning models (XGBoost and transformer-based architectures) to predict retention risks and program efficacy. A parallel implementation of hierarchical Bayesian models will quantify institutional-level effects while accounting for cross-campus heterogeneity. This dual methodology addresses both individual student outcomes and systemic performance indicators, requiring iterative model tuning across 150+ predictor variables. The HPC environment is critical for maintaining data security protocols during cross-institutional analysis, executing memory-intensive natural language processing tasks on 4TB of text data, and reducing model training times from weeks to days through parallelization. Expected outcomes include (1) an open-source framework for ethical multi-institutional data harmonization, (2) validated early-alert systems with improved specificity over current retention models, and (3) quantitative benchmarks for assessing academic program viability under demographic shifts. By advancing computational methods tailored to higher education’s distinct data ecosystems, this work will provide scalable tools to support evidence-based resource allocation and adaptive policy design in postsecondary institutions.
cip_definition: A program of study that prepares an individual to be an institutional researcher at a postsecondary educational institution.
