abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of cultural identity and intersectional gender narratives across Latin American and Caribbean digital archives through advanced computational text analysis. The research addresses the challenge of systematically analyzing vast, multilingual corpora—including historical newspapers, literary works, and grassroots publications—to trace evolving representations of marginalized communities and hybrid cultural expressions. Current methodologies in regional studies lack scalable tools to process heterogeneous, non-standardized texts spanning Spanish, Portuguese, Creole languages, and indigenous linguistic variants. Our approach integrates transformer-based natural language processing models optimized for low-resource languages with graph-based network analysis to map semantic shifts and discourse networks across temporal and geographic axes. High-performance computing resources are critical for training custom multilingual language models on distributed text datasets (>10 TB), conducting parallelized sentiment and topic coherence analyses, and simulating cultural transmission dynamics via agent-based modeling. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible annotated corpus of 20th-century Caribbean feminist writings, quantitative frameworks for assessing cultural hybridity in postcolonial contexts, and visual analytics tools to contextualize identity formation processes. By enabling large-scale interrogation of underrepresented narratives, this work aims to redefine methodological paradigms in area studies while informing contemporary debates on cultural preservation and inclusive historiography in digitization initiatives.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: An integrated program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of the peoples and countries of the Latin American and Caribbean region.

abstract: Inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) are a heterogeneous group of genetic disorders characterized by disruptions in biochemical pathways, leading to complex clinical manifestations and significant morbidity. Current challenges in diagnosis and management stem from phenotypic variability, limited genotype-phenotype correlations, and the lack of predictive tools for treatment response. This project seeks to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to integrate multi-omics data—including genomic, metabolomic, and clinical datasets—and develop computational models for precision diagnosis and therapeutic optimization. The research will focus on three aims: (1) constructing predictive models of metabolic pathway disruptions using machine learning algorithms trained on large-scale patient cohorts, (2) simulating enzyme kinetics and metabolic flux in silico to assess the functional impact of novel genetic variants, and (3) identifying biomarkers for treatment stratification through longitudinal analysis of metabolomic profiles. HPC resources are essential to manage the computational demands of whole-exome sequencing analysis, molecular dynamics simulations of mutant enzymes, and Bayesian network modeling of metabolic networks. Expected outcomes include the creation of a scalable computational framework for rapid variant interpretation, personalized dietary and pharmacologic intervention strategies, and the discovery of novel therapeutic targets for refractory IEMs. By enabling the analysis of high-dimensional datasets and complex simulations, this work will enhance clinical decision-making, reduce diagnostic delays, and improve outcomes for patients with rare metabolic disorders. The tools and models developed will be disseminated as open-source resources to support broader translational research in medical biochemical genetics.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis and medical management of individuals with inborn errors of metabolism, including the provision of direct care and consultative care for individuals of all ages.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance interdisciplinary research in Women’s Studies by analyzing large-scale textual and visual datasets that document feminist cultural production and activism across diverse global contexts. The research problem centers on identifying patterns in feminist discourse and artistic expression that have historically been marginalized or fragmented due to the scale and complexity of archival materials. Traditional qualitative methods struggle to systematically trace thematic shifts, transnational influences, or intersectional dynamics in women’s cultural output from the 20th and 21st centuries, particularly across multilingual or under-digitized collections. To address this, the project will employ computational text analysis, image recognition, and network modeling to process digitized archives of feminist literature, periodicals, manifestos, and visual art from North American, South Asian, and West African contexts. Custom NLP pipelines will be developed to handle multilingual texts, dialect variations, and non-Western feminist terminologies, while computer vision tools will classify visual motifs in art and protest materials. Network graphs will map the circulation of ideas across regions and temporal periods, identifying hubs of influence and underrepresented contributors. The computational workflow requires HPC resources to manage terabyte-scale datasets, train machine learning models on GPU clusters, and run parallelized analyses of cross-cultural correlations. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible digital repository of annotated feminist cultural artifacts, visualizations of discourse networks, and peer-reviewed findings on how regional sociohistorical contexts shaped feminist aesthetics and rhetoric. This work will provide scholars in gender studies and digital humanities with new methodologies to analyze intersectionality at scale, while centering computationally underrepresented voices in global feminist movements. By bridging computational scalability with humanistic inquiry, the project aims to redefine canon-formation processes and inform contemporary equity-oriented cultural policies.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
detailed_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, sociology, politics, culture, and economics of women, and the development of modern feminism in relation to the roles played by women in different periods and locations in North America and the world. Programs may focus on literature, philosophy, and the arts as much as on social studies and policy.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the evolutionary mechanisms underlying morphological and genomic adaptations in hominins through advanced computational modeling and large-scale data integration. A key challenge in physical and biological anthropology is disentangling the complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and selective pressures that shaped anatomical and physiological traits in early Homo and related taxa. Traditional analytical methods struggle to synthesize multidimensional datasets—including high-resolution 3D fossil morphology, ancient DNA fragments, paleoenvironmental proxies, and comparative primate genomics—while accounting for stochastic evolutionary processes. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement agent-based evolutionary simulations, Bayesian phylogenetic comparative models, and machine learning-driven morphometric analyses. The computational workflow will integrate fossil cranial and postcranial datasets from Pleistocene hominins with genomic data from modern and ancient populations to simulate adaptive scenarios under variable climatic and ecological conditions. Parallelized Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) algorithms will assess trait covariance and selection coefficients across simulated populations, while neural networks trained on geometric morphometric data will classify adaptive signatures in fragmentary fossil specimens. This approach requires significant memory allocation and GPU acceleration due to the iterative nature of simulations (10⁶+ agent generations) and the processing of terabyte-scale micro-CT scan repositories. Expected outcomes include identifying critical thresholds in environmental variability that precipitated locomotor and encephalization adaptations, reconstructing adaptive landscapes for key hominin lineages, and publishing open-source tools for fossil data integration. The project will advance methodological frameworks in evolutionary anthropology by enabling probabilistic reconciliation of morphological and genomic evidence at previously unfeasible scales, with implications for understanding human resilience to environmental stress.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of the biological sciences and anthropology to the study of the adaptations, variability, and the evolution of human beings and their living and fossil relatives. Includes instructions in anthropology, human and mammalian anatomy, cell biology, paleontology, human culture and behavior, neuroscience, forensic anthropology, anatomical reconstruction, comparative anatomy, and laboratory science and methods.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of legislative polarization and coalition formation in multiparty democracies using advanced computational modeling and large-scale data analysis. A core challenge in comparative politics lies in understanding how institutional rules (e.g., electoral systems, agenda-setting procedures) interact with ideological preferences to shape legislative outcomes, particularly in contexts of fragmented party systems. Traditional analytical methods struggle to disentangle the nonlinear feedback loops between institutional design, strategic actor behavior, and emergent political phenomena. To address this, we propose developing an agent-based model (ABM) simulating legislative decision-making processes under varying institutional configurations. The ABM will incorporate empirical data on historical voting records, party manifestos, and procedural rules from 15 parliamentary democracies (1990–2020). High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to handle the model’s complexity, including parallelized Monte Carlo simulations across parameter spaces and Bayesian calibration against real-world legislative outcomes. Additionally, we will employ natural language processing (NLP) techniques to analyze parliamentary speech corpora, quantifying rhetorical strategies and issue framing dynamics. These computational approaches will be integrated through network analysis to map how institutional pathways mediate ideological conflict resolution. The project’s outcomes will advance theoretical frameworks in comparative institutions and legislative behavior while providing empirically grounded insights for constitutional design in emerging democracies. By identifying critical leverage points where institutional reforms might mitigate polarization without sacrificing representation, the research has implications for both academic debates and practical policy discussions. Successful execution requires sustained access to GPU-accelerated nodes for deep learning components of the NLP pipeline and high-memory nodes for large-scale network inference tasks, necessitating dedicated HPC allocation beyond standard campus computing infrastructure.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the systematic study of political institutions and behavior. Includes instruction in political philosophy, political theory, comparative government and politics, political parties and interest groups, public opinion, political research methods, studies of the government and politics of specific countries, and studies of specific political institutions and processes.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance precision in ophthalmic dispensing through computational modeling of personalized eyewear dynamics. Current methods for fitting corrective lenses rely heavily on static anatomical measurements and generalized optical formulas, which may inadequately account for dynamic factors such as micro-movements of frames during wear, tear film variability in contact lens applications, or asymmetrical facial biomechanics. These limitations can lead to suboptimal visual correction, discomfort, or prolonged adaptation periods. To address this, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML) to simulate interactions between eyewear, ocular surfaces, and environmental conditions. The project will utilize 3D scans of patient facial anatomy, corneal topography data, and material properties of lens polymers to construct patient-specific models. HPC resources will enable parallelized simulations of frame deformation under mechanical stress, fluid-structure interactions for contact lens tear film stability, and predictive ML algorithms trained on optical outcome datasets. Key challenges include resolving micrometer-scale fluid dynamics at the lens-cornea interface and optimizing GPU-accelerated workflows for real-time clinical applicability. Anticipated outcomes include a validated computational toolkit for predicting optimal frame-lens combinations, reducing iterative trial fittings, and improving adherence to corrective eyewear. This interdisciplinary approach bridges opticianry, biomechanics, and computational optics, offering a novel paradigm for precision eyewear design while addressing gaps in existing ophthalmic dispensing methodologies. The project’s computational demands—particularly in handling high-resolution meshes and iterative ML training—necessitate HPC infrastructure to achieve clinically actionable results within feasible timeframes.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to adapt and fit corrective eyewear, including eyeglasses and contact lenses, as prescribed by ophthalmologists or optometrists; to assist patients in selecting appropriate frames; and to prepare work orders for ophthalmic laboratory technicians. Includes instruction in geometrical optics, ophthalmic optics, anatomy of the eye, optical instrumentation, use and maintenance of adjustment and cleaning tools, prescription interpretation, contact lens adaptation and fitting, prosthesis fitting, facial and eye measuring, pathology identification, record-keeping, and patient and business administrative tasks.

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing computational demands of high-resolution digital imaging and prepress design workflows, which are increasingly limited by conventional computing infrastructure. As the graphic design industry shifts toward ultra-high-definition (UHD/8K) media, dynamic multi-page layouts, and AI-enhanced image processing, existing tools struggle to efficiently render, simulate, and optimize complex design files. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop parallelized workflows for real-time collaborative design environments, automated color management simulations, and machine learning-driven layout optimization. Key computational challenges include GPU-accelerated raster image processing for large-format print preparation, distributed rendering of interactive 3D design previews, and neural network training for predictive typographic alignment across diverse digital platforms. By implementing containerized design automation pipelines on HPC clusters, the project aims to reduce processing times for multi-gigabyte design files by 70-90% compared to current desktop-based workflows. Outcomes will include open-source extensions to industry-standard design software, optimized for scalable computing architectures, and a framework for assessing computational resource allocation in cloud-based publishing environments. This work will directly benefit communication design research by enabling experimentation with computationally intensive techniques such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) for asset creation and physics-based ink deposition modeling for sustainable print production. The requested resources will support both benchmark studies of existing workflows and the development of novel algorithms to bridge gaps between traditional prepress requirements and emerging computational design methodologies.
cip_title: Prepress/ Desktop Publishing and Digital Imaging Design
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to the layout, design and typographic arrangement of printed and/or electronic graphic and textual products. Includes instruction in printing and lithographic equipment and operations, computer hardware and software, digital imaging, print preparation, page layout and design, desktop publishing, and applicable principles of graphic design and web page design.

abstract: Pediatric nephrology faces critical challenges in understanding the molecular and physiological drivers of congenital, inherited, and acquired kidney diseases, which are often heterogeneous and involve multi-organ dysfunction. Current diagnostic and therapeutic strategies are limited by incomplete knowledge of disease mechanisms, variability in treatment responses, and a lack of predictive models tailored to pediatric populations. This project seeks to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to integrate multi-omics data, clinical records, and physiological simulations, enabling the development of precision medicine frameworks for pediatric renal disorders. The research will focus on three interconnected aims: (1) constructing machine learning models to predict disease progression and treatment outcomes in pediatric chronic kidney disease (CKD) and congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT), using whole-genome sequencing, proteomic profiles, and longitudinal clinical data; (2) simulating renal hemodynamics and electrolyte transport in pediatric hypertension through multiscale computational models of nephron function; and (3) identifying novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets via network analysis of transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets from pediatric cohorts with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. These computationally intensive tasks require HPC resources to manage large-scale data integration, parallelize molecular dynamics simulations, and train deep neural networks on high-dimensional datasets. The anticipated outcomes include validated predictive algorithms for CKD progression, mechanistic insights into hypertension pathophysiology, and candidate biomarkers for early intervention. By bridging computational and clinical approaches, this work aims to advance personalized management strategies, reduce long-term morbidity, and inform therapeutic discovery for pediatric kidney diseases. The requested computing infrastructure is essential to handle the data volume, algorithmic complexity, and iterative modeling demands inherent to these objectives.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis and management of infants, children, and adolescents with renal and genito-urinary problems, hypertension and disorders of body fluid physiology.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research on syntactic and semantic patterns in premodern East Asian texts, with a focus on Classical Chinese and its influence on early Japanese and Korean literary traditions. A key challenge in analyzing these texts lies in their linguistic complexity, non-standardized orthographies, and the scarcity of digitized corpora with robust philological annotations. Traditional manual analysis struggles to address the scale of data required to trace diachronic shifts in grammatical structures or quantify cross-regional lexical borrowing. The proposed computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) techniques, including transformer-based models, to automate the parsing of syntactic dependencies and semantic role labeling across heterogeneous text sources. Custom pipelines will be developed to handle variant characters, scribal abbreviations, and multilingual glosses prevalent in historical manuscripts. HPC resources will enable large-scale training of domain-specific language models using distributed deep learning frameworks, as well as the alignment of parallel texts across Chinese, Japanese, and Korean to map transcultural literary exchanges. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible annotated corpus of 10,000+ pages of digitized manuscripts, quantitative frameworks for tracking morphosyntactic evolution in premodern East Asia, and improved OCR models tailored to understudied script variants. This work will provide novel insights into how linguistic contact shaped literary production across the region, while developing computational tools to bridge gaps between traditional philology and digital humanities methodologies. The requested resources are critical for managing memory-intensive tasks such as training multilingual embeddings and conducting Monte Carlo simulations of language change dynamics across millisecond-scale historical intervals.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: East Asian Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, General
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on one or more of the languages of East Asia, including, but not limited to, the Sino-Tibetan, Japanese, and Korean languages. Includes instruction in philology; linguistics; dialects and pidgins; literature; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: This project seeks to advance equitable educational assessment practices by analyzing large-scale, heterogeneous datasets to identify systemic biases in learning outcome evaluations. Traditional statistical methods struggle to model complex, nonlinear interactions in multimillion-row datasets spanning standardized test results, demographic surveys, and digital learning platform logs. We propose developing machine learning architectures to 1) detect latent bias patterns in assessment instruments across diverse student subgroups and 2) simulate how modified evaluation frameworks could reduce observed disparities. The computational workflow integrates natural language processing (NLP) to analyze open-response items, graph neural networks to map relationships between institutional policies and localized achievement gaps, and Bayesian hierarchical models to account for nested data structures (e.g., district-school-classroom hierarchies). High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for training transformer-based models on text responses from 12 million K-12 assessments, conducting Monte Carlo simulations of alternative grading rubrics, and running sensitivity analyses across 150+ demographic cross-sections. Expected outcomes include 1) an open-source bias detection toolkit for assessment designers, 2) empirically validated thresholds for differential item functioning in AI-assisted grading systems, and 3) policy recommendations for weighting socioeconomic covariates in accountability frameworks. By leveraging GPU-accelerated tensor operations and distributed memory parallelism, this work will overcome current limitations in handling sparse, high-dimensional education data while maintaining interpretability constraints required for ethical AI in assessment contexts. The results will directly inform state-level reforms in competency modeling and help institutions audit assessment equity under proposed Title IX regulatory changes.
detailed_field: Educational assessment, evaluation, and research methods
cip_title: Educational Assessment, Evaluation, and Research, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in educational evaluation, research and statistics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to optimize radiation dose and image quality in diagnostic radiologic imaging, addressing the critical challenge of balancing patient safety with diagnostic efficacy. Current protocols for x-ray, CT, and hybrid imaging systems often rely on generalized parameters, which may not account for patient-specific anatomical variability or emerging technologies such as photon-counting detectors. The research will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate radiation transport using Monte Carlo methods, model iterative image reconstruction algorithms, and train deep learning networks for protocol optimization. Multiscale simulations will be conducted to quantify dose deposition across heterogeneous tissues and evaluate noise-resolution trade-offs under varying acquisition parameters. A key innovation involves integrating generative adversarial networks (GANs) to synthesize realistic patient-specific phantoms, enabling large-scale virtual trials without exposing individuals to excess radiation. Additionally, reinforcement learning frameworks will be implemented to dynamically adapt imaging parameters based on real-time feedback from simulated scans. The computational workload necessitates parallel processing of large-scale datasets (>100 TB), including voxelized phantom libraries and raw sensor data from digital radiography and MRI systems. Expected outcomes include validated models for personalized protocol optimization, open-source tools for dose prediction, and quantitative guidelines for emerging technologies like low-dose spectral CT. This work will directly inform clinical practice by establishing data-driven methods to reduce population radiation exposure while maintaining diagnostic accuracy, with particular relevance to pediatric and high-risk populations. The requested HPC resources are essential for achieving the required spatial and temporal resolution in simulations, as well as for training complex neural networks on heterogeneous imaging data. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed platforms and integrated into residency training programs, advancing both radiologic physics research and translational safety initiatives.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnostic applications of x-rays, gamma rays from sealed sources, ultrasonic radiation, and magnetic resonance; and in the use of equipment associated with their production and use, including radiation safety. One of the three subspecialties available to residents in radiologic physics who must select one or more subspecialty areas.

abstract: This project seeks to enhance the effectiveness of scientific and technical communication by analyzing how complex information is processed and retained across digital media formats, with a focus on optimizing user engagement and comprehension. Despite advances in multimedia communication tools, a critical gap remains in understanding how computational design choices—such as interactive data visualization, hyperlinked documentation, or augmented reality (AR) interfaces—impact audience understanding of technical content. To address this, we propose a large-scale computational study leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model user interactions with diverse communication artifacts. Using a mixed-methods approach, we will deploy machine learning models to analyze patterns in eye-tracking datasets, clickstream behavior, and qualitative feedback from usability studies involving simulated technical scenarios (e.g., emergency response protocols, engineering documentation navigation). Concurrently, natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will evaluate semantic coherence and terminological consistency in AI-generated technical content compared to human-authored materials. These computational workflows require parallelized processing of multimodal data (text, video, interaction logs) across thousands of simulated user sessions, necessitating GPU-accelerated nodes for real-time analysis of AR/VR interface interactions and scalable storage for longitudinal tracking. Outcomes will include a framework for predicting communication breakdowns in technical documents and digital interfaces, alongside actionable guidelines for optimizing information design in high-stakes fields such as healthcare or aerospace engineering. By integrating computational analytics with communication theory, this project aims to advance evidence-based practices for technical communicators while demonstrating the transformative role of HPC in non-traditional domains like audience analysis and usability research.
detailed_field: Applied communication, advertising, and public relations
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the communication of technical and scientific knowledge to a variety of audiences through print, video, and digital media; and that prepares individuals to function as technical writers and editors, documentation developers, web designers, and usability specialists. Includes instruction in scientific and technical writing and editing, graphic and information design, web design, audience analysis, document usability and field testing, publications management, and applications to specific technical fields.

abstract: Substance use disorders (SUDs) and co-occurring psychiatric conditions present complex, heterogeneous clinical challenges, with treatment outcomes influenced by dynamic interactions between genetic, neurobiological, environmental, and behavioral factors. Current analytical approaches often fail to capture these multidimensional relationships due to limitations in modeling high-dimensional data or simulating emergent neurobehavioral dynamics. This project seeks high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational psychiatry research aimed at identifying precision treatment targets and optimizing intervention strategies for SUDs. We propose integrating multi-modal datasets—including genomic (GWAS, whole-exome sequencing), neuroimaging (resting-state fMRI, DTI), electronic health records (EHRs), and real-time behavioral monitoring data—from a longitudinal cohort of patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) and major depressive disorder (MDD). Machine learning pipelines will be developed to model nonlinear associations between polygenic risk scores, neural circuit connectivity patterns, and clinical trajectories, while mechanistic simulations will explore how acute and chronic substance exposure alters reward network dynamics. Computational workflows will require parallelized processing of large neuroimaging volumes (>10 TB), distributed training of ensemble predictors for relapse risk stratification, and population-scale pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modeling of buprenorphine-naloxone interactions across genetic subpopulations. HPC resources are essential to handle memory-intensive tasks such as whole-brain connectome analysis, Bayesian network inference for comorbid symptom clusters, and agent-based modeling of social determinants affecting treatment access. Expected outcomes include predictive biomarkers of medication response, optimized patient-specific intervention timing based on neurocomputational profiles, and mechanistic insights into stress-induced craving pathways. This work will establish a scalable computational framework for translational addiction research, directly informing clinical trial designs and personalized therapeutic strategies for dual-diagnosis populations.
cip_definition: Research focused on the evaluation and treatment of individuals with alcohol, drug, or other substance-related disorders, and of individuals with the dual diagnosis of substance-related and other psychiatric disorders.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolving interplay between Canadian constitutional principles and complex, large-scale societal datasets. The core problem lies in understanding how foundational legal frameworks—particularly those rooted in the Canadian Constitution and Commonwealth legal traditions—adapt to dynamic social, cultural, and technological shifts. Traditional legal research methods struggle to systematically map the nonlinear relationships between judicial reasoning, legislative amendments, and emergent public values across decades of case law and policy documents. To address this, the project will employ natural language processing (NLP) techniques to process over 150,000 Canadian court decisions, parliamentary debates, and historical legal texts, identifying latent patterns in judicial rhetoric, precedent adoption, and constitutional interpretation. Concurrently, agent-based modeling will simulate the cascading effects of hypothetical legal reforms on institutional behavior and rights-based disputes. By integrating these computational approaches, the research aims to construct a multidimensional network model of legal evolution, quantifying how specific doctrinal shifts influence systemic resilience or vulnerability. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database linking constitutional clauses to their sociopolitical contexts, predictive frameworks for assessing the downstream impacts of landmark rulings, and methodological innovations in computational legal theory. This work will provide novel insights into the adaptive capacity of Canada’s legal architecture while establishing scalable tools for analyzing jurisprudence as a complex, data-rich system. The requested HPC resources are critical for training transformer-based language models on legal corpora, running high-fidelity policy simulations, and managing the terabyte-scale integration of heterogeneous legal and historical datasets.
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the Canadian legal system, Constitution law, and jurisprudence. Includes instruction in legal history, legal sociology, philosophy of law, Constitutional law, Commonwealth law, legal procedure, and related topics.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize dynamic resource allocation in multi-hospital networks under uncertainty, addressing critical inefficiencies in health system operations. Current approaches to resource sharing—such as staff, equipment, and specialty care access—often rely on static, facility-centric models ill-equipped to handle fluctuating demand, supply chain disruptions, or emergent public health crises. Using high-performance computing (HPC), we propose an agent-based simulation platform that integrates real-time data streams (e.g., patient volume, staff availability, supply inventories) with predictive analytics to model interdependencies across hospitals. The platform will employ reinforcement learning algorithms to iteratively optimize resource redistribution strategies while balancing cost, equity, and operational constraints. Computational challenges include scaling neural networks to simulate thousands of concurrent decision points across heterogeneous institutions and validating models against synthetic crisis scenarios (e.g., natural disasters, pandemic surges). By leveraging GPU-accelerated clusters, we aim to reduce simulation runtime for system-wide decision trees from weeks to hours, enabling rapid scenario testing. Expected outcomes include actionable protocols for adaptive resource sharing, quantified trade-off analyses for policymakers, and open-source tools to simulate region-specific crises. This work bridges computational scalability gaps in health administration, offering a paradigm shift from reactive to proactive resource management in complex care ecosystems. Success would directly inform national guidelines for health system resilience, reducing bottlenecks in care delivery during high-stakes scenarios.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to develop, plan, and manage health care operations and services within health care facilities and across health care systems. Includes instruction in planning, business management, financial management, public relations, human resources management, health care systems operation and management, health care resource allocation and policy making, health law and regulations, and applications to specific types of health care services.

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing demand for high-fidelity, dynamic visualizations in biomedical research, education, and clinical practice by leveraging advanced computational resources. Medical illustrators face challenges in rendering complex anatomical structures, physiological processes, and pathological conditions at scale, particularly when integrating real-time interactivity, multi-modal imaging data, or simulating dynamic biological systems. Traditional workflows struggle with the computational demands of processing high-resolution volumetric datasets (e.g., MRI, CT, microscopy), generating photorealistic 3D models, and simulating biomechanical behaviors such as tissue deformation or fluid dynamics. To overcome these limitations, this project proposes the development of a scalable, GPU-accelerated pipeline for medical visualization and simulation. The pipeline will utilize parallelized algorithms for segmentation and mesh generation from imaging data, physics-based rendering techniques for lifelike material properties, and finite element analysis for biomechanical modeling. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable the processing of terabyte-scale datasets, reduce rendering times for complex scenes, and support machine learning approaches to automate repetitive tasks like anatomical labeling or texture synthesis. Additionally, the project will explore real-time interactive visualization frameworks for virtual reality (VR) surgical training modules, requiring low-latency rendering and collision detection. Outcomes include open-source tools optimized for biomedical visualization workflows, validated models for educational simulations, and benchmarks for computational efficiency in medical illustration tasks. These resources will enhance the precision and accessibility of biomedical communications, directly benefiting medical education, patient counseling, and interdisciplinary research. By integrating HPC capabilities into medical illustration practices, this work aims to establish new standards for computational scalability in the field while addressing critical gaps in visualizing increasingly complex biomedical data.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply the principles and techniques of art and computer-assisted imaging, graphics, and animation to create visual materials to facilitate the recording and dissemination of biomedical knowledge for educational, research, and clinical purposes. Includes instruction in anatomy, physiology, pathology, histology, embryology, neuroanatomy, medical terminology, artistic media and techniques, illustration techniques, three-dimensional modeling, prosthetics, data display design, exhibit design and production, medical photography, multimedia, computer graphics and animation, digital imaging, business management, production technology, and instructional design.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational modeling and simulation in oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMFS), addressing critical challenges in patient-specific surgical planning and postoperative outcome prediction. Current approaches to complex procedures—such as mandibular reconstruction, orthognathic surgery, and prosthetic implantation—often rely on static imaging and generalized biomechanical assumptions, limiting precision in predicting tissue responses, implant stability, and long-term functional outcomes. To overcome these limitations, we propose a multiscale computational framework integrating patient-specific anatomical data from cone-beam CT and intraoral scans with dynamic biomechanical modeling, finite element analysis (FEA), and machine learning (ML)-driven predictive analytics. HPC resources are essential to process high-resolution 3D datasets, simulate real-time mechanical stresses during mastication and speech, and model biological processes such as osseointegration and soft tissue healing under diverse physiological conditions. The computational pipeline will employ GPU-accelerated solvers for FEA, agent-based modeling for cellular responses to surgical interventions, and ensemble ML algorithms trained on retrospective clinical data to identify risk factors for complications such as nonunion, infection, or implant failure. By enabling granular analysis of biomechanical interactions and tissue adaptation, this work aims to generate predictive tools for optimizing surgical techniques, implant designs, and postoperative care protocols. Successful implementation will provide clinicians with actionable insights to reduce revision surgeries, improve functional and aesthetic outcomes, and personalize treatment strategies for pathologies including traumatic injuries, congenital defects, and oncologic resections. The project will also establish an open-source computational toolkit adaptable to broader OMFS research, fostering innovation in a field where advanced modeling remains underrepresented despite its transformative potential for patient care.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the advanced study of the diagnosis and intrusive and adjunctive treatment of diseases, injuries, and defects of the oral and maxillofacial regions, including functional and aesthetic aspects. Includes instruction in pharmacology, analgesia, anesthesia, anxiety control, surgical procedures and techniques, surgical instrumentation, exodontia, oral diseases and malfunctions, soft and hard tissue pathology, dentoalveolar surgery, infection management, and prosthetic implantation.

abstract: Respiratory care therapy faces significant challenges in optimizing personalized treatment strategies for patients with heterogeneous respiratory diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Current clinical protocols often rely on generalized guidelines that may not account for individual variations in lung mechanics, gas exchange efficiency, or comorbidities, leading to suboptimal outcomes. This project proposes to develop patient-specific computational models of respiratory physiology to predict responses to therapeutic interventions, enabling data-driven personalization of care. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement multi-scale simulations integrating 3D airway geometry derived from medical imaging, dynamic lung mechanics, and gas transport algorithms. Machine learning techniques will be applied to analyze large clinical datasets, including ventilator waveforms, arterial blood gas trends, and electronic health records, to identify patterns predictive of therapeutic success. The computational framework will simulate outcomes of varying ventilator settings, pharmacological interventions, and rehabilitation protocols under diverse physiological conditions. Expected outcomes include validated models capable of recommending individualized respiratory care plans, reducing trial-and-error approaches in critical care settings. The project will also generate open-access tools for respiratory therapists to explore virtual scenarios, enhancing clinical training through simulation-based learning. By bridging computational innovation with clinical practice, this work aims to advance precision medicine in respiratory care, improve patient outcomes, and reduce healthcare costs associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation and hospital stays. The scale of data processing, parallelized simulations, and iterative model training necessitates robust HPC infrastructure to achieve clinically relevant turnaround times, making this research feasible only with dedicated computing resources.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of physicians, to assist in developing respiratory care plans, administer respiratory care procedures, supervise personnel and equipment operation, maintain records, and consult with other health care team members. Includes instruction in the applied basic biomedical sciences; anatomy, physiology, and pathology of the respiratory system; clinical medicine; therapeutic procedures; clinical expressions; data collection and record-keeping; patient communication; equipment operation and maintenance; personnel supervision; and procedures for special population groups.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research on the integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and real-time environmental simulations in architectural design processes. The research addresses a critical gap in current computational design methodologies, which often prioritize formal or aesthetic outcomes over dynamic, context-sensitive performance metrics. By developing a novel framework that combines generative adversarial networks (GANs), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and agent-based pedestrian movement modeling, the project aims to create adaptive design systems capable of iteratively optimizing architectural proposals for energy efficiency, thermal comfort, and spatial circulation in dense urban contexts. The computational workflow will process multi-scale datasets, including high-resolution LiDAR scans of existing urban fabric, historical climate data, and real-time sensor inputs from IoT networks, to generate and evaluate thousands of design permutations. This requires parallel processing of complex 3D geometry operations, coupled with machine learning model training on heterogeneous urban datasets. Expected outcomes include an open-source computational toolkit for performance-driven architectural design, validated through case studies in three climatically distinct cities. The research contributes to emerging paradigms in computational architecture by bridging gaps between generative design, environmental simulation, and human behavior modeling—advancing both methodological innovation and practical applications for sustainable urban development. Successful implementation of this framework could significantly reduce the computational barriers currently limiting holistic performance-based design approaches in architectural practice and education.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of architecture, cities, landscapes, designed objects, ornament, architectural photography, and material culture in diverse places and time periods, and the social and aesthetic dimensions of contemporary architecture, landscapes, and cities, emphasizing issues of sustainable environments, new forms of urbanism, and the use of digital media for visualization and analysis. Includes instruction in the fundamentals of architecture, design, environmental and sustainability studies, historic preservation, landscape architecture, studio art, and urban affairs and planning.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance interdisciplinary research on the digital preservation and analysis of intangible cultural heritage within underrepresented Indigenous communities in the Pacific Islands. The research problem centers on the urgent need to document, model, and interpret dynamic cultural practices—such as oral traditions, ritual performances, and ecological knowledge systems—that are at risk of erasure due to globalization and climate displacement. Current methodologies in area studies lack the computational capacity to process multimodal datasets (audio, video, geospatial, and ethnographic field notes) at scale while maintaining ethical frameworks for Indigenous data sovereignty. The project proposes a computational approach integrating machine learning-based speech recognition for endangered Polynesian languages, 3D spectral analysis of choral recordings to map vocal traditions, and agent-based modeling to simulate the transmission of ecological knowledge across generations. HPC resources are critical for training transformer models on low-resource languages, processing terabyte-scale audiovisual archives, and running stochastic simulations that account for cultural variability and environmental stressors. Expected outcomes include an open-access digital repository co-designed with community partners, novel algorithms for culturally sensitive data annotation, and visualizations of knowledge networks that highlight interdependencies between cultural practices and ecosystems. By bridging computational scalability with community-driven research, this work aims to establish new methodologies for ethically grounded, collaborative area studies while directly supporting Indigenous-led preservation initiatives. The resource allocation will enable processing timelines impossible on local infrastructure, reducing model training times by 80% and facilitating real-time collaborative analysis with remote Indigenous scholars.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: Any instructional program in specifically defined area studies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in social science teacher education by modeling the complex dynamics of classroom learning environments and optimizing evidence-based pedagogical strategies. Social science education involves multidimensional interactions among students, teachers, curricula, and sociocultural contexts, generating large-scale datasets that challenge traditional analytical methods. Current approaches often struggle to integrate real-time behavioral data, longitudinal academic performance metrics, and qualitative discourse analysis at scale, limiting the ability to identify patterns or predict the efficacy of instructional interventions. To address this gap, we propose developing agent-based models (ABMs) and machine learning (ML) frameworks to simulate classroom interactions, analyze heterogeneous learning trajectories, and evaluate the impact of teacher training protocols. The ABMs will parameterize variables such as student engagement, peer collaboration, and teacher feedback mechanisms, while ML algorithms will process multimodal data (e.g., student essays, discussion transcripts, and assessment scores) to uncover latent predictors of learning outcomes. HPC resources are critical for scaling these computationally intensive simulations across diverse virtual classroom configurations and iteratively refining models using Bayesian optimization. Expected outcomes include the identification of high-impact teaching practices tailored to underrepresented student populations, the generation of open-access synthetic datasets for educator training, and the creation of adaptive tools for real-time pedagogical decision support. By integrating computational social science methods with teacher education research, this project aims to transform how social science educators are prepared to address equity gaps and foster critical thinking in rapidly evolving educational landscapes. The requested resources will enable processing of terabyte-scale datasets, parallel execution of 10,000+ classroom simulations, and development of GPU-accelerated NLP pipelines—capabilities unfeasible with existing campus infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach specific social science subjects and programs at various educational levels.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model the dynamics of household financial resilience under evolving economic stressors, with a focus on optimizing community-based intervention strategies. The research problem centers on the lack of scalable, data-driven frameworks to predict how families allocate resources—such as income, time, and social capital—in response to systemic shocks like inflation, employment volatility, or public health crises. Existing models in family and consumer sciences often rely on static survey data or simplified economic assumptions, limiting their capacity to simulate complex, interdependent decision-making processes across diverse demographic groups. To address this gap, the project will develop an agent-based modeling (ABM) framework integrating heterogeneous household data (e.g., spending patterns, debt profiles, and social network interactions) with macroeconomic indicators. Computational workflows will employ machine learning to calibrate agent behaviors from longitudinal datasets, followed by large-scale parallel simulations to explore “what-if” scenarios under varying policy conditions. HPC resources are critical for managing the high dimensionality of input data, executing thousands of stochastic simulations to quantify uncertainty, and visualizing multi-agent interactions in near real time. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible toolkit for community organizations to forecast localized household vulnerability and test the efficacy of interventions such as microloan programs, childcare subsidies, or digital literacy campaigns. By bridging computational social science and family resource management, this work aims to advance evidence-based strategies within human sciences business services, particularly for underserved populations. The project’s interdisciplinary approach—spanning behavioral economics, data science, and consumer policy—aligns with emerging priorities in family and consumer sciences to adopt computational rigor while preserving nuanced, human-centric insights.
cip_title: Family and Consumer Sciences/ Human Sciences Business Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in family and consumer sciences/human sciences business services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to enhance physics teacher preparation by investigating how computational modeling and data-driven insights can address persistent challenges in physics pedagogy. A critical barrier in physics education is the gap between abstract conceptual mastery and the ability to teach those concepts effectively, particularly in contexts involving student misconceptions, interdisciplinary connections, or complex systems (e.g., electromagnetism, quantum phenomena). To bridge this gap, we propose developing and deploying high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate classroom learning dynamics, model the efficacy of instructional strategies, and analyze large-scale datasets of student problem-solving behaviors. Agent-based models will simulate diverse classroom scenarios, incorporating variables such as prior knowledge, common misconceptions, and intervention timing. These simulations will be validated against empirical data from physics classrooms, including pre-/post-assessment results and video-recorded teaching demonstrations. Concurrently, machine learning algorithms will process multimodal educational datasets (text responses, conceptual diagrams, and interaction logs from virtual labs) to identify patterns in student reasoning and predict optimal teaching approaches for specific topics. The computational demands of running thousands of parallelized simulations, coupled with the need for real-time analysis of high-dimensional educational data, necessitate access to HPC infrastructure. Outcomes will include (1) a publicly accessible repository of physics teaching simulations tailored to teacher training programs, (2) evidence-based frameworks for addressing misconceptions in mechanics and modern physics, and (3) predictive tools to personalize professional development for pre-service teachers. By integrating computational research with physics education, this work aims to transform how teachers are prepared to navigate complex pedagogical scenarios, ultimately improving secondary and undergraduate students’ conceptual understanding of physics.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach physics programs at various educational levels.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the interplay between cultural production, identity formation, and diasporic networks in the Caribbean through large-scale textual and multimedia data. The research problem centers on the fragmented preservation and understudied dynamics of cultural expressions—such as literature, oral histories, music, and digital media—that reflect the region’s hybrid identities and transnational connections. Traditional humanities methodologies struggle to process the scale and diversity of these materials, which span languages (e.g., English, Spanish, French, Creole), formats, and historical periods. The project proposes a computational cultural analytics framework combining natural language processing (NLP), multimodal machine learning, and network analysis to map patterns of cultural exchange, adaptation, and resistance across the Caribbean and its global diaspora. Key tasks include training multilingual NLP models on Creole and colonial-language corpora, detecting audiovisual motifs in folk and popular music, and reconstructing transnational collaboration networks from digitized archives and social media. HPC resources are critical for processing terabytes of heterogeneous data, running parallelized model training, and simulating cultural diffusion dynamics. Anticipated outcomes include: (1) a public repository of annotated Caribbean cultural datasets; (2) computational tools for analyzing under-resourced languages and multimedia; and (3) evidence-based insights into how regional identity is negotiated through cultural practices in postcolonial and diasporic contexts. This work aims to advance interdisciplinary Caribbean Studies by bridging qualitative theories of hybridity and transculturation with data-driven methods, while fostering equitable access to computational resources for researching marginalized cultural systems. The scalability of the approach will also provide a template for studying other linguistically diverse, postcolonial regions.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples inhabiting the major islands and archipelagoes of the Caribbean Sea and related coastal borderlands, including immigration patterns and Pre-Columbian, colonial, and modern societies.

abstract: Neurological disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and epilepsy involve complex interactions between molecular, cellular, and systemic networks that remain poorly understood. Current clinical approaches often lack the precision to predict disease progression or optimize individualized treatment strategies. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to integrate multi-modal neuroimaging, electrophysiological, and genomic datasets, enabling the development of predictive models for neurological disease dynamics. A key challenge is the computational demand of analyzing high-resolution brain imaging (7T MRI, DTI), whole-genome sequencing, and longitudinal electrophysiological recordings (EEG, EMG) across large patient cohorts. Existing methods struggle to reconcile the spatial-temporal scales of these datasets or identify subtle, cross-modal biomarkers. Our computational approach employs machine learning frameworks, including graph neural networks and ensemble methods, to model disease-specific perturbations in brain connectivity and genetic risk profiles. Multi-scale simulations will integrate molecular pathways (e.g., protein aggregation in neurodegeneration) with circuit-level dysfunction observed in neuroimaging. HPC resources are critical for optimizing hyperparameters, training deep learning architectures on GPU clusters, and running parallelized simulations of disease progression under varying therapeutic interventions. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of novel biomarkers for early differentiation of Alzheimer’s subtypes, (2) predictive models linking ALS genetic variants to patterns of motor network degradation, and (3) optimized stimulation parameters for drug-resistant epilepsy via in silico testing of neural network dynamics. By enabling large-scale integration of heterogeneous clinical data, this work aims to advance precision neurology paradigms, reduce trial-and-error in treatment selection, and accelerate translational insights into mechanisms of neurological disease. The requested computing resources will directly support the processing of >10 TB of raw neuroimaging data, genome-wide association studies across 5,000+ patients, and real-time simulations of intervention effects at cellular resolution.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis and treatment of all types of disease or impaired function of the brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, muscles and autonomic nervous system, as well as the blood vessels that relate to these structures.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a multiyear study analyzing the structural drivers of urban social inequality and evaluating the efficacy of community-based policy interventions. The research addresses a critical gap in applied sociology: scalable, dynamic modeling of how intersecting factors—such as housing access, public infrastructure investment, and labor market shifts—affect marginalized populations over time. Traditional sociological methods struggle to integrate real-time, heterogeneous datasets or simulate complex feedback loops between policy decisions and community outcomes. To overcome these limitations, we propose a computational approach combining agent-based modeling (ABM) with machine learning-driven analysis of longitudinal demographic, economic, and public administrative data. The ABM framework will simulate decision-making processes of households, employers, and policymakers under varying intervention scenarios, incorporating geospatial data from municipal records and anonymized social survey responses. Deep learning models will concurrently process unstructured data from community stakeholder meetings and social media to identify emergent concerns and validate simulation parameters. HPC resources are essential for managing the scale of this work, including parallel processing of 10+ years of census microdata, real-time calibration of models with streaming input from city agencies, and sensitivity analyses across 50,000+ agent interactions per simulation cycle. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible toolkit for municipalities to predict equity impacts of housing policies, workforce programs, and infrastructure investments. By bridging computational social science with participatory action research, this project will advance methodological innovation in applied sociology while generating actionable evidence to reduce systemic disparities. The resource-intensive nature of these simulations—requiring sustained GPU capacity and large-memory nodes—necessitates dedicated HPC support to achieve rigorous, policy-relevant results.
detailed_field: Sociology, demography, and population studies nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of sociological theory, methods, skills, and research to resolve particular issues in real-world settings. Includes instruction in data collection, group and organizational dynamics, participatory action research, program evaluation, sociological research methods, and sociological theory.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize personalized dietary interventions for patients with complex metabolic conditions, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address gaps in current dietetic planning methods. Current approaches to designing individualized nutrition plans often rely on generalized guidelines and manual adjustments, which struggle to account for dynamic interactions between genetic, biochemical, and lifestyle factors. This limitation is particularly acute for patients with comorbidities such as diabetes, renal disease, and gastrointestinal disorders, where dietary requirements are highly interdependent and sensitive to small changes. To address this, we propose a machine learning model trained on multi-omics data (genomic, metabolomic, and microbiome profiles), electronic health records, and real-time biometric data from wearable devices. The model will integrate nutrient metabolism simulations using flux balance analysis, optimized via parallelized computing to predict patient-specific responses to dietary components. HPC resources will enable the processing of large-scale datasets, iterative model training, and stochastic simulations to quantify uncertainty in recommendations. Expected outcomes include a scalable tool for generating adaptive meal plans that minimize adverse interactions while meeting clinical targets, validated through retrospective analysis of patient outcomes from partner clinics. Additionally, the project will yield open-access datasets and workflows to support competency development in computational nutrition for dietetic technicians. By bridging data-driven methods with applied dietetics, this work aims to enhance the precision and efficiency of dietary interventions while providing training in advanced computational techniques for future practitioners.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of registered dietitians and nutritionists, to implement nutritional and dietetic plans and provide direct client and patient services. Includes instruction in human nutrition, client interviewing and record keeping, dietary planning, food preparation and safety, food worker supervision, food service establishment monitoring and inspection, and applicable procedures and regulations.

abstract: Dental prostheses, including crowns, bridges, and orthodontic appliances, require precise customization to ensure patient comfort, functionality, and longevity. However, traditional design and fabrication workflows face challenges in predicting biomechanical performance, optimizing material behavior, and personalizing devices for complex anatomical variations. This project seeks to address these limitations by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop advanced computational models for simulating and optimizing dental prosthesis design. The research focuses on three core objectives: (1) multi-scale modeling of stress distribution and wear patterns in ceramic and polymer-based prostheses under masticatory forces, (2) machine learning-driven optimization of digital prosthesis designs to minimize interfacial strain with patient-specific jaw and dentition geometries, and (3) predictive analysis of long-term material fatigue in hybrid prostheses combining 3D-printed alloys and composite resins. Computational workflows will integrate finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for adhesive flow simulations during bonding, and generative adversarial networks (GANs) trained on clinical tomography datasets to propose design adaptations. The HPC environment is critical for handling large-scale parametric studies involving heterogeneous material properties, dynamic loading conditions, and probabilistic anatomical variations across diverse patient populations. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for prosthesis failure risk, open-source computational design templates to reduce manual adjustments in CAD/CAM workflows, and evidence-based guidelines for material selection in complex clinical cases. By bridging computational engineering with dental laboratory practice, this work aims to enhance the precision of prosthodontic interventions, reduce iterative fabrication costs, and improve patient outcomes through data-driven personalization of restorative devices. The requested resources will support GPU-accelerated simulations, high-throughput parameter optimization, and storage of multimodal clinical imaging data paired with biomechanical datasets.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of dentists, to design and construct dental prostheses such as caps, crowns, bridges, dentures, splints, and orthodontic appliances. Includes instruction in dental anatomy, dental materials, ceramics technology, impressions, complete dentures, partial dentures, orthodontics, crowns and bridges, sculpture, bonding and assembly techniques, and equipment operation.

abstract: The study of collective behavior in eusocial insect colonies presents a unique challenge in understanding decentralized decision-making processes under dynamic environmental conditions. This project focuses on modeling the emergent problem-solving capabilities of termite colonies during nest construction and repair, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate multi-agent interactions at biologically relevant scales. Current models lack the granularity to capture real-time feedback between individual behavioral plasticity and colony-level resilience, particularly when colonies face spatially heterogeneous stressors such as partial nest damage or resource scarcity. To address this, we propose an agent-based framework integrating empirical data on termite sensory thresholds, task-switching dynamics, and local communication via vibroacoustic signaling. The computational model will simulate 10^4–10^5 agents across three-dimensional nest architectures, incorporating fluid dynamics principles to model humidity gradients that influence building behavior. HPC resources are critical for parallelizing Monte Carlo simulations testing adaptive responses to stochastic disturbances, with parameter spaces exceeding 10^7 combinations. Expected outcomes include identifying phase transitions in collective repair strategies and quantifying energy trade-offs between coordinated rebuilding and nest abandonment. Results will advance fundamental knowledge of self-organization in biological systems while informing bio-inspired engineering approaches for resilient swarm robotics. This work bridges zoology, complex systems theory, and computational physics, establishing a novel framework for studying macroscopic biological phenomena inaccessible to traditional experimental or theoretical methods alone.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in zoology/animal biology, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project investigates the interplay between collective visual attention dynamics and environmental design in public spaces, leveraging computational modeling to understand how psychological principles of perception and social behavior shape crowd movement patterns. While urban design often prioritizes physical efficiency, the cognitive and emotional factors influencing how individuals navigate shared environments remain understudied, particularly at scale. We propose developing a high-fidelity agent-based model (ABM) that integrates eye-tracking data, spatial cognition metrics, and real-world pedestrian flow datasets to simulate decision-making processes in diverse architectural contexts. The model will employ deep reinforcement learning frameworks to capture how individuals dynamically allocate attention to environmental cues (e.g., signage, crowd density gradients, aesthetic landmarks) while balancing goal-directed navigation with spontaneous exploration. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for training neural networks on multimodal behavioral datasets (10,000+ simulated agents per iteration) and running parallelized simulations across parameterized urban layouts. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework quantifying how specific design elements modulate collective visual engagement and wayfinding efficiency, validated against 3D-reconstructed movement data from partnered civic centers. This work bridges environmental psychology, computational neuroscience, and architectural theory, offering evidence-based strategies for creating public spaces that harmonize functional demands with psychologically informed experiential quality. The resulting open-source toolkit will enable urban planners to prototype designs through a human cognition lens while advancing methodological convergence between behavioral modeling and spatial analytics.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the scientific study of individual and collective behavior, the physical and environmental bases of behavior, and the analysis and treatment of behavior problems and disorders. Includes instruction in the principles of the various subfields of psychology, research methods, and psychological assessment and testing methods.

abstract: Parasitic diseases remain a critical global health burden, with emerging resistance to existing therapeutics underscoring the urgent need for novel intervention strategies. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the molecular mechanisms underpinning host-parasite interactions and chemotherapeutic resistance in two understudied helminth species: *Schistosoma mansoni* and *Ancylostoma duodenale*. A key challenge lies in resolving the structural dynamics of parasite-specific proteins implicated in immune evasion and drug metabolism, particularly those with high conformational flexibility or transient binding sites that evade traditional crystallographic methods. We propose an integrative computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, free-energy perturbation (FEP) calculations, and machine learning-enhanced virtual screening to model parasite protein targets at unprecedented spatiotemporal resolutions. MD simulations will be performed on GPCR-like neuropeptide receptors unique to schistosomes, using all-atom explicit solvent models to capture ligand-binding pathways over microsecond timescales. Concurrently, FEP will quantify the binding affinity landscapes of anthelmintic candidates against hookworm glutathione S-transferase isoforms associated with benzimidazole resistance. These analyses will integrate multi-omics datasets—including cryo-EM density maps of parasite membranes and host immunoglobulin repertoires—to contextualize molecular interactions within physiological host environments. The computational workflow demands large-scale parallelization, requiring >50,000 CPU-core hours per target system and GPU-accelerated sampling for enhanced phase-space exploration. Expected outcomes include the identification of conserved allosteric sites in parasite signaling proteins and prioritized small molecules with predicted sub-nanomolar binding to resistance-conferring enzymes. This work will directly inform downstream in vitro validation of lead compounds and guide the rational design of next-generation antiparasitics. By elucidating resistance mechanisms and host-specific adaptation strategies, the project advances foundational knowledge in ecological parasitology while addressing translational gaps in chemotherapeutic development. Access to HPC resources is essential to overcome current limitations in simulating membrane-bound parasite systems and achieving the statistical rigor required for robust free-energy calculations.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of biological organisms living in ecologically exploitative and competitive relationships with host organisms, and the role of parasites in causing injury, disease, and environmental damage. Includes instruction in vector biology, immunoparasitology, medical parasitology, molecular biology of parasitical associations, veterinary and comparative parasitology, chemotherapeutics, and ecological and systematic parasitology.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance precision in animal grooming practices through the development of a biophysical simulation framework for optimizing grooming protocols. Current approaches to grooming—particularly for specialized contexts such as show animals, working dogs, or pets with dermatological sensitivities—rely heavily on anecdotal expertise and trial-and-error experimentation. This limits scalability, reproducibility, and the ability to predict outcomes for novel coat types or health conditions. Our research addresses this gap by constructing computational models that simulate interactions between grooming tools, products, and animal integumentary systems. Using finite element analysis (FEA), we will model the mechanical stresses of brushing, shearing, and bathing on diverse coat morphologies (e.g., double-coated breeds, curly-haired varieties) under variable hydration and temperature conditions. Concurrently, molecular dynamics simulations will evaluate the penetration and efficacy of grooming products (shampoos, conditioners, topical treatments) across species-specific skin barrier structures. These simulations will be validated against empirical data from 3D-scanned coat samples and biometric sensor arrays applied during live grooming trials. The computational pipeline will integrate machine learning to identify optimal tool-product combinations for minimizing skin irritation, maximizing coat health, and achieving aesthetic outcomes. By enabling predictive, data-driven grooming strategies, this work aims to reduce occupational hazards for groomers, improve animal welfare, and establish quantitative benchmarks for an industry currently lacking standardized protocols. The project’s HPC requirements stem from the need to process high-resolution volumetric datasets of coat structures, run parallelized multi-physics simulations, and train deep learning models on heterogeneous data streams. Outcomes will include open-access simulation tools and a decision-support system for groomers, with potential applications in veterinary dermatology and regulatory policy development for grooming product safety.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide cosmetic services for household pets, show animals, work animals and animal athletes. Includes instruction in skin, coat, and pelt grooming and styling; skin care; hoof, nail, and claw care; animal massage; minor first aid and veterinary referral; animal grooming products and applications; health and safety; and applicable regulations.

abstract: Grapevine cultivation and winemaking face critical challenges in adapting to climate variability and managing disease pressures while maintaining sustainable production practices. This project seeks to address these challenges by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model complex interactions between grapevine genomics, microbial communities during fermentation, and environmental stressors. The research problem centers on identifying genetic markers associated with disease resistance and climate adaptability in grapevines, as well as optimizing fermentation dynamics influenced by microbial consortia under varying climatic conditions. Current approaches lack the computational power to integrate multi-omics datasets (genomics, transcriptomics, metagenomics) with high-resolution environmental data at scale.
