The research will implement agent-based modeling to simulate adversarial decision cycles, coupled with graph neural networks to analyze network resilience patterns in hybrid threat environments. Computational experiments will focus on three operational challenges: (1) predictive modeling of information cascade thresholds in decentralized communication networks, (2) optimization of counter-messaging strategies through multi-objective reinforcement learning, and (3) vulnerability assessment of coalition command-and-control architectures under persistent cyber denial conditions. The HPC environment will enable parallel execution of 10^4+ scenario variants incorporating real-world data from field exercises, scaled through synthetic data generation techniques. Expected outcomes include a validated IO impact prediction toolkit capable of identifying critical intervention points in sub-hour timeframes, probabilistic models of cognitive domain escalation pathways, and quantitative metrics for infrastructure hardening prioritization. This work directly addresses the Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2) imperative to accelerate information advantage through computational modeling, while maintaining strict adherence to ethical AI principles through embedded audit layers and bias mitigation protocols. Resource allocation will support GPU-accelerated graph computations, large-language model fine-tuning for automated narrative analysis, and high-fidelity network traffic simulations at operationally relevant scales.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the strategic and operational use of information relative to the support of military and strategic policy and objectives. Includes instruction in information technology, decision theory and applications, military operations, command and control technology, network operations, network systems integration, computer network defense, space communications technology, and applications to specific military operational tasks.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of modeling large-scale, dynamic communication patterns in digital public relations and advertising campaigns, where traditional computational tools struggle to process real-time, multi-platform data at the speed and scale required for actionable insights. The research problem centers on the inability of existing frameworks to predict emergent audience behaviors or optimize cross-channel messaging strategies in environments characterized by high-volume, unstructured data (e.g., social media, streaming platforms, and interactive ad exchanges). To overcome these limitations, the project will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement agent-based modeling simulations and machine learning pipelines tailored to analyze terabytes of heterogeneous communication data. Computational methods will include natural language processing (NLP) for sentiment and thematic analysis of user-generated content, graph neural networks to map information diffusion across networks, and reinforcement learning algorithms to simulate adaptive audience responses under varying campaign conditions. By leveraging parallelized workflows and GPU-accelerated model training, the project aims to identify patterns in engagement dynamics, predict viral messaging thresholds, and test crisis communication strategies in synthetic yet realistic scenarios. Expected outcomes include a scalable computational framework for real-time campaign optimization, validated against historical case studies from corporate and nonprofit communication contexts. The findings will advance theoretical understanding of nonlinear communication effects in digital ecosystems while providing practitioners with evidence-based tools to allocate resources efficiently, mitigate reputational risks, and maximize message resonance in increasingly fragmented media landscapes. This work underscores the critical role of HPC in addressing complex, data-driven challenges unique to modern organizational communication research.
detailed_field: Applied communication, advertising, and public relations
cip_title: Public Relations, Advertising, and Applied Communication, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in organizational communication, public relations, and advertising, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the therapeutic efficacy of complex herbal formulations used in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) for chronic inflammatory conditions. While TCM practices such as multi-herb synergism are clinically utilized, their pharmacological complexity—hundreds of bioactive compounds interacting with diverse cellular targets—poses a significant challenge for mechanistic validation using conventional experimental approaches. The research problem centers on resolving this complexity through computational systems biology to identify critical compound-target networks, cross-herb interactions, and downstream immunomodulatory pathways. A hybrid workflow will integrate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, machine learning-based binding affinity prediction, and multi-scale network modeling. MD simulations will prioritize stable interactions between TCM-derived phytochemicals and inflammation-related proteins (e.g., NF-κB, COX-2, NLRP3), validated against existing experimental binding data. Graph neural networks will map compound-target-disease associations across 30+ herbs in a representative anti-inflammatory formulation, while agent-based modeling will simulate immune cell behavior under combinatorial phytochemical exposure. HPC resources are essential for handling the exponential combinatorial space (10^6+ potential compound pairs), millisecond-scale MD trajectories, and stochastic network simulations. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of high-priority synergistic herb pairs and putative multi-target mechanisms, (2) a predictive framework for optimizing TCM formulation bioactivity, and (3) publicly accessible databases linking TCM phytochemistry to immune modulation signatures. This work addresses a critical gap in validating traditional medical systems through computational rigor, offering translational insights for integrating evidence-based complementary therapies into precision medicine paradigms for chronic inflammatory diseases.
cip_title: Alternative and Complementary Medicine and Medical Systems, General
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the theories, science, and practice of alternative and complementary medicine and medical systems. Includes instruction in understanding acupuncture, herbal medicine, naturopathy, homeopathy, and other alternative and complementary medicine modalities; mind-body therapies; nutrition; comparison of conventional and alternative medicine; and medical ethics; and may include training in specific alternative and complementary medicine modalities.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical challenges in modeling the radiative and hydrodynamic processes governing the evolution of massive stellar systems and their surrounding environments. A key limitation in simulating these systems arises from the complex interplay of multi-scale physics, including non-equilibrium radiation transfer, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) instabilities, and the coupled feedback between stellar populations and the interstellar medium. Current simulations often rely on simplified approximations for radiative transfer or neglect high-energy processes due to computational constraints, leading to uncertainties in predicting observational signatures of star-forming regions, supernova remnants, and accretion disks. To overcome these limitations, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework combining 3D radiation-MHD simulations with Monte Carlo radiative transfer methods. The code will leverage adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) to resolve small-scale turbulent structures and incorporate wavelength-dependent opacity data for relativistic particles and dust grains. A novel aspect of this work involves coupling non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) ionization calculations with large-scale dynamics, enabling self-consistent modeling of photon-matter interactions in hypervelocity shocks and optically thick environments. The computational workflow will utilize MPI-OpenMP hybrid parallelism across GPU-accelerated nodes to manage memory-intensive radiation transport calculations. Expected outcomes include new insights into the role of radiation pressure in disrupting protostellar disks, improved constraints on dust formation mechanisms in supernova ejecta, and publicly accessible synthetic observables (spectra, light curves) for comparison with JWST and ALMA datasets. By resolving previously intractable scales of radiative feedback, this work will advance predictive models of galactic chemical evolution and inform next-generation telescope surveys. The requested allocation of 2.5 million node-hours on a Tier-2 HPC system will support parameter space exploration across stellar masses, metallicities, and turbulence regimes, generating 500+ TB of high-fidelity simulation data.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theoretical and observational study of the structure, properties, and behavior of stars, star systems and clusters, stellar life cycles, and related phenomena. Includes instruction in cosmology, plasma kinetics, stellar physics, convolution and non-equilibrium radiation transfer theory, non-Euclidean geometries, mathematical modeling, galactic structure theory, and relativistic astronomy.

abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying enzyme-substrate interactions and DNA-protein binding dynamics is critical for elucidating fundamental biological processes, yet experimental approaches alone often fail to resolve transient conformational states or quantify energy landscapes at atomic resolution. This project aims to investigate the structural and energetic determinants of helicase-mediated DNA unwinding and its regulation by cofactors, a system central to replication and repair. We propose to employ all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, enhanced sampling techniques, and free energy calculations to characterize the mechanochemical coupling and nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in a model helicase complex. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to achieve microsecond-scale simulations of multi-component systems (>500,000 atoms) and perform Markov state model analysis to map rare transitions. Parallelized workflows using AMBER and GROMACS will integrate experimental cryo-EM density maps as spatial restraints, while alchemical metadynamics will quantify ATP hydrolysis-driven remodeling of protein-DNA interfaces. Expected outcomes include identifying critical residues mediating processivity, predicting allosteric networks that synchronize motor domains, and modeling how post-translational modifications alter unwinding efficiency. These insights will advance mechanistic understanding of replication fidelity and provide a computational framework for studying helicase dysregulation linked to genetic disorders. The requested resources will enable parameterization of coarse-grained models for long-timescale studies and support machine learning approaches to classify functional conformational states from simulation trajectories. By bridging atomic-scale dynamics with cellular function, this work will establish predictive models of macromolecular interactions relevant to synthetic biology and enzyme engineering applications.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the structure and function of biological macromolecules and the role of molecular constituents and mechanisms in supramolecular assemblies and cells. Includes instruction in such topics as molecular signaling and transduction, regulation of cell growth, enzyme substrates and mechanisms of enzyme action, DNA-protein interaction, and applications to fields such as biotechnology, genetics, cell biology, and physiology.

abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, with interventional cardiology relying on precise hemodynamic assessments to guide revascularization. Current diagnostic tools, such as invasive fractional flow reserve (FFR), are limited by procedural risks and cost, while non-invasive imaging often lacks patient-specific physiologic accuracy. This project aims to develop a computational framework integrating high-resolution imaging data with hemodynamic simulations to predict coronary blood flow and ischemia severity, enabling non-invasive, personalized treatment planning. The primary challenge lies in modeling the complex, dynamic interactions between coronary anatomy, myocardial perfusion, and microvascular resistance at scale, which demands high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Using patient-specific coronary CT angiography and intravascular imaging data, we will construct 3D anatomic models of coronary arteries and simulate blood flow via computational fluid dynamics (CFD) coupled with finite element analysis of vessel wall mechanics. Multi-scale modeling will link macroscale hemodynamics to microvascular resistance using reduced-order models calibrated against clinical FFR and perfusion measurements. Machine learning algorithms will iteratively optimize boundary conditions and automate segmentation of imaging datasets. These simulations require parallelized workflows across thousands of CPU cores due to the computational intensity of transient, turbulence-resolving CFD and the need for probabilistic sensitivity analyses across heterogeneous patient cohorts. Expected outcomes include a validated platform for non-invasive FFR prediction with <5% error relative to invasive measurements, identification of high-risk anatomic-physiologic mismatch patterns, and predictive models for post-stent restenosis based on hemodynamic shear stress profiles. The HPC-enabled pipeline will process 500+ patient datasets annually, far exceeding the capacity of local workstations. By integrating anatomic, hemodynamic, and outcomes data, this work will advance precision guidance for coronary interventions, reduce unnecessary procedures, and establish a framework for real-time simulation in clinical decision support systems. Successful implementation will directly inform clinical trial design for image-derived FFR adoption and contribute open-source tools for cardiovascular computational modeling.
cip_definition: Research focused on the use of specialized imaging and other diagnostic techniques to evaluate blood flow and pressure in the coronary arteries and chambers of the heart, and in the use of technical procedures and medications to treat abnormalities that impair the function of the cardiovascular system.

abstract: The safe and efficient management of hazardous materials requires advanced predictive tools to address the complex interplay of chemical, physical, and environmental factors influencing waste behavior. Current methods for optimizing hazardous waste disposal and containment systems often rely on simplified models, which inadequately capture nonlinear interactions, degradation kinetics, or multi-phase transport phenomena under variable field conditions. This project seeks to develop a high-fidelity computational framework to simulate hazardous material interactions with engineered containment systems and natural environments, enabling data-driven strategies for waste stabilization, transport risk mitigation, and long-term storage. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will implement multiphysics models integrating reactive transport equations, machine learning-enhanced material degradation predictors, and stochastic uncertainty quantification. Key simulations will focus on (1) thermochemical stability of composite waste matrices under thermal and mechanical stress, (2) probabilistic mapping of contaminant plume dispersion in heterogeneous subsurface environments, and (3) accelerated aging studies for novel bioremediation substrates. The computational workflow will utilize GPU-optimized solvers for large-scale parameter sweeps and ensemble simulations, validated against experimental datasets from partner laboratories. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for optimizing waste treatment protocols, risk assessment matrices for regulatory compliance, and open-source modules for simulating biohazard transport in infrastructure-adjacent environments. By addressing critical gaps in system-level modeling of hazardous material dynamics, this research will directly support technological advancements in waste processing facilities, emergency response planning, and remediation site design, while reducing reliance on costly empirical trial-and-error approaches.
cip_title: Hazardous Materials Management and Waste Technology
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and other professionals engaged in identifying and disposing of hazardous materials. Includes instruction in environmental safety principles, biohazard identification, testing and sampling procedures, laboratory techniques, instrumentation calibration, hazardous waste disposal procedures and systems, safety and protection procedures, equipment maintenance, and report preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in semi-automated data entry workflows by developing adaptive computational models that optimize human-machine collaboration in microcomputer-based environments. Traditional data entry systems rely on static software interfaces and rigid workflows, which struggle to accommodate variability in input formats, user skill levels, or real-time error correction needs. The research will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to train ensemble machine learning models that dynamically adjust interface parameters, predictive text suggestions, and error detection thresholds based on continuous analysis of user interaction patterns. Using distributed computing frameworks, we will process terabyte-scale datasets of keystroke dynamics, cursor movements, and correction patterns collected from diverse microcomputer applications (spreadsheets, database interfaces, legacy systems). The computational pipeline will integrate natural language processing for context-aware field prioritization and computer vision techniques for layout recognition in semi-structured documents. A key innovation involves developing GPU-accelerated reinforcement learning agents that simulate human decision-making processes during data validation tasks, enabling proactive workflow adjustments without disrupting user attention. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework for adaptive data entry systems that reduces repetitive strain injuries by 18-25% through ergonomic interface adaptations, decreases procedural errors by 30% via real-time anomaly detection, and improves throughput by 15% in heterogeneous input environments. The HPC infrastructure is critical for handling the combinatorial complexity of modeling individualized user profiles while maintaining sub-200ms latency requirements for responsive interface adjustments. This work bridges gaps between human-computer interaction research and practical microcomputer applications, offering scalable solutions for industries reliant on legacy data entry systems undergoing digital transformation.
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to perform basic data and text entry using standard and customized software products. Includes instruction in keyboarding skills, personal computer and work station operation, reading draft texts and raw data forms, audio and tape dictation, and various interactive software programs used for tasks such as word processing, spreadsheets, databases, and others.

abstract: This project seeks to address the critical challenge of optimizing pedagogical strategies for less commonly taught languages (LCTLs) through computational modeling of language acquisition patterns and instructional efficacy. While foreign language teacher education programs emphasize methodologies for major languages, LCTLs—such as Mandarin, Arabic, or Swahili—present unique complexities due to differences in linguistic structure, cultural context, and resource availability. Current approaches often rely on generalized frameworks ill-suited to these languages, resulting in inconsistent learner outcomes. To bridge this gap, we propose a data-driven study leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multimodal datasets of classroom interactions, learner assessments, and teacher feedback across diverse LCTL contexts. Natural language processing (NLP) techniques will be applied to model phonological, syntactic, and semantic acquisition patterns in learners, while machine learning algorithms will identify correlations between instructional methods (e.g., task-based vs. grammar-translation approaches) and proficiency gains. Agent-based simulations will further test the scalability of adaptive teaching strategies in virtual classroom environments with varying student-to-teacher ratios and resource constraints. The computational workload necessitates HPC resources due to the scale of multilingual text/audio processing (10,000+ hours of classroom data), the iterative training of deep neural networks for proficiency prediction, and parallelized simulation of pedagogical scenarios. Anticipated outcomes include (1) evidence-based frameworks for tailoring LCTL instruction to specific linguistic and cultural features, (2) predictive models to guide real-time pedagogical adjustments, and (3) open-access tools for generating adaptive teaching materials. This work directly supports the development of specialized competencies in foreign language teacher education, enhancing equity in access to quality LCTL instruction globally.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach foreign languages programs at various educational levels, other than French, German or Spanish.

abstract: Maternal and child health disparities persist globally, driven by complex interactions between biological, social, and environmental factors. This project seeks to advance predictive modeling of adverse maternal and child health outcomes by integrating heterogeneous data sources—including electronic health records, demographic surveys, and environmental exposure datasets—to identify high-risk populations and optimize intervention strategies. A key challenge lies in scaling computationally intensive analyses across large, multi-modal datasets while accounting for spatial, temporal, and socio-behavioral variables. To address this, we propose developing an adaptive machine learning framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to train ensemble models that combine deep neural networks with interpretable causal inference methods. The computational workflow will involve preprocessing terabyte-scale health datasets, implementing distributed training of graph-based models to capture community-level health dynamics, and running agent-based simulations to evaluate intervention scenarios. HPC capabilities are critical for managing memory-intensive operations during feature extraction from longitudinal records, parallelizing Monte Carlo simulations for policy impact assessments, and reducing runtime for hyperparameter optimization across nested cross-validation folds. Expected outcomes include: (1) a scalable pipeline for identifying prenatal risk factors associated with preterm birth and neonatal mortality in underserved populations; (2) geospatial-temporal models quantifying the interaction between environmental stressors (e.g., air quality, heat islands) and maternal comorbidities; and (3) open-source tools enabling reproducible analysis of equity-focused intervention trade-offs. By enabling rapid iteration on complex models that synthesize clinical and public health data, this work will directly inform state-level maternal health initiatives and federal perinatal quality collaboratives, bridging computational innovation with translational health policy. The requested resources will support GPU-accelerated model training, large-scale data storage, and high-throughput batch processing essential for achieving statistically robust, generalizable results.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of public health specializations, public policy studies, and the social and behavioral sciences to issues of health affecting women, children, and families; and prepares individuals to function as maternal and child health specialists. Includes instruction in research design and testing, program evaluation, public policy analysis, public finance, economics of health care, community health, family development and dynamics, women's studies, social psychology, fetal and child development, biostatistics, health education and promotion, nutrition, neonatal development, psychology, and social services delivery.

abstract: The sustainable management of watershed ecosystems under climate change and anthropogenic pressures requires advanced predictive tools to inform policy decisions. Current challenges include integrating multi-scale hydrological, ecological, and socio-economic data to model complex feedback loops and assess the long-term impacts of management strategies. Existing models often lack the spatial resolution or computational scalability to evaluate regional watershed dynamics under diverse climate scenarios and policy interventions. This project seeks to address these gaps by developing a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework to simulate watershed resilience and optimize conservation policies. The research will focus on the [specific region/system, if applicable], employing a coupled modeling approach that combines hydrodynamic simulations, machine learning-based climate projection downscaling, and agent-based representations of land-use decision-making. HPC resources will enable parallelized execution of ensemble scenarios across decadal timescales, incorporating high-resolution remote sensing data (e.g., LiDAR, multispectral imagery) and stochastic climate inputs. Computational workflows will quantify trade-offs between water allocation policies, biodiversity conservation targets, and infrastructure development pathways. Expected outcomes include scalable models to identify critical thresholds in ecosystem services, such as sediment retention and flood mitigation capacities, under varying management regimes. The results will directly support state and federal agencies in designing adaptive policies that balance ecological integrity with human resource needs. By leveraging HPC capabilities to process terabytes of heterogeneous data and run computationally intensive multi-objective optimizations, this project aims to advance the integration of computational science into environmental governance, providing a replicable framework for evidence-based natural resources management.
detailed_field: Environmental/ natural resources management and policy
cip_title: Environmental/ Natural Resources Management and Policy, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in environmental or natural resources management and policy, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing dynamic resource allocation in large organizations operating under volatile market conditions. Traditional resource management frameworks often struggle to adapt to real-time fluctuations in demand, workforce availability, and operational constraints, leading to inefficiencies in cost control and service delivery. To overcome these limitations, we propose a computational approach combining multi-agent simulation and reinforcement learning (RL) to model complex decision-making hierarchies and identify adaptive allocation strategies. The project will develop a scalable simulation environment where autonomous agents represent departments, teams, or individual employees, each with unique skills, constraints, and objectives. RL algorithms will then iteratively optimize resource distribution policies across thousands of parallelized scenarios, accounting for stochastic demand patterns, workforce mobility, and shifting organizational priorities. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to manage the combinatorial complexity of these simulations, which involve millions of interdependent variables and require rapid convergence of RL models. Expected outcomes include a validated framework for real-time resource allocation that balances operational costs, employee utilization, and service quality metrics. The results will advance theoretical understanding of agility in organizational decision-making structures, particularly in service industries facing unpredictable demand cycles. Practically, the project will deliver open-source tools for scenario testing and policy prototyping, enabling managers to stress-test allocation strategies under diverse market conditions. By integrating computational scalability with business management theory, this work aims to bridge gaps between strategic planning and operational execution in complex enterprises.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on developing and expanding the theory and research in regards to the planning, organizing, directing , and controlling the functions and processes of a firm or organization.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamic interplay between human gut microbiome evolution and urbanization-driven environmental changes, integrating biological, anthropological, and environmental datasets to model how modern urban lifestyles alter microbial diversity and associated health outcomes. Rapid urbanization has reshaped dietary habits, environmental exposures, and social behaviors, yet the systemic impact on human-associated microbiomes—critical to metabolic, immune, and cognitive functions—remains poorly quantified. We propose a computational framework combining agent-based modeling, high-throughput metagenomic analysis, and geospatial data integration to simulate microbiome adaptation across heterogeneous urban populations. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process multi-terabyte genomic datasets from global cohorts, train machine learning models on microbiome-environment interactions, and run large-scale simulations incorporating variables such as dietary patterns, pollution gradients, and socioeconomic disparities. A novel aspect of this work is the incorporation of ethnographic data on cultural practices (e.g., food preparation, antibiotic use) into microbial community dynamics models, bridging biological and sociocultural determinants of health. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of urbanization-sensitive microbial taxa linked to non-communicable diseases, (2) predictive maps of microbiome-driven health risks under future urban development scenarios, and (3) an open-source computational toolkit for simulating host-microbiome-environment feedback loops. This work addresses a critical gap in human biology by quantifying how bidirectional interactions between biological systems and constructed environments shape population health. The requested HPC resources are essential for handling the project’s scale, enabling parallelized genomic analyses, and optimizing complex systems models that integrate stochastic, spatially explicit datasets. Findings will inform public health strategies targeting microbiome resilience and provide a template for interdisciplinary studies at the biology-society interface.
cip_definition: An interdisciplinary program that focuses on understanding the human being from the biological, social science, and humanities perspectives and that addresses contemporary issues related to biology and society, such as global health and disease, environmental policy, bioethics, and biotechnology.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of health-related message dissemination and public engagement across digital media platforms, with a focus on identifying patterns that influence the effectiveness of health advocacy campaigns. The research problem centers on the challenge of analyzing large-scale, unstructured communication data—including social media posts, public health campaign materials, and user-generated content—to understand how message framing, source credibility, and audience characteristics interact to shape public perceptions of health risks and preventive behaviors. Traditional methods in health communication struggle to process the volume and complexity of such data, limiting insights into real-time public responses and adaptive messaging strategies. To address this gap, we propose a computational approach leveraging natural language processing (NLP) and network analysis techniques to model the spread and reception of health messages across diverse populations. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for training machine learning models on multi-terabyte text datasets, simulating information diffusion networks, and conducting sentiment and thematic analyses at scale. The project will utilize GPU-accelerated computing to optimize NLP tasks, such as topic modeling and emotion detection, while parallel processing will enable dynamic network simulations to test how variations in message content or delivery channels affect engagement. Expected outcomes include the development of predictive frameworks to guide the design of targeted health campaigns, with applications to vaccine hesitancy mitigation, chronic disease prevention, and crisis communication. By integrating computational methods with communication theory, this work aims to advance evidence-based strategies for improving message clarity, trustworthiness, and behavioral impact, directly contributing to public health priorities. The requested HPC resources will support both the technical demands of large-data analytics and the iterative refinement of models to ensure scalability across linguistic and cultural contexts.
detailed_field: Applied communication, advertising, and public relations
cip_definition: A program that focuses on how people, individually and collectively, understand and accommodate to health and illness and the role of communication and media in shaping professional health care messages and public acceptance of these messages. Includes instruction in the development and use of health-related and care-related messages and media; the goals and strategies of health care promotion; relationships, roles, situations, and social structures in the context of health maintenance and promotion; and applications to disease prevention, health advocacy, and communications concerning treatments.

abstract: The development of advanced biopharmaceutical processes and biomolecular systems requires precise control over molecular interactions, yet current experimental approaches struggle to resolve the dynamic, multi-scale behavior of these systems. This project seeks to address this gap by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model and optimize enzyme-catalyzed drug synthesis pathways and protein-engineered biomaterials. Specifically, we aim to resolve the mechanistic basis of catalytic efficiency in non-aqueous enzymatic reactions and predict the self-assembly behavior of peptide-polymer hybrids for targeted drug delivery. Traditional molecular dynamics (MD) methods lack the scalability to simulate these systems at biologically relevant timescales, while coarse-grained models often sacrifice critical atomic-level details. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hybrid computational framework integrating all-atom MD simulations with enhanced sampling techniques, machine learning-driven free energy calculations, and reactive force field (ReaxFF) modeling. These simulations will be executed on HPC clusters to enable millisecond-scale sampling of enzyme conformational dynamics, solvent effects in non-aqueous bioreactors, and stress-strain responses of engineered biomaterials under physiological conditions. The computational workflow will utilize GROMACS and LAMMPS with GPU-accelerated parallelization, requiring access to >10,000 core-hours per simulation ensemble. Expected outcomes include the identification of rate-limiting steps in enzymatic drug precursor synthesis, design rules for solvent-resistant enzyme mutants, and predictive models for tuning the release kinetics of polymer-based drug carriers. This work will directly inform experimental efforts in our lab to develop continuous biomanufacturing platforms and responsive therapeutic delivery systems, with broader implications for sustainable pharmaceutical production and precision medicine. The requested computing resources are critical to achieving the resolution and throughput necessary to bridge molecular-scale insights with process-scale engineering applications.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of systems at the interface of chemical engineering and biology, with an emphasis at the molecular level, such as biopharmaceutical processes, protein engineering, metabolic engineering, gene therapy, biomaterials, cell and tissue engineering, and drug delivery. Includes instruction in chemical engineering, thermodynamics, organic chemistry, biochemistry, momentum and heat transfer, cellular and molecular biotechnology, process design, and chemical reactor design.

abstract: The proposed research investigates the interplay between urban microbiome dynamics and localized climate resilience through an integrative computational framework, bridging microbial ecology, atmospheric science, and urban systems modeling. Rapid urbanization has created complex feedback loops between anthropogenic landscapes, microbial communities, and microclimate patterns, yet predictive models remain underdeveloped due to data resolution challenges and disciplinary silos. This project addresses the critical gap in quantifying how microbial functional traits—such as heat-resistant metabolism or moisture-modulating biofilm production—mediate urban heat island effects and stormwater retention at neighborhood scales. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we will develop a multi-agent simulation platform that couples 1) spatially explicit microbial metagenomic data (TB-scale sequencing datasets from distributed sensor networks) with 2) fluid dynamics models of urban airflow and 3) machine learning predictors of community-scale metabolic outputs. The computational approach employs hybrid MPI-OpenMP parallelization to handle heterogeneous data integration across biological, physical, and climatic domains, while graph neural networks will map microbial interaction networks onto microclimate outcomes. Validation will utilize time-series LiDAR thermal scans and groundwater infiltration measurements from six metropolitan test zones. By establishing scalable workflows for merging biological complexity with geophysical systems, this work aims to produce the first predictive framework for microbiome-enhanced urban climate adaptation strategies. Expected outcomes include quantifiable thresholds for microbial community interventions to mitigate extreme heat events and optimize green infrastructure performance. The computational architecture developed will enable future cross-domain studies of biological-physical couplings in anthropogenic ecosystems, addressing a critical need for interdisciplinary tools in urban sustainability science. Resource allocation is essential for managing memory-intensive phylogenetic network analyses concurrently with high-resolution climate simulations, requiring sustained access to GPU-accelerated nodes and distributed memory systems.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of scientific computing and its application. Includes instruction in scientific visualization, multi-scale analysis, grid generation, data analysis, applied mathematics, numerical algorithms, high performance parallel computing, and numerical modeling and simulation with applications in science, engineering and other disciplines in which computation plays an integral role.

abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects over 850 million people globally, with heterogeneous progression rates complicating treatment strategies. Current risk prediction models rely on limited clinical variables, failing to capture multi-scale interactions between molecular mechanisms, physiological processes, and patient-specific factors. This project seeks to develop an integrative computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model CKD progression and predict individualized outcomes. We will employ machine learning algorithms trained on multi-omics datasets (genomics, proteomics, metabolomics) from longitudinal cohort studies, combined with mechanistic models simulating renal hemodynamics, fibrosis pathways, and metabolic dysregulation. The HPC environment will enable large-scale parameter optimization across these hybrid models using de-identified electronic health records (n≈250,000) and high-resolution biosensor data. Ensemble methods will identify critical biomarkers and physiological thresholds governing disease transitions, while graph neural networks will map inter-organ crosstalk contributing to CKD comorbidities. The resulting predictive platform will be validated against renal function trajectories in three prospective clinical trials. This work aims to establish a new paradigm for dynamic risk stratification in nephrology, enabling earlier interventions tailored to molecular drivers and systemic interactions. Successful implementation could reduce the proportion of patients progressing to end-stage renal disease by 15–20% within five years, significantly lowering healthcare burdens. The computational infrastructure developed will also serve as a scalable template for studying other complex chronic diseases with multi-organ involvement.
cip_definition: Research focused on Nephrology

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing dynamic resource allocation and workforce scheduling in hybrid office environments, where fluctuating staff presence, evolving space requirements, and budgetary constraints complicate operational efficiency. Traditional rule-based or manual approaches often fail to account for the combinatorial complexity of variables, including personnel roles, workspace utilization, equipment availability, and real-time demand shifts. To overcome these limitations, we propose a computational framework integrating agent-based modeling (ABM) and mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) to simulate office operations and generate data-driven scheduling and space allocation strategies. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute large-scale simulations that model hundreds of interdependent variables—such as employee mobility patterns, shared resource conflicts, and energy costs—across diverse scenarios. Parallelized optimization algorithms will iteratively refine solutions to minimize overhead costs while maintaining productivity benchmarks and employee satisfaction metrics. The project will leverage anonymized sensor data from partner organizations to calibrate models, ensuring practical relevance. Expected outcomes include a scalable decision-support tool capable of recommending adaptive office configurations and staffing plans under uncertainty. This research directly contributes to the Office Management and Supervision field by advancing computational methods for space management and labor coordination, offering actionable insights to reduce operational costs and enhance workplace flexibility. The proposed work aligns with organizational trends toward hybrid work models, providing a foundation for evidence-based supervision strategies in business administration.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to supervise and manage the operations and personnel of business offices and management-level divisions. Includes instruction in employee supervision, management, and labor relations; budgeting; scheduling and coordination; office systems operation and maintenance; office records management, organization, and security; office facilities design and space management; preparation and evaluation of business management data; and public relations.

abstract: This project seeks to develop and validate computational models to optimize adaptive learning systems (ALS) in diverse educational contexts, addressing the current gap in scalable, real-time personalization of digital learning environments. While ALS platforms increasingly leverage learner analytics, existing systems often rely on static algorithms or limited datasets, resulting in suboptimal recommendations for learners with varying needs, cultural backgrounds, or accessibility requirements. To address this, we propose a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that dynamically integrates multimodal interaction data (e.g., eye-tracking patterns, clickstream behaviors, and formative assessment performance) with contextual metadata about learning environments. The research will utilize high-performance computing resources to train deep neural networks on heterogeneous datasets spanning 15,000+ learner interactions across three open-source learning platforms, while maintaining privacy-preserving federated learning protocols. Computational experiments will test hypotheses about the impact of temporal feature engineering and attention mechanisms on model accuracy in predicting learning outcomes. A parallel agent-based modeling component will simulate how different resource allocation strategies affect system performance under varying institutional constraints. Expected outcomes include 1) validated architectures for low-latency adaptation in web-based instructional systems, 2) open-source tools for simulating educational technology deployments, and 3) evidence-based frameworks for balancing computational costs with pedagogical benefits in ALS design. This work directly advances the program’s focus on evidence-based educational technology integration by providing scalable methods to personalize learning while maintaining computational feasibility for resource-constrained institutions. Results will be disseminated through interactive visualization portals to support learning designers’ decision-making processes.
detailed_field: Educational/ instructional technology and media design
cip_definition: A program that focuses on designing and integrating technology into educational curricula. Includes instruction in foundations of educational technology, design, utilizing technology for assessment, multimedia instruction, computer applications, human-computer interaction, web-based instruction, distance education, and designing and producing educational software and materials.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in the computational analysis of Baltic languages, with a focus on understudied and extinct varieties such as Old Prussian and Curionian. Despite their historical and cultural significance, these languages remain underrepresented in digital philology and natural language processing (NLP) research due to fragmented textual records, non-standard orthographies, and limited computational tools tailored to their linguistic features. The research problem centers on reconstructing phonological, morphological, and syntactic patterns in these languages to advance scholarly understanding of their evolution and interrelationships. To achieve this, the project will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process digitized corpora of historical texts, inscriptions, and comparative data from extant Baltic languages. Computational methods will include the development of transformer-based models for automated morphological parsing, phylogenetic algorithms to model language divergence, and semantic network analysis to trace lexical shifts across time and dialects. The scale of data—spanning centuries of textual fragments and multilingual parallel texts—requires distributed computing for efficient storage, preprocessing, and iterative model training. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of annotated Old Prussian and Curionian texts, probabilistic reconstructions of unattested phonological systems, and open-source NLP pipelines optimized for Baltic language structures. These resources will directly support philological research, language revitalization initiatives, and applications in cross-lingual information retrieval for regional archives. By integrating computational linguistics with traditional philological expertise, the project aims to establish a methodological framework for analyzing low-resource historical languages, with implications for both Baltic studies and digital humanities methodologies. The requested HPC allocation is essential to manage memory-intensive tasks, such as training deep learning models on heterogeneous textual data and running large-scale comparative simulations, which cannot feasibly be executed on local infrastructure.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the languages of the Baltic peoples, including, but not limited to, the modern languages of Latvian and Lithuanian, and extinct languages such as Old Prussian and Curionian. Includes instruction in philology; literature; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the role of mechanical stress in modulating tumor progression and metastasis within physiologically relevant microenvironments, integrating principles of biomechanics, oncology, and physiology. Tumors experience heterogeneous mechanical forces due to growth-induced compression, extracellular matrix remodeling, and interstitial fluid pressure, which influence cellular signaling, invasion, and therapeutic resistance. However, existing models often oversimplify these interactions by neglecting the dynamic, multiscale coupling between tissue-scale mechanics and subcellular responses. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework combining finite element modeling (FEM) of tumor mechanics with agent-based simulations (ABS) of cancer cell behavior. The FEM component will simulate time-dependent stress-strain distributions within 3D tumor geometries derived from clinical imaging, incorporating viscoelastic material properties and fluid-structure interactions. The ABS module will model mechanosensitive cellular decision-making (e.g., proliferation, migration, apoptosis) in response to localized mechanical cues predicted by FEM. This bidirectional coupling requires iterative data exchange at submicron spatial and subsecond temporal resolutions across millions of computational cells, necessitating parallelized workflows on HPC clusters. Expected outcomes include identification of critical stress thresholds that trigger metastatic phenotypes, predictive maps of therapy-resistant niches, and quantitative links between tumor mechanical heterogeneity and genomic instability. By elucidating how biomechanical forces synergize with oncogenic pathways, this work will advance targeted strategies to mechanically disrupt tumor progression. The computational framework will be validated against in vitro models of breast and pancreatic cancer under controlled loading conditions, with future translation to patient-specific simulations. Access to HPC resources is essential to achieve the required scale and resolution, enabling unprecedented integration of mechanical and biological tumor dynamics.
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the biological, anatomical, and mechanical structure and function of the mechanical aspects of biological systems. Includes courses in anatomy, physiology, kinesiology, mechanics, measurement and instrumentation, and research methods.

abstract: This project seeks to optimize sustainable textile waste reduction in wholesale fashion merchandising through dynamic pricing and inventory strategies, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model complex, multi-agent supply chain ecosystems. The fashion industry faces escalating pressure to mitigate overproduction and textile waste, particularly at the wholesale level, where mismatches between bulk orders and retailer demand lead to unsold inventory and environmental harm. Current strategies rely on static pricing or heuristic demand forecasting, which fail to adapt to real-time shifts in consumer trends, supplier constraints, or geopolitical disruptions. To address this, we propose an interdisciplinary computational framework integrating agent-based modeling (ABM), reinforcement learning (RL), and large-scale sentiment analysis of social media and economic datasets. HPC resources will enable simulations of thousands of wholesale buyers, suppliers, and retailers operating under dynamic conditions, including climate policy shocks and viral trend cycles. The ABM component will capture heterogeneous decision-making behaviors, while RL algorithms will train adaptive pricing agents to balance profitability with waste reduction. Sentiment data, scraped from platforms like Instagram and TikTok, will inform demand predictions at granular regional and demographic levels. By parallelizing these workflows across GPU clusters, we aim to identify pricing-inventory policies that reduce overstock by ≥30% in simulated wholesale environments while maintaining profit margins. Outcomes will provide actionable strategies for wholesalers to align purchasing contracts with emerging sustainability regulations and volatile consumer preferences. This research bridges computational social science, operations research, and environmental management, advancing both business efficiency and circular economy objectives in a critically understudied domain.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to promote product lines/brands, and organize promotional campaigns, at the wholesale level to attract retailer interest, wholesale purchasing, and supply contracts. Includes instruction in wholesaling, wholesale advertising, selling, and customer relations.

abstract: Immunopathologic diseases, including autoimmune disorders and transplant rejection, involve complex interactions between immune cells, molecular pathways, and clinical variables that remain inadequately characterized. Current challenges in predicting patient-specific immunotherapy responses or post-transplant outcomes stem from limitations in modeling dynamic immune processes across genomic, proteomic, and clinical datasets. This project proposes to develop an integrated computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multi-modal immunopathology data, with the goal of identifying predictive biomarkers and optimizing therapeutic strategies. The research will focus on two interconnected aims: (1) constructing patient-specific immune network models using single-cell RNA sequencing, serum proteomics, and clinical histopathology data from cohorts with autoimmune vasculitis and renal transplant recipients, and (2) simulating immune response trajectories under varying therapeutic regimens through mechanistic modeling. Computational methods will combine deep learning architectures for feature extraction from high-dimensional pathology images, Bayesian network inference for identifying critical immune pathway interactions, and parallelized agent-based simulations of immune cell dynamics. The HPC environment is essential for managing datasets exceeding 500 TB, running iterative model optimizations, and executing large-scale in silico clinical trials comparing immunosuppression protocols. Expected outcomes include validated computational models capable of predicting graft rejection risk with >85% accuracy in retrospective validation cohorts and identifying optimal combination therapies for refractory autoimmune cases. By enabling the integration of real-time diagnostic data with dynamic systems immunology models, this work aims to advance precision management of immunologic diseases while reducing reliance on trial-and-error treatment approaches. The requested resources will support GPU-accelerated model training, high-memory nodes for whole-genome association analyses, and scalable storage for multi-institutional collaborative datasets.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis, treatment and laboratory management of immunologic diseases. Includes instruction in diagnostic surgical pathology, management of organ transplantation and immunotherapy.

abstract: Physical therapy rehabilitation outcomes are hindered by heterogeneous patient biomechanical profiles and insufficient personalization of therapeutic interventions. Traditional protocols, often based on population-level data, fail to address individual variations in musculoskeletal dynamics, leading to prolonged recovery and suboptimal functional outcomes. This project seeks to bridge this gap by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to develop a computational framework for optimizing patient-specific rehabilitation strategies. The research integrates multiscale biomechanical modeling—combining motion capture, electromyography, and medical imaging data—with machine learning to simulate the effects of therapeutic exercises, neuromuscular retraining, and biophysical agents on tissue healing and functional recovery. HPC resources will enable large-scale finite element simulations of musculoskeletal stress distributions, neural network training on heterogeneous clinical datasets, and real-time optimization of treatment parameters across diverse patient cohorts. Expected outcomes include predictive models that identify optimal intervention sequences, dosage, and progression tailored to individual biomechanical and physiological constraints. By establishing a link between computational biomechanics and clinical decision-making, this work aims to advance precision rehabilitation paradigms, reduce trial-and-error in therapy design, and improve recovery efficiency. The resulting open-source tools will provide a foundation for scalable, data-driven approaches in physical therapy, with potential applications in post-surgical rehabilitation, chronic injury management, and preventive care. This interdisciplinary effort merges clinical expertise with computational innovation, addressing a critical niche in health sciences where personalized therapeutic design intersects with emerging technologies.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to evaluate, examine, diagnose, and alleviate physical functional impairments and limitations caused by injury or disease through the design and implementation of therapeutic interventions to promote fitness and health. Includes instruction in anatomy, behavioral sciences, biology, biomechanics, biophysical agents, care plan development and documentation, cellular histology, clinical evaluation and measurement, clinical reasoning, communication, exercise physiology, kinesiology, neuroscience, pharmacology, pathology, physiology, professional standards and ethics, rehabilitation psychology, and therapeutic exercise.

abstract: Medical imaging is fundamental to modern diagnostics, yet the increasing complexity and volume of radiological data strain conventional analysis methods, leading to delays and variability in clinical interpretations. This project addresses these challenges by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to develop scalable, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven tools for automated medical image analysis. The research focuses on optimizing deep learning models to detect and characterize pathologies—such as tumors, vascular anomalies, and neurodegenerative lesions—across multi-modal imaging datasets (e.g., MRI, CT, and PET). Key computational challenges include processing high-resolution 3D volumes, managing heterogeneous data formats, and ensuring robust generalization across diverse patient populations. To overcome these, we propose a hybrid pipeline integrating GPU-accelerated preprocessing for noise reduction and spatial normalization, distributed training of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with federated learning frameworks, and Bayesian uncertainty quantification to enhance model reliability. The HPC infrastructure will enable rapid iteration on petascale datasets from multi-institutional collaborations while preserving data privacy. Expected outcomes include validated AI tools that reduce diagnostic turnaround times, improve detection accuracy for early-stage malignancies, and identify novel imaging biomarkers predictive of disease progression. By providing open-source algorithms and computational workflows, this work will empower radiologists to harness large-scale data effectively, advancing precision diagnostics and bridging gaps between imaging research and clinical practice. The requested resources are critical to achieving the computational throughput necessary for translating these innovations into patient care.
cip_definition: Research focused on Radiology

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize personalized meal planning for individuals with complex dietary constraints, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to address gaps in current dietitian assistant workflows. Current manual methods for meal planning struggle to efficiently balance nutritional requirements, ingredient availability, patient preferences, and regulatory standards, particularly for populations with overlapping medical, cultural, or socioeconomic needs (e.g., diabetic patients requiring renal-friendly, halal-compliant diets). The research problem centers on scaling real-time optimization across high-dimensional parameter spaces while integrating dynamic inputs such as fluctuating nutrient databases, regional food costs, and patient biometric feedback. Using a hybrid approach combining constrained evolutionary algorithms and transformer-based preference modeling, the project will simulate multi-objective meal plans under probabilistic scenarios (e.g., supply chain disruptions, seasonal ingredient shifts). HPC resources will enable parallelized testing of >10^6 recipe permutations per case, incorporating real-world data from electronic health records, USDA nutrient databases, and patient-reported outcome metrics. Expected outcomes include an open-source optimization engine capable of generating compliant meal variants 40-60x faster than manual methods, validated against registered dietitian assessments. The computational pipeline will also produce sensitivity analyses to prioritize critical nutritional variables for specific health conditions. By bridging clinical nutrition, operations research, and machine learning, this work aims to establish scalable decision-support tools for dietitian teams while advancing methodologies for constraint-heavy resource allocation in healthcare settings. Results will be disseminated through interdisciplinary journals and modular software packages adaptable to institutional dietary management systems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to assist registered dietitians in planning, preparing and serving meals to individuals with specific dietary needs. Includes instruction in equipment use, food preparation, diet regulations, food handling, safety and sanitary standards and administrative techniques and procedures.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance biomechanical and clinical research in podiatric medicine, addressing critical gaps in understanding the interplay between foot pathologies, therapeutic interventions, and dynamic lower extremity function. The research focuses on developing multiscale computational models to simulate the biomechanical behavior of the foot under varying pathological and treatment conditions, including diabetic foot ulcers, Charcot neuroarthropathy, and post-surgical rehabilitation. Current limitations in predicting tissue stress distributions, bone remodeling dynamics, and orthotic efficacy stem from the computational complexity of modeling heterogeneous tissues, nonlinear material properties, and patient-specific gait patterns. To overcome these challenges, the project will implement finite element analysis (FEA) coupled with machine learning algorithms to optimize simulations of foot mechanics across diverse patient cohorts. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of high-resolution 3D imaging datasets (MRI/CT), stochastic modeling of soft tissue interactions, and real-time analysis of gait sensor data. Key deliverables include predictive frameworks for ulcer risk stratification, virtual testing environments for orthotic design, and biomechanical insights into surgical outcomes. By integrating clinical data with computational modeling, this work aims to establish personalized treatment protocols, reduce trial-and-error in device fabrication, and improve postoperative recovery timelines. The outcomes will directly inform evidence-based guidelines in podiatric practice, enhancing preventive care and functional outcomes for patients with complex lower extremity disorders. Access to HPC infrastructure is essential to manage the terabyte-scale datasets, iterative model calibrations, and parameter sweeps required for robust, generalizable results in this high-dimensional research space.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of podiatric medicine, involving the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of diseases, disorders, and injuries to the foot and lower extremities. Includes instruction in the basic medical sciences, anatomy of the lower extremity, functional orthopedics, foot biomechanics, podiatric radiology, dermatology, podiatric surgery, podopediatrics, sports medicine, physical diagnosis, emergency medicine and traumatology, practice management, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address challenges in analyzing the linguistic evolution and dialectal diversity of Japanese across historical periods. Japanese philological studies face significant computational barriers due to the complexity of its writing systems (e.g., kanji, kana), morphological structures, and dialect variations, compounded by the scarcity of machine-readable corpora for pre-modern texts. The research aims to develop scalable natural language processing (NLP) pipelines to analyze syntactic, morphological, and lexical patterns in digitized texts spanning Ancient, Medieval, and Modern Japanese, including understudied regional dialects. Computational methods will include training transformer-based models for diachronic language modeling, employing probabilistic algorithms for dialect classification, and automating the alignment of historical orthographies with contemporary phonetic representations. These tasks require parallelized processing of terabyte-scale text datasets and iterative model training, necessitating HPC infrastructure for GPU-accelerated workloads and large-memory nodes. Expected outcomes include (1) a diachronic corpus annotated with linguistic features, (2) quantitative insights into language shift mechanisms, particularly during the Edo-Meiji transition, and (3) open-access tools for dialect preservation, relevant to communities maintaining endangered regional varieties. The project bridges computational linguistics and area studies, offering methodologies transferable to other under-resourced languages while advancing Japan-specific humanistic scholarship. By enabling large-scale analysis previously constrained by manual methods, this work will inform pedagogical resources, enhance NLP applications for historical texts, and contribute to interdisciplinary debates on language standardization and cultural identity.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Japanese language. Includes instruction in philology; Ancient, Medieval, and Modern Japanese; dialects; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: Pediatric patients exhibit unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles due to developmental physiological changes, genetic variability, and disease heterogeneity. Current dosing guidelines for many medications remain extrapolated from adult studies, leading to suboptimal efficacy or safety in children. This project seeks to address this gap by developing precision dosing models tailored to pediatric populations through advanced computational methods. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze large-scale clinical, genomic, and pharmacometric datasets, enabling the integration of multi-omics data, electronic health records (EHRs), and real-world evidence. Key objectives include (1) constructing population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) models using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling, (2) applying machine learning to identify genetic and clinical covariates influencing drug response, and (3) simulating individualized dosing strategies via physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling. Computational workflows will require parallel processing for Bayesian parameter estimation, Monte Carlo simulations to predict exposure-response relationships across developmental stages, and validation against retrospective clinical outcomes. HPC resources are critical to manage the computational intensity of these tasks, particularly for optimizing algorithms across diverse pediatric subpopulations (e.g., neonates, adolescents) and rare disease cohorts. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for dose individualization of high-risk medications (e.g., anticoagulants, immunosuppressants), reducing adverse drug reactions and therapeutic failures. The project will generate open-access tools for pediatric pharmacotherapy optimization, fostering scalable methodologies for future research. By bridging developmental pharmacology with computational innovation, this work aims to establish a framework for evidence-based dosing in pediatric care, directly addressing a longstanding challenge in clinical medicine.
cip_definition: Research focused on pediatric pharmacy.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for optimizing adaptive programming interfaces that leverage real-time user cognitive load data to personalize coding environments. While traditional programming tools prioritize static efficiency metrics, emerging interdisciplinary work at the intersection of cognitive ergonomics, human-computer interaction, and programmatic adaptability remains underexplored. The research problem centers on mitigating cognitive fatigue during extended programming tasks by dynamically adjusting interface elements—such as code layout, autocompletion prompts, and debugging feedback—based on biometric and behavioral inputs (e.g., eye-tracking, keystroke dynamics, and EEG-derived attention signals). The computational approach integrates machine learning models trained on multimodal user interaction data with real-time optimization algorithms to balance code-generation efficiency against cognitive strain thresholds. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for two phases: (1) large-scale parallel processing of heterogeneous training data (collected from 500+ programming sessions across diverse expertise levels) to build user-specific cognitive load predictors, and (2) GPU-accelerated simulations of interface adaptation strategies under varying task complexity scenarios. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework for cognitive-aware programming environments validated through controlled user studies, demonstrating statistically significant reductions in task abandonment rates (target: 22-35%) and error frequency (target: 15-25%) compared to static interfaces. The work establishes a novel methodology for quantifying programmer-device interaction through computational cognitive models, with broader implications for adaptive systems in education, accessibility technologies, and high-stakes software development environments. Resource requests target 200,000 node-hours on GPU clusters for deep reinforcement learning workflows and 50 TB of temporary storage for processing real-time biometric streams during simulation cycles.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in computer programming, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to address the critical gap in computational resources for analyzing understudied Turkic, Uralic-Altaic, Caucasian, and Central Asian languages, many of which are low-resource or endangered. Current linguistic research in these regions is hindered by fragmented datasets, limited digitized corpora, and a lack of tools for automated morphological, syntactic, and semantic analysis. To overcome these challenges, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop scalable computational models for cross-linguistic comparison and diachronic analysis. Our approach integrates machine learning techniques—including transformer-based architectures and probabilistic graphical models—with parallelized processing of multilingual text corpora, oral narratives, and historical manuscripts. Key tasks include training language-specific embeddings, automating the annotation of agglutinative morphological structures, and simulating language contact effects across Central Asia’s diverse linguistic landscape. The computational demands of these tasks, particularly the need for distributed training on large-scale datasets and real-time alignment of phonetic variations, necessitate HPC infrastructure. Expected outcomes include an open-access repository of annotated texts for 10+ languages (e.g., Chuvash, Tuvan, Balkar, and Georgian dialects), probabilistic maps of syntactic convergence zones, and tools for detecting lexical borrowing patterns. These resources will directly support linguistic preservation initiatives and advance theoretical understanding of typological variation across Eurasia. By enabling previously infeasible analyses of language evolution and contact dynamics, this project will foster interdisciplinary collaborations between computational linguists, area studies scholars, and communities engaged in language revitalization efforts.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: Turkic, Uralic-Altaic, Caucasian, and Central Asian Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in the Turkic, Uralic-Altaic, Caucasian, and Central Asian languages, literatures, and linguistics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop and validate computational models to evaluate the effectiveness of large-scale educational interventions, with a focus on identifying factors that mediate equity and learning outcomes in heterogeneous student populations. Current evaluation frameworks struggle to integrate mixed-methods data (e.g., longitudinal academic records, qualitative stakeholder feedback, and real-time behavioral metrics from digital learning platforms) while accounting for contextual variables such as socioeconomic disparities and institutional resource allocation. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled approach combining multilevel Bayesian inference, natural language processing (NLP) for qualitative data, and agent-based simulations of intervention scalability. The computational demands arise from (1) processing terabytes of unstructured text from open-response surveys and classroom observations, (2) running parallelized Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling for hierarchical models with >10⁵ parameters, and (3) simulating district-wide policy impacts under thousands of counterfactual scenarios. Leveraging GPU-accelerated NLP transformers and distributed-memory clusters will reduce model training times from weeks to days while enabling sensitivity analyses impractical on local hardware. Expected outcomes include a publicly deployable toolkit for dynamically visualizing equity trade-offs in program designs and evidence-based recommendations for optimizing resource distribution in Title I schools. The project will advance evaluation methodology by formalizing nonlinear interactions between intervention components and contextual variables—a critical gap in current quasi-experimental approaches. By utilizing HPC resources to handle the scale and complexity of modern educational data ecosystems, this work aims to provide actionable insights for reducing outcome gaps while establishing computational reproducibility standards in education research.
detailed_field: Educational assessment, evaluation, and research methods
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the principles and procedures for generating information about educational programs, personnel and methods, and the analysis of such information for planning purposes. Includes instruction in evaluation theory, evaluation research design and planning, administering evaluations and related data collection activities, data reporting requirements, data analysis and interpretation, and related economic and policy issues.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research on early identification of reading difficulties through computational modeling of language and literacy development in young learners. The research problem centers on the challenge of analyzing complex, high-dimensional datasets—including speech recordings, eye-tracking metrics, and written responses—to detect subtle patterns predictive of atypical reading trajectories. Traditional statistical methods are insufficient for modeling the dynamic interactions between phonological, syntactic, and semantic development at scale, particularly when integrating longitudinal data from diverse learner populations. To address this, the project will employ machine learning techniques, including transformer-based neural networks and graph analytics, to process multimodal datasets from 5,000+ K-3 students. These models will simulate language acquisition pathways and identify critical inflection points where targeted interventions could mitigate reading challenges. Computational demands include training deep learning architectures on longitudinal speech-text paired data, clustering atypical vs. typical literacy profiles using unsupervised methods, and validating models against clinical diagnostic benchmarks. HPC resources are essential for managing distributed training across GPU nodes, processing terabytes of audio-visual data, and running iterative simulations to test hypothetical intervention scenarios. Expected outcomes include (1) open-source tools for automated analysis of literacy behaviors, (2) evidence-based thresholds for early risk detection, and (3) a framework for personalizing phonics-based instruction based on computational profiles.
