These systems raise fundamental questions about collective meaning-making, cultural transmission, and identity formation in post-textual environments, yet remain understudied due to the technical challenges of analyzing large-scale, heterogeneous multimedia datasets. The research will employ computational visual semiotics, combining computer vision techniques for pattern recognition in image corpora with graph-based network analysis of usage contexts across temporal and platform boundaries. High-performance computing resources are essential for processing petabytes of user-generated content from federated platforms (including ActivityPub networks and blockchain-based communities), requiring GPU-accelerated feature extraction, transformer-based multimodal embedding, and dynamic network modeling at scale. Expected outcomes include 1) a computational framework for identifying emergent visual grammars across decentralized networks, 2) quantitative models of cultural innovation diffusion in iconographic systems, and 3) ethical guidelines for preserving ephemeral digital vernaculars. By bridging humanities-focused cultural analysis with scalable computational methods, this work aims to establish new paradigms for studying twenty-first-century cultural production while addressing preservation challenges posed by proprietary platform dependencies and digital obsolescence. The resource request supports both the development of custom vision-language models tailored to grassroots digital aesthetics and the creation of an open repository for analyzing at-risk community-generated visual cultures.
cip_title: Liberal Arts and Sciences, General Studies and Humanities, Other
cip_definition: Any single instructional program in liberal arts and sciences, general studies and humanities, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the biomechanical and biophysical mechanisms underlying Asian Bodywork Therapy (ABT) modalities, such as acupressure and Tui na, through computational modeling and simulation. Despite widespread clinical use, the physiological effects of ABT techniques—particularly their interactions with tissue dynamics, neural signaling, and systemic energy pathways (e.g., Qi flow)—remain poorly quantified. Traditional studies rely on small-scale empirical data or subjective outcomes, limiting reproducibility and mechanistic insight. To address this gap, we propose a computational framework integrating patient-specific anatomical models, finite element analysis (FEA), and machine learning (ML) to simulate and optimize ABT interventions. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process high-resolution medical imaging data, model tissue deformation and fluid dynamics during pressure application, and analyze multiscale physiological responses across diverse populations. Simulations will incorporate variable parameters such as force magnitude, direction, and duration, as well as individualized anatomical variations (e.g., muscle density, vascular networks). Concurrently, ML algorithms will identify patterns in existing clinical datasets linking ABT techniques to biomarkers of pain modulation, inflammation, and autonomic nervous system activity. The integration of FEA and ML outputs aims to generate predictive models of therapy efficacy, enabling personalized treatment protocols. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated computational pipeline for mapping ABT biomechanics, (2) quantitative evidence of dose-response relationships in pressure-based therapies, and (3) open-access tools for practitioners to refine techniques using simulated scenarios. By bridging traditional practices with computational biophysics, this work will establish a foundation for evidence-based optimization of ABT, enhancing its integration into multidisciplinary care and informing regulatory standards for training and safety. The project’s computational demands—particularly the need for parallelized simulations of heterogeneous tissue interactions and large-scale ML training—necessitate HPC resources to achieve clinically relevant resolution and scalability.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide relief and improved health and well-being based on Chinese medical principles through one or more of the traditional bodywork therapies of Asia. Includes instruction in acupressure, AMMA(r) Therapy, Chi Nei Tsang, Five Element Shiatsu, Integrative Eclectic Shiatsu, Japanese Shiatsu, Jin Shin Do(r) Bodymind Acupressure(tm), Macrobiotic Shiatsu, Anma Therapy, Thai massage, Tui na, Zen Shiatsu, Qigong, Okazaki(r) Restorative Massage, principles of Western and Chinese medicine, patient counseling and observation, practice management, applicable regulations, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders represent a leading cause of global disability, yet diagnostic imaging approaches for conditions such as osteoarthritis, spinal degeneration, and traumatic injuries remain limited in their ability to detect early pathological changes or predict disease progression. Current clinical protocols rely heavily on subjective interpretation of conventional MRI and CT, which lack sensitivity to microstructural tissue alterations. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing advanced computational models to analyze quantitative imaging biomarkers derived from high-resolution musculoskeletal datasets. We propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process and integrate multi-parametric MRI sequences (T1/T2 mapping, diffusion-weighted imaging) and biomechanical simulation data across a retrospective cohort of 1,200 patients and prospective data from 200 new participants. Deep learning architectures will be trained to identify patterns predictive of early degenerative joint disease, vertebral endplate failure, and muscle atrophy progression, while finite element modeling will simulate load distribution in pathological bone and cartilage. Computational demands include processing >50 TB of 3D imaging data, running iterative simulations of tissue stress-response, and optimizing neural networks through hyperparameter tuning across thousands of parallelized trials. Anticipated outcomes include validated algorithms for automated detection of subclinical fractures, predictive models of disc herniation risk based on biomechanical stressors, and quantitative imaging criteria for pediatric growth plate injury prognosis. This work will establish novel computational frameworks to enhance diagnostic precision in musculoskeletal radiology, enabling earlier intervention and personalized treatment strategies. The requested HPC allocation is critical for managing memory-intensive workflows, reducing model training times from weeks to days, and ensuring reproducibility through large-scale validation. Results will be disseminated through open-access tools for biomarker analysis, directly supporting clinical translation of quantitative imaging in musculoskeletal care.
cip_definition: Research focused on that prepares diagnostic radiologists in the diagnosis and treatment of disorders or injuries of the joints, bones, muscles, and spine in adults and children.

abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of global mortality, with mechanistic complexity arising from multi-scale interactions spanning molecular pathways, cellular dynamics, and organ-level pathophysiology. Current clinical approaches often lack the resolution to predict individualized disease trajectories or optimize therapies. This project proposes an integrative computational framework to model cardiac dysfunction, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to bridge molecular, cellular, and clinical datasets. The primary research problem centers on identifying mechanistically grounded biomarkers for arrhythmia risk and heart failure progression, which are poorly predicted by existing clinical tools. We will develop multi-scale models of cardiac electrophysiology and biomechanics, calibrated using patient-derived imaging, genomic, and hemodynamic data. Key computational methods include finite-element simulations of myocardial tissue, agent-based modeling of fibroblast-myocyte interactions in fibrotic hearts, and deep learning architectures to integrate multi-omics data with clinical outcomes. HPC resources are critical for parameter optimization across 10^4–10^5 cellular configurations, whole-heart simulations at submillimeter spatial resolution, and Bayesian inference workflows to quantify uncertainty in personalized model predictions. A parallel aim involves real-time processing of 4D flow MRI datasets (>1 TB/patient) to simulate coronary blood flow dynamics under varying physiologic and pharmacologic conditions. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models linking genetic variants to arrhythmia susceptibility via in silico ion channel perturbation studies, (2) automated pipelines for stratifying heart failure subtypes using unsupervised learning on EHR-derived features, and (3) open-source simulation tools for virtual stent deployment and hemodynamic outcome prediction. By enabling time-resolved simulations of cardiac electromechanics across unprecedented spatial scales, this work will advance precision cardiology through mechanism-based risk stratification and treatment optimization. The computational infrastructure developed will be disseminated via a cloud-based platform, allowing clinical researchers to test hypotheses in simulated patient cohorts. This project directly addresses the NIH’s mandate for translational bioinformatics in CVDs, with potential to reduce invasive diagnostic procedures and accelerate therapeutic innovation.
cip_definition: Research focused on Cardiology

abstract: This project seeks to employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of ritual practices in underrepresented diasporic religious traditions, focusing on the intersection of oral performance, material culture, and community identity. The research centers on the Ifá-Orisha tradition, a West African diasporic spiritual system with global manifestations, examining how its ritual protocols—transmitted orally and through embodied practice—adapt to sociocultural disruptions such as migration and digital mediation. While prior studies have relied on qualitative ethnography, this project innovates by applying computational methods to a multimodal corpus spanning decades: audio recordings of divination chants, 3D-scanned ritual objects, and video documentation of ceremonies from Nigeria, Cuba, Brazil, and the United States. Key challenges include processing non-Roman script transcriptions of Yoruba incantations, identifying patterns in ritual gesture sequences via motion-capture data, and modeling the diffusion of symbolic motifs across geographically dispersed communities. The HPC environment will enable large-scale natural language processing (NLP) of Yoruba incantations using transformer models trained on liturgical texts, computer vision analysis of ritual object iconography via convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and network science approaches to map variations in ceremonial practices. Anticipated outcomes include a publicly accessible digital archive of annotated ritual materials, probabilistic models of cultural transmission pathways, and visualizations of how core theological concepts manifest differently across diasporic nodes. By computationally tracing the resilience and innovation of an oral religious tradition, this work aims to advance methodological frameworks for studying non-textual, practice-based theological systems while preserving endangered cultural heritage. The project underscores the critical role of HPC in addressing complex humanities questions that require processing unstructured, high-dimensional data across temporal and spatial scales inaccessible to traditional analytical methods.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in theological and ministerial studies not elsewhere classified, including preparation for religious vocations in faiths other than Christianity and Judaism.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical gaps in the computational analysis of linguistic diversity across French dialects and creoles. While French is a globally distributed language, its regional variations—such as Metropolitan French, Canadian French, and African and Caribbean Creoles—exhibit complex phonological, syntactic, and lexical divergences that remain understudied at scale. Traditional methods struggle to process the vast, heterogeneous corpora required to model these variations, particularly when analyzing historical texts, contemporary spoken data, and sociolinguistic interactions. This research aims to develop a unified computational framework to systematically map linguistic features across space, time, and social contexts, enabling comparative analysis of dialectal evolution and creole formation. The project will employ natural language processing (NLP) techniques, including transformer-based models for morphosyntactic tagging and dialect identification, combined with phonetic alignment algorithms to trace sound shifts in historical recordings. Parallelized corpus construction pipelines will integrate digitized texts, speech datasets, and sociodemographic metadata, while machine learning classifiers will identify patterns of language contact and change. HPC resources are essential to train models on distributed datasets spanning multiple terabyte-scale archives, optimize hyperparameters for low-resource dialects, and run computationally intensive simulations of language variation. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of annotated linguistic features, predictive models of dialectal divergence, and tools to support endangered creole preservation efforts. By bridging computational linguistics with French philology, this work will advance scholarly understanding of language dynamics while providing practical resources for educators, policymakers, and technology developers working in multilingual Francophone contexts.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the French language and related dialects and creoles. Includes instruction in philology; Metropolitan French; Canadian French; African and Caribbean Creoles; dialects; and applications in business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing software verification and validation (V&V) for large-scale, distributed systems through the development of a novel computational framework that integrates formal methods with machine learning (ML). Traditional V&V techniques struggle with scalability and efficiency when applied to modern software systems characterized by concurrency, real-time constraints, and dynamic environments. To overcome these limitations, the proposed research will design parallel algorithms for model checking and runtime verification, augmented by ML-driven prioritization of critical code paths and fault scenarios. The framework will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable exhaustive exploration of state spaces, probabilistic analysis of failure modes, and training of neural networks for anomaly detection in system logs. Key computational methods include distributed symbolic execution, Monte Carlo simulations for reliability estimation, and graph-based representations of software behavior optimized for GPU acceleration. The project will validate the approach using case studies from cloud-based microservice architectures and embedded control systems, measuring metrics such as verification time, fault coverage, and false-positive rates. Successful outcomes will provide a scalable, open-source toolchain for rigorous software assurance, directly benefiting safety-critical domains like autonomous systems and cybersecurity. By combining formal rigor with data-driven adaptability, this work aims to advance computational methodologies in software engineering while demonstrating how HPC infrastructures can bridge gaps between theoretical verification and practical system complexity. Resource requests include GPU nodes for ML training, high-memory CPUs for symbolic analysis, and distributed storage for terabyte-scale trace datasets.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply scientific and mathematical principles to the design, analysis, verification, validation, implementation, and maintenance of computer software systems using a variety of computer languages. Includes instruction in discrete mathematics, probability and statistics, computer science, managerial science, and applications to complex computer systems.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the interdisciplinary study of molecular gastronomy, a field blending culinary arts, chemistry, and materials science to innovate food design and sensory experiences. While molecular gastronomy has transformative potential for culinary practices and consumer engagement, its computational modeling remains underdeveloped due to the complexity of multi-phase interactions (e.g., emulsions, gels, foams) and the lack of tailored simulation frameworks. Traditional experimental approaches are resource-intensive and limited in probing dynamic, non-equilibrium systems critical to achieving precise textures, flavors, and visual effects. This research aims to bridge this gap by developing a computational pipeline to simulate and optimize novel culinary processes, such as spherification or temperature-dependent gelation, at microscale resolutions. The project will employ hybrid numerical methods, combining lattice Boltzmann simulations for fluid dynamics, molecular dynamics for interfacial interactions, and machine learning to map parameter spaces (e.g., pH, ionic strength, shear rates) to sensory outcomes. By parallelizing these workflows across HPC architectures, the team will resolve time-dependent behaviors of hydrocolloids, proteins, and lipid assemblies under conditions mimicking real-world culinary environments. Anticipated outcomes include a validated open-source toolkit for predictive culinary material design, reducing trial-and-error experimentation in recipe development. The work will also establish quantitative correlations between molecular-scale phenomena and macroscopic sensory properties, offering foundational insights for personalized nutrition and sustainable food engineering. This project highlights the role of HPC in democratizing innovation for culinary professionals while positioning computational gastronomy as a benchmark for interdisciplinary research in non-traditional STEM domains.
cip_title: Culinary, Entertainment, and Personal Services, Other.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in culinary, entertainment, and personal services not listed above.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in the documentation and computational analysis of understudied Indigenous languages of the Americas, many of which are endangered and lack sufficient digital resources. Despite their linguistic complexity and cultural significance, these languages—spanning families such as Mayan, Uto-Aztecan, Andean-Equatorial, and others—remain underrepresented in computational linguistics due to limited accessible data and the challenges of modeling agglutinative morphosyntax, non-linear phonology, and oral literary traditions. The research will employ high-performance computing (HPC) to develop scalable natural language processing (NLP) tools tailored to these languages, enabling large-scale corpus analysis, automated morphological parsing, and cross-linguistic comparison. Key computational tasks include training transformer-based models on newly digitized texts and oral narratives, constructing phylogenetically informed language models to trace historical relationships, and simulating dialectal variations under shifting sociolinguistic conditions. The project will integrate interdisciplinary data, including legacy recordings, transcribed oral literatures, and community-generated materials, requiring parallel processing for alignment and annotation. Outcomes will include open-access computational lexicons, annotated multimedia corpora, and adaptive NLP pipelines designed in collaboration with Indigenous language stakeholders. These resources aim to support both academic research in typology and language revitalization initiatives, bridging computational methodologies with community-driven priorities. By leveraging HPC capabilities to handle sparse data and complex linguistic structures, this work advances equitable language technology development while contributing to the preservation of Indigenous knowledge systems.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: American Indian/ Native American Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics
cip_definition: A program that focuses on one or more of the languages native to the Western Hemisphere, with an emphasis on American Indian languages, but including other Native American languages. Includes instruction in philology; oral and written literatures; Inuit and Aleut languages; North American language families, including, but not limited to, Algonkian, Athabascan, Siouan, Muskogean, Iroquoian, Kumeyaay, Yuman, Mayan, Zapotecan, and Uto-Aztecan; South American language families, including, but not limited to, Andean-Equatorial, Ge-Pano-Carib, and Macro-Chibchan; and other minor languages.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the stability and transfer of heritable information in bacteriophage populations under environmental stress. While phage genomes are highly compact, their ability to rapidly acquire mutations or horizontally transferred genetic elements contributes to adaptability, yet the regulatory processes that balance genome stability with plasticity remain poorly understood. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will analyze large-scale genomic datasets from phage populations subjected to mutagenic conditions (e.g., UV exposure, chemical mutagens) to identify conserved regulatory motifs and mutation hotspots. Computational models will simulate the dynamics of DNA replication and repair processes under varying stress intensities, integrating empirical data on mutation rates, recombination frequency, and gene expression. These simulations will employ parallelized algorithms to track probabilistic outcomes of replication errors and repair pathway efficacy across millions of simulated generations. Additionally, network analysis tools will map interactions between phage-encoded stability factors (e.g., terminases, integrases) and host machinery to pinpoint evolutionary constraints on genome architecture. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework linking specific genetic elements to mutation tolerance, insights into selective pressures driving horizontal gene transfer in viral populations, and mechanistic explanations for stress-induced genomic instability. This work will advance foundational knowledge in molecular genetics by elucidating how phage genomes maintain functional integrity despite rapid evolution, with broader implications for understanding genetic adaptation in pathogenic viruses. The scale of genomic data and complexity of stochastic modeling necessitate HPC resources to achieve statistically robust, high-resolution analyses.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of genetic structures and mechanisms of organisms, including bacteria, phages, and viruses. Includes instruction in the replication, expression, transfer, structure, maintenance, and stability of heritable information in DNA, RNA, and proteins; the regulation of these processes; and neurogenetics.

abstract: This project seeks to advance pedagogy in Communication Arts and Literature education by investigating how large-scale computational analysis of multimodal classroom interactions can inform the design of equitable, adaptive teaching strategies. A critical challenge in teacher education lies in systematically evaluating how instructional techniques—such as discourse scaffolding, feedback methods, or culturally responsive dialogue—impact student engagement and competency development across diverse learning contexts. Traditional qualitative analyses of classroom data (e.g., discussion transcripts, writing portfolios, or speech recordings) are labor-intensive and limited in scale, hindering generalizable insights. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process and analyze multimodal educational datasets from K-12 and postsecondary classrooms. Natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will be developed to quantify patterns in student-teacher interactions, including syntactic complexity in written feedback, pragmatic features of oral communication, and semantic shifts in literary analysis tasks. Deep learning models will further examine nonverbal cues in video-recorded teaching simulations to correlate pedagogical gestures with learner outcomes. By parallelizing these workflows across GPU nodes, we aim to process over 10,000 hours of classroom data from statewide partnerships, enabling longitudinal comparisons of instructional efficacy. Outcomes will include (1) evidence-based frameworks for optimizing communication pedagogy across literacy, public speaking, and digital media domains; (2) open-source tools to help educators visualize interaction patterns and personalize instruction; and (3) scalable benchmarks for assessing equitable participation in discourse-heavy disciplines. This computational approach directly supports teacher candidates in refining practice through data-driven reflection, while advancing interdisciplinary innovation at the intersection of educational linguistics and computational social science.
cip_title: Communication Arts and Literature Teacher Education
cip_definition: A program of study that prepares individuals to teach oral expression, literature, and writing to students at various education levels. Includes instruction in interpersonal communication, intercultural communication, language learning, listening instructional techniques, public speaking, reading instructional techniques, writing instructional techniques, and practical teaching experience.

abstract: The integration of digital dentistry and CAD/CAM technologies has transformed dental diagnostics, treatment planning, and restorative workflows. However, challenges persist in optimizing the biomechanical performance and long-term durability of digitally designed dental restorations, particularly under dynamic occlusal forces and material fatigue. Current clinical workflows lack predictive computational models capable of simulating complex, patient-specific biomechanical interactions at scale, limiting the personalization and efficiency of CAD/CAM workflows. This project seeks to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop multiscale, data-driven simulations of dental restoration behavior. The research will employ finite element analysis (FEA) to model stress distribution in restorations across diverse anatomical geometries, coupled with machine learning algorithms trained on clinical datasets to predict material degradation and failure probabilities. Large-scale parametric studies will evaluate the performance of hybrid materials and novel lattice structures under simulated masticatory cycles. HPC resources are critical to process high-resolution 3D scans, execute parallelized simulations across thousands of material-geometry combinations, and analyze terabytes of biomechanical data. Expected outcomes include (1) validated computational frameworks for optimizing CAD/CAM restoration designs, (2) predictive models linking digital treatment planning parameters to clinical outcomes, and (3) open-source datasets correlating simulation results with longitudinal patient data. This work will advance personalized digital dentistry by enabling clinically actionable insights into restoration longevity, reducing iterative design cycles, and informing evidence-based material selection. The computational tools developed will be disseminated to dental researchers and clinicians, fostering innovation in digital treatment workflows while minimizing costly physical prototyping. By bridging computational engineering and clinical dentistry, this project aims to establish scalable methodologies for improving patient-specific restorative outcomes through data-driven digital workflows.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the use of digital and CAD/CAM technology in dental treatment. Includes instruction in digital diagnostic and treatment planning techniques, CAD/CAM restoration, and patient management.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the computational and neural mechanisms underlying real-time language comprehension, with a focus on how syntactic ambiguity resolution interacts with working memory constraints. A key challenge in psycholinguistics is modeling the dynamic interplay between probabilistic language processing and finite cognitive resources, particularly in naturalistic contexts. While behavioral and neuroimaging studies provide insights, existing computational models often oversimplify memory architecture or fail to scale to complex sentence structures. To address this gap, we propose developing a hybrid neural network framework integrating transformer-based language models with biologically plausible memory systems. The research will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to 1) train and fine-tune large language models on psycholinguistically annotated corpora, 2) simulate trial-level behavioral data (e.g., reading times, error patterns) across diverse syntactic constructions, and 3) perform Bayesian model comparison of alternative memory architectures. The computational models will be constrained by both behavioral datasets from self-paced reading experiments and existing fMRI data on memory-intensive language tasks. Resource-intensive components include parallelized parameter space exploration across memory decay rates and capacity limits, as well as Monte Carlo simulations assessing model fit robustness. Expected outcomes include a validated computational account of memory-language interactions, open-source tools for simulating resource-constrained language processing, and novel predictions about individual differences in sentence comprehension efficiency. This work will advance cognitive theories of language understanding while developing methods to bridge artificial neural network approaches with human cognitive modeling. The requested HPC allocation is critical given the need for simultaneous training of multiple model variants, large-scale synthetic data generation, and computationally intensive Bayesian inference over high-dimensional parameter spaces.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the mechanisms and processes of learning and thinking, and associated information encoding, decoding, processing and transmitting systems. Includes instruction in theories of cognition and intelligence; studies of cognitive processes such as memory, sensation, perception, pattern recognition, problem solving, and conceptual thinking; cybernetics; psycholinguistics; and the study of biological and social communications mechanisms and processes.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing dynamic stage environments in live theatrical performances through advanced computational modeling and simulation. Traditional stagecraft methods often rely on static designs and manual adjustments, which limit responsiveness to real-time variables such as actor movements, audience perspectives, and acoustic interactions. To overcome these constraints, we propose the development of a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework that simulates multidimensional stage dynamics, including spatial acoustics, lighting propagation, and audience sightline analysis. By integrating real-time motion capture data with physics-based models, the system will predict and visualize how adjustments to set configurations, actor blocking, or technical elements (e.g., movable platforms, reflective surfaces) affect performance quality across diverse venue geometries. The computational pipeline will employ parallelized ray-tracing algorithms for acoustic and optical simulations, coupled with machine learning models trained on historical performance data to recommend adaptive design solutions. This approach requires significant HPC resources due to the need for high-resolution, low-latency simulations across variable parameters, including 3D spatial meshes of theater architectures and time-series analyses of performer trajectories. Expected outcomes include a suite of open-source tools for theater practitioners to prototype and test stage designs virtually, reducing reliance on physical mock-ups and enabling data-driven artistic decisions. The project will validate these tools through case studies with regional theater partners, measuring impacts on production efficiency and audience immersion metrics. By bridging computational innovation with theatrical practice, this work aims to expand the creative possibilities of stagecraft while establishing a methodological framework for computational research in performance-based disciplines.
detailed_field: Dance, drama, theatre arts, and stagecraft
cip_title: Dramatic/ Theatre Arts and Stagecraft, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in dramatic/theatre arts and stagecraft, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in Consultation-Liaison (CL) Psychiatry by modeling the bidirectional interactions between psychiatric symptoms and complex medical illnesses. A critical challenge in this field is the lack of predictive frameworks that integrate dynamic, multimodal clinical data—including electronic health records (EHRs), neuroimaging, and biomarkers—to identify patients at highest risk of psychiatric complications during medical treatment or to optimize psychopharmacological interventions in medically vulnerable populations. To address this, we propose developing computational models using machine learning (ML) and network analysis to analyze longitudinal datasets from 5,000+ patients with comorbid psychiatric and medical conditions (e.g., cancer, autoimmune disorders, post-transplant care). Key computational tasks include natural language processing (NLP) of unstructured clinical notes to extract psychiatric symptom trajectories, federated learning across multi-institutional EHRs to preserve privacy, and Bayesian network modeling to infer causal pathways linking inflammatory markers, medication regimens, and neuropsychiatric outcomes. HPC resources are essential for training deep learning architectures on high-dimensional neuroimaging data (e.g., fMRI to assess delirium risk post-surgery) and for running large-scale simulations of intervention scenarios. Expected outcomes include validated predictive algorithms for depression exacerbation in oncology patients and delirium prevention protocols in critical care, both prioritized for real-world clinical integration. By quantifying how psychiatric and medical factors interact over time, this work aims to generate scalable tools for personalized intervention, reducing hospital readmissions and improving quality of life in medically complex populations. The computational pipelines developed will also serve as a template for future studies at the intersection of psychiatry and systemic medical illness, a domain underrepresented in precision medicine research.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis and treatment of psychiatric disorders and symptoms in complex medically ill patients. This includes treatment of patients with acute or chronic medical, neurological, obstetrical, or surgical illness in which psychiatric illness is affecting their medical care and/or quality of life, and patients who have a psychiatric disorder that is the direct consequence of a primary medical condition, a somatoform disorder, or psychological factors affecting a general medical condition.

abstract: The increasing complexity of manufacturing systems demands advanced computational tools to optimize process efficiency, material utilization, and energy consumption in production environments. This project seeks to address critical bottlenecks in computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) workflows by developing high-fidelity simulations of multi-axis machining processes and additive manufacturing systems. Traditional experimental approaches to parameter optimization are time-intensive and cost-prohibitive, particularly when scaling to industrial production volumes. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, this research will implement parallelized finite element analysis (FEA) models to predict tool wear, thermal distortion, and residual stresses in subtractive manufacturing operations. Concurrently, lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) simulations will be deployed to analyze powder bed dynamics and melt pool behavior in metal additive manufacturing. These computational models will integrate machine learning algorithms trained on heterogeneous datasets—including sensor data from CNC machines and in-process monitoring systems—to enable real-time adaptive control predictions. The proposed workflows require distributed memory architectures to manage large-scale meshing operations and transient multiphysics simulations with microsecond temporal resolution. Anticipated outcomes include validated predictive frameworks for minimizing material waste in machining operations, optimizing energy-efficient laser sintering parameters, and reducing post-processing requirements for hybrid manufacturing systems. By bridging gaps between simulation fidelity and practical deployability, this work aims to advance digital twin capabilities for small-to-medium manufacturing enterprises, directly supporting the program’s focus on accessible engineering solutions. The requested computing resources will enable parametric studies at unprecedented scales, reducing reliance on physical prototyping while providing students with hands-on experience in HPC-driven manufacturing research.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills to the identification and resolution of production problems in the manufacture of products. Includes instruction in machine operations, production line operations, engineering analysis, systems analysis, instrumentation, physical controls, automation, computer-aided manufacturing (CAM), manufacturing planning, quality control, and informational infrastructure.

abstract: The increasing complexity of gastrointestinal and hepatic diseases, such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), necessitates advanced computational approaches to integrate multi-dimensional data for personalized treatment strategies. Current clinical models often fail to account for the interplay between genomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and longitudinal clinical data, limiting their predictive accuracy. This project seeks to address these limitations by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and validate machine learning algorithms capable of synthesizing heterogeneous datasets. We will aggregate and preprocess multi-omics data from cohorts of patients with NAFLD, HCV-related cirrhosis, and IBD, alongside electronic health records encompassing imaging, histopathology, and treatment outcomes. Deep learning architectures, including transformer-based models and graph neural networks, will be trained to identify predictive biomarkers, stratify disease subtypes, and forecast progression to complications such as hepatocellular carcinoma or treatment-resistant flares. Computational workflows will be optimized for parallel processing on HPC clusters to handle the scale of data (>100 TB) and the complexity of models requiring millions of parameters. The anticipated outcomes include the creation of open-source predictive tools validated against prospective clinical data, novel insights into molecular drivers of disease heterogeneity, and a framework for real-time decision support in clinical workflows. By enabling the analysis of previously intractable datasets, this research aims to advance precision medicine in gastroenterology and hepatology, ultimately improving risk stratification and therapeutic targeting for complex digestive diseases.
cip_definition: Research focused on Gastroenterology and Hepatology

abstract: This project seeks to develop a predictive modeling framework to optimize care delivery workflows and reduce adverse patient outcomes in settings reliant on nursing assistants and patient care aides. Nursing aides are critical frontline providers in long-term and acute care facilities, yet high patient-to-staff ratios, time-sensitive tasks, and variability in patient deterioration patterns create challenges in prioritizing care. Current protocols often rely on static schedules or reactive interventions, which may delay response to emerging risks such as falls, pressure injuries, or sepsis. To address this, we propose a machine learning approach leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multimodal patient data—including electronic health records, real-time vital signs, and mobility metrics—to dynamically predict patient risk states and recommend task prioritization. A hybrid neural network architecture will integrate temporal (e.g., hourly vital trends) and contextual (e.g., medication schedules, mobility limitations) data streams, trained on retrospective datasets from partnered healthcare facilities. HPC resources are essential to process terabytes of heterogeneous data, optimize hyperparameters across parallelized simulations, and validate models against diverse clinical scenarios through in silico trials. Expected outcomes include a real-time decision support tool that identifies high-risk patients and suggests context-aware task sequences for nursing aides, balancing acuity needs with workflow efficiency. Successful implementation could reduce preventable adverse events by 15–25% in pilot facilities while providing empirical insights into workload distribution patterns. This work directly aligns with nursing science priorities to enhance auxiliary staff effectiveness through scalable computational tools, ultimately improving patient safety in resource-constrained environments.
cip_title: Nursing Assistant/ Aide and Patient Care Assistant/ Aide
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to perform routine nursing-related services to patients in hospitals or long-term care facilities, under the training and supervision of a registered nurse or licensed practical nurse.

abstract: Preventive medicine aims to reduce disease burden through early intervention, yet a critical gap remains in leveraging large-scale, multidimensional health data to predict risk and optimize prevention strategies at the population level. This project proposes to develop a computational framework integrating electronic health records (EHRs), genomic data, and environmental exposures to model disease trajectories and evaluate targeted interventions for cardiovascular disease (CVD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) in diverse populations. Current approaches struggle with the computational demands of analyzing heterogeneous datasets spanning millions of patients, hundreds of genetic loci, and time-varying environmental factors while accounting for complex interactions. We will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement parallelized machine learning pipelines for risk prediction, including ensemble methods and neural networks optimized for sparse, longitudinal EHR data. Agent-based modeling will simulate population health outcomes under different prevention scenarios, requiring iterative parameter sweeps across demographic and socioeconomic variables. A key innovation involves federated learning architectures to process distributed EHR data across multiple health systems without compromising patient privacy. The computational workflow will utilize GPU-accelerated nodes for deep learning tasks and high-memory CPU nodes for genome-wide association studies (GWAS) integrating polygenic risk scores with clinical variables. Expected outcomes include (1) validated predictive models with improved accuracy for CVD/T2D onset, (2) scalable tools for simulating intervention impacts across subpopulations, and (3) open-source software enabling resource-efficient analysis of preventive strategies in real-world settings. By addressing computational bottlenecks in handling multimodal health data, this work will advance evidence-based prevention paradigms and provide a template for data-driven public health decision-making.
cip_definition: Research focused on Preventive Medicine

abstract: The human gut microbiome is a critical mediator of dietary effects on host physiology, yet the mechanisms underlying diet-microbiome-host interactions in metabolic dysfunction remain poorly understood. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a multiscale, systems-level model integrating microbial metagenomic, metabolomic, and host physiological data to predict how specific dietary components modulate microbiome dynamics and contribute to metabolic outcomes in obesity-related disorders. Current limitations in modeling these interactions stem from the combinatorial complexity of dietary inputs, strain-specific microbial metabolic networks, and nonlinear host responses, necessitating computational approaches capable of handling high-dimensional data and stochastic simulations. We propose a hybrid pipeline combining genome-scale metabolic reconstruction of 500+ gut microbial taxa, Bayesian inference of metabolite exchange networks, and agent-based modeling of spatially resolved microbial communities under varying nutrient conditions. HPC resources will enable parallelized flux balance analysis across microbial genomes, Monte Carlo sampling of community metabolic states, and integration of host liver-adipose tissue crosstalk using ordinary differential equation systems. Validation will utilize longitudinal multi-omics datasets from clinical cohorts with varying dietary interventions. Expected outcomes include identification of keystone microbial taxa driving diet-induced metabolic inflammation, predictive algorithms linking fiber-fatty acid ratios to microbiome stability, and a publicly accessible computational toolkit for simulating personalized diet-microbiome interactions. This work bridges nutritional biochemistry, computational ecology, and systems biology to address critical gaps in designing microbiota-targeted dietary therapies, with potential applications in precision nutrition for metabolic syndrome and obesity comorbidities. The scale of combinatorial simulations—encompassing ~10^6 microbial community configurations and host metabolic states—exceeds the capacity of standard computing infrastructure, underscoring the necessity of HPC allocation.
cip_definition: A scientific program that focuses on the utilization of food for human growth and metabolism, in both normal and dysfunctional states, from the interdisciplinary perspective of the agricultural, human, biological, and biomedical sciences. Includes instruction in food science, biochemistry, physiology, dietetics, food and nutrition studies, biotechnology, biophysics, and the clinical sciences.

abstract: The optimization of bioprocesses for sustainable biomanufacturing remains a critical challenge in biotechnology, particularly in scaling microbial fermentation and protein synthesis for industrial applications. Traditional experimental approaches are limited by the high dimensionality of biological systems, which involve complex interactions between genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors. This project proposes an integrative computational framework to model and optimize microbial strain performance, enzyme kinetics, and bioreactor dynamics using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Leveraging genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs), molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and machine learning (ML), we will analyze multi-omics datasets to predict strain engineering targets for enhanced product yields in antibiotic synthesis and recombinant protein expression. MD simulations will elucidate structural dynamics of key enzymes in cellulose degradation and protein folding, informing rational design of thermostable variants. Concurrently, agent-based modeling will simulate microbial population behavior under varying bioreactor conditions to identify optimal nutrient delivery and aeration strategies. The computational pipeline will require parallelized workflows for large-scale parameter sweeps and ensemble simulations, necessitating GPU-accelerated nodes and high-memory resources. Expected outcomes include predictive models for strain optimization, validated via experimental collaborator data, and open-source tools for simulating bioprocess scalability. This work will advance precision biomanufacturing by reducing trial-and-error experimentation, accelerating the translation of lab-scale discoveries to industrial production. The resource allocation will directly support the development of scalable, energy-efficient biotechnologies with applications in pharmaceutical development, biofuel synthesis, and circular bioeconomy initiatives.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply scientific principles and technical skills in support of biologists and biotechnologists in research, industrial, and government settings. Includes instruction in fermentation technology, cell culturing, protein purification, biologic synthesis, assaying and testing, quality control, industrial microbiology, bioprocessing, chromatography and bioseparation, genetic technology, laboratory and hazardous materials safety, and computer applications.

abstract: The integration of advanced computational methods with physical science research is critical to overcoming limitations in simulating multi-scale phenomena inherent to next-generation materials and processes. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the dynamic behavior of metastable materials under extreme thermodynamic conditions, a problem currently constrained by the computational intensity of tracking atomic interactions across experimentally relevant timescales. The research will employ hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations, enhanced by machine learning-driven force fields, to model phase transitions and defect propagation in high-entropy alloys and glassy systems. These methods require parallelized computation across thousands of cores to handle the iterative optimization of interatomic potentials and the statistical sampling of rare events. By coupling adaptive sampling algorithms with GPU-accelerated MD frameworks, the project aims to achieve microsecond-scale simulations at near-ab initio accuracy, enabling the prediction of material failure mechanisms and stability thresholds. The outcomes will directly inform the design of alloys with tailored mechanical properties for aerospace and energy applications, reducing reliance on costly trial-and-error experimentation. Furthermore, the development of open-source workflow tools for automated parameter calibration and uncertainty quantification will enhance reproducibility in computational materials science. The scale of data generated—anticipated to exceed 500 TB of trajectory and metadata—necessitates distributed storage and in-situ analysis capabilities provided by HPC infrastructure. This work bridges gaps between atomistic modeling and industrial material testing, advancing the foundational role of computational science in physical technology innovation. Successful execution will establish scalable protocols for simulating non-equilibrium systems, with broader implications for catalysis, nanotechnology, and quantum material discovery.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in physical science technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the emergent dynamics of decentralized workforce ecosystems, a novel interdisciplinary area intersecting organizational behavior, computational social science, and network theory. Traditional human resources frameworks struggle to model the complexity of modern, fluid work structures—such as hybrid gig-platform hybrids, AI-augmented teams, and blockchain-governed decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs)—where decision-making, incentives, and communication channels operate non-hierarchically. The research problem centers on developing predictive models to quantify resilience and productivity trade-offs in these systems, which exhibit nonlinear interactions at scale. Using agent-based modeling (ABM) and multilayer network analysis, we will simulate workforce ecosystems under varying conditions, including dynamic resource allocation, stochastic task arrival rates, and heterogeneous agent strategies. Computational experiments will integrate real-world HR datasets (e.g., platform worker performance metrics, collaboration tool metadata) with synthetic agents representing human and AI actors. The HPC environment is critical for parallelizing simulations across thousands of parameter combinations while maintaining temporal granularity in interaction tracking. Expected outcomes include (1) a taxonomy of failure modes in decentralized work structures, (2) adaptive resource allocation algorithms optimized for stability in volatile environments, and (3) metrics quantifying the "coordination entropy" of hybrid human-AI teams. Results will advance strategic HR practices for organizations adopting Web3 and AI-driven work models, while contributing methodological innovations in computational organizational science. The project’s scale—encompassing ~10^6 agent simulations with real-time adaptation mechanisms—necessitates dedicated GPU-accelerated nodes and distributed memory architectures to achieve practical runtime for sensitivity analyses.
cip_title: Human Resources Management and Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in human resources management, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop an adaptive framework for optimizing heterogeneous computing resources in dynamic industrial IoT environments, where traditional system analysis methods struggle to balance real-time operational demands with evolving computational workloads. Industrial automation increasingly relies on edge-to-cloud infrastructures that integrate legacy operational technology (OT) with modern IT systems, creating unpredictable latency spikes, resource contention, and inefficiencies in data processing pipelines. The research will employ agent-based simulation models to map multi-layered workflows across hybrid architectures, coupling digital twin representations of physical systems with reinforcement learning algorithms to autonomously allocate computational tasks. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for scaling these simulations to realistic industrial scenarios involving 10,000+ concurrent edge devices, distributed analytics nodes, and time-sensitive control loops. The computational approach will iteratively train resource allocation policies under simulated stress conditions—including equipment failures, network partitioning, and abrupt load shifts—while preserving backward compatibility with legacy supervisory control systems. Outcomes will include a toolkit for dynamically provisioning containerized services across heterogeneous hardware, validated through case studies in smart manufacturing and energy grid management. This work bridges gaps between systems analysis methodologies and emergent cyber-physical computing paradigms, offering empirically tested strategies to reduce operational latency by 30–50% in pilot deployments while maintaining legacy system interoperability. The resulting models will advance predictive resource allocation in environments where traditional static provisioning fails, directly supporting the integration of AI-driven analytics into industrial ecosystems without requiring full infrastructure overhauls.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply programming and systems analysis principles to the selection, implementation, and troubleshooting of customized computer and software installations across the life cycle. Includes instruction in computer hardware and software; compilation, composition, execution, and operating systems; low- and high-level languages and language programming; programming and debugging techniques; installation and maintenance testing and documentation; process and data flow analysis; user needs analysis and documentation; cost-benefit analysis; and specification design.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for modeling emergent behavioral patterns in decentralized digital communication networks, a nascent interdisciplinary domain intersecting social dynamics, information diffusion, and computational social science. The research problem centers on understanding how non-hierarchical, large-scale digital interactions—such as those in federated social platforms or encrypted messaging ecosystems—reshape collective decision-making processes, trust formation, and conflict resolution. Traditional social science methodologies struggle to capture the multi-scale temporal dynamics and nonlinear feedback loops inherent in these systems, necessitating advanced computational approaches. The project will employ agent-based modeling (ABM) enhanced by graph neural networks (GNNs) to simulate interaction networks with up to 10^6 nodes, integrating empirical data from anonymized metadata trails to parameterize agents’ behavioral rules. A novel hybrid architecture will combine discrete-event simulation for micro-level interactions with continuous-time network evolution models, requiring high-performance computing (HPC) resources for parallelized scenario testing and sensitivity analyses. Computational challenges include optimizing memory allocation for sparse adjacency matrices in dynamically rewiring networks and implementing adaptive sampling techniques to reduce stochastic uncertainty in ABM outputs. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated open-source toolkit for simulating decentralized social systems, (2) quantitative metrics for resilience to misinformation cascades in non-modular communication topologies, and (3) evidence-based insights into emergent governance structures in digital communities. The work advances social science methodology by formalizing computational techniques to study systems that lack centralized authority—a critical gap as traditional institutional frameworks are increasingly supplemented or supplanted by distributed digital networks. Resource requests focus on GPU-accelerated nodes for GNN training cycles and high-memory nodes for network persistence across long-duration simulations.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the design of research studies, measurement of variables, data analysis, and formulation of models. Includes instruction in experimental, quasi-experimental, and case study methods; historical research; participant observation; questionnaire design; sampling theory; and statistical methods.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the long-term evolution of political decision-making patterns and their relationship to historical crises through the computational analysis of multi-century, cross-regional archival datasets. Combining methods from computational history, network science, and political institutionalism, we propose to analyze structured records of legislative votes, treaty formations, and policy responses to environmental/economic shocks across three geopolitical regions (Europe, Southeast Asia, and South America) from 1600–1950. The central research problem addresses how path dependencies in governance systems emerge from crisis responses, and whether these patterns exhibit measurable similarities across distinct cultural-historical contexts. Current manual historiography struggles to systematically compare such complex, longitudinal processes, particularly when analyzing interactions between formal institutions and informal power networks. Our computational approach employs transformer-based language models fine-tuned on multilingual historical documents to extract structured event data, coupled with temporal network analysis to model institutional relationships. Key innovations include the development of a novel graph neural network architecture capable of processing temporally discontinuous historical records and a counterfactual simulation framework for testing institutional resilience hypotheses. The project requires high-performance computing resources to manage three core challenges: 1) processing over 15 million pages of digitized primary sources across six languages, 2) training multi-modal models that integrate textual, spatial, and socioeconomic data, and 3) running ensemble simulations of political system evolution under varying historical constraints. Expected outcomes include an open-access knowledge graph tracing institutional adaptations across case studies, quantitative frameworks for assessing historical contingency in political development, and methodological advances in computational historical analysis. This work aims to provide policymakers and historians with new analytical tools for understanding the systemic impacts of crisis responses while establishing computational social science infrastructure for transhistorical comparative research.
cip_definition: A program with a general synthesis of history and political science or a specialization which draws from history and political science. Includes instruction in comparative government and politics, historiography, historical research methods, political science, political theory, records administration, and systematic study of political institutions and behavior.

abstract: This project seeks to address the critical challenge of optimizing patient-specific prosthetic implants for maxillofacial reconstruction, where anatomical complexity and biomechanical heterogeneity often lead to suboptimal functional outcomes and implant failure. Current generic or semi-custom designs inadequately account for dynamic load distributions, micro-motion at bone-implant interfaces, and site-specific tissue remodeling, contributing to complications such as aseptic loosening and stress shielding. To overcome these limitations, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework integrating multiscale biomechanical modeling, topology optimization, and machine learning to generate patient-adaptive implant designs. High-resolution CT/MRI data will inform 3D finite element models simulating mastication, speech, and parafunctional loading scenarios. HPC resources will enable iterative topology optimization algorithms to minimize stress concentrations while preserving porosity for osseointegration, constrained by manufacturability criteria. Concurrently, neural networks trained on retrospective clinical datasets will predict site-specific bone remodeling patterns to iteratively refine implant geometry. Validations will include computational benchmarking against existing designs and in silico trials across a virtual cohort representing diverse craniofacial morphologies. Expected outcomes include a scalable pipeline for generating mechanically robust, biologically integrated implants, reducing revision surgeries by an estimated 30-40% in complex cases. This interdisciplinary approach bridges computational mechanics, materials science, and clinical surgery, offering a paradigm shift toward precision rehabilitation of maxillofacial defects. The requested HPC allocation will support the intensive computational demands of parallelized simulations, optimization loops, and large-scale data synthesis, which exceed the capacity of local institutional clusters. Successful implementation will advance both clinical care and foundational knowledge of bone-implant interactions in dynamic biomechanical environments.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the advanced study of the diagnosis and intrusive and adjunctive treatment of diseases, injuries, and defects of the oral and maxillofacial regions, including functional and aesthetic aspects. Includes instruction in pharmacology, analgesia, anesthesia, anxiety control, surgical procedures and techniques, surgical instrumentation, exodontia, oral diseases and malfunctions, soft and hard tissue pathology, dentoalveolar surgery, infection management, and prosthetic implantation.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the evolution of transnational cultural flows and identity formation across Europe from the early modern period to the present, with a focus on underrepresented communities and intersectional identities. The research problem centers on gaps in understanding how localized cultural practices—mediated through texts, visual media, and oral histories—intersected with broader European colonial and migratory contexts, particularly in marginalized groups such as diasporic communities, women, and hybrid cultural networks. Current scholarship often relies on fragmented qualitative analyses, limiting systematic exploration of large, multilingual corpora and multimodal sources. To address this, the project proposes a computational humanities approach leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Machine learning models, including transformer-based architectures, will be trained to analyze semantic patterns in digitized texts (e.g., pamphlets, personal correspondence) across six languages, while computer vision techniques will classify iconographic motifs in art and material culture from archival collections. Network analysis will map the diffusion of cultural symbols and narratives across time and space, incorporating geospatial data from migration records. HPC capabilities are critical for processing terabytes of heterogeneous data, running parallelized NLP pipelines, and training multimodal models that integrate textual, visual, and spatial features. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible knowledge graph tracing cultural exchange pathways, quantitative frameworks for assessing hybridity in cultural production, and visualizations of gendered or ethnically coded symbolic repertoires. By computationally bridging micro-level cultural practices with macro-historical trends, this work aims to advance interdisciplinary methodologies in European cultural studies while centering marginalized voices in narratives of European identity. The resource request supports GPU-intensive model training, large-scale database integration, and iterative simulation of cultural transmission dynamics across 400 years.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples of the European Continent, including the study of European migration patterns and colonial empires.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational workflows to address the growing demands of high-resolution, real-time media processing in photographic and film/video production. Current workflows struggle to efficiently manage ultra-high-definition (8K+) video streams, multi-camera synthetic environments, and AI-driven postproduction tasks, which require rapid processing of large datasets. The research problem centers on overcoming latency, storage bottlenecks, and computational limitations that hinder creative flexibility and technical precision in time-sensitive production environments. To address this, the project proposes leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to parallelize and optimize three core processes: (1) real-time rendering of complex visual effects (VFX) using GPU-accelerated ray tracing, (2) machine learning (ML)-based restoration of archival film via neural networks trained on degraded/restored frame pairs, and (3) dynamic simulation of virtual production environments for previsualization. Computational methods will include distributed processing of raw video data across nodes, in-memory caching for frame-sequential tasks, and hybrid CPU/GPU pipelines for ML inference. The project will utilize containerized workflows to ensure compatibility with industry-standard software (e.g., DaVinci Resolve, Unreal Engine). Expected outcomes include a scalable framework for processing 8K footage at sub-frame latency, a publicly accessible dataset of film degradation patterns paired with ML restoration models, and performance benchmarks for virtual production simulations. This work will directly enhance pedagogical resources by enabling student-led research in computational cinematography while providing industry practitioners with open-source tools to reduce postproduction timelines. The requested HPC allocation is critical to handling petascale visual data and achieving the fine-grained parallelism required for these computationally intensive tasks, which cannot feasibly be executed on local workstations.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to the operation and maintenance of camera and lighting equipment and the production of finished still, video, and film products under the supervision of photographers, directors, and editors. Includes instruction in equipment setup and maintenance; lighting; power supplies; studio and film set tasks such as camera operator, grip, and best boy; plate and negative handling and development; laboratory procedures; and digital software applications.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying dysregulated endocrine signaling in livestock species, a critical contributor to metabolic disorders that impact animal health and agricultural productivity. Despite advances in veterinary pathophysiology, the dynamic interplay between hormone receptors, intracellular signaling cascades, and genetic variability in non-model species remains poorly characterized. We propose a multi-scale computational approach integrating molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, machine learning (ML)-enabled genomic variant analysis, and agent-based modeling of tissue-level hormonal responses. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to simulate hormone-receptor binding kinetics across experimentally derived conformational states (µs-ms timescales), train deep neural networks on multi-omics datasets from bovine and porcine models, and parameterize 3D organoid-scale models of adrenal and pancreatic tissues. The MD simulations will leverage GPU-optimized workflows to resolve residue-specific interactions in glucocorticoid and insulin receptor variants linked to disease phenotypes. Concurrently, ML models will identify regulatory elements in 45 newly sequenced genomes from stress-resistant livestock populations. By coupling these outputs, we aim to predict how genetic diversity modulates endocrine resilience under metabolic stress. This work will generate the first open-access computational framework for species-specific endocrine modeling in veterinary physiology, directly informing targeted breeding strategies and therapeutic interventions. The requested resources will enable processing of ~800 TB of genomic and structural biology data, execution of >10^6 simulation replicates, and validation against in vivo electrophysiology datasets. Outcomes are expected to advance precision veterinary medicine while providing foundational tools to bridge molecular physiology and clinical applications in agricultural species.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the functional dynamics of animal biological systems and their relationship to the diagnosis and treatment of disease and injury. Includes instruction in mammalian and non-mammalian physiology, laboratory physiology, physiological responses to the environment, endocrinology, animal biotechnology, mechanisms of hormone action, organ systems, metabolism, and pathophysiology.

abstract: Cancer treatment optimization remains a critical challenge in oncology pharmacy due to tumor heterogeneity, dynamic drug resistance mechanisms, and the narrow therapeutic indices of many chemotherapies. Current approaches to personalizing drug regimens often rely on static genomic or clinical parameters, which inadequately capture the complex, time-dependent interactions between tumor evolution, drug pharmacokinetics-pharmacodynamics (PK/PD), and patient-specific factors. This project proposes to develop a computational framework integrating multi-scale modeling and machine learning to predict optimal drug dosing schedules and combinations for individual patients. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to support large-scale simulations of tumor growth dynamics under varying drug exposures, parameterized by clinical genomic data, electronic health records, and in vitro drug response assays from a retrospective cohort of 1,200 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer. A systems pharmacology model will couple ordinary differential equation-based representations of intracellular signaling pathways (e.g., EGFR, VEGF) with spatial agent-based models of tumor-immune ecosystem interactions. Bayesian neural networks will then be trained on simulation outputs to infer patient-specific adaptive dosing policies that balance efficacy and toxicity. Molecular dynamics simulations of drug-protein binding affinities, enabled by GPU-accelerated nodes, will further refine predictions for patients with rare resistance mutations. The computational pipeline will be validated against prospective clinical outcomes from an institutional phase II trial evaluating adaptive capecitabine/bevacizumab regimens. Successful implementation will yield a predictive tool to dynamically optimize oncology drug regimens, potentially reducing adverse events by 20-30% while maintaining therapeutic efficacy. This resource will be disseminated as open-source software to enable precision dosing trials across cancer types, addressing an urgent need in clinical oncology pharmacy practice.
cip_definition: Research focused on oncology pharmacy.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the application of machine learning and large-scale data analytics in optimizing behavioral interventions for individuals with developmental disabilities and autism. Applied behavior analysis (ABA) relies on the systematic analysis of behavioral patterns to design personalized interventions, yet existing methods for processing multidimensional datasets—including longitudinal behavioral assessments, sensor-based activity logs, and video-coded social interactions—are constrained by computational limitations. Current tools struggle to efficiently model complex, time-varying relationships between interventions, environmental factors, and behavioral outcomes, particularly when scaling to heterogeneous populations. This project proposes a computational framework integrating reinforcement learning, network analysis, and agent-based modeling to simulate and predict intervention efficacy across diverse behavioral contexts. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of high-resolution behavioral datasets (e.g., eye-tracking, vocalization patterns) and large-scale Monte Carlo simulations to identify optimal intervention parameters under varying conditions. Key objectives include developing predictive models of skill acquisition trajectories, automating the detection of critical behavioral transition points, and quantifying the impact of environmental variables on intervention outcomes. The computational pipeline will incorporate multi-agent simulations to model social dynamics in group-based ABA settings, coupled with natural language processing to analyze qualitative data from therapist notes and caregiver reports. Outcomes will provide empirically validated guidelines for dynamically adapting interventions based on real-time data streams, reducing the latency between behavioral assessment and intervention adjustment. This work will directly address scalability challenges in ABA by producing open-source tools for resource-constrained clinical settings, ultimately enhancing the precision and accessibility of behavior-analytic services. The requested resources will support GPU-accelerated model training, distributed storage for multi-institutional datasets, and high-throughput processing of real-world behavioral data, enabling translational advances at the intersection of computational science and applied psychology.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of principles of learning and behavior to enhance the development, abilities, and choices of children and adults; and that prepares individuals to address the behavioral needs of individuals, especially those with developmental disabilities and autism. Includes instruction in behavior analysis and learning, behavioral and functional assessment, developmental psychology, applied behavioral analysis in developmental disabilities and autism, applied behavioral analysis in mental health and aging, research methods, evaluation of interventions, and professional and ethical issues.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing injury prevention strategies in athletic training by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model the complex interplay between biomechanical stress, recovery protocols, and individualized physiological thresholds. Current approaches to injury mitigation often rely on generalized guidelines, which fail to account for the high variability in athletes’ musculoskeletal resilience, movement patterns, and adaptive capacities. To bridge this gap, we propose a computational framework that integrates motion capture data, wearable sensor outputs, and physiological biomarkers to simulate tissue-level stress accumulation across diverse athlete populations. Using finite element analysis and agent-based modeling, the project will simulate thousands of training scenarios to identify critical thresholds for overuse injuries—such as tendinopathies or stress fractures—under varying training loads and recovery intervals. Machine learning algorithms will be employed to classify risk profiles and recommend personalized adjustments to technique, workload, and recovery practices. The HPC environment is essential for processing high-dimensional datasets in real time and running computationally intensive multiscale models that link macro-level movement dynamics to micro-level tissue responses.
