Expected outcomes include a scalable predictive tool for coaches and sports medicine practitioners to tailor injury prevention programs, reducing downtime and enhancing long-term athlete performance. By advancing the integration of computational modeling into sports science, this work aims to establish a paradigm shift from reactive to proactive injury management, with implications for both elite athletics and community-level physical education programs.
detailed_field: Parks, recreation, leisure, fitness, and sport studies and management
cip_title: Sports, Kinesiology, and Physical Education/ Fitness, General
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on activities and principles that promote physical fitness, achieve and maintain athletic prowess, and accomplish related research and service goals. Includes instruction in human movement studies, motivation studies, rules and practice of specific sports, exercise and fitness principles and techniques, basic athletic injury prevention and treatment, and organizing and leading fitness and sports programs.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize quality control (QC) protocols in manufacturing processes through high-fidelity simulations of production systems and defect analysis. Traditional QC methods often rely on manual inspections or localized statistical sampling, which can miss subtle anomalies in complex, high-throughput manufacturing environments. To address this gap, we propose integrating sensor-derived production data with physics-based models of material behavior and machine learning (ML) techniques to predict defect formation in real time. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate multi-stage manufacturing workflows under diverse operating conditions, including thermal, mechanical, and environmental stressors. Key computational tasks include finite element analysis of component deformation, Monte Carlo simulations of process variability, and training ML classifiers to correlate sensor patterns with defect probabilities. By parallelizing these workflows, we aim to identify critical control points where minor adjustments could prevent cascading quality failures. The outcomes will include an open-source toolkit for QC process optimization, validated against experimental data from partner manufacturing facilities. This work is expected to reduce waste in production systems by 15–30%, improve compliance with international quality standards, and provide a scalable computational model for adaptive QC systems in industries ranging from automotive parts to construction materials. Access to HPC resources is essential to manage the computational intensity of coupled multi-physics simulations and the large-scale data integration required for robust ML training. The project aligns with the Engineering Technologies field by advancing applied computational methods to enhance real-world quality assurance practices.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and other professionals engaged in maintaining consistent manufacturing and construction standards. Includes instruction in quality control systems management principles, technical standards applicable to specific engineering and manufacturing projects, testing procedures, inspection procedures, related instrumentation and equipment operation and maintenance, and report preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical challenges in solar energy system optimization by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model and simulate advanced photovoltaic (PV) materials and thermal energy storage configurations. Despite the rapid growth of solar technologies, inefficiencies in energy conversion and storage persist due to material limitations, interfacial losses, and dynamic environmental conditions. Current experimental approaches struggle to resolve these multiscale, nonlinear interactions efficiently, necessitating computational methods to accelerate discovery. The research will employ atomistic simulations to investigate defect dynamics and charge transport in emerging perovskite-silicon tandem PV materials, using density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamics (MD) to predict stability and performance under operational stressors. Concurrently, finite element analysis (FEA) will model phase-change materials in thermal storage systems, optimizing heat transfer fluid pathways and evaluating degradation mechanisms under cyclic loading. Machine learning models trained on simulation datasets will identify correlations between material properties, system geometries, and long-term efficiency. By integrating these approaches, the project aims to establish predictive frameworks for designing durable, high-efficiency solar energy systems tailored to regional climatic conditions. The requested HPC resources will enable large-scale parallel computations, reducing simulation timescales from months to days while maintaining the resolution required to capture nanoscale phenomena and system-level dynamics. Expected outcomes include validated models for accelerated material screening, prototype designs for improved thermal storage integration, and open-source tools to guide solar system deployment in underserved regions. This work directly supports the Solar Energy Technology program’s mission by bridging theoretical insights with scalable engineering solutions, ultimately advancing the reliability and affordability of solar power infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and other professionals engaged in developing solar-powered energy systems. Includes instruction in solar energy principles, energy storage and transfer technologies, testing and inspection procedures, system maintenance procedures, and report preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the study of large-scale visual culture dynamics and generative art processes, bridging computational methods with art historical and media studies research. The core research problem centers on analyzing patterns of stylistic evolution and cultural influence across digitized art collections spanning multiple centuries, geographies, and media types—including photography, digital art, and hybrid visual forms—that exceed the analytical capacity of conventional art historical methods. Current approaches struggle to process high-resolution image datasets (10,000+ works) while modeling nonlinear relationships between technical innovations, sociopolitical contexts, and aesthetic trends. The proposed computational framework integrates three components: 1) A convolutional neural network pipeline for cross-modal feature extraction from heterogeneous visual sources, 2) Graph-based network analysis to map temporal and geographic diffusion of compositional strategies, and 3) Agent-based modeling to simulate hypothetical evolutionary pathways in art movements under varying cultural constraints. These methods require parallelized GPU computing for training multimodal embeddings and processing 3D-scanned archival materials at scale. Anticipated outcomes include new quantitative models of artistic influence validated against art historical scholarship, interactive visualization tools for exploring generative art spaces, and a public dataset linking computational signatures with curatorial metadata. The research addresses critical gaps in analyzing post-digital art practices while developing transferable methodologies for computational media studies. By enabling systematic comparison of aesthetic patterns across unprecedented temporal and cultural spans, this work aims to redefine the scale at which humanistic inquiry can engage with visual cultural heritage, offering new frameworks for understanding creativity in algorithmic media environments.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the introductory study and appreciation of the visual arts. Includes instruction in art, photography, and other visual communications media.

abstract: This project seeks to develop an integrative computational framework to model the dynamic interactions between socio-economic behaviors and ecological systems in rapidly urbanizing regions, with a focus on identifying leverage points for sustainable transitions. Urban systems are complex, adaptive entities where human decision-making, infrastructure evolution, and environmental feedbacks co-evolve, yet existing models often treat these components in isolation, limiting their utility for holistic policy design. Our research addresses this gap by coupling agent-based modeling (ABM) with high-resolution geospatial analytics and biophysical simulations to capture nonlinear relationships between land-use patterns, resource flows, and community resilience. The computational challenges arise from scaling spatially explicit ABMs to metropolitan-level populations (10^6+ agents) while integrating real-time climate data streams and heterogeneous socio-demographic datasets. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to manage the combinatorial complexity of parameter spaces, enable Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses across diverse urbanization scenarios, and optimize multi-objective sustainability outcomes through evolutionary algorithms. Expected outcomes include: (1) a validated open-source toolkit for urban sustainability modeling that bridges micro-scale behavioral dynamics with macro-scale ecological impacts; (2) identification of critical thresholds in waste-to-energy infrastructure deployment that balance carbon reduction goals with equitable access; and (3) predictive insights into how participatory governance structures influence the adoption rates of green technologies across income strata. By creating a testbed for "digital twin" experimentation of urban policies, this work aims to advance methodological integration across computational social science, environmental engineering, and spatial ecology while providing actionable guidance for city planners operating under deep uncertainty about climate change impacts. The requested allocations will support GPU-accelerated simulations of coupled human-natural systems at unprecedented spatiotemporal resolutions, directly addressing scalability barriers in current interdisciplinary sustainability science.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the concept of sustainability from an interdisciplinary perspective. Includes instruction in sustainable development, environmental policies, ethics, ecology, landscape architecture, city and regional planning, economics, natural resources, sociology, and anthropology.

abstract: Emerging phytopathogens pose escalating threats to global food security, yet current surveillance frameworks lack predictive power to anticipate novel disease emergence in rapidly changing agroecosystems. This project addresses the critical gap in modeling pathogen adaptability at the intersection of climate-driven selection pressures and host microbiome resilience, focusing on soil-borne fungal pathogens in staple cereal crops. We propose developing a high-resolution agent-based model integrating three understudied dimensions: (1) evolutionary trajectories of effector gene clusters under simulated drought-heatwave regimes, (2) dynamic interactions between pathogen secretory proteomes and rhizosphere microbial networks, and (3) spatiotemporal mapping of virulence trait transmission through soil hyphal networks. The computational framework will synthesize multi-omics datasets from experimental mesocosms (metatranscriptomics, exometabolomics) with geospatial soil health indices across three continental cropping zones. Machine learning architectures, including graph neural networks trained on microbial interaction networks and transformer models for effector protein sequence prediction, will be deployed on HPC clusters to handle the combinatorial complexity of biotic-abiotic interactions. Key innovations include a novel soil pore-scale simulation module capturing moisture gradient effects on hyphal communication and a co-evolutionary algorithm predicting parallel adaptation in host-microbiome-pathogen tripartite systems. Expected outcomes include predictive risk maps identifying geographic hotspots for sudden disease emergence, molecular targets for microbiome-mediated resistance priming, and a publicly accessible digital twin platform for simulating intervention strategies. This work will advance fundamental understanding of pathogen adaptive landscapes while providing actionable intelligence for preemptive disease management—a critical need as traditional resistance breeding cycles struggle to match accelerating pathogen evolution rates. Successful implementation requires sustained access to GPU-accelerated computing resources capable of simultaneous execution of 50,000+ parameterized evolutionary simulations and large-language model training on protein sequence corpora.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of plant diseases and plant health, and the development of disease control mechanisms from an agricultural perspective. Includes instruction in plant anatomy and physiology, pathogenesis, molecular plant virology, molecular genetics, bacterial epidemiology, causal agent identification, host/agent interactions, disease resistance and response mechanisms, developing plant disease treatments, disease prevention, and disease physiology and control.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address systemic inefficiencies in medical insurance coding workflows, with a focus on optimizing the accuracy and interoperability of coded clinical data. Despite advancements in electronic health records (EHRs), persistent challenges in coding consistency—such as variability in ICD/CPT code assignment, contextual misinterpretation of clinical documentation, and time lags in claims processing—undermine billing integrity, healthcare analytics, and reimbursement fairness. Using anonymized insurance claims datasets paired with linked clinical narratives, we propose a computational framework to model coding decision pathways, quantify error propagation, and simulate the downstream impacts of coding discrepancies on payer-provider workflows. Machine learning models (e.g., transformer-based NLP for clinical text analysis and graph neural networks to map coding dependencies) will be trained on multi-institutional datasets to identify high-risk patterns in code assignment. Agent-based simulations will replicate coder-payer interactions under varying regulatory constraints and EHR interface designs. The computational workload demands parallelized processing of terabyte-scale claims data, iterative model training across heterogeneous data types, and real-time simulation of complex adaptive systems—tasks requiring HPC infrastructure for GPU-accelerated NLP, distributed memory scaling, and high-throughput job scheduling. Anticipated outcomes include predictive tools to flag error-prone coding scenarios, evidence-based recommendations for EHR template redesign, and generative AI prototypes to assist coders in resolving ambiguous documentation. By bridging computational modeling and health information management, this work aims to reduce administrative waste, enhance data quality for translational research, and establish scalable methods for auditing emerging AI-driven coding tools. The resource allocation will directly support the development of open-source benchmarking tools tailored to coding specialists, fostering transparency in a field critical to healthcare sustainability.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to perform specialized data entry, classification, and record-keeping procedures related to medical diagnostic, treatment, billing, and insurance documentation. Includes instruction in medical records and insurance software applications, basic anatomy and physiology, medical terminology, fundamentals of medical science and treatment procedures, data classification and coding, data entry skills, and regulations relating to Medicare and insurance documentation.

abstract: This project investigates the interplay between decentralized social media architectures and emergent collective decision-making processes, focusing on how platform design influences consensus formation in polarized information environments. While existing studies have centered on mainstream platforms, the rapid growth of federated and blockchain-based social networks presents novel dynamics that challenge traditional models of digital discourse. The research employs large-scale agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate interaction patterns across 10^6 synthetic users with heterogeneous belief-updating algorithms, incorporating neurocognitive constraints on information processing. High-performance computing resources are critical for parameter space exploration across 1) varying network topologies (scale-free, small-world, and emergent decentralized structures), 2) multiple incentive systems for content sharing, and 3) evolving trust calibration mechanisms. Simulations will integrate real-world data from ActivityPub-based platforms through federated learning techniques, requiring distributed computation across GPU clusters. Expected outcomes include a taxonomy of platform architectures that either mitigate or amplify belief polarization, validated through multi-agent reinforcement learning experiments. The computational framework will advance methodological capabilities for studying socio-technical systems at scale, providing evidence-based design principles for next-generation social platforms. Results will contribute foundational insights to the emerging field of computational social architecture, addressing critical gaps in understanding how technical infrastructures co-evolve with human collective behaviors beyond current centralized paradigms.
cip_definition: Any program in general social sciences, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of algorithmic labor coordination in platform-based gig economies, focusing on how computational systems shape worker autonomy, wage volatility, and collective action potential. While existing labor studies research has qualitatively examined gig work conditions, this study employs large-scale computational modeling to quantify the emergent effects of platform algorithms on labor markets. The research problem centers on the lack of transparency in how real-time task allocation, surge pricing mechanisms, and performance metrics create systemic inequities across demographic groups and geographic regions. Using anonymized ride-hailing and delivery platform datasets (simulated where proprietary data is unavailable), we will develop agent-based models that simulate worker decision-making under competing algorithmic constraints. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for running thousands of parallelized simulations that account for heterogeneous worker populations, dynamic pricing environments, and evolving labor regulations. Machine learning techniques will be applied to identify patterns of algorithmic bias in historical wage data, while natural language processing will analyze worker forum discussions to map grievance escalation pathways. Expected outcomes include a framework for predicting tipping points in labor mobilization efforts and a policy toolkit for regulating adaptive pricing systems. This computationally intensive approach advances labor studies by bridging discrete case analyses with systemic modeling of platform economies, offering new methodologies to assess how business-driven AI systems reconfigure power relationships in 21st-century work structures. The project will generate open-source simulation tools to help worker advocacy groups test intervention strategies in silico before real-world implementation.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of various aspects of work, labor organization and policy, and labor movements from the perspective of the social sciences and history. Includes instruction in labor history; political and ideological issues; worker movements and social organizations; civil rights; labor law and policy studies; labor economics; international and comparative labor studies; and applications to specific industries, groups, locations, and time periods.

abstract: Radionuclide-based therapies and diagnostic procedures require precise modeling of radiation interactions at cellular and subcellular scales to optimize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing off-target toxicity. Current clinical practices rely on generalized anatomical phantoms and static pharmacokinetic assumptions, which inadequately capture patient-specific heterogeneities in tumor morphology, radionuclide biodistribution, and radiation sensitivity. This project proposes to develop a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework for multi-scale, patient-specific dosimetry that integrates dynamic pharmacokinetic modeling, Monte Carlo radiation transport simulations, and machine learning-driven predictive analytics. The computational workflow will leverage clinical imaging data (PET/SPECT/CT) to construct voxelized phantoms, simulate radionuclide decay cascades, and model energy deposition patterns across biologically relevant spatial resolutions (µm-mm). Parallelized algorithms will address the computational intensity of tracking secondary particle emissions from emerging alpha-emitting isotopes like ²²⁵Ac and ¹⁴⁹Tb, which exhibit complex decay schemes. A neural network architecture will concurrently analyze historical patient data to predict inter-individual variations in radiopharmaceutical uptake and clearance. The HPC infrastructure is essential for processing terabytes of multimodal imaging data, executing billions of particle histories in Monte Carlo simulations, and training high-dimensional predictive models. Expected outcomes include validated protocols for personalized dose escalation in neuroendocrine tumor therapies, probabilistic risk maps for normal tissue toxicity, and open-source tools for optimizing radionuclide production targets. By resolving spatial-temporal dosimetry uncertainties inherent to current treatment planning systems, this work aims to improve clinical outcomes for 15-20% of patients experiencing subtherapeutic dosing or radiation-related adverse events. The resulting computational platform will also provide a foundation for evaluating novel theranostic agents and adaptive radiotherapy approaches, directly advancing precision nuclear medicine.
cip_definition: Research focused on the therapeutic and diagnostic applications of radionuclides (except those used in sealed sources for therapeutic purposes); and in the use of equipment associated with their production and use, including radiation safety. One of the three subspecialties available to residents in radiologic physics who must select one or more subspecialty areas.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of judicial decision-making patterns within the Canadian legal system, with a focus on constitutional law and its intersection with Indigenous legal traditions. The study addresses a critical gap in understanding how computational methods can illuminate systemic trends in judicial reasoning, particularly in cases involving Charter challenges and the interpretation of Section 35 Aboriginal rights. By employing natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) techniques, the project will process a corpus of over 150,000 Canadian court decisions spanning federal, provincial, and territorial jurisdictions from 1982 to present. Computational models will be developed to identify latent patterns in legal argumentation, temporal shifts in the application of legal tests, and the influence of interdisciplinary expert testimony on judicial outcomes. A novel component involves network analysis of legal citation practices to map the integration of Indigenous legal principles into mainstream jurisprudence. The HPC infrastructure is essential for training transformer-based models on legal text, running parallel simulations of hypothetical case outcomes under varying doctrinal frameworks, and processing high-dimensional datasets linking judicial decisions to sociopolitical contexts. Anticipated outcomes include a publicly accessible database of annotated legal decisions, predictive models of judicial reasoning in emerging areas like climate litigation, and quantitative frameworks for assessing legal coherence in pluralistic legal systems. This interdisciplinary approach bridges computational social science and legal theory, offering empirically grounded insights into the dynamism of Canadian constitutional law while advancing methodological innovation in legal informatics.
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the Canadian legal system, Constitution law, and jurisprudence. Includes instruction in legal history, legal sociology, philosophy of law, Constitutional law, Commonwealth law, legal procedure, and related topics.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model and simulate the dynamic interactions of pigments, binders, and substrates in oil and acrylic painting processes, addressing a critical gap in understanding how material behaviors influence artistic outcomes. Traditional approaches to studying these interactions rely on empirical experimentation, which is time-intensive, resource-limited, and often unable to isolate variables such as environmental conditions, chemical stability, or layered application effects. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, this research will employ multiphysics simulations to replicate the drying, cracking, and color-shifting phenomena of paints under diverse compositional and environmental scenarios. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models will simulate paint flow and blending on digital canvases, while molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will analyze binder-pigment interactions at microstructural scales. Machine learning models, trained on empirical data from historical artworks and controlled laboratory experiments, will predict long-term material degradation patterns and optimize pigment formulations for durability and visual effect. The project will also integrate 3D spectral rendering to visualize how simulated paintings evolve over time under varying lighting conditions. By correlating computational outputs with physical test cases, this work aims to establish predictive tools for artists and conservators, enabling data-driven decisions in material selection and preservation strategies. The scalability of these simulations—particularly the MD and CFD components—demands significant parallel processing capabilities, necessitating access to HPC infrastructure with GPU-accelerated nodes. Outcomes will include open-access datasets, a modular simulation toolkit for the visual arts community, and peer-reviewed insights into the interplay between painting materials and aesthetic longevity. This interdisciplinary effort bridges computational science and studio practice, advancing both technical and creative methodologies in contemporary painting.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals creatively and technically to express emotions, ideas, or inner visions by the application of paints and related chemical color substances to canvases or other materials. Includes instruction in color and color mixing, surface preparation, composition, oil and acrylic media, watercolor media, painting techniques, and personal style development.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational modeling in landscape architecture, focusing on the dynamic interplay between ecological systems, human-designed landscapes, and climate variability. Traditional design methods often rely on static environmental datasets or simplified simulations, limiting the ability to predict long-term ecological performance under stochastic climate conditions. This project addresses this gap by developing a multi-agent simulation framework that integrates real-time hydrological data, vegetative growth algorithms, and human behavioral patterns to model landscape resilience at urban scales. The computational approach combines geospatial analysis, machine learning for predictive scenario generation, and agent-based modeling to simulate interactions between soil erosion, plant communities, and pedestrian movement in high-density urban green spaces. Key challenges include processing high-resolution LiDAR and satellite imagery to parameterize micro-scale terrain variations, as well as optimizing parallelized simulations for diverse climate scenarios (e.g., extreme precipitation events, drought cycles). The HPC infrastructure will enable iterative testing of design interventions across 10,000+ stochastic climate realizations, providing probabilistic assessments of landscape durability and ecosystem service delivery. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for adaptive landscape design, validated against case studies in flood-prone coastal cities, and novel metrics quantifying the economic value of ecological redundancy in public spaces. By bridging computational ecology with design practice, this work aims to establish evidence-based standards for climate-responsive landscapes while demonstrating the transformative potential of HPC in non-STEM design disciplines. The results will directly inform municipal resilience planning and offer a replicable methodology for integrating complex systems science into landscape architecture education and professional workflows.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of landscape architecture and research in various aspects of the field. Includes instruction in geology and hydrology; soils, groundcovers, and horticultural elements; project and site planning; landscape design, history, and theory; environmental design; applicable law and regulations; and professional responsibilities and standards.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance structural integrity and efficiency in ironworking through computational modeling and simulation. Ironworkers face persistent challenges in designing and installing metal structures that balance cost, safety, and compliance with evolving building codes. Traditional trial-and-error methods for optimizing load-bearing capacity, weld integrity, and dynamic stress distribution are time-intensive and limited in their ability to predict complex real-world behaviors. To address this, we propose a computational framework combining finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML) to model structural performance under diverse environmental and operational conditions. High-fidelity simulations will assess thermal stresses in welded joints, wind-induced vibrations in tall ornamental structures, and fatigue failure in reinforced beams under cyclic loading. ML algorithms trained on simulation data will identify optimal material configurations and fabrication sequences, reducing material waste and labor costs. The HPC environment is critical for scaling these resource-intensive models, particularly when simulating large-scale structures or incorporating stochastic variables such as seismic activity or variable crane load dynamics during installation. Outcomes will include open-access datasets of validated structural simulations, predictive tools for failure risk assessment, and a digital twin framework to guide real-time decision-making during construction. By integrating computational rigor with ironworking expertise, this research aims to establish new best practices for resilient, code-compliant metal structures while enhancing training protocols for future ironworkers through data-driven insights. The requested computing resources will enable the iterative refinement of models, ensuring their applicability to both standardized and custom fabrication scenarios in the field.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to make and install structural, ornamental, and reinforcing metal structures and supports. Includes instruction in drafting, technical mathematics, blueprint interpretation, welding, riveting, beam placement, ornamental design, structural reinforcement, crane operation, safety, and applicable codes and standards.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of informal employee networks and their impact on organizational resilience during large-scale disruptions, such as pandemics or supply chain crises. Traditional human resources management (HRM) frameworks often overlook the role of emergent, self-organizing networks in shaping workforce adaptability, relying instead on formal hierarchies and policy-based interventions. To address this gap, we propose a computational study integrating organizational behavior theory, network science, and agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate how informal communication patterns influence collective problem-solving, knowledge sharing, and stress propagation in distributed teams. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to model organizations at scale, simulating millions of agent interactions across parameterized scenarios that vary team structures, crisis severity, and hybrid work configurations. Using anonymized HR datasets from multinational firms, we will calibrate agent behaviors to reflect real-world decision-making patterns, then test interventions such as dynamic resource reallocation, AI-mediated mentorship matching, and decentralized crisis response protocols. The computational workflow leverages graph neural networks to predict network fragility points and reinforcement learning to optimize adaptive HR policies. Expected outcomes include a validated framework for quantifying informal network resilience, actionable insights for designing agile HR systems in volatile environments, and open-source tools for simulating workforce dynamics under stress. This work bridges computational social science and HRM, offering a novel paradigm to address 21st-century challenges in talent sustainability. By elucidating how micro-level interactions scale to organizational outcomes, the project aims to advance evidence-based strategies for building crisis-ready workforces while demonstrating the transformative potential of HPC in strategic human capital research.
cip_title: Human Resources Management/ Personnel Administration, General
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to manage the development of human capital in organizations, and to provide related services to individuals and groups. Includes instruction in personnel and organization policy, human resource dynamics and flows, labor relations, sex roles, civil rights, human resources law and regulations, motivation and compensation systems, work systems, career management, employee testing and assessment, recruitment and selection, managing employee and job training programs, and the management of human resources programs and operations.

abstract: The preservation of historic structures and landscapes necessitates balancing complex, often competing factors, including material degradation, environmental stressors, socio-economic pressures, and regulatory constraints. Current methodologies for modeling these interactions rely on simplified assumptions or fragmented datasets, limiting their utility in dynamic urban environments. This project seeks to address these challenges by developing a computational framework to simulate and predict the long-term impacts of conservation strategies, climate change, and urban development on historic sites. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will integrate multi-scale datasets—including 3D LiDAR scans, environmental sensor data, archival records, and socio-economic indicators—into a unified geospatial-temporal model. Computational methods will include finite element analysis (FEA) to assess material stress under varying climate scenarios, machine learning algorithms to identify patterns in deterioration rates, and agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate stakeholder decision-making processes. The HPC environment is critical for handling the high-resolution spatial data, parallelizing computationally intensive simulations, and iterating through thousands of scenario combinations to identify optimal preservation pathways. Expected outcomes include predictive tools to prioritize at-risk structures, quantify trade-offs between conservation and development goals, and inform policy decisions. By creating an open-source computational platform, this research will provide preservationists, urban planners, and policymakers with scalable, data-driven strategies to safeguard cultural heritage amid growing environmental and economic uncertainties. The project’s interdisciplinary approach—bridging architectural history, materials science, and computational social science—exemplifies the transformative potential of HPC in non-traditional STEM fields, offering a model for integrating advanced computing into humanities-driven research.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the design and implementation of plans to restore and maintain historic buildings, districts, and landscapes in a way that balances conservation and preservation with commercial and development interests. Includes instruction in architectural history, building conservation, cultural resource management, economics, historical documentation and preservation, land-use and zoning codes, public policy, public relations, real estate law, and taxation.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the development of next-generation ceramic materials with tailored mechanical and thermal properties for extreme environment applications, such as energy generation systems and high-temperature industrial processes. A critical challenge in ceramic sciences is predicting and optimizing microstructural evolution under thermo-mechanical stress, as experimental characterization of atomic-scale phenomena in refractory materials remains costly and limited. To address this, we propose a multiscale computational framework combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, phase-field modeling, and machine learning to investigate defect dynamics, grain boundary interactions, and crack propagation mechanisms in silicon carbide (SiC) and alumina (Al₂O₃) composites. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute large-scale MD simulations (10⁶–10⁷ atoms) capturing nanosecond-scale events at temperatures exceeding 2000 K, coupled with phase-field models resolving mesoscale microstructure evolution. Machine learning interatomic potentials will be trained on density functional theory (DFT) datasets to enhance simulation accuracy while maintaining computational feasibility. The study will quantify how dopant segregation, interfacial anisotropy, and residual stresses influence fracture toughness and creep resistance. Expected outcomes include predictive models linking processing parameters (sintering temperature, additive composition) to operational performance metrics, enabling data-driven design of ceramics with enhanced thermal stability and damage tolerance. By elucidating fundamental structure-property relationships in these material systems, the research will directly inform the synthesis of ceramics for advanced turbine coatings, nuclear reactor components, and industrial wear-resistant tools. The requested computing resources will support parameter space exploration exceeding current laboratory capabilities, accelerating the translation of computational insights into scalable manufacturing protocols.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of inorganic non-metallic materials, such as porcelains, cements, industrial ceramics, ceramic superconductors, abrasive, and related materials and systems.

abstract: The proliferation of unstructured cultural heritage data—including digitized manuscripts, oral histories, and multimedia artifacts—presents a critical challenge in organizing and analyzing these resources to uncover patterns of societal knowledge transmission. This project seeks to develop a scalable computational framework for modeling the semantic and temporal evolution of cultural narratives across heterogeneous, multilingual datasets. While existing tools in information retrieval and natural language processing often prioritize contemporary textual data, this work focuses on adapting and integrating methods for noisy, non-standardized historical materials, including OCR-scanned texts, transcribed folklore, and annotated iconography. The research employs a hybrid approach combining transformer-based language models fine-tuned on historical linguistics with graph neural networks to map conceptual relationships across time and media types. Key computational challenges include handling irregular temporal sampling, mitigating biases in fragmented archival sources, and enabling cross-modal alignment between textual and visual data. High-performance computing resources are essential for training multi-modal embeddings at scale, conducting Monte Carlo simulations to quantify narrative drift uncertainty, and optimizing dynamic graph structures representing century-scale knowledge flows. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for cultural analytics, novel metrics for quantifying semantic preservation in digitized heritage collections, and case studies demonstrating how marginalized narratives persist or transform within global knowledge systems. This work bridges information science, computational historiography, and digital preservation, offering methodological advances for institutions managing cultural big data while providing empirical insights into the long-term dynamics of collective memory formation.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on computing, computer science, and information science and systems. Such programs are undifferentiated as to title and content and are not to be confused with specific programs in computer science, information science, or related support services.

abstract: The increasing complexity of managing adult patients with multiple chronic conditions necessitates advanced computational approaches to optimize clinical decision-making and resource allocation. This project addresses the challenge of predicting disease progression and treatment response in non-surgical adult populations with heterogeneous conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, and autoimmune disorders. Current clinical prediction tools often fail to integrate multi-modal patient data—including electronic health records (EHRs), wearable device metrics, psychosocial factors, and genomic biomarkers—into unified models, limiting their accuracy and utility in real-world practice. We propose developing machine learning (ML) frameworks to analyze longitudinal patient datasets from three tertiary care centers, encompassing over 250,000 de-identified records. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for training transformer-based models on unstructured EHR text via natural language processing, while simultaneously processing high-dimensional biomarker data and time-series inputs from continuous glucose monitors and blood pressure sensors. Computational workflows will employ federated learning techniques to preserve data privacy across institutions and Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning. Anticipated outcomes include (1) risk stratification models identifying patients at highest risk for acute decompensation or poor treatment adherence, (2) personalized therapeutic recommendations based on comorbidity networks and social determinants of health, and (3) simulation environments for testing practice management strategies under varying resource constraints. The project will establish an open-source clinical ML pipeline optimized for HPC architectures, enabling replication across health systems. By enhancing predictive accuracy for complex medical trajectories, this work aims to reduce hospital readmissions, improve chronic disease management, and inform value-based care initiatives in general internal medicine. Successful implementation requires sustained access to GPU clusters for deep learning tasks and high-memory nodes for large-scale patient cohort simulations.
cip_definition: Research focused on the provision of general medical services to adult patients with a wide range of non-surgical clinical problems. May included related research in behavioral aspects of diseases, patient and family counseling and practice management.

abstract: This research project seeks to enhance the precision and efficiency of image-guided interventions in interventional radiology through advanced computational modeling and real-time data analysis. Current challenges in integrating multi-modal imaging data (e.g., fluoroscopy, MRI, CT) during minimally invasive procedures—such as stent placement, embolization, and abscess drainage—limit the ability to dynamically predict device-tissue interactions, optimize navigation pathways, and anticipate complications. These limitations contribute to prolonged procedure times, increased radiation exposure, and suboptimal patient outcomes. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a computational framework for real-time, image-guided therapy planning and execution. The project will utilize GPU-accelerated deep learning algorithms to automate the segmentation of anatomical structures and pathological features from multi-modal imaging datasets. Finite element modeling and computational fluid dynamics simulations will be employed to predict device behavior (e.g., stent expansion, catheter tracking) and physiological responses (e.g., blood flow changes, embolic agent dispersion) under diverse clinical scenarios. Additionally, reinforcement learning models will be trained on retrospective patient data to optimize procedural parameters, such as imaging angle selection and device trajectory. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallel processing of high-resolution 3D imaging data (≥1 TB per patient cohort) and reduce simulation runtime from hours to minutes, facilitating intraprocedural adaptation. Expected outcomes include a validated predictive platform for personalized intervention planning, demonstrated through retrospective validation and prospective pilot studies in vascular and oncologic interventions. This work aims to reduce procedural complications by 20–30%, minimize radiation dose through AI-driven fluoroscopy optimization, and establish a scalable computational toolkit for advancing image-guided therapy research. The requested resources are critical for handling the computational intensity of multi-physics simulations and large-scale neural network training, which cannot be feasibly executed on local clinical workstations.
cip_definition: Research focused on image-guided therapies, using fluoroscopy, digital radiography, computed tomography, sonography, and magnetic resonance imaging, to guide small devices inserted into the body through very small openings. These therapies include angioplasty, stent placement, thrombolysis, embolization, biliary and genitourinary drainages, and abscess drainages. Does NOT require prior completion of a residency program in diagnostic radiology.

abstract: Woodworking practices have historically relied on empirical methods to predict material behavior, optimize toolpaths, and ensure structural integrity in finished products. However, the anisotropic nature of wood, coupled with variable environmental factors like humidity and temperature, introduces complex nonlinear dynamics that challenge traditional trial-and-error approaches. This project seeks to develop a high-fidelity computational framework to model wood deformation, stress distribution, and tool interaction at unprecedented resolution, enabling data-driven design and manufacturing processes. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will implement finite element analysis (FEA) simulations to capture multi-scale mechanical responses in wood under varying grain orientations, moisture levels, and machining forces. These simulations will integrate machine learning models trained on experimental datasets—including digital image correlation measurements and CNC machining telemetry—to predict optimal cutting parameters, minimize material waste, and prevent tool wear. The computational workflow will also couple hygrothermal models with structural analyses to assess long-term durability of joinery systems under cyclic environmental loads. By parallelizing these resource-intensive simulations across HPC nodes, we aim to generate a parametric library of material performance profiles applicable to furniture design, architectural components, and heritage restoration. Expected outcomes include open-source simulation tools tailored to woodworking education, a decision-support system for sustainable material selection, and predictive metrics to reduce energy consumption in kiln-drying processes. This research bridges gaps between traditional craftsmanship and computational engineering, offering scalable methodologies to preserve material resources while advancing precision in wood-based manufacturing.
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to lay out and shape stock; assemble wooden articles or subassemblies; mark, bind, saw, carve, and sand wooden products; repair wooden articles, and use a variety of hand and power tools.

abstract: The increasing complexity of modeling subsurface geological processes at high resolution presents a critical computational challenge in understanding lithospheric dynamics and associated seismic hazards. This project seeks to advance the simulation of fault zone interactions and stress propagation within heterogeneous rock matrices through the development of a scalable, physics-informed numerical framework. The research problem centers on resolving the multiscale coupling between long-term tectonic strain accumulation and short-term seismic rupture events, which requires capturing nonlinear material behaviors across spatial scales from meters to kilometers and temporal scales spanning seconds to millennia. To address this, we propose a hybrid computational approach combining finite element discretization with adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) and parallelized iterative solvers. The model will integrate constitutive relationships derived from laboratory rock mechanics data, enabling explicit representation of friction laws, fracture propagation, and poroelastic effects. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to manage the anticipated 10^8–10^9 degree-of-freedom simulations, leveraging GPU-accelerated nodes for matrix assembly and distributed memory architectures via MPI for domain decomposition. Validation against geodetic InSAR datasets and historical seismic catalogs will constrain model parameters through inverse optimization techniques. Expected outcomes include: (1) quantification of stress transfer thresholds between adjacent fault segments in active tectonic regions, (2) probabilistic forecasts of rupture cascades under varying fluid injection scenarios, and (3) open-source release of optimized solver routines for the geodynamics community. The computational infrastructure requested will enable unprecedented resolution of strain localization patterns near critical mineralogical phase boundaries, directly contributing to improved seismic hazard assessment frameworks. By elucidating how microscale rock properties influence macroscale tectonic behavior, this work bridges a fundamental gap in physics-based earthquake forecasting while providing generalizable methods for HPC-enabled geomechanical modeling.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the earth; the forces acting upon it; and relationships between the solids, liquids and gases comprising it.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance diagnostic and therapeutic innovations in ophthalmic and optometric care. A critical challenge in this field lies in the analysis of complex, multi-modal datasets—such as high-resolution retinal imaging, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and dynamic visual field assessments—which are essential for early detection and monitoring of conditions like glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy. Current computational tools struggle to efficiently integrate these datasets while maintaining the precision required for clinical decision-making. This research proposes the development of machine learning frameworks, including deep neural networks and ensemble models, to automate the detection of pathological features and predict disease progression. Additionally, the project will employ biomechanical simulations to model ocular tissue responses to intraocular pressure changes and surgical interventions, which demand significant computational power for high-fidelity, three-dimensional simulations. By utilizing HPC resources, the team will process terabytes of anonymized patient data, train computationally intensive models with hyperparameter optimization, and run iterative simulations to validate hypotheses. Expected outcomes include scalable algorithms for real-time diagnostic support, open-source tools for optometric device calibration, and mechanistic insights into post-surgical outcomes. These contributions aim to reduce diagnostic latency, enhance personalized treatment plans, and improve accessibility to precision optometric care in underserved populations. The requested allocation will directly address the resource-intensive demands of parallelized model training and large-scale data integration, enabling translational advancements in ophthalmic support services and allied health education.
cip_title: Ophthalmic and Optometric Support Services and Allied Professions, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in ophthalmic and optometric support services and allied professions, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop a scalable computational framework for dynamic risk assessment and real-time hazard prediction in complex industrial systems, addressing critical gaps in current process safety methodologies. Traditional risk analysis tools often rely on static models with simplified assumptions, limiting their ability to adapt to evolving operational conditions or capture cascading failure mechanisms in interconnected systems. To overcome these limitations, we propose an integrated approach combining multi-physics simulations, machine learning, and probabilistic graph-based analysis optimized for high-performance computing (HPC) environments. The research will focus on modeling high-consequence scenarios in process-intensive facilities, such as equipment degradation under variable stressors, human-system interaction errors, and transient thermal-fluid phenomena during emergency shutdowns. Computational workflows will leverage distributed-memory parallelism to perform ensemble simulations of failure propagation pathways across thousands of parametric variations, while graph neural networks will analyze historical incident data to identify latent risk patterns. The HPC infrastructure will enable 3D transient simulations of multiphase flows and structural responses at unprecedented spatiotemporal resolutions, coupled with real-time uncertainty quantification through Monte Carlo methods. Expected outcomes include an open-source risk prediction toolkit capable of processing sensor data streams for adaptive safety decision support, validated against industrial case studies from pharmaceutical manufacturing and energy storage sectors. By enabling high-fidelity modeling of complex safety-critical interactions, this work aims to establish new benchmarks for predictive process safety analytics, reducing the likelihood of catastrophic incidents through computationally driven insights into emergent risks. The requested computing resources will directly support the development of these computationally intensive models, which exceed the capabilities of conventional workstations due to their need for teraflop-scale processing and petabyte-scale scenario databases.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers engaged in developing methods to mitigate damage, reduce risks, and prevent accidents. Includes instruction in design for injury prevention, engineering for process safety, environmental psychology, function-based risk analysis, fundamentals of industrial engineering, operations research, probability and statistics, risk assessment and reduction, and safety engineering.

abstract: This project seeks to enhance earth science teacher education by integrating high-performance computing (HPC) to address critical gaps in preparing educators to teach complex, data-driven earth systems. Current pedagogical approaches often lack the computational tools necessary to model dynamic processes such as climate change, geophysical interactions, and hydrological cycles, limiting teachers’ ability to convey these concepts effectively. To bridge this gap, we propose developing a suite of scalable computational workflows and interactive simulations that leverage HPC resources to model earth systems at unprecedented spatial and temporal resolutions. These tools will be embedded within a curriculum designed to train pre-service and in-service teachers in computational thinking, data analysis, and the use of authentic scientific datasets. The project will utilize climate model outputs (e.g., CMIP6), satellite remote sensing data, and geospatial repositories, processed through parallelized Python-based pipelines optimized for GPU-accelerated clusters. Machine learning methods will be applied to classify geological features and predict ecosystem responses under varying climate scenarios, enabling teachers to demonstrate real-world scientific inquiry. By providing access to HPC infrastructure, the project will empower educators to design classroom activities that mirror current research practices, fostering student engagement with cutting-edge earth science challenges. Anticipated outcomes include measurable improvements in teachers’ computational literacy, the creation of open-access educational modules, and a framework for integrating HPC-driven pedagogy into science education standards. This work will establish a replicable model for advancing STEM teacher preparation through computationally intensive, inquiry-based learning, ultimately equipping future generations to address pressing environmental issues with data-informed decision-making.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach earth science programs at various educational levels.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize athlete performance and organizational decision-making in sport and fitness administration through advanced analytics and simulation. The research problem centers on the inefficiency of traditional, intuition-driven approaches to managing athlete workloads, facility operations, and strategic planning in dynamic sports environments. Current methodologies often lack the capacity to integrate heterogeneous data streams—such as biometric wearables, training logs, facility usage patterns, and financial constraints—into actionable models. To address this gap, the project proposes a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled system that combines agent-based modeling, machine learning, and real-time data assimilation. The computational approach will involve three phases: (1) creating multi-scale simulations of athlete-physiology interactions under varying training loads and recovery protocols, (2) developing predictive models for facility resource allocation using historical attendance and event data, and (3) implementing ensemble forecasting techniques to evaluate competing strategies for roster management and budget optimization. By leveraging parallel processing capabilities, the system will iteratively refine decision pathways across temporal scales—from in-game tactical adjustments to multi-year organizational planning. Expected outcomes include a validated toolkit for quantifying injury risk mitigation strategies, a dynamic pricing algorithm for facility utilization, and scenario-planning interfaces for coaching staff and administrators. The research occupies an emerging niche at the intersection of sports management, operational analytics, and computational physiology, distinct from conventional public health or engineering domains. Successful implementation could redefine evidence-based practices in athlete development and sport business operations while establishing scalable methodologies for resource-constrained organizations. Access to HPC resources is critical due to the need for rapid parameter-space exploration across high-dimensional datasets and the real-time requirements of potential deployment scenarios.
detailed_field: Parks, recreation, leisure, fitness, and sport studies and management
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply business, coaching and physical education principles to the organization, administration and management of athletic programs and teams, fitness/rehabilitation facilities and health clubs, sport recreation services, and related services. Includes instruction in program planning and development; business and financial management principles; sales, marketing and recruitment; event promotion, scheduling and management; facilities management; public relations; legal aspects of sports; and applicable health and safety standards.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of identifying and diagnosing atypical reading development in early childhood education through advanced computational modeling of linguistic and cognitive processes. Current diagnostic tools for reading difficulties often rely on static assessments, which lack the granularity to capture dynamic interactions between phonological awareness, vocabulary acquisition, and decoding skills. To overcome this limitation, we propose developing machine learning models trained on multimodal datasets—including longitudinal reading assessments, eye-tracking data, and spoken language samples—to map trajectories of typical and atypical literacy development. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for processing these heterogeneous datasets, which encompass terabytes of audio, video, and text from 5,000+ K–3 learners in diverse linguistic environments. Neural networks will be deployed to detect subtle patterns in phonemic errors, gaze fixation durations, and syntactic complexity that correlate with emerging reading difficulties. Parallelized feature extraction pipelines will analyze speech recordings for prosodic and morphosyntactic markers, while transformer-based models will evaluate written responses for semantic coherence and orthographic processing. The computational outputs will inform the creation of dynamic risk profiles to guide early intervention strategies. By leveraging HPC capabilities for large-scale data integration and real-time model retraining, this work aims to produce scalable diagnostic tools that help educators personalize literacy instruction. Anticipated outcomes include open-source algorithms for processing educational language data and evidence-based frameworks for integrating computational analytics into teacher training programs. This research directly aligns with the Language and Literacy Education program’s focus on bridging theoretical knowledge of reading development with practical pedagogical innovations, offering transformative potential for both teacher preparation and student outcomes.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach language and literacy subject matter areas, at various educational levels. Includes instruction in language development, typical and atypical reading development, and diagnosing reading difficulties.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a predictive modeling framework for optimizing personalized support strategies for individuals with developmental disabilities. Current approaches to designing care plans in developmental services rely heavily on manual assessment and iterative adjustments, which can delay effective interventions and strain limited resources. The research problem centers on integrating heterogeneous data—including behavioral logs, health records, caregiver observations, and environmental factors—to generate dynamic, adaptive models that predict individual responses to specific support interventions. By synthesizing data from psychology, sociology, and behavioral analysis, the project addresses a gap in computational tools tailored to non-clinical, community-based care settings. The computational approach employs agent-based modeling to simulate individual behaviors and interactions within diverse scenarios, coupled with machine learning techniques to identify patterns in longitudinal outcomes. HPC resources are critical for scaling these simulations to account for high-dimensional variables (e.g., sensory sensitivities, communication styles, and social determinants of health) and for enabling real-time parameter adjustments during model training. Expected outcomes include a validated open-source toolkit for simulating intervention efficacy, which could reduce trial-and-error periods in care planning and improve resource allocation for community organizations. Additionally, the project aims to uncover latent relationships between environmental factors and behavioral outcomes, offering novel insights for developmental services training programs. By bridging computational social science with applied disability support, this work advances an emerging interdisciplinary niche, demonstrating how HPC can address complex, human-centered challenges beyond traditional science and engineering domains.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply practical knowledge and skills to support individuals with a variety of physical, mental or developmental disabilities in a family or community setting. Includes instruction in health care, basic nutrition, pharmacology, nursing, autism, mental health, psychology, sociology, behavioral analysis, communication, intervention, counseling and community services, and developmental services, such as literacy and life skills training.

abstract: The application of protective and decorative coatings to structural surfaces involves complex interactions between materials, environmental conditions, and application techniques. Traditional empirical approaches to optimizing coating performance—such as adhesion, durability, and aesthetic outcomes—are time-intensive, resource-heavy, and often fail to account for the multivariate nature of real-world conditions. This project proposes a computational research initiative to model and simulate the physicochemical processes governing coating behaviors, enabling predictive insights into material performance under diverse environmental and operational scenarios. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we aim to develop multiscale models that integrate molecular dynamics simulations of coating-substrate interactions, computational fluid dynamics analyses of application processes (e.g., spraying, rolling), and machine learning frameworks to correlate environmental variables (humidity, temperature, pollution) with long-term coating degradation. These models will be validated against experimental data from controlled laboratory tests and field studies. The computational approach addresses critical gaps in understanding how micro-scale material properties (e.g., polymer chain mobility, pigment dispersion) influence macro-scale outcomes like crack propagation, moisture resistance, and color retention. By simulating thousands of parameter combinations, the project will identify optimal coating formulations and application protocols for specific environmental and structural conditions, reducing reliance on trial-and-error methods. Expected outcomes include a predictive toolset for selecting coatings that maximize longevity and compliance with sustainability standards, directly benefiting industry practices in surface preparation, waste reduction, and regulatory adherence. The HPC infrastructure is essential to handle the high-dimensional parameter space, large datasets from hyperspectral imaging of coating failures, and the parallel processing demands of real-time simulation workflows. This research aligns with the program’s focus on advancing technical methodologies in painting and wall covering while addressing environmental and economic challenges in the field.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to finish exterior and interior structural surfaces by applying protective or decorative coating materials, such as paint, lacquer, and wallpaper. Includes instruction in surface preparation; selecting, preparing, and applying paints and other coatings; hanging wallpaper; equipment operation and maintenance; finish selection; safety and clean-up; environmental effects on finishes; adhesion properties; and applicable codes and standards.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the dynamics of cultural production and diasporic identity formation across sub-Saharan Africa and its global diasporas. Despite growing digitization efforts, large-scale computational studies of African cultural artifacts—including oral histories, visual arts, music, and multilingual texts—remain scarce due to fragmented datasets and the computational complexity of integrating multimodal sources. This research addresses this gap by employing machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) techniques to map patterns of cultural exchange, adaptation, and preservation within and beyond the African continent. The project will aggregate and process digitized collections from archives, community repositories, and contemporary digital media, focusing on understudied linguistic and artistic traditions. Key computational tasks include training transformer-based models on low-resource African languages, clustering visual motifs in art and textiles using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and simulating network models to trace the diffusion of cultural narratives across diasporic communities. These analyses require HPC capabilities to manage distributed storage, parallelize model training, and process terabytes of unstructured data. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of annotated cultural materials, computational tools tailored for African linguistic and artistic datasets, and new interdisciplinary frameworks for understanding how diasporas reconstitute cultural memory in digital spaces. By centering computational methods on African-led cultural production, this work aims to challenge homogenizing narratives in global cultural studies and provide infrastructure for equitable digital scholarship. The project’s findings will directly inform curriculum development in African Studies and collaborative preservation initiatives with cultural practitioners in Nigeria, Kenya, and the Caribbean diaspora.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples of the African Continent, usually with an emphasis on Africa south of the Sahara, and including the African diasporas overseas.

abstract: This project seeks to address persistent health disparities in urban communities by analyzing the complex interplay of social, environmental, and clinical factors influencing preventable chronic diseases. Despite evidence linking socioeconomic inequities to adverse health outcomes, community-level interventions remain constrained by insufficiently granular predictive models. To overcome this, we propose a computational epidemiology approach integrating multi-source data—including electronic health records, geospatial environmental exposures, census-derived social determinants, and public health surveillance metrics—to simulate and optimize intervention strategies. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for processing these large-scale, heterogeneous datasets and running agent-based models (ABMs) that simulate population-level health behaviors under varying resource allocation scenarios. The ABMs will incorporate dynamic networks representing community interactions, stochastic disease progression algorithms, and policy-sensitive parameters to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of preventive programs targeting hypertension, diabetes, and asthma. Machine learning pipelines will identify high-risk subpopulations and forecast intervention impacts using ensemble methods optimized for parallel computing. Expected outcomes include scalable frameworks for predicting localized health risks, evidence-based recommendations for prioritizing community health resources, and open-source tools enabling reproducible health equity analyses. By quantifying how specific resource allocations mitigate disparities, this work will directly inform municipal health departments and community organizations in designing targeted prevention campaigns. The requested computing resources will enable iterative model calibration, sensitivity analyses across diverse demographic contexts, and real-time visualization of intervention trade-offs—tasks infeasible with standard institutional computing infrastructure. This project aligns with public health priorities by bridging computational innovation and community-driven preventive medicine, ultimately advancing data-driven strategies to reduce inequitable disease burdens.
cip_definition: A program that prepares public health specialists to plan and manage health services in local community settings, including the coordination of related support services, government agencies, and private resources. Includes instruction in public health, community health services and delivery, health behavior and cultural factors, local government operations, human services, health communication and promotion, health services administration in local settings, environmental health, preventive and comparative medicine, epidemiology, biostatistics, family and community health, and applicable law and regulations.

abstract: Plants rely on intricate mechanical and hydrodynamic processes within their cells to adapt to environmental stressors, yet the multiscale dynamics of these systems remain poorly understood. This project seeks to model the biomechanical behavior of plant cell wall-fluid interactions during rapid osmotic stress responses, a critical process for survival in fluctuating environments. Using high-performance computing (HPC), we will simulate the coupled mechanical deformation of cellulose microfibrils and cytoplasmic fluid flow in 3D cellular geometries derived from experimental cryo-electron tomography data of *Arabidopsis thaliana* root hairs. The computational framework integrates finite element methods for solid mechanics, lattice Boltzmann simulations for viscous fluid dynamics, and stochastic models for ion transport across dynamically changing membranes. By resolving nanosecond-scale molecular interactions alongside minute-long tissue-level stress redistribution, these multiscale simulations will uncover how localized wall loosening propagates hydraulic signals through adjacent cells—a phenomenon hypothesized to coordinate systemic drought avoidance behaviors. Key challenges include optimizing parallelized solvers for irregular cellular geometries and validating models against microfluidic pressure perturbation experiments. Successful implementation will provide the first quantitative map of energy dissipation thresholds in plant cell networks under hydraulic shock, offering insights into evolutionary constraints on cell wall architecture. Outcomes will directly inform bioinspired material designs for soft robotics and advance predictive models of crop resilience to climate-driven water volatility. This work bridges plant biophysics, computational mechanics, and soft matter engineering, establishing a new paradigm for studying plant environmental sensing through HPC-enabled mechanohydraulic analysis.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of plants, related microbial organisms, and plant habitats and ecosystem relations. Includes instruction in plant anatomy and structure, phytochemistry, cytology, plant genetics, plant morphology and physiology, plant ecology, plant taxonomy and systematics, paleobotany, and applications of biophysics and molecular biology.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize community health interventions addressing the intersection of mental health disparities and social determinants in multilingual, underserved populations. Community health workers (CHWs) serving as liaisons between healthcare systems and marginalized communities face challenges in personalizing interventions due to fragmented data on socioenvironmental stressors, cultural contexts, and health service accessibility. We propose an agent-based modeling (ABM) approach integrated with natural language processing (NLP) to simulate community-level health behaviors and intervention outcomes. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are required to process heterogeneous datasets—including anonymized clinical interactions, community surveys in six languages, and geospatial service utilization patterns—and to run large-scale simulations capturing dynamic interactions between individuals, CHWs, and health systems. The ABM will incorporate machine learning-derived risk stratification models trained on longitudinal mental health outcomes, while NLP pipelines will analyze qualitative field notes from CHWs to identify cultural and linguistic barriers to care. Sensitivity analyses will evaluate how variations in intervention timing, CHW-to-population ratios, and multilingual resource allocation impact projected health equity outcomes. Expected outcomes include an open-source tool for simulating culturally tailored intervention strategies and evidence-based thresholds for optimizing CHW deployment in low-resource settings.
