All developed code and validation datasets will be made openly available to the engineering design community.
cip_definition: An instructional program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to engineering problems involving marrying or coordinating multiple dissimilar systems to carry out single functions or achieve common purposes, organizing system components for maximum flexibility and utility, planning engineering projects involving multiple tasks and design solutions, planning design testing and evaluation procedures, resolving specification and requirement conflicts, and choosing among competing theoretical solutions. Note: this program was re-instated after being deleted from CIP 2000; previously, it was coded as 14.2901.

abstract: Franchising represents a critical yet understudied axis of modern economic systems, characterized by complex interdependencies among legal frameworks, operational scalability, and localized market dynamics. Traditional franchise management models often rely on static, aggregated data, limiting their ability to predict systemic risks or optimize network-wide decisions in real time. This project proposes the development of a dynamic, multi-agent simulation framework to model franchise ecosystems at unprecedented scale, integrating heterogeneous variables such as regional regulatory constraints, supply chain volatility, consumer sentiment shifts, and cross-franchise resource competition. The research problem centers on identifying non-linear tipping points in franchise network resilience—specifically, how micro-level operational decisions propagate through geographically distributed systems under economic stressors like inflation shocks or localized demand collapse. Computational methods will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to execute parallelized simulations across three dimensions: 1) agent-based modeling of franchisee-operator interactions using game-theoretic principles, 2) machine learning-driven scenario forecasting trained on historical franchise failure/recovery patterns, and 3) real-time geospatial optimization of shared resource allocation (e.g., distributed warehousing, multi-unit staffing). The simulation environment will ingest live economic indicators and anonymized transaction streams from partner franchise networks, requiring petascale processing capabilities to maintain temporal fidelity across 10,000+ simulated franchise units. Expected outcomes include a predictive analytics toolkit capable of identifying at-risk franchise clusters 6-18 months before conventional financial metrics detect instability, alongside adaptive resource distribution algorithms that reduce systemic waste by 15-20% in benchmark testing. By bridging computational social science with operational research, this work aims to establish a new paradigm for data-driven franchise governance while demonstrating how HPC-enabled simulation can address emergent complexity in decentralized business architectures.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to manage and operate franchises. Includes instruction in legal requirements, set-up costs and capitalization requirements, financing, and applications to specific franchise opportunities.

abstract: This project seeks to address computational bottlenecks in processing high-fidelity 3-D models for industrial design and manufacturing applications, where traditional computing systems struggle with the scalability of complex geometries, real-time simulations, and multi-objective optimization. The research focuses on leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable rapid iterative design, analysis, and validation of resource-intensive 3-D models, particularly for additive manufacturing and large-scale structural systems. Key computational challenges include the parallelization of finite element analysis (FEA) for stress testing lattice-based structures, dynamic mesh refinement for multi-resolution 3-D scans, and machine learning-driven topology optimization under material constraints. The proposed methods integrate distributed computing frameworks to accelerate CAD-based simulations, GPU-accelerated rendering for real-time design visualization, and scalable algorithms for generative design workflows that balance performance metrics such as weight, durability, and production cost. By deploying these HPC-enabled workflows, the project aims to reduce computational time for industrial-scale 3-D model iterations by 60–80% compared to current single-node systems, while improving predictive accuracy in material behavior simulations. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for distributed 3-D model processing, validated benchmarks for HPC resource allocation in design tasks, and case studies demonstrating optimized manufacturing workflows for automotive component prototyping and architectural formwork systems. This work will directly enhance the accessibility of advanced computational design methodologies for small-to-medium enterprises, bridging gaps between theoretical model complexity and practical production feasibility in engineering technology domains.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills in the use of three-dimensional (3-D) computer technology to create technical illustrations and models used in manufacturing, design, production, and construction. Includes instruction in 3-D computer-aided design (CAD), 3-D printing, 3-D model design and construction, and 3-D scanning.

abstract: This project seeks to develop computational models to analyze how social studies educators design and implement curricula that address complex sociopolitical systems, with the goal of enhancing pedagogical strategies for teaching civic reasoning and historical analysis. A critical challenge in social studies education lies in equipping teachers to scaffold students’ understanding of dynamic, interconnected societal phenomena—such as political polarization or historical causality—using pedagogies that bridge abstract concepts with real-world contexts. Current approaches often rely on static frameworks or anecdotal case studies, limiting educators’ ability to anticipate how instructional choices influence students’ systems-level thinking. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate classroom learning dynamics and model the efficacy of diverse teaching strategies at scale. Agent-based modeling will be employed to represent student cohorts interacting with curriculum components, enabling the exploration of emergent outcomes under varied pedagogical conditions (e.g., project-based learning vs. structured debates). Natural language processing techniques will analyze large corpora of classroom discourse and lesson plans to identify patterns in how teachers frame sociopolitical complexity. By integrating these computational methods, the project will generate predictive insights into how specific instructional designs affect students’ critical engagement with social studies content. Expected outcomes include (1) a framework for optimizing lesson sequencing in civics and history education, (2) scalable tools for simulating classroom response to controversial or ambiguous content, and (3) evidence-based guidelines for teacher training programs to address gaps in systems thinking pedagogy. The computational demands of processing multimodal educational data (text, interaction logs, and simulated environments) necessitate parallelized workflows and large-scale memory allocation, which HPC infrastructure uniquely provides. Findings will directly inform the development of adaptive professional development resources for social studies educators, ultimately aiming to improve students’ capacity to engage with societal challenges as informed citizens.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach general social studies programs at various educational levels.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model the cascading impacts of evolving international tax regulations on cross-border corporate structures, with a focus on digitally driven multinational enterprises (MNEs). The research addresses a critical gap in legal and policy analysis: the absence of dynamic, multi-jurisdictional simulations capable of predicting how iterative changes in tax laws—such as OECD Pillar Two global minimum tax rules or unilateral digital services taxes—interact with corporate operational frameworks. Traditional legal scholarship relies on static case studies or qualitative comparisons, which struggle to account for the nonlinear feedback loops between regulatory shifts, corporate tax optimization strategies, and jurisdictional competition. To address this, the project will develop agent-based models (ABMs) simulating MNE decision-making under heterogeneous tax regimes, integrating real-world data on bilateral tax treaties, transfer pricing policies, and corporate financial disclosures. Computational legal analytics will be applied to parse regulatory texts from 50+ jurisdictions using natural language processing (NLP) techniques, creating structured inputs for the ABMs. Monte Carlo methods will stress-test scenarios where concurrent policy changes in key economies (e.g., U.S., EU, and ASEAN states) collide with adaptive corporate behaviors. The HPC environment is essential for scaling these simulations across thousands of permutations while maintaining granular detail on entity-level legal obligations. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework to quantify systemic risks of regulatory arbitrage, insights into unintended consequences of policy fragmentation, and visualizable policy "heat maps" to guide multilateral coordination efforts. By combining computational modeling with doctrinal legal analysis, this work aims to establish a new paradigm for anticipatory governance in international tax law, offering actionable tools for both policymakers and MNEs navigating an increasingly volatile regulatory landscape.
cip_title: International Business, Trade, and Tax Law
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the law, policies, and regulations governing transnational business and commercial practices, including the specialized tax law related to international financial transactions.

abstract: This project seeks to develop and validate computational models to optimize individualized instruction for elementary students with disabilities, addressing the challenge of efficiently tailoring evidence-based teaching strategies to diverse learning needs. Current methods for designing individualized education plans (IEPs) rely heavily on manual, time-intensive processes that may not fully account for complex interactions between instructional approaches, student characteristics, and learning outcomes. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze multi-modal educational datasets—including standardized assessment scores, behavioral observation logs, and teacher-reported intervention data—from 15,000+ anonymized K-6 special education records. Machine learning techniques (e.g., reinforcement learning, hierarchical clustering) will be applied to identify patterns in effective instructional strategies across neurodevelopmental profiles, while agent-based modeling will simulate classroom scenarios to predict intervention efficacy under varying resource constraints. The computational workflow requires parallel processing of high-dimensional data to train predictive models that account for longitudinal student progress, teacher feedback loops, and curriculum alignment. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework for generating data-driven IEP recommendations, validated against a longitudinal cohort of 200 students in partner school districts. This work will advance special education practice by providing teachers with scalable tools to personalize instruction while maintaining fidelity to pedagogical best practices. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling the combinatorial complexity of modeling individualized learning trajectories and testing hypothetical intervention scenarios, which exceed the capabilities of standard educational research software. Results will directly inform teacher training programs on integrating computational insights into special education curriculum design and classroom implementation.
cip_title: Education/ Teaching of Individuals in Elementary Special Education Programs
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the design and provision of teaching and other educational services to children with special learning needs or disabilities who are in the elementary grades. Includes instruction in diagnosing learning disabilities; developing individual education plans; curriculum development, instructional strategies, and classroom management for elementary special education; and teaching elementary education subject matter.

abstract: Endocrine and metabolic disorders, including type 2 diabetes, obesity, and thyroid dysfunction, exhibit complex molecular and physiological heterogeneity that complicates diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. Current clinical classifications often fail to capture this variability, leading to suboptimal therapeutic outcomes. This project proposes a computational framework to integrate multi-omics data (genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics) with clinical electronic health records (EHRs) to identify patient-specific molecular subtypes and predictive biomarkers for endocrine disorders. The primary challenge lies in analyzing high-dimensional datasets with nonlinear interactions across temporal and spatial scales, which demands advanced machine learning (ML) and scalable computational infrastructure. We will develop a hybrid deep learning model combining graph neural networks (GNNs) to model biological networks and transformer architectures to process longitudinal EHR data. This approach will be validated using a cohort of 15,000 patients with type 2 diabetes and comorbid obesity from the NIH All of Us Research Program, with replication in thyroid disorder datasets. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to train these models on terabytes of raw sequencing data, perform hyperparameter optimization via Bayesian methods, and conduct in silico simulations of metabolic pathways perturbed by identified genetic variants. Expected outcomes include (1) novel stratification of endocrine disorders into mechanistically distinct subgroups, (2) predictive algorithms for treatment response leveraging federated learning across institutions, and (3) open-source tools for dynamic visualization of multi-omics-clinical interactions. The computational workflows will be containerized for reproducibility, with GPU-accelerated scaling tested on HPC clusters. By linking molecular signatures to real-world outcomes, this work aims to advance precision endocrinology, reduce trial-and-error prescribing, and identify high-risk patients for early intervention. Successful implementation will require sustained access to HPC resources capable of parallel processing, large-memory nodes for genome-wide association study (GWAS) meta-analyses, and high-throughput pipelines for metabolomic feature extraction.
cip_definition: Research on disorders of the internal (endocrine) glands such as the thyroid and adrenal glands, and to deal with disorders such as diabetes, metabolic and nutritional disorders, obesity, pituitary diseases, and menstrual and sexual problems. Requires prior completion of a residency program in internal medicine.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational textual analysis in Talmudic Studies, a field characterized by complex intertextual relationships, layered commentaries, and evolving legal-ethical discourse. Traditional methods of Talmudic analysis rely on manual close reading, which limits scalability when tracing conceptual networks across vast corpora spanning centuries. The research problem centers on developing scalable computational frameworks to model semantic, logical, and jurisprudential patterns in Talmudic literature and its reception history. Using natural language processing (NLP) adapted to rabbinic Aramaic and Hebrew, combined with graph-based network analysis, the project will map argumentative structures, cross-referential dependencies, and conceptual shifts within and across key texts. HPC resources are essential for training transformer-based language models on digitized manuscripts and critical editions, enabling semantic similarity detection and automated source linkage at scale. Further computational work will involve agent-based modeling to simulate historical debates documented in the Talmud, testing hypotheses about dialogic reasoning norms. Expected outcomes include an open-access database of annotated textual networks, visualization tools for interdisciplinary scholarship, and methodological frameworks bridging computational humanities with Jewish legal philosophy. This work aims to transform the study of Talmudic reasoning processes, offering new pathways to analyze how ethical principles are dynamically constructed through multilayered discourse. By integrating advanced computing with traditional hermeneutics, the project will enhance scholarly capacity to trace the evolution of Jewish legal thought while fostering interdisciplinary collaborations in digital religious studies.
cip_definition: A program focused on intense study of the Talmud that fosters values, critical thinking, and scholarship skills; prepares students for entry into a broad spectrum of graduate and professional schools; and prepares students for entry into a variety of careers including the Rabbinate. Includes instruction in Jewish law, Jewish jurisprudence, ethics, philosophy, and related disciplines.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in predictive modeling of occupational hazards by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate complex workplace safety scenarios. Current approaches to risk assessment in occupational safety and health often rely on static datasets or simplified analytical models, limiting their ability to anticipate emerging risks in dynamic environments such as construction sites, manufacturing facilities, or emergency response scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we propose the development of a multi-scale computational framework integrating computational fluid dynamics (CFD), finite element analysis (FEA), and machine learning (ML) to model real-time interactions between environmental factors, equipment, and human workers. The HPC resources will enable large-scale simulations of airborne contaminant dispersion, structural failure mechanisms under stress, and ergonomic strain patterns across diverse populations. Additionally, ML algorithms will be trained on synthetic and historical injury datasets to identify latent risk factors and predict accident probabilities under varying operational conditions. The computational workflows will be validated against experimental data from sensor networks deployed in industrial settings. Expected outcomes include optimized safety protocols for mitigating exposure to chemical, physical, and biomechanical hazards, as well as an open-source toolkit for probabilistic risk assessment adaptable to small- and medium-sized enterprises. By providing unprecedented resolution in simulating high-consequence, low-probability events—such as equipment malfunctions coupled with human error—this research will directly enhance the evidence base for proactive safety interventions. The project aligns with the Occupational Safety and Health Technology program’s mission to bridge engineering principles and practical safety solutions, while advancing technical capacity in hazard modeling for workforce training and regulatory compliance applications.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and other professionals engaged in maintaining job-related health and safety standards. Includes instruction in safety engineering principles, inspection and monitoring procedures, testing and sampling procedures, laboratory techniques, applications to specific work environments, and report preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to enhance geography education by developing computational tools to model and analyze complex geospatial datasets for classroom integration, addressing a critical gap in accessible, data-driven pedagogical resources. Despite the growing availability of geospatial data from satellites, sensors, and citizen science platforms, K-12 educators often lack the technical capacity to process these datasets into meaningful lesson materials. The research problem centers on bridging this divide by creating scalable methods to transform raw spatial data into interactive, curriculum-aligned visualizations and simulations. The computational approach leverages high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process multi-terabyte datasets using parallelized workflows in Python and R, integrating machine learning (e.g., convolutional neural networks) to identify pedagogically relevant spatial patterns in land-use change, climate variability, and urban dynamics. Agent-based modeling frameworks (e.g., NetLogo) will simulate student interactions with geospatial interfaces to optimize usability across diverse learning environments. Proposed work includes benchmarking computational efficiency of data downsampling algorithms, training predictive models to flag region-specific geographic phenomena for lesson customization, and generating synthetic datasets to represent underrepresented locales. Expected outcomes include an open-access repository of computationally preprocessed geospatial teaching modules, validated through partnerships with 15 teacher-training programs. By reducing computational barriers to real-world data integration, this project aims to empower educators to foster spatial literacy and evidence-based reasoning skills. The HPC infrastructure is essential for handling memory-intensive geoprocessing tasks and large-scale parameter testing of educational simulation models, which would be infeasible on standard academic computing systems. Results will advance geography teacher education by demonstrating scalable intersections between computational earth science and classroom practice.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach geography at various grade levels.

abstract: Clinical Nurse Specialists (CNSs) are critical in optimizing patient outcomes through advanced clinical decision-making, yet resource constraints and complex care environments limit their capacity to predict and mitigate adverse events in real time. This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model patient deterioration risks and intervention efficacy in acute care settings, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multimodal health data. The research problem centers on integrating real-time electronic health record (EHR) data, wearable sensor outputs, and longitudinal patient histories to identify early warning signals of clinical decline—a task requiring large-scale data processing and predictive analytics beyond the capabilities of standard clinical systems. The computational approach will employ machine learning (ML) techniques, including ensemble models and neural networks, to synthesize heterogeneous datasets and simulate patient trajectories under varying intervention scenarios. Key tasks include parallelized training of ML models on retrospective EHR data, validation against prospective clinical outcomes, and agent-based modeling to evaluate the impact of CNS-led interventions on care workflows. The project will utilize GPU-accelerated computing for model optimization and deploy scalable storage solutions for terabyte-level datasets. Expected outcomes include validated predictive algorithms for sepsis, acute respiratory failure, and delirium risks, tailored to prioritize CNS clinical actions. By enabling dynamic risk stratification and intervention planning, this work aims to reduce preventable complications, shorten hospital stays, and inform scalable decision-support tools for nurses. The HPC resources are essential to manage the computational intensity of real-time data assimilation, multi-parameter simulations, and validation across diverse patient cohorts. This research aligns with national priorities to enhance clinical reasoning in nursing and advance data-driven care delivery models, with implications for healthcare cost reduction and patient safety improvement.
cip_definition: A program that prepares registered nurses to deliver direct patient and client care in clinical settings. Includes instruction in clinical pharmacotherapeutics, advanced clinical practice, holistic nursing, nursing practice and health care policy, administration and consultation services, health assessment, patient stabilization and care, and patient education.

abstract: The development of advanced polymeric materials with tailored properties requires a fundamental understanding of multi-scale structure-property relationships during processing. Current experimental methods face limitations in resolving dynamic molecular interactions and phase transitions under industrially relevant flow conditions, such as those encountered in extrusion or injection molding. This project seeks to address this gap by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate polymer processing across atomistic, mesoscopic, and continuum scales. We propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of chain orientation dynamics, coarse-grained models for flow-induced crystallization kinetics, and finite element analysis (FEA) of macroscopic thermal-mechanical stresses. The HPC resources will enable parallelized simulations of polymer melts with chemically specific architectures (e.g., branched polyolefins, block copolymers) under shear and extensional flows, capturing time-dependent morphological evolution at unprecedented resolution. Machine learning techniques will be applied to extract predictive relationships between processing parameters, hierarchical structures, and final material properties from the simulation datasets. Expected outcomes include validated models for optimizing processing conditions to achieve targeted crystallinity distributions, mechanical anisotropy, and barrier properties in semi-crystalline polymers. The results will directly inform the design of energy-efficient manufacturing protocols for high-performance packaging films and lightweight automotive components. By establishing an open-source computational workflow for polymer process-structure-property prediction, this work will accelerate the development of sustainable polymer systems with reduced reliance on empirical trial-and-error approaches. The requested computing resources are critical due to the memory-intensive nature of long-timescale MD simulations and the need for coupled multi-physics simulations across spatial scales.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of synthesized macromolecular compounds and their application to specific engineering uses, including the development of industrial materials with tailored properties, the design of lightweight structural components, the use of liquid or solid polymers, and the analysis and control of polymerization processes.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the understanding of nonequilibrium quantum many-body dynamics in strongly correlated systems, a foundational challenge in modern physics. While theoretical frameworks exist, the computational complexity of solving time-dependent many-body Schrödinger equations for large systems remains a critical barrier. This research will employ high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate quantum dynamics in ultracold atomic lattices and spin chains, systems that exhibit emergent phenomena such as many-body localization and quantum phase transitions. The computational approach combines tensor network algorithms, specifically matrix product states (MPS) and time-dependent variational principles (TDVP), optimized for parallel execution on GPU clusters. These methods enable efficient representation of entangled quantum states while mitigating exponential scaling of Hilbert space dimensions. Key objectives include probing thermalization dynamics in disordered systems, characterizing the stability of quantum coherence under nonlinear interactions, and identifying signatures of prethermalization in quenched geometries. The simulations will leverage adaptive time-stepping and distributed memory architectures to handle system sizes exceeding 100 lattice sites—a scale intractable with current single-node resources. Expected outcomes include predictive models for nonequilibrium quantum transport and metastable states, with implications for quantum information storage and engineered quantum materials. By benchmarking against recent experimental results from trapped-ion platforms, this work will also bridge gaps between theoretical predictions and observable phenomena. The requested computing resources are essential to achieve the required numerical precision and statistical sampling across parameter spaces, enabling transformative insights into the universal behavior of quantum matter far from equilibrium.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the major topics, concepts, processes, and interrelationships of physical phenomena as studied in any combination of physical science disciplines.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the socio-political networks and economic transformations in colonial Latin America (16th–18th centuries) through large-scale archival data integration. The research problem centers on identifying patterns of resource extraction, labor systems, and institutional collaboration across Spanish and Portuguese territories, which are poorly understood due to the fragmented and multilingual nature of surviving records. Traditional methods struggle to synthesize data from thousands of digitized manuscripts, trade logs, and colonial censuses, limiting historians’ ability to trace systemic connections between regions like Potosí, Minas Gerais, and administrative hubs in Seville or Lisbon. To address this, the project will employ natural language processing (NLP) tools optimized for early modern Spanish and Portuguese, combined with network analysis algorithms, to map relationships between colonial actors, institutions, and commodities. Key computational tasks include training custom NLP models to extract named entities and economic terms from heterogeneous texts, constructing dynamic network graphs to visualize shifting power structures, and applying spatial analysis to trade routes using GIS-linked datasets. These workflows require parallel processing and large-memory nodes to handle ~10 TB of unstructured data and resolve ambiguities in paleographic texts. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of cross-referenced colonial interactions, visualizations of resource flows, and quantitative insights into how imperial policies shaped regional inequalities. By integrating computational methods with archival scholarship, this project aims to advance debates on colonialism’s long-term impacts while establishing scalable digital humanities frameworks for understudied Iberian-language sources.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history of the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking areas of the world, including the Iberian, Latin American, and Lusophone worlds.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing real-time personalization and dynamic supply chain management in large-scale e-commerce platforms using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Modern e-commerce systems generate vast, heterogeneous datasets—including customer behavior logs, inventory telemetry, and third-party market signals—that require rapid integration and analysis to enable responsive decision-making. Existing methods struggle to balance computational efficiency with the accuracy of multi-objective optimization models under real-world constraints, such as latency thresholds and privacy-preserving data handling. To overcome these limitations, we propose developing a scalable computational framework leveraging parallelized reinforcement learning (RL) and agent-based simulations. The project will utilize HPC resources to train deep RL models on historical transaction datasets (spanning 100M+ user interactions) while simulating concurrent supply chain scenarios under variable demand shocks. Key computational tasks include distributed hyperparameter optimization for recommendation systems, Monte Carlo simulations of inventory routing problems, and privacy-aware federated learning across synthetic customer cohorts. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated model for real-time personalization that reduces latency by 30% while maintaining >95% accuracy in A/B tests, (2) dynamic pricing algorithms resilient to supply chain volatility, and (3) open-source tools for privacy-preserving e-commerce analytics. These results will advance both academic research in electronic commerce operations and practical frameworks for enterprise-scale platforms, particularly in improving resource allocation during peak traffic periods and crisis-induced market shifts. The HPC infrastructure is critical for managing memory-intensive graph computations (customer-product networks) and large-scale sensitivity analyses that cannot be feasibly executed on local clusters. By bridging computational scalability gaps in current e-commerce architectures, this work aims to establish new benchmarks for responsive, ethical, and adaptive online business systems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to plan, manage, supervise, and market electronic business operations, products, and services provided online via the Internet. Includes instruction in business administration, information technology, information resources management, web design, computer and Internet law and policy, computer privacy and security, e-trading, insurance, electronic marketing, investment capital planning, enterprise operations, personnel supervision, contracting, and product and service networking.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to enhance the security and reliability of mechanical and electronic locking systems, addressing vulnerabilities in traditional and emerging lock technologies. Despite centuries of innovation, locks remain susceptible to sophisticated physical, digital, and hybrid attacks, particularly as smart locks integrate IoT connectivity and legacy mechanical components. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate multi-physics interactions within lock mechanisms, model probabilistic attack scenarios, and optimize novel tamper-resistant designs. Finite element analysis (FEA) will assess stress distributions in locking components under forced entry conditions, while Monte Carlo methods will evaluate the statistical efficacy of combination manipulation techniques. For electronic systems, agent-based models will simulate cyber-physical attacks on embedded firmware, and lattice Boltzmann methods will model thermal vulnerabilities in safe materials. Machine learning pipelines will process terabyte-scale datasets of lock failure cases to identify latent design weaknesses. The computational workload requires parallelized GPU-accelerated simulations to resolve micron-scale tolerances in mechanical interactions and real-time cryptanalysis of proprietary key-generation algorithms. Expected outcomes include predictive frameworks for rating lock susceptibility to emerging attack vectors, generative designs for high-security key profiles, and adaptive algorithms to dynamically update safe combination protocols. By integrating computational engineering with locksmithing praxis, this work aims to establish a new paradigm for proactive security hardening in physical access systems, directly benefiting manufacturers, locksmith professionals, and standards organizations. The requested HPC resources are critical due to the need for parameter sweeps across 10^6+ mechanical configuration variants and the cryptographic complexity of analyzing post-quantum lock authentication protocols.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to make, repair, maintain, modify, and open locks; to make keys; to enter and change lock and safe combinations; and install and repair safes.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model the socio-spatial dynamics of equitable housing design in rapidly urbanizing regions, integrating behavioral, economic, and aesthetic factors. Current approaches to evaluating housing equity often rely on static demographic data or qualitative assessments, limiting their ability to predict how built environment features—such as unit layouts, shared infrastructure placement, or access to communal spaces—interact with evolving social and economic pressures. We propose an agent-based modeling (ABM) system coupled with generative design algorithms to simulate how housing configurations influence long-term community resilience, resource distribution, and occupant well-being. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to handle the combinatorial complexity of design variables (e.g., spatial hierarchies, material choices, policy constraints) and large-scale behavioral datasets, including anonymized mobility patterns and household resource usage. The ABM will incorporate dynamic networks of occupant interactions, simulating scenarios under varying constraints such as climate stressors, economic inequality gradients, and policy interventions. Machine learning techniques will be applied to optimize generative design outputs against equity metrics derived from agent behaviors and preference surveys. Expected outcomes include predictive models linking specific design features to measurable social outcomes, a toolkit for policymakers to evaluate housing prototypes computationally, and novel metrics for quantifying "equitable density" in urban planning contexts. By bridging computational social science with architectural analytics, this work addresses a gap in evidence-based housing design tools that account for both human-centered needs and systemic urban challenges. The project’s computational demands—including parallelized simulations of 10,000+ agent populations, high-resolution spatial optimization, and real-time visualization of multi-parameter trade-offs—necessitate dedicated HPC allocations to achieve scalability and practical relevance for global housing stakeholders.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the behavioral, social, economic, functional, and aesthetic aspects of housing, interiors, and other built environments. Includes instruction in analyzing, planning, designing, furnishing, and equipping residential, work, and leisure spaces to meet user needs and the study of related public policies.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to resolve dynamic structural mechanisms underlying the assembly and function of macromolecular complexes involved in cellular stress response pathways. A central challenge in structural biology is capturing transient, multi-scale conformational changes in large protein-RNA assemblies, such as those mediating mRNA quality control. Traditional experimental techniques like cryo-EM provide static snapshots but lack the temporal resolution to map allosteric communication or folding intermediates during substrate processing. To address this, we propose an integrative computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, coarse-grained modeling, and free energy calculations to study the 26S proteasome regulatory particle and its interaction with misfolded protein substrates. All-atom MD simulations will model ATP-dependent conformational shifts in the AAA+ ATPase ring at microsecond timescales, while enhanced sampling techniques will characterize free energy landscapes of substrate translocation. Coarse-grained models will extend analysis to millisecond regimes, capturing large-scale rearrangements of the 19S regulatory cap. These simulations require extensive parallelization across GPU nodes due to system sizes exceeding 5 million atoms and the need for replica-exchange protocols. HPC resources will also support cryo-EM data processing for validation, utilizing iterative 3D classification and flexible fitting algorithms to correlate computational predictions with experimental density maps. Expected outcomes include mechanistic insights into how nucleotide cycling drives mechanical unfolding of substrates, identification of critical interfacial residues for targeted mutagenesis, and predictive models of regulatory particle dysregulation linked to neurodegenerative diseases. By bridging dynamic structural data with functional assays, this work will advance rational design of small-molecule modulators to probe proteostasis pathways, with broader implications for understanding molecular recognition and chaperone-mediated protein degradation.
detailed_field: Biochemistry, biophysics, and molecular biology nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of submolecular and molecular components and assemblies of living systems and how they are organized into functional units such as cells and anatomic tissues. Includes instruction in glycoprotein, carbohydrate, protein, and nucleic acid structures and chemistry; cytoskeletal structure; nuclear and intracellular structures; molecular recognition; molecular chaperones; transcription and folding; multicellular organization; microtubules and microfilaments; cell differentiation; immunophysics; and DNA sequencing.

abstract: Radioisotopic pathology relies on advanced in vitro analyses to quantify radionuclide interactions in biological samples, yet current methodologies face challenges in scaling to high-throughput datasets, modeling dynamic isotope-tissue interactions, and optimizing laboratory protocols for safety and precision. This project seeks to address these gaps by developing computational frameworks to analyze multi-modal data from radioisotope assays, simulate radiation transport in heterogeneous biological matrices, and automate quality control processes. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to (1) train machine learning models on mass spectrometry and gamma spectroscopy datasets for rapid isotope quantification, (2) perform Monte Carlo simulations of radiation dispersion in synthetic tissue models to refine storage and handling protocols, and (3) integrate pharmacokinetic models with clinical metadata to predict inter-patient variability in ex vivo isotope retention. By parallelizing these workflows across GPU and CPU clusters, the project aims to overcome current bottlenecks in processing times for large-scale radiobiological datasets, which can exceed conventional computing capabilities when modeling complex decay chains or multi-isotope systems. Expected outcomes include optimized algorithms for minimizing radiation exposure risks in laboratory workflows, validated predictive models for isotope-tissue binding affinities, and open-source tools for automating quality assurance in radioisotopic pathology labs. These advances will enhance the reproducibility of in vitro radionuclide studies, support regulatory compliance in clinical laboratories, and inform the development of safer, more efficient diagnostic protocols. The requested computing resources will enable iterative model training, large-scale parameter space exploration, and validation against experimental data from collaborating clinical sites, directly addressing the computational demands inherent in radioisotopic research while fostering translational applications in precision oncology and metabolic disorder diagnostics.
cip_definition: Research focused on the use of radionuclides in the study of body fluids, excreta, or tissues quantified outside the body. May included related research in laboratory management and safety, quality control, instrumentation, isotope storage and in vitro analyses.

abstract: The proposed research seeks to address critical gaps in predicting the health and ecological risks of emerging environmental toxicants, including per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and heavy metal mixtures, which exhibit complex interactions in biological and environmental systems. Traditional experimental methods struggle to capture the multi-scale dynamics of toxin transport, bioaccumulation, and molecular toxicity mechanisms across species and environments. This project will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop integrative computational models that simulate toxin behavior from molecular interactions to ecosystem-level impacts. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will characterize toxin binding affinities to metabolic enzymes and receptors, while physiologically based toxicokinetic (PBTK) models parameterized with environmental monitoring data will predict bioaccumulation patterns in aquatic and terrestrial organisms. A parallelized environmental fate model will integrate geospatial data on soil chemistry, hydrology, and industrial emissions to map toxin dispersion and degradation pathways. Machine learning algorithms will identify synergistic effects of co-occurring pollutants using toxicogenomic datasets from cross-species exposure studies. Computational outputs will be validated against in vitro toxicity assays and field biomarker measurements. This work will advance predictive frameworks for prioritizing high-risk toxins, quantifying exposure thresholds, and informing remediation strategies. By elucidating mechanistic links between environmental toxin behavior and adverse health outcomes, the project directly supports evidence-based policies for hazardous material management and ecosystem protection. The scale of data integration and the need for real-time simulation of toxin-receptor interactions across millions of conformations necessitate HPC capabilities to achieve biologically relevant resolution and throughput. Outcomes will provide foundational insights into dermal and reproductive toxicology, nutrient-toxin interactions, and adaptive responses in non-model species, addressing urgent challenges in environmental health science.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the health effects associated with exposure to toxic chemicals and systems occurring in the natural, work, and living environments; the management of environmental toxins and toxicity; and the development of protections for humans, animals, and plants. Includes instruction in applied ecology; microbiology; toxin transport, fate, and degradation; dermal toxicology; reproductive and genetic toxicology; atmospheric and environmental chemistry; metals toxicology; environmental mutagens and biotransformation; nutrient interaction; chemical sensitivity, disorders, and disease; risk assessment; animal waste management; environmental health; and hazardous materials management.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) methodologies for analyzing dynamic, multi-source spatial data in security and intelligence contexts. The research addresses the challenge of integrating heterogeneous geospatial datasets—such as satellite imagery, crowdsourced social media feeds, environmental sensor streams, and historical conflict records—into unified predictive models. Traditional geospatial tools struggle to process these datasets at scale due to disparities in resolution, update frequency, and semantic structure, particularly when analyzing human-terrain interactions in rapidly evolving scenarios. The proposed work combines machine learning, spatial statistics, and distributed computing to develop adaptive frameworks for real-time pattern detection and anomaly prediction. Key computational objectives include training transformer-based models on multi-temporal satellite imagery to identify subtle landscape changes indicative of emerging risks, optimizing graph neural networks for modeling cross-domain spatial dependencies, and implementing GPU-accelerated raster/vector data fusion pipelines. The project will utilize parallel processing architectures to handle petabyte-scale geospatial repositories, with containerized workflows ensuring reproducibility across security-focused research environments. Expected outcomes include novel algorithms for automated feature extraction from low-quality or partially obscured imagery, probabilistic risk maps integrating human activity patterns with physical geography variables, and open-source tools for scalable spatiotemporal analysis. This work aims to establish computational benchmarks for next-generation GEOINT systems, providing actionable intelligence support while addressing ethical considerations in automated spatial surveillance. By bridging gaps between geospatial science, artificial intelligence, and high-performance computing, the project will deliver frameworks applicable to disaster response, infrastructure monitoring, and geopolitical forecasting, with emphasis on interpretability and adaptability in resource-constrained operational settings.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to analyze security and intelligence problems using a geographic perspective by relating human actions to cultural, political, economic, social, and physical landscapes. Includes instruction in aerial photography analysis, cartography, geographic information systems (GIS), physical geography, remote sensing, spatial programming, and quantitative methods in geographic research.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in social studies teacher education by modeling the impact of pedagogical strategies on student learning outcomes in diverse classroom environments. A critical challenge in social studies education is designing instructional approaches that equitably address complex socio-historical concepts—such as systemic inequality, geopolitical conflicts, and cultural dynamics—while accounting for varying student backgrounds, prior knowledge, and engagement patterns. Traditional qualitative and small-scale quantitative methods struggle to capture the multidimensional interactions between teaching practices, curricular content, and learner variability at scale. To address this, we propose a computational framework combining agent-based modeling (ABM) and machine learning (ML) to simulate classroom dynamics under diverse pedagogical scenarios. The ABM component will represent students as heterogeneous agents with attributes informed by empirical data from public school demographics, state assessment records, and anonymized student surveys. Instructional strategies, aligned with state and national social studies standards, will be encoded as dynamic variables affecting agent interactions. ML algorithms will then analyze simulation outputs to identify patterns linking specific pedagogical interventions to predicted learning gains, particularly for historically marginalized student groups. HPC resources are essential to execute thousands of parallel simulations, enabling sensitivity analyses across demographic, curricular, and instructional variables. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated computational model of social studies classroom ecosystems, (2) evidence-based recommendations for optimizing teacher training modules, and (3) open-access tools for educators to test virtual implementations of lesson plans. By bridging computational social science and teacher education, this work aims to provide scalable, data-driven insights into equitable pedagogical design, ultimately strengthening the preparation of social studies educators to navigate complex, real-world classrooms.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach general social studies programs at various educational levels.

abstract: Emerging IoT-driven workflows in distributed environments require adaptive system architectures that balance latency, energy efficiency, and reliability across heterogeneous edge-to-cloud infrastructures. Current resource allocation frameworks struggle to model the dynamic interdependencies between application-specific quality-of-service requirements, hardware variability, and intermittent connectivity in such systems. This project proposes a computational systems analysis approach to design and simulate context-aware resource orchestration strategies for hybrid edge-cloud ecosystems. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will develop discrete-event simulations modeling multi-tiered workflows across synthetic and real-world device topologies. The computational framework will integrate hardware performance profiles, network telemetry datasets, and machine learning models to predict optimal task partitioning under constraints including energy budgets, thermal limits, and failure probabilities. Key innovations include a modular architecture for testing diverse allocation heuristics and a novel cost function incorporating both technical metrics (e.g., end-to-end latency distributions) and operational factors (e.g., device maintenance costs). Simulations will scale to >10^5 node configurations using parallelized workload generators and distributed optimization solvers. Expected outcomes include quantifiable performance benchmarks for different edge deployment paradigms, open-source tools for comparative systems analysis, and evidence-based guidelines for configuring resilient hybrid infrastructures. This work addresses critical gaps in lifecycle management of adaptive computing systems, particularly for applications in industrial IoT and mobile sensor networks where traditional cloud-centric models prove inadequate. The HPC-enabled simulations will provide unprecedented resolution into emergent behaviors at the hardware-software boundary, informing both academic research and practical implementation strategies for next-generation distributed systems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply programming and systems analysis principles to the selection, implementation, and troubleshooting of customized computer and software installations across the life cycle. Includes instruction in computer hardware and software; compilation, composition, execution, and operating systems; low- and high-level languages and language programming; programming and debugging techniques; installation and maintenance testing and documentation; process and data flow analysis; user needs analysis and documentation; cost-benefit analysis; and specification design.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze large-scale historical datasets and model complex socio-cultural transformations in pre-modern Eurasia (c. 1200–1800 CE). The research addresses a critical gap in historical methodology: the systematic integration of fragmented archival records, trade logs, and climate proxy data to reconstruct interconnected patterns of migration, resource distribution, and knowledge exchange. Traditional qualitative approaches struggle to synthesize these heterogeneous datasets, which span multiple languages, calendrical systems, and spatial scales. The computational workflow employs natural language processing (NLP) to extract entities and relationships from digitized manuscripts, paired with agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate decision-making processes in agrarian and urban communities under varying environmental and political conditions. Key technical challenges include aligning temporal inconsistencies across sources, handling incomplete or contradictory records via probabilistic reasoning, and optimizing parallelized simulations of population dynamics at continental scales. The HPC environment is essential for processing over 15 TB of primary source corpora, training transformer-based models for multilingual text analysis, and running ensemble simulations to assess historical counterfactuals. Expected outcomes include 1) a publicly accessible knowledge graph linking individuals, institutions, and environmental events across Eurasia, 2) quantitative frameworks for evaluating competing theories about state formation and crisis periods, and 3) methodological benchmarks for computational historiography. By enabling data-driven interrogation of cross-regional connectivity, this project aims to advance understanding of how decentralized networks sustained cultural continuity amid geopolitical fragmentation—a finding with implications for modern global history education and heritage preservation strategies.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the general study and interpretation of the past, including the gathering, recording, synthesizing and criticizing of evidence and theories about past events. Includes instruction in historiography; historical research methods; studies of specific periods, issues and cultures; and applications to areas such as historic preservation, public policy, and records administration.

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing complexity of modern electrical power transmission systems, which face challenges such as aging infrastructure, increasing renewable energy integration, and dynamic load demands. Traditional methods for designing and validating electrical installations often rely on static models or simplified simulations, limiting their ability to predict cascading failures, optimize grid resilience, or evaluate the long-term impacts of distributed energy resources. To overcome these limitations, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a scalable, multiphysics simulation framework tailored for power transmission networks. The computational approach integrates finite element analysis (FEA) for thermal and mechanical stress modeling in transmission lines, agent-based simulations for fault propagation under varying environmental conditions, and machine learning algorithms to optimize real-time load balancing. By coupling these methods, the framework will simulate interactions between physical components (e.g., transformers, insulators) and grid-wide operational dynamics at unprecedented spatial and temporal resolutions. Key objectives include identifying failure-prone configurations in high-renewable penetration scenarios, validating code-compliant installation practices under extreme weather patterns, and generating adaptive maintenance schedules to minimize downtime. The HPC environment is critical for handling the computational intensity of modeling large-scale networks with millions of nodes, as well as for training neural networks on historical grid performance data. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for risk assessment in power transmission design, data-driven recommendations for updating installation standards, and a publicly accessible database of simulated failure modes correlated with National Electrical Code (NEC) compliance metrics. This work will directly support vocational training programs by providing empirically validated case studies and enhancing the precision of safety protocols taught in electrical installation curricula.
cip_title: Electrical and Power Transmission Installation/ Installer, General
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to install indoor and outdoor residential, commercial, and industrial electrical systems, and associated power transmission lines. Includes instruction in electricity, safety procedures, wiring, insulation and grounding, schematic blueprint interpretation, equipment operation and maintenance, and applicable codes and standards.

abstract: The increasing complexity of digital evidence in forensic investigations necessitates advanced computational tools to analyze heterogeneous, high-volume datasets. This project seeks to develop a scalable framework for integrating fragmented digital evidence—such as IoT device logs, cloud storage metadata, and encrypted communications—with traditional forensic data (e.g., DNA, fingerprint, and toxicology records) to reconstruct timelines and interactions in criminal cases. Current methods lack the capacity to process multi-modal data streams efficiently, particularly when addressing time-sensitive investigations involving terabytes of unstructured data from diverse sources. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to deploy machine learning models optimized for forensic contexts. These models will automate pattern recognition across disparate data types, identify correlations between digital and physical evidence, and mitigate biases in probabilistic linkage analysis. Key computational challenges include parallelizing feature extraction from encrypted files, optimizing graph-based algorithms for network analysis, and validating results against legally admissible forensic standards. The project will utilize GPU-accelerated nodes for training deep learning architectures on anonymized case data and CPU clusters for simulating large-scale evidence integration scenarios. Outcomes will include open-source tools for forensic practitioners to prioritize leads, visualize evidence networks, and assess confidence levels in reconstructed event sequences. By enhancing the scalability and reproducibility of digital-physical evidence synthesis, this work aims to establish a benchmark for computational forensics that aligns with evolving legal and ethical requirements while addressing resource constraints in public-sector forensic laboratories.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of the physical, biomedical, and social sciences to the analysis and evaluation of physical evidence, human testimony and criminal suspects. Includes instruction in forensic medicine, forensic dentistry, anthropology, psychology, entomology, pathology, forensic laboratory technology and autopsy procedures, DNA and blood pattern analysis, crime scene analysis, crime scene photography, fingerprint technology, document analysis, witness and suspect examination procedures, applicable law and regulations, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and validate computational models aimed at optimizing respiratory care protocols for patients with heterogeneous lung pathologies. A critical challenge in respiratory therapy is tailoring ventilator settings and aerosolized medication delivery to individual patient physiology, particularly in cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and post-surgical recovery. Current clinical decision-making relies on generalized guidelines, which may not account for the complex interplay of airway mechanics, regional lung compliance, and gas exchange dynamics. To address this, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating patient-specific anatomical data from medical imaging, physiological parameters from clinical monitors, and fluid-structure interaction models to simulate ventilation-perfusion mismatches and drug deposition patterns. The HPC environment will enable large-scale parallelization of finite element analyses for airway biomechanics and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of nebulized particle transport across bifurcating bronchial trees. Machine learning algorithms will be deployed on HPC clusters to identify predictive biomarkers from retrospective clinical datasets, correlating simulated outcomes with real-world patient responses. Expected outcomes include (1) validated models for personalized positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) titration, (2) optimized nebulizer type and particle size selection based on patient-specific airway geometry, and (3) an open-source computational toolkit for respiratory therapy education. By bridging computational engineering with clinical practice, this work aims to reduce ventilator-induced lung injury risks, improve therapeutic efficacy, and provide respiratory therapy students with advanced simulation tools for scenario-based training. The scale of parameter space exploration and real-time coupling of 3D simulations with physiological control systems necessitates dedicated HPC resources to achieve clinically relevant resolutions and throughput.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to administer general respiratory care procedures under the supervision of respiratory therapists in a variety of clinical settings. Includes instruction in patient data collection and monitoring, airway management, installation of nebulizers and other respiratory assistance devices, application and monitoring of breathing gases, equipment operation and maintenance, safety and sanitation procedures, and applicable regulations.

abstract: Regulatory science faces a critical challenge in evaluating complex, rapidly evolving medical technologies—such as AI-driven diagnostics or gene-edited therapies—where traditional approval frameworks struggle to balance safety, efficacy, and innovation. This project proposes a computational approach to model and simulate regulatory decision pathways for emerging technologies, enabling data-driven policy optimization. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we will develop agent-based models (ABMs) to simulate interactions between regulators, developers, and clinical trial data streams under varying regulatory scenarios. These ABMs will integrate real-world FDA submission datasets, synthetic clinical trial data generated via generative adversarial networks (GANs), and dynamic risk-benefit algorithms that account for evolving post-market evidence. A parallelized computational workflow will assess thousands of regulatory parameter combinations (e.g., evidence thresholds, adaptive trial designs, real-world evidence integration protocols) to identify optimal pathways that minimize time-to-decision while maintaining safety standards. Validation will involve retrospective analysis of historical device/drug approvals and forward-looking case studies on AI-based medical imaging systems. The HPC environment is essential for scaling Monte Carlo simulations across multidimensional parameter spaces and managing petabytes of structured/unstructured regulatory document data. Outcomes will include an open-source computational toolkit for predictive regulatory analytics, quantitative benchmarks for evidence requirements in novel technology domains, and policy recommendations for adaptive licensing frameworks. This work aims to transform regulatory science into a proactive, simulation-informed discipline capable of accelerating patient access to breakthrough technologies without compromising scientific rigor.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to manage the regulatory process for companies innovating and developing cutting edge products in science, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, and medicine. Includes instruction in regulatory affairs, clinical documentation, human and animal subject protection, Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations, data management and analysis, good manufacturing practices, and quality management.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a high-fidelity computational framework to optimize energy system efficiency in mixed-use urban environments, addressing the critical challenge of balancing energy demand, cost, and sustainability in rapidly evolving grids. Current energy system models often lack the resolution to account for dynamic interactions between building-scale consumption patterns, renewable energy integration, and grid stability, particularly in regions with aging infrastructure. To bridge this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement a multi-layered simulation approach integrating building energy models, machine learning-driven demand forecasting, and transient grid stability analysis. The computational workflow will utilize parallelized finite element simulations to model heat transfer and electromechanical losses in distribution networks, coupled with reinforcement learning algorithms to optimize real-time energy dispatch strategies. Large-scale datasets from IoT-enabled sensors across three pilot districts will inform boundary conditions and validation protocols. The HPC environment is essential for handling the project’s scale, which involves ~10^6 degree-of-freedom thermal models, minute-resolution time-series analysis across 5-year weather datasets, and Monte Carlo simulations assessing 10,000+ stochastic demand scenarios. Expected outcomes include a validated open-source toolkit for municipal energy planners, identifying infrastructure retrofit priorities that reduce aggregate energy losses by 15–25% in test cases, and policy-ready metrics for renewable penetration thresholds under dynamic pricing regimes. By enabling previously intractable resolutions of temporal-spatial tradeoffs in district-scale systems, this work aims to directly support decarbonization goals while maintaining grid reliability—a cornerstone challenge in modern energy systems technology. The requested resources will accelerate parameter optimization phases by 8–10x compared to local cluster capabilities, ensuring robust results within grant timelines.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and other professionals engaged in developing energy-efficient systems or monitoring energy use. Includes instruction in principles of energy conservation, instrumentation calibration, monitoring systems and test procedures, energy loss inspection procedures, energy conservation techniques, and report preparation.

abstract: The increasing demand for sustainable energy technologies necessitates advancements in controlled nuclear fusion, where plasma confinement and stability remain critical challenges. This project seeks to develop high-fidelity simulations of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) instabilities in tokamak plasmas, specifically addressing the interplay between edge-localized modes (ELMs) and turbulent transport. Current predictive models lack the resolution to capture multiscale interactions between global MHD phenomena and localized turbulence, limiting their accuracy in experimental scenarios. To bridge this gap, we propose a hybrid computational framework combining 3D nonlinear MHD simulations with gyrokinetic turbulence modeling, enabled by high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The simulations will leverage adaptive mesh refinement to resolve boundary layer dynamics near plasma-facing components while maintaining global stability constraints. A key innovation involves coupling the NIMROD code for MHD with the GENE code for microturbulence via a novel iterative interface, which requires parallelization across thousands of CPU cores to manage memory-intensive data exchanges. The HPC allocation will support parameter scans across magnetic configuration space, including varying triangularity and safety factor profiles, to identify optimal regimes for ELM suppression. Expected outcomes include (1) validated predictive criteria for instability thresholds under reactor-relevant conditions, (2) quantitative analysis of heat flux patterns on divertor surfaces, and (3) open-source release of optimized coupling algorithms for the fusion modeling community. By elucidating multiscale plasma behavior, this work will directly inform the design of next-generation fusion devices, accelerating progress toward commercially viable fusion energy. The computational demands—exceeding 2 million core-hours annually—necessitate dedicated HPC allocations to achieve the required spatiotemporal resolution and statistical convergence.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of physics to a technical discipline or with the interface between physics and other disciplines.

abstract: This project seeks to develop computational models to optimize the design, fabrication, and acoustic performance of musical instruments, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address challenges in material science, structural dynamics, and sound engineering. Traditional instrument fabrication relies heavily on empirical methods and artisan expertise, which, while effective, limit systematic exploration of novel materials, geometries, and repair techniques. The research problem centers on overcoming these limitations by simulating complex physical interactions—such as vibrational modes in stringed instruments, airflow dynamics in woodwinds, and stress distribution in joint structures—to inform data-driven design and repair protocols. Computational methods will include finite element analysis (FEA) for stress and resonance modeling, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for air column behavior in wind instruments, and machine learning algorithms trained on acoustic datasets to predict optimal material pairings and structural adjustments. High-resolution simulations of multi-scale phenomena, such as the interaction of varnish layers with wood substrates in violins or the effects of microfractures on tonal quality in brass instruments, require parallelized processing and large-scale memory allocation. The project will validate models against experimental data from 3D-printed prototypes and sensor-equipped instruments. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for custom instrument fabrication, improved repair workflows for degraded or damaged instruments, and a public database of material acoustic properties to support makers and conservators. By bridging computational engineering with craft-based disciplines, this work aims to advance sustainable practices through material optimization, extend the lifespan of historical instruments, and democratize access to high-precision fabrication insights for educational and professional communities. The requested HPC resources are critical to achieving the necessary resolution and parametric scope for these simulations, which exceed the capacity of local computing infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to make, repair, maintain, and tune acoustic and electric musical instruments. Includes instruction in methods and equipment for making musical instruments, electronic instrument amplification systems, techniques of cleaning, and methods of tuning musical instruments.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address a critical gap in organizational decision-making under volatility, a pervasive challenge in contemporary business environments. Traditional analytical models often fail to capture the nonlinear dynamics and interdependencies inherent in complex systems, such as global supply chains or adaptive organizational structures. To overcome this limitation, the project employs large-scale agent-based modeling (ABM) simulations to analyze how firms can optimize resource allocation and strategic flexibility in the face of stochastic disruptions, including market shocks, geopolitical risks, and technological discontinuities. The computational framework integrates heterogeneous agents representing stakeholders, competitors, and environmental factors, with behavioral parameters derived from empirical datasets spanning 15 industries. Key methodological innovations include parallelized Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses to quantify uncertainty propagation and machine learning-driven scenario clustering to identify robust decision pathways. The proposed HPC infrastructure will enable simulations at unprecedented scales—up to 10^6 agents with dynamically evolving interaction networks—while maintaining temporal granularity for multi-year strategic horizons. Anticipated outcomes include (1) a validated open-source ABM toolkit for enterprise resilience planning, (2) empirically grounded thresholds for strategic flexibility investments across organizational archetypes, and (3) policy matrices linking computational findings to real-world decision protocols. By bridging complexity theory and computational management science, this work aims to establish new standards for data-driven organizational design while demonstrating how HPC capabilities can transform traditional business strategy paradigms. The resource request prioritizes GPU-accelerated nodes for neural network training within the ABM framework and high-memory nodes for real-time optimization of multi-objective decision surfaces.
cip_title: Business Administration, Management and Operations, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in business and administration, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project addresses the challenge of optimizing real-time photorealistic rendering for large-scale, dynamic virtual environments by integrating perceptual models of human vision with adaptive computational resource allocation. Traditional rendering pipelines prioritize geometric and physical accuracy, often consuming excessive computational resources to generate details imperceptible to human observers under specific viewing conditions. The proposed work bridges computer graphics, visual perception psychology, and high-performance computing to develop a novel framework that dynamically allocates rendering effort based on perceptual saliency metrics. The core computational methodology combines Monte Carlo path tracing with neural gaze prediction models and foveated rendering techniques, requiring iterative simulations across diverse scene complexities and viewer behavior patterns. High-performance computing resources are essential for training perception-aware quality assessment models using multi-terabyte datasets of eye-tracking data and rendered sequences, as well as for parallelized testing of adaptive algorithms across parameter spaces. Expected outcomes include a publicly available benchmark suite quantifying perceptual efficiency gains, open-source implementations of perception-driven resource distribution algorithms, and guidelines for hardware-accelerated rendering architectures. This work advances the frontier of computationally sustainable graphics by establishing systematic methods to align rendering expenditure with human visual capabilities, with potential applications in extended reality systems, autonomous vehicle simulations, and immersive telepresence environments requiring both high fidelity and energy efficiency.
