To address this gap, we propose the development of a high-fidelity, agent-based simulation platform that models passenger behavior, crew interactions, and environmental factors under diverse emergency conditions. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute large-scale Monte Carlo simulations that incorporate probabilistic human decision-making algorithms, real-time physiological stress responses, and multi-agent coordination dynamics. The computational framework will integrate machine learning techniques to analyze historical incident data, optimizing evacuation pathways and crew resource management strategies. Key outcomes include the identification of critical failure points in existing protocols, data-driven recommendations for procedural updates, and the creation of adaptive training modules that respond to simulated passenger demographics and aircraft configurations. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this project will generate granular insights into time-sensitive decision-making processes, enabling flight attendants to mitigate risks more effectively. The resulting models will be validated against empirical data from partner airlines, ensuring practical relevance. This work directly aligns with aviation safety imperatives, offering scalable tools to reduce human error, improve emergency preparedness, and ultimately save lives in crisis scenarios. The computational demands—including parallel processing of thousands of stochastic simulations and real-time rendering of 3D cabin environments—necessitate dedicated access to GPU-accelerated clusters and large-memory nodes.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to the performance of a variety of personal services conducive to the safety and comfort of airline passengers during flight, including verifying tickets, explaining the use of safety equipment, providing passenger services, and responding to in-flight emergencies.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the biomechanical and molecular mechanisms underlying osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) for chronic musculoskeletal pain syndromes, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model multiscale physiological interactions. While OMT is clinically effective for conditions like chronic low back pain, its systemic effects—spanning cellular mechanotransduction, inflammatory modulation, and neural network adaptation—remain poorly quantified. Current limitations stem from the inability to integrate heterogeneous datasets (e.g., force kinetics from OMT interventions, proteomic profiles, and functional MRI data) into unified dynamical models. The research problem centers on resolving how localized mechanical stimuli during OMT propagate biophysical signals across tissue, organ, and systemic scales to produce therapeutic outcomes. We propose a computational pipeline combining molecular dynamics simulations of mechanosensitive ion channels, finite element modeling of fascial strain distribution, and graph-based neural network analysis of pain modulation pathways. HPC resources will enable high-throughput simulations of protein conformational changes under varying mechanical loads, agent-based modeling of immune cell recruitment in response to simulated fascial deformation, and machine learning-driven integration of multi-omic datasets from patient cohorts. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework linking OMT parameters (e.g., force vector, duration) to molecular and systemic responses, identifying biomarkers for treatment optimization. This work will advance osteopathic medicine by providing mechanistic validation of holistic treatment principles and establishing computational tools for personalized OMT protocol design. The project’s interdisciplinary approach—bridging biomechanics, systems biology, and clinical osteopathy—addresses a critical gap in understanding manual therapies through scalable, data-driven models.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of osteopathic medicine, involving a combination of medical principles and procedures and osteopathic principles of holistic medicine and the relationship of the musculoskeletal system to general health. Includes instruction in the basic medical sciences, preventive medicine, family and community medicine, medical informatics, disease systems, organ and physiologic systems, osteopathic principles and practice, osteopathic manipulative treatment, musculoskeletal and skin systems, clinical specialty rotations, medical ethics, and professional standards and practice management.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in dynamic resource allocation for distributed computing systems, a critical challenge in modern computing environments where heterogeneous workloads and fluctuating demands strain traditional static allocation models. Current approaches often lack the responsiveness needed to optimize hardware utilization, leading to energy waste, latency spikes, and underprovisioning risks in applications ranging from cloud services to edge computing networks. To overcome these limitations, we propose developing an adaptive resource management framework that integrates real-time telemetry data with predictive machine learning models. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate large-scale distributed systems under diverse workload scenarios, training neural networks to forecast resource needs while accounting for hardware constraints and energy efficiency targets. Computational experiments will evaluate allocation strategies across simulated data center architectures and IoT-edge configurations, measuring metrics including task completion times, energy consumption, and fault tolerance. By iteratively refining models through GPU-accelerated training and validation cycles, the project aims to produce allocation algorithms capable of reducing resource overprovisioning by ≥30% in benchmark tests while maintaining service-level agreements. Outcomes will include open-source optimization tools compatible with container orchestration platforms and a reference architecture for intelligent resource scheduling. This work directly supports the Engineering Technologies field by advancing practical methodologies for maintaining complex computer systems, with applications in industrial automation, smart infrastructure, and scalable computing education platforms. Successful implementation could lower operational costs for computing infrastructure providers while improving the sustainability of large-scale deployments.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of professionals who use computer systems. Includes instruction in basic computer design and architecture, programming, problems of specific computer applications, component and system maintenance and inspection procedures, hardware and software problem diagnosis and repair, and report preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in understanding the dynamics of T cell receptor (TCR) signaling heterogeneity and its role in immune dysregulation during chronic viral infections. While advances in single-cell technologies have revealed transcriptional diversity among T cell populations, the computational integration of multi-omics datasets (e.g., TCR repertoire sequencing, epigenetic profiling, and cytokine secretion data) remains a bottleneck. Current models lack the resolution to map how stochastic variations in TCR signaling thresholds influence clonal expansion, exhaustion, or anergy—key determinants of adaptive immune failure. To bridge this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework combining agent-based modeling of TCR-peptide-MHC interactions with Bayesian inference of signaling network dynamics. Simulations will parameterize kinetic rates of kinase activation, co-receptor recruitment, and feedback inhibition using existing proteomic datasets from influenza- and HIV-specific CD8+ T cells. Parallelized parameter sweeps will quantify how signaling noise propagates to transcriptional variability, linking in silico predictions to experimental single-cell RNA-seq datasets from patient-derived T cells. Additionally, we will employ graph neural networks to classify TCR sequences associated with functional exhaustion versus sustained cytotoxicity, training on structurally resolved TCR-antigen complexes from public databases. The HPC environment is essential for scaling these analyses to millions of TCR clonotypes and simulating spatial-temporal signaling events at physiological timescales. Expected outcomes include a predictive atlas of TCR signaling states that stratify infection outcomes and identify molecular checkpoints amenable to immunotherapeutic intervention. This work will directly inform translational efforts to reprogram exhausted T cells in chronic infections and autoimmune disorders, aligning with the program's focus on host-pathogen interactions and immune response regulation. The computational pipelines developed will be disseminated as open-source tools for the immunology community.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on scientific study of the biological mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of disease, host-pathogen interactions, and host response to disease. Includes instruction in antigen and antibody structure and function, effector mechanisms, receptors, histocompatibility, host-pathogen recognition, disease modeling, autoimmune systems, antibody formation, cytotoxic responses, regulation of immune response, virulence determinants, intercellular signaling, immunosuppression, immunotherapy, immunogenetics, disease markers, transplantation, antibody humanization, and microbial pathogenesis.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of urban infrastructure resilience under compound stressors, integrating social behavioral patterns with physical network interdependencies. While traditional urban studies emphasize policy or economic frameworks, this research focuses on computational modeling of human-infrastructure feedback loops during crises such as heatwaves, floods, or grid failures—a niche intersecting computational social science, urban systems engineering, and risk analysis. The core problem lies in understanding how adaptive behaviors (e.g., population mobility, resource-sharing practices) amplify or mitigate cascading infrastructure failures, particularly in underserved neighborhoods where data granularity is limited. The study will employ agent-based modeling (ABM) paired with graph neural networks (GNNs) to simulate multi-scale interactions between residents, critical service providers, and infrastructure nodes (power, water, transit) across a synthetic urban environment calibrated to real-world demographic and geospatial data. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve stochastic simulations at city-block resolution over multi-week event horizons, incorporating high-dimensional parameters for social vulnerability indices and infrastructure decay rates. Computational workflows will leverage containerized ensembles to test intervention scenarios, including decentralized microgrid adoption and mobile service deployment strategies. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible simulation framework for evaluating equity-focused resilience policies, alongside empirical insights into threshold effects linking collective action to systemic recovery trajectories. By quantifying latent synergies between social cohesion and infrastructure redundancy, this work aims to advance predictive tools for urban planners operating in multi-hazard environments while contributing methodological innovations in coupling ABM with GNN-based anomaly detection. The project will generate open-source code repositories and curated training datasets to support replication in diverse urban contexts.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of social science principles to the study of urban institutions and the forces influencing urban social and political life. Includes instruction in urban theory, the development and evolution of urban areas, urban sociology, principles of urban and social planning, and the politics and economics of urban government and services.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize precision machining and material performance in internal combustion engines, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical challenges in engine durability, efficiency, and emissions. Modern engine design requires balancing competing demands of thermal efficiency, mechanical stress tolerance, and emission control, particularly in commercial and high-performance automotive applications. Traditional experimental approaches to component testing—such as cylinder head crack propagation analysis, crankshaft fatigue modeling, or piston-cylinder thermal deformation studies—are constrained by cost, time, and the inability to capture multi-physics interactions at operational scales. This research will employ finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to model stress distributions, heat transfer, and fluid-structure interactions in engine components under dynamic operating conditions. HPC resources will enable high-resolution simulations of microstructural material behavior during machining processes (e.g., cylinder block surface finishing) and operational cycles, integrating machine learning algorithms to predict wear patterns and optimize component geometries. Key focus areas include simulating the effects of machining tolerances on combustion efficiency, evaluating novel alloy performance under cyclic thermal loads, and validating computational models against experimental data from engine dynamometer tests. The anticipated outcomes include a predictive toolkit for identifying failure-prone geometries, reducing iterative prototyping costs, and informing curriculum updates in engine machining programs with data-driven design principles. By bridging computational engineering and hands-on machinist training, this work aims to advance sustainable engine technologies while preparing technicians for emerging digital manufacturing workflows. The scalability of these models will directly benefit industry partners seeking to accelerate the development of low-emission diesel and hybrid engines.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to the building and reconstruction of automotive and commercial vehicle engines. Includes instruction in cylinder head and block, crack repair, crankshaft inspection and repair, connecting rods and pistons, balancing, block preparation, disassembly and repair, engine assembly, gas and diesel technology, and inspection and machining.

abstract: The increasing complexity of modern security systems, which integrate multi-sensor networks, real-time data processing, and adaptive threat detection algorithms, necessitates advanced computational approaches to optimize their design, deployment, and maintenance. Current industry practices for installing and configuring security systems often rely on heuristic methods, leading to suboptimal sensor placement, inefficient resource allocation, and elevated rates of false alarms. This project seeks to address these challenges by developing a computational framework that leverages high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate, analyze, and optimize security system configurations across diverse environments. The research will employ agent-based modeling to simulate intruder behaviors and environmental interactions, coupled with machine learning algorithms trained on synthetic and real-world datasets to predict system vulnerabilities and failure modes. Monte Carlo simulations will assess probabilistic threat scenarios, while parallelized optimization routines will determine ideal sensor placements and alarm thresholds. The computational workload demands scalable processing capabilities due to the high dimensionality of parameter spaces and real-time data throughput requirements. By utilizing HPC resources, the project aims to generate actionable insights for technicians, including prescriptive installation guidelines, adaptive repair protocols, and predictive inspection schedules. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible simulation toolkit for training purposes, quantitative performance benchmarks for common security system architectures, and novel algorithms to reduce false positive rates by at least 30% in tested configurations. This work will directly enhance the technical rigor of security system education programs while providing industry stakeholders with evidence-based strategies to improve system reliability and cost-effectiveness.
cip_title: Security System Installation, Repair, and Inspection Technology/ Technician
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to install and repair household, business, and industrial security alarms, sensors, video and sound recording devices, identification systems, protective barriers, and related technologies.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of multigenerational family systems under stress using advanced computational modeling, with a focus on understanding resilience patterns and systemic feedback loops. Family systems, as complex adaptive systems, exhibit nonlinear interactions influenced by cultural, psychological, and socioeconomic variables. Traditional qualitative or survey-based methods often struggle to capture these interdependencies at scale, particularly when analyzing longitudinal or cross-cultural data. To address this gap, we propose developing an agent-based model (ABM) simulating family decision-making processes, emotional transmission, and resource-sharing behaviors across generations. The model will integrate empirical datasets from sociology and psychology, including trauma response metrics, household economic data, and intergenerational communication patterns. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to parameterize thousands of family archetypes, run Monte Carlo simulations testing intervention scenarios (e.g., policy changes, therapeutic approaches), and perform sensitivity analyses on emergent system behaviors. Computational challenges include managing stochastic interactions among agents with heterogeneous belief systems, scaling network analyses for extended kinship structures, and processing high-dimensional time-series outputs. Expected outcomes include identifying critical leverage points for enhancing family resilience, quantifying the systemic impacts of socioeconomic policies on family cohesion, and generating predictive frameworks for risk stratification in social work contexts. This work bridges computational social science with family systems theory, offering a novel methodology for studying relational dynamics that could inform both clinical practice and policymaking. The resulting open-source simulation toolkit will provide a foundation for interdisciplinary research into complex familial interactions that traditional disciplinary approaches cannot adequately model.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the family as a social unit in its developmental, dynamic, comparative, and structural aspects, and the significance of the family as a system that impacts individuals and society. Includes instruction in related principles of sociology, psychology, behavioral sciences, and the humanities.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model the dynamics of urban crime hotspots and evaluate decentralized policing strategies under varying social and environmental conditions. While traditional crime analysis often relies on static spatial data, this research integrates real-time sensor data, anonymized mobility patterns, and community-reported incident logs to simulate emergent crime dynamics at an unprecedented granularity. The core challenge lies in processing heterogeneous, high-velocity datasets spanning law enforcement records (10+ TB/month), environmental sensor feeds (air quality, lighting infrastructure status), and geotagged social media sentiment to identify latent predictors of criminal activity. Using agent-based modeling enhanced with graph neural networks, we will simulate interactions between potential offenders, bystanders, and patrol units across a synthetic urban environment calibrated with multi-year crime statistics from three metropolitan regions. High-performance computing resources are critical for running parallelized Monte Carlo simulations to test how resource allocation strategies—such as fluctuating patrol densities or community-led surveillance initiatives—affect both crime displacement patterns and public trust metrics. The computational pipeline leverages containerized workflows for data fusion, dynamic graph construction, and reinforcement learning-based policy optimization. Expected outcomes include a validated open-source toolkit for scenario-based policing strategy analysis and evidence-based recommendations for balancing predictive policing efficacy with procedural justice considerations. By quantifying how minor adjustments in patrol distribution influence long-term community perceptions of safety, this work aims to bridge gaps between computational criminology theory and adaptive policy design, offering municipal agencies a decision-support system responsive to evolving urban landscapes.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the criminal justice system, its organizational components and processes, and its legal and public policy contexts. Includes instruction in criminal law and policy, police and correctional systems organization, the administration of justice and the judiciary, and public attitudes regarding criminal justice issues.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of information dissemination across 17th-century European scholarly networks and its impact on political and intellectual developments. Traditional historical methods face challenges in systematically analyzing the vast corpus of surviving correspondence and publications from this period, which includes thousands of letters, pamphlets, and treatises. To address this, the project will employ computational text analysis, social network modeling, and agent-based simulations to reconstruct and analyze the flow of ideas among scholars, institutions, and political actors. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for processing multilingual texts through natural language processing pipelines, identifying semantic patterns, and mapping evolving network connections across temporal and geographic dimensions. The agent-based model will simulate how information spread through these networks under varying sociopolitical constraints, requiring iterative parameter adjustments and large-scale parallel processing. Expected outcomes include the identification of previously unrecognized hubs of intellectual exchange, quantitative assessments of censorship effects on knowledge diffusion, and visualizations of network resilience during key historical events such as the Thirty Years' War. By integrating computational methods with archival research, this study aims to establish a new framework for analyzing historical information ecosystems, providing insights into how networked communication shaped early modern state formation and scientific revolution. The proposed work will also produce open-source tools tailored for historical network analysis, enabling future researchers to apply similar methodologies to other periods and regions. This interdisciplinary approach demonstrates the transformative potential of HPC resources in advancing historical scholarship through large-scale data synthesis and complex systems modeling.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in history, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Aircraft armament systems represent a critical component of modern military operations, requiring precise integration of mechanical, electronic, and computational subsystems. However, current maintenance and operational protocols for these systems rely heavily on static schedules and reactive diagnostics, leading to inefficiencies in resource allocation, unplanned downtime, and potential safety risks. This project proposes the development of a dynamic, data-driven predictive maintenance framework using high-performance computing (HPC) to optimize the lifecycle management of aircraft weapon systems. The research addresses the challenge of processing heterogeneous datasets—including real-time sensor telemetry, historical maintenance logs, environmental corrosion metrics, and component wear simulations—to predict failure modes and prioritize maintenance interventions. Computational methods will integrate machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks to map interdependencies among subsystems) with physics-informed digital twins that simulate stress propagation in composite weapon materials under operational conditions. HPC resources will enable large-scale parameter sweeps to evaluate probabilistic failure scenarios across diverse climatic and operational contexts, as well as parallelized optimization algorithms to balance mission readiness with maintenance costs. Expected outcomes include a scalable decision-support tool capable of reducing unplanned maintenance events by 30–40%, extending component lifespans through corrosion-mitigation strategies, and improving safety compliance by identifying latent risks in aging armament systems. The project’s computational workflows will be designed for interoperability with existing military logistics platforms, ensuring direct applicability to operational environments. By bridging advanced analytics with domain-specific constraints of military technology, this work advances a novel paradigm for sustainment of critical defense infrastructure while aligning with emerging priorities in predictive operational analytics.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the principles, technology and maintenance of aircraft weapons systems and associated peripherals. Includes instruction in basic science and quantitative methods, computer science, electronics, engineering graphics, fluid power, heavy equipment operation, armament systems, weapon materials and processes, weapon safety, corrosion control, aircraft systems maintenance, and maintenance management.

abstract: The proposed research seeks to advance the understanding of reaction mechanisms in catalytic organic transformations through high-fidelity computational modeling, addressing critical gaps in characterizing short-lived intermediates and transition states that are experimentally inaccessible. Current limitations in simulating complex reaction networks—particularly those involving dynamic solvent effects, multi-configurational electronic states, and non-equilibrium conformational sampling—require robust high-performance computing (HPC) resources to achieve the necessary accuracy and timescale resolution. This project will employ quantum mechanical (QM) methods, including density functional theory (DFT) and coupled-cluster theory, to model electronic structures, combined with ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) to capture solvation and entropy effects. Enhanced sampling techniques, such as metadynamics and umbrella sampling, will be implemented to map free energy landscapes for key proton-transfer and bond-rearrangement steps. These simulations will integrate with experimental kinetic data from collaborators to validate predicted activation barriers and intermediate lifetimes. The computational workflow will leverage GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry packages (e.g., CP2K, ORCA) and custom Python scripts for automated trajectory analysis, necessitating large-scale parallelization and extensive memory allocation. Expected outcomes include (1) atomistic insights into solvent-mediated selectivity in asymmetric catalysis, (2) predictive models for optimizing catalyst design, and (3) open-access datasets of simulated reaction coordinates to support machine learning initiatives in reaction prediction. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling the 10^4–10^5 core-hour demands of multi-scale simulations, enabling statistically rigorous sampling across conformational and electronic degrees of freedom. This work will directly inform experimental efforts in sustainable chemistry while developing transferable protocols for merging mechanistic theory with real-time spectroscopic data, bridging a persistent gap in computational organic chemistry.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of principals of mathematical algorithms, statistics, and large databases to integrate chemical theory and modeling with experimental observations. Includes instruction in chemistry or a related scientific field, computer training, a familiarity with chemical principles, including conformational analysis, acid–base equilibria, physical organic chemistry, molecular structure, thermodynamics, and stereochemistry.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the neurophysiological and biomechanical mechanisms underlying mind-body therapies, such as yoga, tai chi, and somatic movement practices, to establish evidence-based frameworks for optimizing therapeutic protocols. Despite widespread application, the integrative effects of these therapies on dynamic body-brain interactions remain poorly quantified, particularly in diverse populations. To address this gap, we propose a computational study combining motion capture data, physiological monitoring (e.g., EEG, heart rate variability), and patient-reported outcomes to model how specific movement sequences and mindfulness practices modulate stress responses, motor control, and cognitive-emotional states. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process and integrate multi-modal datasets spanning terabytes of kinematic, neuroimaging, and biometric data. Machine learning pipelines will be developed to identify patterns linking movement quality, autonomic nervous system activity, and self-reported well-being, while finite element modeling will simulate tissue stress distributions during therapeutic movements to assess injury risk and biomechanical efficiency. Agent-based models will further explore how individualized movement adaptations influence long-term neuroplasticity. Expected outcomes include predictive algorithms to personalize mind-body interventions for chronic pain and anxiety populations, as well as open-source tools for educators to design safer, more effective training programs. By quantifying previously anecdotal therapeutic principles, this work aims to advance rigor in movement therapy research and expand access to precision-based mind-body health strategies. The scale of data aggregation and concurrent simulations necessitates HPC capabilities to achieve real-time analysis and iterative model refinement, which are infeasible with standard laboratory computing infrastructure.
cip_title: Movement and Mind-Body Therapies and Education, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in movement and mind-body therapies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze large-scale media datasets and model the dissemination of science, health, and environmental narratives across digital platforms. Journalists in these fields face challenges in tracking how complex issues—such as climate change impacts, public health crises, or emerging technologies—are framed, amplified, or distorted through social networks and media ecosystems. Current tools for analyzing media discourse often lack the scalability to process terabytes of unstructured text, video, and social media data, limiting researchers’ ability to identify patterns of misinformation, partisan bias, or public engagement gaps. This project addresses these limitations by developing computational workflows to map narrative networks, quantify sentiment shifts, and simulate the spread of information under varying editorial or algorithmic conditions. Methods include natural language processing (NLP) pipelines for topic modeling and entity recognition, graph-based algorithms to trace cross-platform content diffusion, and agent-based models to test how journalistic interventions alter public perception. HPC resources are critical for training transformer-based models on diverse corpora (e.g., news archives, Twitter/X threads, broadcast transcripts) and running parallelized simulations of information ecosystems. Anticipated outcomes include (1) a publicly accessible framework for analyzing science and environmental journalism at scale, (2) evidence-based insights into how editorial practices interact with algorithmic amplification, and (3) actionable recommendations for improving the accuracy and reach of science communication. By enabling real-time analysis of global media landscapes, this work will equip journalists, educators, and policymakers with tools to counter misinformation and enhance public discourse on critical scientific and environmental issues.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on reporting on science, health, or environmental policy issues; investigating environmental problems and their causes; and public relations. Includes instruction in communication law, health reporting skills, interactive journalism, integrated marketing communication, journalism methods, media ethics, persuasion and political communication, science, health and the environment, social marketing, and video journalism.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) to optimize medication dispensing workflows in community pharmacy settings, with a focus on mitigating human error risks inherent to pharmacy technician roles. Despite advancements in pharmacy automation, error rates in medication dispensing remain a critical concern, with workflow complexity, interruptions, and time pressures disproportionately impacting technician-driven tasks. Current approaches rely on retrospective error analysis, limiting proactive intervention. We propose a computational framework integrating agent-based modeling (ABM) and machine learning (ML) to simulate real-world pharmacy environments, model technician-patient-pharmacist interactions, and predict error-prone scenarios. The ABM component will incorporate dynamic variables such as prescription volume, staffing ratios, and task prioritization protocols, while ML algorithms trained on anonymized dispensing error datasets will identify latent risk patterns. HPC resources are essential to process high-dimensional data streams from simulated workflows (e.g., 10,000+ parallelized scenarios) and optimize hyperparameters for ensemble ML models. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated predictive model for dispensing error hotspots, (2) evidence-based workflow redesign recommendations to reduce cognitive load, and (3) an open-source simulation toolkit for adaptive training module development. By bridging computational science and pharmacy operations, this work addresses an unmet need in patient safety research, offering scalable solutions to enhance technician performance without expanding traditional clinical or pharmaceutical science domains. The resulting tools will directly inform competency frameworks for pharmacy technician education programs while advancing methodological synergies between health systems engineering and frontline healthcare delivery.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of pharmacists, to prepare medications, provide medications and related assistance to patients, and manage pharmacy clinical and business operations. Includes instruction in medical and pharmaceutical terminology, principles of pharmacology and pharmaceutics, drug identification, pharmacy laboratory procedures, prescription interpretation, patient communication and education, safety procedures, record-keeping, measurement and testing techniques, pharmacy business operations, prescription preparation, logistics and dispensing operations, and applicable standards and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the understanding of quantum reaction dynamics in heterogeneous chemical systems, a critical challenge in chemical physics where traditional experimental methods struggle to resolve atomistic details of short-lived intermediates and transition states. We aim to computationally model nonadiabatic energy transfer processes at molecule-surface interfaces and solvated environments, systems central to catalytic and photochemical applications. Current limitations in simulating such processes stem from the high computational cost of accurately treating coupled electronic and nuclear motion across multiple scales while preserving quantum coherence effects. To address this, we propose a hybrid computational framework combining real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) with trajectory surface hopping dynamics, accelerated by machine-learned potential energy surfaces. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute massively parallel simulations of molecular ensembles under varying interfacial geometries and thermodynamic conditions. The allocation will enable large-scale ab initio calculations using software packages like Q-Chem and in-house modified versions of LAMMPS, which are optimized for GPU-accelerated architectures. Key deliverables include quantitative predictions of solvent-mediated charge transfer rates in metal-organic complexes and surface-alignment effects on reaction branching ratios in photocatalysis. These results will directly test recent theoretical predictions about the role of decoherence in suppressing unwanted recombination pathways at interfaces. The outcomes will provide foundational insights for designing energy-efficient catalytic systems and advance methodological standards for simulating quantum dynamics in spatially inhomogeneous environments. By integrating chemical physics principles with scalable computational workflows, this work bridges critical gaps between quantum mechanical accuracy and mesoscale phenomena relevant to next-generation chemical technologies.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of structural phenomena combining the disciplines of physical chemistry and atomic/molecular physics. Includes instruction in heterogeneous structures, alignment and surface phenomena, quantum theory, mathematical physics, statistical and classical mechanics, chemical kinetics, and laser physics.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in understanding the role of structural genomic variation (SGV) in shaping complex traits and adaptation in domesticated and wild animal populations. While single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are well-studied in animal genetics, the contribution of large-scale structural variants—including deletions, duplications, inversions, and translocations—to phenotypic diversity, fitness, and evolutionary trajectories remains poorly characterized. Current limitations stem from the computational complexity of detecting SGV across diverse genomes and modeling its interactions with regulatory elements. We propose a multi-stage computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze whole-genome sequencing data from 15 agriculturally and ecologically significant animal species, including bovids, equids, and avian taxa. Long-read sequencing datasets will be processed using scalable alignment and variant-calling pipelines optimized for distributed memory architectures. Graph-based pan-genome representations will be constructed to capture population-level SGV, followed by integrative analyses linking variants to gene expression datasets (RNA-seq, ATAC-seq) and trait databases. To model evolutionary dynamics, spatially explicit forward-time simulations will quantify how recombination rates, selection pressures, and demography interact to shape SGV distributions. Machine learning models trained on these outputs will predict the functional impact of structural variants on development, metabolism, and disease resilience. This work will establish novel computational workflows for SGV analysis in non-model organisms, identify candidate structural variants underlying key domestication and adaptation phenotypes, and provide comparative insights into the evolutionary constraints shaping animal genomes. The requested HPC resources are essential for managing data storage (~500 TB), parallelizing genome-wide analyses, and running computationally intensive simulations. Outcomes will directly inform selective breeding programs, conservation strategies, and biomedical models of human genetic disorders with structural variant etiologies.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the genetics of multicellular animal life forms from the experimental, comparative, and clinical (veterinary and medical) viewpoints. Includes instruction in molecular genetics, gene expression, gene regulation, genomics, epigenetic phenomena, DNA recombination and repair, genetic interactions at the microbial and higher levels, and molecular evolution.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research on optimizing persuasive communication strategies in dynamic digital environments. Public relations and advertising campaigns increasingly rely on real-time analysis of multi-modal datasets—including social media interactions, consumer behavior metrics, and sentiment trends—to tailor messages for diverse audiences. However, traditional computational tools struggle to process these datasets at scale, limiting the ability to model complex audience responses or predict the cascading effects of messaging across platforms. This research addresses this gap by developing machine learning models to analyze how message framing, visual rhetoric, and platform-specific dynamics collectively influence engagement and persuasion outcomes. The computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) for text-based content, computer vision techniques for image/video analysis, and graph-based algorithms to map information diffusion networks. These methods require parallelized processing of terabytes of heterogeneous data, including historical campaign archives and real-time social media streams, to train deep learning architectures (e.g., transformer-based models) for predictive and prescriptive analytics. By simulating audience segmentation scenarios and A/B testing message variants in virtual environments, the project aims to identify optimal strategies for maximizing reach and impact while minimizing unintended consequences, such as misinformation amplification. Outcomes will provide actionable frameworks for adaptive communication design, enabling practitioners to dynamically adjust campaigns based on computational insights. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling memory-intensive workloads, reducing model training times, and scaling analyses to global audience datasets. This work bridges computational innovation with communication theory, offering novel methodologies for data-driven persuasion research in non-technical academic domains.
detailed_field: Applied communication, advertising, and public relations
cip_title: Public Relations, Advertising, and Applied Communication
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on organizational communication, public relations, and advertising; and that prepares individuals to function in a wide range of public and private sector positions requiring the skills of persuasive communication. Includes instruction in communications, public relations, and advertising theory; principles and techniques of persuasion; message/image design; marketing strategy; professional writing; public speaking and multi-media presentation skills; digital communications; and applied research.

abstract: This project seeks to develop an integrated modeling framework to evaluate the effectiveness of renewable energy transition policies under climate change uncertainties, with a focus on grid reliability, economic feasibility, and emissions reduction targets. As nations commit to decarbonization, policymakers face critical challenges in balancing intermittent renewable energy integration, storage needs, and fossil fuel phase-out timelines while maintaining energy security. Current models often lack the spatial-temporal resolution to capture localized climate impacts on energy demand and supply, limiting their utility for region-specific policy design. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled system dynamics model coupled with machine learning techniques. The framework will simulate hourly energy demand patterns under diverse climate scenarios (RCP 2.6, 4.5, 6.0), incorporating granular weather data, infrastructure degradation risks, and evolving technology costs. Agent-based modeling components will assess market responses to carbon pricing and renewable subsidies, while optimization algorithms will identify cost-minimized pathways for grid storage deployment. The HPC infrastructure is essential for processing multi-petabyte climate datasets from CMIP6, running Monte Carlo simulations across 50+ policy combinations, and resolving nonlinear interactions between energy systems and environmental constraints at 1km² resolution. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible policy decision tool that quantifies trade-offs between emission reduction timelines, grid stability, and socioeconomic costs across different governance structures. This work will directly inform national climate action plans by identifying resilient energy portfolios that align with Paris Agreement targets while mitigating risks of stranded assets. The computational outputs will advance methodological integration of environmental economics with climate science, providing novel insights into the spatial justice implications of energy transitions.
detailed_field: Environmental/ natural resources management and policy
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the systematic analysis of public policy issues related to climate change, energy policy, environmental economics, global sustainability, and security. Includes instruction in climate change, clean energy technologies, environmental policy, environmental law, environmental economics, food security, fossil fuels, renewable and sustainable energy sources, and water issues.

abstract: Climate change and evolving agricultural practices are driving rapid shifts in pest population dynamics, exacerbating challenges in managing pesticide resistance and non-target species impacts. Current pest management strategies often rely on reactive, generalized approaches, leading to excessive chemical use, environmental contamination, and economic losses. This project proposes to develop a predictive, multi-scale computational framework to optimize integrated pest management (IPM) strategies by modeling pest behavior, evolutionary trajectories, and intervention efficacy. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will integrate agent-based modeling (ABM) with machine learning (ML) to simulate pest population responses to environmental variables, host plant interactions, and control tactics across spatial and temporal scales. Genomic data from pest species will inform resistance gene spread models, while convolutional neural networks (CNNs) will process remote sensing data to map weed infestations and habitat suitability. Molecular dynamics simulations will assess candidate biopesticides for target specificity and degradation profiles, reducing non-target effects. The computational workflow demands parallelized processing of large ecological datasets, real-time parameter optimization, and ensemble modeling to quantify uncertainty. Expected outcomes include predictive tools to prioritize region-specific IPM combinations, identify resistance mitigation thresholds, and design precision spraying protocols. This work will advance adaptive pest management systems that minimize chemical inputs while maintaining crop yields, directly supporting agricultural resilience. By bridging entomology, plant pathology, and computational science, the project will generate open-source models and training resources for the plant protection research community. Resource allocation is critical for scaling simulations across representative agroecosystems and validating models against experimental field trials.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_title: Plant Protection and Integrated Pest Management
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of scientific principles to the control of animal, insect and weed infestation of domesticated plant populations and other settings, including agricultural crops; the prevention/reduction of attendant economic loss; and the control of environmental pollution and degradation related to pest infestation and pest control measures. Includes instruction in entomology, applicable animal sciences, plant pathology and physiology, weed science, crop science, and environmental toxicology.

abstract: This project seeks to evaluate the economic efficiency of conservation policies under climate change uncertainty by developing an integrated modeling framework that combines dynamic econometric analysis, high-resolution climate projections, and large-scale optimization. Existing approaches often oversimplify spatial-temporal interactions between ecological systems and economic behavior, limiting their capacity to inform adaptive resource management. The research will address this gap by constructing a computationally intensive model that simulates decentralized decision-making by agricultural and industrial agents under shifting climate regimes, while incorporating feedbacks between regional biodiversity loss, land use change, and ecosystem service valuation. The computational methodology employs parallelized Monte Carlo simulations to quantify policy impacts across 10,000+ stochastic climate scenarios, Bayesian hierarchical models to analyze heterogeneous agent responses derived from satellite land cover data and microeconomic surveys, and evolutionary algorithms to identify Pareto-optimal resource allocation strategies. High-performance computing resources are essential for processing multi-terabyte environmental datasets (including NOAA climate records and ESA Sentinel-2 imagery), solving high-dimensional dynamic optimization problems with non-convex constraints, and running ensemble projections at 1km² resolution across three major U.S. watersheds. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible toolkit for comparing the cost-effectiveness of market-based conservation instruments (e.g., habitat banking, precision irrigation subsidies) under varying climate pathways, with explicit quantification of equity-efficiency trade-offs. Results will advance coupled human-environment systems modeling through novel integration of stochastic dominance analysis and spatially explicit biophysical thresholds, providing actionable insights for agencies managing climate-resilient resource allocation. The computational framework will be designed for scalability to global biodiversity hotspots, with intermediate outputs peer-reviewed in environmental economics journals and presented to the USDA and EPA through policy briefs.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of economic concepts and methods to the analysis of issues such as air and water pollution, land use planning, waste disposal, invasive species and pest control, conservation policies, and related environmental problems. Includes instruction in cost-benefit analysis, environmental impact assessment, evaluation and assessment of alternative resource management strategies, policy evaluation and monitoring, and descriptive and analytic tools for studying how environmental developments affect the economic system.

abstract: The study of xenobiotic metabolism and its role in chemical toxicity remains a critical challenge in pharmacology and toxicology, particularly in predicting adverse drug reactions and environmental toxin bioactivation. Current in vitro and animal models often fail to capture the complexity of human metabolic pathways, enzyme polymorphisms, and tissue-specific responses. This project seeks to develop a computational framework integrating enzyme kinetics, metabolic network modeling, and machine learning to predict biotransformation pathways and toxicity outcomes for structurally diverse xenobiotics. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to simulate large-scale, multi-compartment pharmacokinetic models that account for dynamic enzyme-substrate interactions, competitive inhibition, and tissue-specific expression profiles of cytochrome P450 isoforms and phase II conjugating enzymes. Molecular dynamics simulations will be employed to assess binding affinities of toxicants and their metabolites to critical targets, such as neurotoxicant interactions with ion channels or immunopharmacological effects on cytokine signaling. Additionally, agent-based models will evaluate population-level variability in detoxification capacity influenced by genetic and environmental factors. The computational pipeline will be validated against experimental data from primary hepatocyte cultures and in vivo toxicity studies. Expected outcomes include the identification of high-risk metabolic pathways for industrial chemicals and therapeutics, predictive tools for assessing interindividual susceptibility to chemical toxicity, and mechanistic insights into enzyme-mediated bioactivation of procarcinogens. This work will advance the development of safer pharmaceuticals and evidence-based regulatory guidelines for chemical exposures, directly addressing unmet needs in precision toxicology. The scale of parameter space exploration, real-time integration of heterogeneous datasets, and iterative model optimization necessitate dedicated HPC resources to achieve biologically meaningful resolution within feasible timeframes.
cip_definition: A program with an integrated, combined approach to the study of pharmacological and toxicological issues in biology and the biomedical sciences. Includes instruction in topics such as solvents, xenobiotic metabolism, chemical toxicity, neurotoxicology, immunopharmacology, biotransformation, tissue culture and in vitro studies, biomolecular analysis, bioactivation and inactivation, enzyme regulation, chemoprevention and chemotherapy, industrial and chemical studies, radiation health, and bioinformatics.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model the complex interactions between dietary patterns, nutrient absorption dynamics, and individualized metabolic responses, with the goal of advancing precision nutrition frameworks. Traditional nutritional research often relies on population-level data or simplified in vitro models, which fail to capture the nonlinear, multi-scale interactions between dietary components, gut microbiota, host metabolism, and genetic factors. The computational challenge lies in integrating heterogeneous datasets—including multi-omics profiles, time-series biometric data, and food composition databases—into predictive models that account for individual variability in nutrient utilization and health outcomes. Using agent-based modeling and machine learning techniques, we will simulate nutrient-metabolite interactions at the cellular and systemic levels, parameterized by empirical data from clinical cohorts. Key computational tasks include optimizing differential equation systems for nutrient kinetics, training neural networks on high-dimensional dietary-metabolic associations, and conducting Monte Carlo simulations to assess the robustness of personalized dietary recommendations under varying physiological conditions. The HPC environment is critical for handling the scale of these computations, particularly for parallel processing of stochastic simulations and large-scale parameter sweeps. Expected outcomes include a novel computational platform for dynamically tailoring nutrition interventions based on real-time biomarker feedback, as well as mechanistic insights into how micronutrient synergies or antagonisms influence metabolic health. This work bridges gaps in nutritional systems biology by providing tools to decode the emergent properties of diet-host-microbiome networks, with potential applications in mitigating diet-related chronic diseases and optimizing food product development for diverse populations. By situating computational nutrition within an HPC context, this project aims to establish a methodological foundation for next-generation dietary guidelines that transcend one-size-fits-all paradigms.
cip_title: Foods, Nutrition, and Wellness Studies, General
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the role of foods and nutrition in human health and wellness. Includes instruction in nutritional care and education, the planning and provision of food services, the development of consumable food products, life-span nutrition and wellness, the principles of nutritional assessment, and food safety and food composition.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for advancing high-resolution, large-scale photographic image synthesis and analysis, with a focus on simulating complex lighting environments and optimizing dynamic composition in digital photography. Current approaches to rendering photorealistic scenes with nuanced light interactions—particularly in mixed natural-artificial lighting or multi-spectral conditions—are limited by the computational demands of ray-tracing algorithms and the need for real-time adjustments in composition. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to parallelize physically based rendering workflows, enabling iterative optimization of scene parameters (e.g., light angles, spectral distribution, sensor noise models) at unprecedented scale. The project will employ Monte Carlo path-tracing methods accelerated via GPU clusters, coupled with machine learning models trained on HPC-generated datasets to predict optimal compositional adjustments under variable lighting constraints. A key innovation involves integrating computational photography techniques with generative adversarial networks (GANs) to simulate film-grain textures and chemical development artifacts in digital workflows, bridging historical photographic processes with modern computational tools. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for photographers to prototype complex lighting scenarios in virtual environments, reducing physical trial-and-error in studio setups. Additionally, the computational models will enable novel analyses of archival photographic collections by automating the detection of lighting techniques and material degradation patterns across large image corpora. This work directly supports pedagogical goals in advanced digital photography courses while contributing to interdisciplinary research at the intersection of computational imaging, heritage preservation, and visual arts practice. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling memory-intensive rendering tasks (10–50 GB/scene) and training deep learning models on terabyte-scale image datasets, which exceed the capacity of local departmental hardware.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the principles and techniques of communicating information, ideas, moods, and feelings through the creation of images on photographic film, plates, and digital images and that may prepare individuals to be professional photographic artists. Includes instruction in camera and equipment operation and maintenance, film and plate developing, light and composition, films and printing media, color and special effects, photographic art, photographic history, use of computer applications to record or enhance images and applications to the photography of various subjects.

abstract: Individuals with neuromotor impairments face significant challenges in achieving functional independence due to the limitations of existing assistive technologies, which often lack adaptive responsiveness to dynamic user needs and environmental contexts. This project proposes the development of a machine learning-driven framework to optimize real-time control of hybrid exoskeleton-orthosis systems for upper limb rehabilitation. The research problem centers on overcoming the computational bottlenecks in processing multimodal sensor data—including electromyography, inertial motion capture, and pressure distribution—to generate personalized, context-aware assistance strategies. Current approaches rely on pre-programmed heuristics or simplified physiological models, which fail to accommodate the variability in user intent detection, joint torque requirements, and compensatory movement patterns across diverse impairment profiles. To address this, we will implement a hierarchical reinforcement learning architecture trained on high-fidelity biomechanical simulations derived from clinical motion analysis datasets. The computational workflow requires parallelized training of deep neural networks across multiple GPU nodes to handle the high-dimensional state-action space encompassing musculoskeletal dynamics, device mechanics, and user performance metrics. High-performance computing resources will enable large-scale hyperparameter optimization and validation through synthetic patient digital twins representing a spectrum of neuromuscular pathologies. Expected outcomes include a novel adaptive control framework demonstrating <50ms latency in real-world testing and a 30% improvement in movement smoothness metrics compared to conventional systems. This work will establish computational pipelines for patient-specific assistive technology optimization while advancing rehabilitation engineering methodologies through the integration of biomechanical modeling and AI-driven control systems. The resulting open-source tools and simulation datasets will provide critical resources for the emerging field of intelligent rehabilitation interfaces.
cip_title: Assistive/ Augmentative Technology and Rehabilitation Engineering
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply the principles of psychology, engineering, and occupational therapy to the design and implementation of technological interventions and systems to promote patient rehabilitation and function. Includes instruction in ergonomics, seating and mobility design, universal and near environment systems design, rehabilitation research, rehabilitation biomechanics, access and communications design, microprocessor-based technologies, neurological trauma, standards and testing, and service delivery management.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in funeral service education and practice through computational modeling of grief dynamics and funeral home operational efficiency. While funeral service integrates elements of psychology, sociology, and business management, the field lacks data-driven frameworks to optimize grief counseling strategies and resource allocation in funeral home operations. Current training and service models rely heavily on qualitative, anecdotal approaches, limiting scalability and personalization. This research addresses these gaps by developing agent-based models (ABMs) to simulate client-counselor interactions under diverse cultural, demographic, and psychological conditions, alongside discrete-event simulations (DES) to analyze logistical workflows in funeral homes. The ABMs will incorporate anonymized historical data from grief counseling sessions, demographic datasets, and ethnographic studies to parameterize agent behaviors, while DES will model facility workflows, staff scheduling, and supply chain logistics under variable demand scenarios. By parallelizing these simulations across HPC nodes, the project aims to identify patterns in effective grief intervention techniques and generate predictive models for operational bottlenecks. Expected outcomes include evidence-based recommendations for adaptive counseling protocols and dynamic resource allocation strategies tailored to community-specific needs. Additionally, the computational framework will be adapted into an open-source toolkit for funeral service education, enabling students to explore "what-if" scenarios in virtual environments. This work bridges a critical gap in applying computational social science and operations research to funeral service—a domain where ethical, cultural, and emotional sensitivities necessitate precision and adaptability often unaddressed by conventional methodologies.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for professional licensure as funeral directors and as managers of funeral homes, cemeteries, and related services.  Includes instruction in the sociology of death and dying, psychology of grief and grief counseling, history of funeral service, funeral direction, business law, funeral service law, funeral home management, accounting and related computer operations, and funeral services marketing and merchandising.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamic interplay between distributed cognitive processes and environmental affordances in shaping collective decision-making within culturally diverse groups. While traditional cognitive science often focuses on individual cognition or homogeneous populations, this research addresses a critical gap by modeling how heterogeneous cultural frameworks, embedded in variable ecological contexts, co-evolve with group-level cognitive strategies. The core computational challenge lies in simulating multi-agent systems where agents operate under distinct, culturally inherited perceptual priors, dynamically adapting their problem-solving heuristics through both social learning and real-time environmental feedback. To achieve this, we will develop a high-performance agent-based modeling framework integrating (1) biophysically plausible neural network models of individual decision-making, (2) stochastic cultural transmission dynamics, and (3) ecological niche construction processes. The simulations will employ evolutionary algorithms to explore emergent coordination patterns across timescales, from rapid situational adaptation to intergenerational knowledge transmission. Computational demands arise from simultaneously tracking millions of neural activation states across diverse agent populations, modeling complex environment-agent couplings through spatially explicit landscapes, and performing sensitivity analyses across parameter spaces governing cultural-evolutionary dynamics. Expected outcomes include predictive models of how specific cultural-environmental configurations foster resilient collective cognition, with applications to designing inclusive decision-support systems and understanding cognitive diversity in ecological transition zones. This work establishes a novel methodological bridge between cultural neuroscience, ecological psychology, and complex systems theory, requiring HPC resources to manage the combinatorial complexity inherent in truly interdisciplinary cognitive science research.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in cognitive science, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize the allocation of public housing resources in rapidly urbanizing regions, addressing systemic inefficiencies that perpetuate socioeconomic disparities. Current approaches often rely on static demographic data and heuristic decision-making, which fail to capture dynamic interactions between housing policies, economic shifts, and population mobility. The research problem centers on creating adaptive, evidence-driven models to improve equity in housing distribution while accounting for real-time constraints such as budget volatility and infrastructure capacity. Using high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will implement agent-based simulations coupled with machine learning to model individual household decision-making, regional economic trends, and policy impacts at scale. The computational approach integrates multi-source data—including census records, real estate transactions, and public service usage logs—into a parallelized optimization pipeline. Reinforcement learning algorithms will iteratively test policy scenarios, while graph-based network analyses will map interdependencies between housing access, transportation systems, and employment opportunities. The project requires HPC capabilities to manage large-scale parameter spaces (10,000+ concurrent agents) and perform Monte Carlo simulations assessing uncertainty in long-term policy outcomes. Expected outcomes include an open-source decision support tool enabling municipal agencies to simulate housing allocation strategies under diverse economic and demographic conditions. Validation will occur through partnerships with three city governments, using historical data to benchmark model accuracy. By quantifying trade-offs between equity metrics, fiscal constraints, and political feasibility, this work aims to establish a new paradigm for dynamic resource allocation in public administration. The computational infrastructure developed will provide a template for applying HPC to complex social policy challenges, with potential extensions to healthcare access and disaster relief logistics.
cip_definition: Any program in public administration, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, with complex conditions such as myocardial infarction and malignant arrhythmias posing significant challenges in diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic optimization. Current clinical models often lack the resolution to capture dynamic interactions between cellular-level pathophysiology, tissue remodeling, and systemic hemodynamics. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop multiscale computational models that integrate molecular, cellular, and organ-level data to simulate disease progression and treatment responses in heterogeneous patient populations. The research will employ finite element modeling to simulate cardiac electrophysiology and biomechanics, coupled with machine learning algorithms trained on multi-omic datasets (genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic) and longitudinal electronic health records. Key objectives include identifying biomarkers predictive of arrhythmic events, optimizing personalized anticoagulation strategies for post-infarction patients, and simulating the hemodynamic impact of novel interventional therapies. The computational workflow requires large-scale parameter sweeps to account for patient-specific variability, real-time analysis of high-resolution imaging data (MRI/CT), and ensemble modeling to quantify uncertainty in clinical predictions. By enabling the integration of disparate data types at unprecedented scale, HPC resources will facilitate the development of validated, clinically actionable models that bridge translational gaps between bench research and bedside care. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for risk prediction, virtual trial platforms to accelerate therapeutic development, and mechanistic insights into sex-specific disparities in cardiovascular outcomes. This work aligns with national priorities to reduce cardiovascular disease burden through precision medicine and has the potential to inform clinical guidelines for managing complex cardiac conditions.
cip_definition: Research on how to specialize in diseases of the heart and blood vessels and to manage complex cardiac conditions such as heart attacks and life-threatening, abnormal heartbeat rhythms.

abstract: This project seeks to address the computational challenges of analyzing complex, high-dimensional social science datasets to model societal inequality dynamics. Traditional statistical methods often struggle with the scale, heterogeneity, and interdependencies inherent in modern social data, such as longitudinal surveys, administrative records, and geospatial indicators. The research aims to develop scalable Bayesian hierarchical models with spatial-temporal components to quantify how economic, demographic, and policy factors interact across multiple scales (individual, community, regional). A key innovation is the integration of stochastic processes and non-parametric techniques to handle missing data, sampling biases, and nonlinear relationships common in social datasets. The computational approach relies on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and variational inference algorithms, optimized for parallel processing on high-performance computing (HPC) clusters. This enables efficient sampling from posterior distributions with millions of parameters while accounting for complex covariance structures and autocorrelation. The project will utilize open-source tools (e.g., Stan, NumPyro) adapted for GPU-accelerated workflows to reduce runtime for large-scale simulations. Expected outcomes include (1) publicly available software for social scientists to fit interpretable inequality models without sacrificing computational feasibility, (2) granular estimates of policy impacts on inequality trends across diverse populations, and (3) methodological advances in regression-based techniques for sparse, imbalanced social data. By leveraging HPC resources, this work will overcome memory and runtime barriers that limit conventional statistical analyses, providing empirically grounded insights into the drivers of inequality. Results will inform targeted interventions and advance quantitative social science methodology through reproducible case studies using census microdata, labor force statistics, and global development indicators.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the social scientific applications of relationships between groups of measurements, and similarities and differences, using probability theory and techniques derived from it. Includes instruction in quantitative social science methodologies, the principles in probability theory, binomial distribution, regression analysis, standard deviation, stochastic processes, non-parametric statistics, sampling theory, and statistical techniques.

abstract: Child care and support services management faces complex challenges in optimizing resource allocation, improving service accessibility, and ensuring equitable outcomes across diverse socioeconomic contexts. Traditional policy evaluation methods often rely on static datasets or simplified models, limiting their ability to account for dynamic interactions between family needs, workforce availability, funding constraints, and regulatory frameworks. This project proposes the development of an agent-based modeling (ABM) framework enhanced by machine learning to simulate the multi-scale impacts of child care policies and operational strategies. The research will integrate heterogeneous data sources—including demographic records, regional economic indicators, and anonymized service utilization patterns—to parameterize agents representing families, providers, and regulatory bodies. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute large-scale simulations that capture variability across urban, suburban, and rural environments while testing thousands of policy permutations. Computational workflows will employ parallelized Monte Carlo methods to assess uncertainty in outcomes such as waitlist reduction, provider retention rates, and cost-effectiveness of subsidy structures. A secondary phase will apply natural language processing (NLP) to analyze unstructured feedback from caregiver surveys and regulatory documents, identifying latent themes influencing service quality perceptions. Expected outcomes include a validated decision-support tool for policymakers, capable of forecasting the second-order effects of funding reallocations or staffing interventions. This work bridges computational social science with public service management, establishing a novel methodology for evaluating child care systems through adaptive simulation. The project’s computational demands—including memory-intensive ABM iterations and NLP model training—require dedicated HPC infrastructure to achieve timely results. Findings will contribute to evidence-based strategies for reducing service disparities while maintaining operational feasibility, with implications for similar resource allocation challenges in non-profit and public sector management.
cip_title: Child Care and Support Services Management
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the provision and management of child care services and that prepares individuals to plan, design, and manage child care facilities and programs that meet children's developmental needs and interests and that provide safe and healthy environments. Includes instruction in child development and psychology; home- and institution-based child care; identification of diseases, injuries, and psychological trauma and applicable referrals; parent relations; personnel and business management principles; and related laws and policies.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational frameworks for optimizing next-generation spacecraft trajectory designs and propulsion systems, addressing critical challenges in multi-body orbital mechanics and plasma-based propulsion. Current mission architectures, particularly those involving cislunar operations or multi-stage deep-space missions, face limitations in balancing computational efficiency with the high-fidelity modeling required for nonlinear gravitational fields, time-varying thrust vectors, and stochastic perturbations. The research will implement a hybrid computational approach combining high-resolution direct numerical simulations of Hall-effect thruster plasmas with parallelized evolutionary algorithms for trajectory optimization. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable large-scale parameter sweeps of ionized xenon flow dynamics using particle-in-cell (PIC) methods, coupled with GPU-accelerated solutions to three-body orbital transfer problems through pseudo-spectral optimal control techniques. Validation will leverage adaptive mesh refinement for resolving plasma-wall interactions in thrusters and machine learning surrogates to accelerate convergence in trajectory search spaces. Expected outcomes include optimized variable-specific-impulse propulsion profiles for crewed Mars transfer vehicles and improved stability criteria for low-power electric propulsion systems in small satellite constellations.
