Expected outcomes include an open-access knowledge graph linking philosophical claims to their textual origins and later adaptations, as well as quantitative frameworks for assessing the epistemic boundaries of Hindu theological debates. This work will provide a foundation for reinterpreting Hinduism’s intellectual history through data-driven models of philosophical change, offering scholars new tools to contextualize primary sources and trace the emergence of contested ideas in global religious thought.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the group of South Asian theologies and philosophies collectively known as Hinduism; together with the religious history and cultural and social manifestations of the faith. Includes instruction in Hindu theology and philosophy (dharma); literature (Vedas, Upanishads, Epics, and commentaries); the Hindu Pantheon, sects, and movements; schools and disciplines; and related arts and sciences.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the historical and contemporary linguistic evolution of regional Spanish and Portuguese dialects across Latin America, with a focus on understudied contact zones between Indigenous, African, and European language traditions. The research addresses a critical gap in Hispanic and Lusophone linguistics: the lack of large-scale, computationally intensive studies examining how syntactic, phonetic, and lexical features develop in multilingual contexts over time. Current methodologies struggle to process the complex interplay of sociolinguistic variables in terabyte-scale corpora spanning four centuries of texts, oral histories, and modern speech recordings. Our team proposes a hybrid computational approach combining neural language models fine-tuned on historical texts, phonetic alignment algorithms optimized for non-European sound systems, and agent-based simulations of language contact scenarios. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallel processing of 19th-century manuscript scans through optical character recognition (OCR) pipelines, acoustic analysis of endangered language recordings from the Amazon and Andes regions, and comparative syntax modeling across 30+ dialectal variants. Expected outcomes include the first diachronic map of grammatical convergence patterns in Ibero-American creoles, a publicly accessible database of annotated speech features linked to sociocultural metadata, and predictive models of language shift in marginalized communities. This work will directly support preservation initiatives for Afro-Bolivian Spanish and Brazilian Vernacular Portuguese while advancing computational methods for low-resource language analysis. The requested resources—particularly GPU nodes for transformer model training and high-memory nodes for corpus linguistics workflows—are essential to handle the project’s unique requirements in processing heterogeneous, multilingual data at unprecedented scale. Results will be disseminated through the open-source LinguaConnect toolkit, designed specifically for Hispanic and Lusophone linguistic research.
detailed_field: Hispanic/ Latin American languages, literatures, and linguistics
cip_title: Hispanic and Latin American Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, General
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the languages and literatures of the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking areas of the world, including the Iberian, Latin American, and Lusophone worlds. Includes instruction in Spanish and Portuguese language and linguistics; regional and Latin American dialects; and Spanish, Portuguese, Spanish American, Luso-Brazilian, and Chicano literature.

abstract: The increasing complexity of interventional cardiology procedures, such as percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI) and transcatheter valve therapies, demands advanced computational tools to optimize patient-specific treatment planning and outcomes. Current clinical methods for evaluating coronary hemodynamics—including fractional flow reserve (FFR) and intravascular imaging—are limited by their inability to model dynamic, patient-specific blood flow interactions with coronary anatomy and implanted devices at high resolution. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing a multi-scale computational framework integrating high-fidelity hemodynamic simulations, machine learning (ML), and real-world clinical data to predict procedural outcomes and guide intervention strategies. The research will leverage anonymized patient datasets comprising angiograms, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and invasive pressure measurements to construct 3D patient-specific coronary models. These models will drive finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to quantify wall shear stress, pressure gradients, and stent-device interactions under varied physiological conditions. Concurrently, ML models will be trained on retrospective procedural data to identify patterns linking anatomical features, hemodynamic parameters, and clinical outcomes. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to manage the computational burden of these simulations, which involve millions of mesh elements and transient, multi-physics analyses, as well as to process terabyte-scale imaging datasets and optimize ML architectures. Expected outcomes include predictive tools to stratify patients at risk of post-procedural complications (e.g., in-stent restenosis, thrombosis) and virtual testing platforms for pre-interventional device selection. By enabling precision modeling of coronary pathophysiology, this work aims to reduce trial-and-error in clinical practice, improve procedural success rates, and establish a foundation for AI-driven interventional guidance systems. The results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals and open-source computational tools, fostering collaboration across the cardiovascular research community.
cip_definition: Research focused on the use of specialized imaging and other diagnostic techniques to evaluate blood flow and pressure in the coronary arteries and chambers of the heart, and in the use of technical procedures and medications to treat abnormalities that impair the function of the cardiovascular system.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model and optimize adaptive management strategies for urban green spaces under dynamic socio-environmental pressures. As cities face increasing demands for equitable recreational access, climate resilience, and biodiversity conservation, traditional park management approaches struggle to balance competing priorities. The research addresses this gap by creating a spatially explicit, agent-based model that simulates visitor behavior, ecological processes, and infrastructure wear patterns across heterogeneous park systems. Using high-performance computing resources, we will integrate multi-source data streams including anonymized mobility traces, vegetation health sensors, and maintenance records to parameterize interactions between human activities and landscape dynamics at unprecedented resolution. Machine learning techniques will be applied to identify nonlinear relationships between management interventions (e.g., trail rerouting, facility placement) and long-term outcomes across ecological, social, and operational metrics. The computational architecture will enable parallel simulation of thousands of scenario combinations while accounting for stochastic weather patterns and evolving user demographics. Expected outcomes include a decision-support tool that predicts optimal resource allocation strategies under varying climate projections and budget constraints, with particular attention to equity in recreational access for marginalized communities. This work advances computational social-ecological systems modeling by bridging leisure management practice with complex systems science, offering novel methodologies for maintaining urban green infrastructure in an era of rapid environmental change.
detailed_field: Parks, recreation, leisure, fitness, and sport studies and management
cip_title: Parks, Recreation, and Leisure Facilities Management, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in parks, recreation, and leisure facilities management, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a large-scale computational analysis of Canadian literary texts, with a focus on tracing thematic and stylistic evolution across regions, periods, and oral traditions. While Canadian literature has been extensively studied through close reading, broader patterns in its development—particularly the interplay between formal literary production and folkloric or oral narratives—remain underexplored due to the sheer volume and linguistic diversity of materials. This research addresses this gap by employing natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) techniques to analyze a curated corpus of over 50,000 digitized texts, including novels, poetry, Indigenous oral histories (transcribed from archival recordings), and regional folk tales. Key computational tasks include topic modeling to identify shifting thematic preoccupations (e.g., wilderness, multiculturalism), sentiment analysis to track tonal changes across historical periods, and network analysis to map influences between authors and traditions. The scale of data, coupled with the need to process multilingual content (e.g., code-switching in Québécois and Indigenous texts) and audio-derived transcripts, necessitates HPC resources for parallelized text processing, training custom transformer-based models (e.g., BERT variants fine-tuned on Canadian English and French dialects), and storing intermediate outputs. Expected outcomes include (1) identifying previously unrecognized connections between literary movements and socio-political events, (2) quantifying the impact of oral traditions on canonical authors, and (3) generating visualizable datasets that map regional stylistic divergences. Results will be disseminated through an open-access interactive platform, enabling scholars to query trends and access annotated texts. By integrating computational methods with literary theory, this project aims to redefine scholarly understanding of Canadian literature’s development while establishing scalable methodologies for analyzing hybrid textual-oral corpora in the humanities.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the literature and literary development, both formal and folkloric, of Canada from its origins to the present. Includes instruction in period and genre studies, author studies, literary criticism, and regional and oral traditions.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational legal analytics in the domain of Family/Child/Elder Law, an interdisciplinary field intersecting legal theory, policy analysis, and sociodemographic data science. The research addresses a critical gap in the systematic evaluation of how dynamic legal frameworks—spanning custody disputes, elder guardianship, and child welfare policies—generate inequitable outcomes across marginalized populations. Traditional legal scholarship often relies on manual case analysis or small-sample qualitative studies, limiting scalability and predictive rigor. To overcome this, we propose a computational approach integrating natural language processing (NLP), graph-based network modeling, and machine learning (ML) to analyze large-scale legal corpora, including court decisions, legislative texts, and administrative records. The HPC infrastructure will enable processing of terabyte-scale datasets, spanning decades of case law and policy revisions, to identify latent patterns in judicial reasoning, temporal shifts in statutory interpretation, and systemic biases in procedural outcomes. Agent-based modeling will simulate the cascading effects of hypothetical policy changes on family structures and resource allocation, incorporating demographic variables such as income, race, and geographic location. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models quantifying the impact of specific legal precedents on case resolution timelines and equity metrics, (2) an open-access toolkit for visualizing policy-driven disparities in custody and guardianship proceedings, and (3) evidence-based recommendations for legislative reforms to mitigate algorithmic bias in automated decision-support systems used by courts. By bridging computational scalability with sociolegal inquiry, this work aims to establish a replicable framework for data-driven jurisprudence, offering stakeholders—from policymakers to advocacy groups—actionable insights into the intersection of law, technology, and familial well-being.
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the law, policies, and regulations affecting domestic relations across the lifespan.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance an interdisciplinary investigation into the dynamics of cultural and intellectual exchange across premodern Afro-Eurasian societies. The research problem centers on analyzing fragmented, multilingual textual and material records (e.g., trade logs, religious manuscripts, artistic motifs) to trace the diffusion of ideas, technologies, and social practices between 500–1500 CE. Existing scholarship lacks systematic computational frameworks to integrate these heterogeneous datasets, which span archaeology, linguistics, and historiography. The project will develop scalable natural language processing (NLP) pipelines to parse and align digitized texts in Arabic, Sanskrit, and classical Chinese, combined with network analysis models to map connectivity patterns across trade routes and urban hubs. Computational challenges include handling non-Latin scripts, fragmentary or damaged source materials, and spatial-temporal data normalization across disparate scholarly corpora. The HPC environment is critical for training transformer-based models on low-resource historical languages, running agent-based simulations of cultural transmission, and visualizing multilayer networks at continental scales. Expected outcomes include (1) an open-access digital repository of annotated, cross-referenced primary sources; (2) quantitative metrics for assessing the role of environmental factors versus institutional actors in shaping intercultural exchange; and (3) methodological frameworks for reconciling humanistic interpretations with computational pattern detection. By bridging computational social science and digital humanities approaches, this work aims to redefine narratives about globalization’s antecedents while demonstrating how HPC can catalyze resource-intensive, multidisciplinary inquiry in liberal arts contexts. The results will inform curriculum development in global history and computational humanities programs, emphasizing data-driven perspectives on cultural complexity.
cip_title: Liberal Arts and Sciences/ Liberal Studies
cip_definition: A program that is a structured combination of the arts, biological and physical sciences, social sciences, and humanities, emphasizing breadth of study. Includes instruction in independently designed, individualized, or regular programs.

abstract: The spread of entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) as biocontrol agents against agricultural pests is constrained by limited understanding of their tri-trophic interactions with insect hosts and plant rhizospheres under dynamic environmental conditions. This project seeks to model the molecular and ecological drivers of EPN-host-plant signaling cascades using a multi-scale computational framework. We aim to resolve how soil temperature gradients, root exudate chemistry, and insect immune responses collectively modulate nematode foraging efficiency and infection success. High-performance computing resources will enable spatially explicit agent-based simulations of nematode population dynamics in heterogeneous soil matrices, integrated with genome-scale metabolic network models of symbiotic bacteria (Xenorhabdus spp.) to predict toxin production thresholds under nutrient stress. Concurrently, machine learning pipelines will analyze hyperspectral imaging datasets from host plants exposed to EPN infestations, identifying spectral signatures linked to induced systemic resistance. The computational workflow will be validated against empirical data from microcosm experiments tracking Steinernema carpocapsae infections in fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) larvae across varying soil moisture regimes. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework for optimizing EPN field persistence, novel biomarkers for non-destructive monitoring of rhizosphere interactions, and genotype-environment mapping of bacterial symbiont resilience under drought scenarios. By bridging nematode behavioral ecology, microbial systems biology, and plant phenomics, this work addresses a critical gap in developing climate-adaptive biocontrol strategies while advancing computational methods for analyzing soil-borne multipartite symbioses.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of nematode (roundworm) and insect species/populations in respect of their life cycles, morphology, genetics, physiology, ecology, taxonomy, population dynamics, and environmental and economic impacts. Includes instruction in applicable biological and physical sciences as well as insect toxicology and the biochemical control of insect populations.

abstract: Soil health and microbial community dynamics are critical yet poorly understood drivers of agricultural productivity and carbon sequestration in agroecosystems. Current models lack resolution to predict how soil microbiomes interact with physicochemical variables under climate stressors, limiting our ability to design adaptive land management strategies. This project seeks to address this gap by developing a high-resolution computational framework to simulate microbial-soil interactions at scale, enabling predictive insights into soil resilience under varying agricultural practices and climate scenarios. The research leverages high-performance computing (HPC) to integrate multi-omics datasets (metagenomic, metatranscriptomic) with spatially explicit soil hydrology and biogeochemical models. Agent-based modeling will simulate microbial community responses to nutrient cycling, moisture fluctuations, and crop residue management, while machine learning algorithms will identify key functional traits linked to soil organic matter stabilization. Parallelized workflows will process terabytes of environmental sensor data and genomic sequences to parameterize models across diverse soil types and cropping systems. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable model quantifying microbial contributions to soil carbon dynamics under drought and intensive farming, (2) predictive tools to optimize tillage, irrigation, and cover cropping practices for enhanced soil health, and (3) open-access datasets linking microbial diversity to agroecosystem functionality. By resolving fine-scale microbial processes within whole-soil profiles, this work will advance fundamental understanding of soil biogeochemistry while directly informing precision agriculture strategies. The computational demands of coupling genomic, hydrological, and climate data necessitate HPC resources to achieve the spatial-temporal resolution required for actionable insights. Results will be disseminated through stakeholder partnerships with agricultural extension services, ensuring translational impact on sustainable soil management.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: Any instructional program in the soil sciences, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project proposes a computational investigation of cross-regional cultural narratives in premodern and early modern Asia, focusing on the transmission of gendered archetypes and their evolution in literary and visual sources. While textual and artistic records from 1000–1800 CE reflect dynamic exchanges of cultural ideals across Asian societies, systematic analysis of these narratives remains fragmented due to the multilingual, multimodal, and geographically dispersed nature of primary materials. Leveraging high-performance computing, this study will process a curated corpus of 15,000+ digitized texts (poetry, folktales, religious commentaries) and 8,000+ visual works (scroll paintings, temple reliefs, illustrated manuscripts) from Chinese, Japanese, Persian, and Sanskrit traditions. A hybrid pipeline combining multilingual transformer models (for text) and graph neural networks (for iconographic relationships) will be developed to trace the adaptation of gender-related motifs—such as fertility symbols, warrior ideals, and cosmological pairings—across linguistic and artistic contexts. Spatial-temporal analysis modules will map regional variations in narrative prominence against historical trade routes and religious networks. The computational workflow addresses challenges in cross-modal alignment, requiring parallel processing of text-image pairs from heterogeneous digitization standards. Expected outcomes include 1) identification of previously unrecognized intercultural pathways in gendered symbol transmission, 2) quantitative models correlating narrative shifts with documented sociopolitical transformations, and 3) public visualization tools for exploring motif trajectories. This work advances Asian cultural studies by enabling macroscale comparative analysis of identity constructs while developing methodologies for ethically engaged computational humanities. The scale of data integration and need for simultaneous training of multimodal architectures necessitates HPC resources beyond local cluster capabilities, particularly for memory-intensive graph processing and low-latency cross-repository data federation.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples of the Asian Continent, including the study of the Asian diasporas overseas.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing ensemble performance outcomes through advanced computational modeling of conductor-led musical interactions. While traditional conducting pedagogy emphasizes experiential learning and subjective feedback, there remains a critical gap in quantitatively analyzing how gestural, temporal, and dynamic decisions by conductors propagate through ensembles of varying sizes and instrumentation. The research will develop high-fidelity simulations of performer-conductor dynamics using motion capture data from live rehearsals, audio signal processing of ensemble recordings, and machine learning techniques to model real-time adaptation processes. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for processing multi-modal datasets encompassing 3D kinematic conductor gestures, synchronized audio streams from 50+ instrument sections, and individual performer response latencies measured under diverse acoustic conditions. Parallelized workflows will train neural networks to identify patterns in successful error-correction strategies during complex tempo modulations, while finite element models will simulate wave propagation effects in large orchestral settings. Expected outcomes include a computational framework for predicting ensemble cohesion metrics, which will inform the development of AI-assisted rehearsal analytics tools for conducting students. By bridging data-driven insights with artistic pedagogy, this work aims to establish new methodologies for assessing conducting efficacy, particularly in contexts involving non-standard notation or improvisatory elements. The requested computing resources will enable large-scale parameter sweeps across ensemble configurations and repertoire styles, which are computationally prohibitive on local workstations. Results will be disseminated through open-source conducting simulation tools and interdisciplinary publications linking performance informatics with music education practices.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to master the art of leading bands, choirs, orchestras and other ensembles in performance, and related music leadership. Includes instruction in score analysis and arranging, rehearsal and performance leadership, music coaching, arrangement and performance planning, ensemble operations management, and applications to specific school or professional ensembles.

abstract: This project seeks to address unresolved questions in computational complexity theory regarding the practical limits of solving NP-hard optimization problems under resource constraints. While theoretical frameworks classify these problems as intractable in the worst case, real-world instances often exhibit structures that permit efficient approximation or heuristic solutions. However, characterizing the boundaries of tractability for such instances remains an open challenge. We propose a computational study to systematically explore the relationship between problem structure, algorithmic strategies, and runtime performance across a spectrum of NP-hard problems, including graph coloring, traveling salesman, and satisfiability. The project will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to execute large-scale simulations of classical and quantum-inspired algorithms, such as simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers. These simulations will analyze runtime distributions, solution quality, and scalability across problem sizes up to 10^6 variables, generating empirical data to refine complexity-theoretic models. Computational workloads will parallelize parameter sweeps over algorithm configurations and problem ensembles using MPI-based task farming, with individual trials requiring up to 48 hours on multi-core nodes. Memory-intensive phases, such as constraint matrix operations for mixed-integer programming, will utilize distributed-memory architectures. Expected outcomes include (1) a taxonomy of structural features correlating with practical tractability, (2) optimized heuristic portfolios for common NP-hard problem classes, and (3) statistical evidence informing refinements to the polynomial hierarchy. Results will be disseminated through computational complexity venues and open-source algorithm libraries, bridging theoretical insights with practical optimization tools for scientific and industrial applications. This work directly advances the program’s mission by elucidating the nature of computation through rigorous empirical analysis at scales previously inaccessible to purely theoretical methods.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on computability theory, complexity theory, and the nature of computation.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the intersectional cultural narratives and linguistic patterns of underrepresented diasporic communities in digital archives. While existing scholarship in area studies has prioritized textual or qualitative methods, the scale and complexity of transnational digital cultural production—including multilingual social media corpora, digitized oral histories, and community-led archival initiatives—demand advanced computational tools to identify latent themes, semantic networks, and temporal shifts in self-representation. The research problem centers on gaps in understanding how marginalized groups negotiate hybrid identities across decentralized digital spaces, particularly when working with non-Roman scripts, low-resource languages, and multimodal data (e.g., image-text interactions). Using a mixed-methods framework, the project will apply transformer-based natural language processing (NLP) models fine-tuned for code-switching detection, distributed topic modeling across parallelized datasets, and graph-based analysis of cross-cultural semantic linkages. Computational workflows will integrate Python-based NLP libraries (e.g., Stanza, Transformers) with custom algorithms for noise reduction in crowd-sourced historical texts, optimized for GPU-accelerated processing. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable pipeline for analyzing diasporic digital cultural artifacts across linguistic and temporal boundaries, (2) quantitative frameworks to map the evolution of collective memory in migrant communities, and (3) public-facing visualizations of transnational narrative networks to inform cultural preservation initiatives. By enabling large-scale pattern recognition in heterogeneous, multilingual datasets, HPC resources are critical to advancing methodological innovation in intersectional area studies while centering ethical computational practices for marginalized knowledge systems. The project’s computational outputs will be disseminated through open-access platforms to support community archivists and interdisciplinary researchers working at the nexus of cultural studies and digital humanities.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: Any instructional program in specifically defined area studies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Archival institutions face escalating challenges in managing exponentially growing volumes of digitized and born-digital records, particularly those with complex formats (e.g., multimedia, dynamic web content, or interactive datasets). Traditional archival workflows struggle to scale efficiently, risking data degradation, incomplete metadata generation, and accessibility barriers. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop computational frameworks for automating and optimizing archival processes, with a focus on preserving context-rich digital materials and enabling scalable access. The research centers on three interconnected objectives: (1) designing machine learning models to identify, classify, and extract metadata from heterogeneous digital collections, (2) simulating long-term digital preservation environments to test format migration strategies under diverse technological constraints, and (3) creating parallelized workflows for integrity verification of large-scale archival holdings. Computational methods will include natural language processing for contextual analysis of unstructured text, computer vision techniques for image and video appraisal, and distributed computing architectures to manage petabytes of data. HPC resources are critical to train models on diverse archival corpora, replicate multi-decade preservation scenarios, and process high-resolution multimedia assets efficiently. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for automated metadata enhancement, predictive models to prioritize at-risk digital objects, and benchmarks for evaluating computational preservation efficacy. By integrating archival theory with scalable computational practices, this project aims to redefine stewardship paradigms for complex digital collections, reduce manual labor in archival workflows, and ensure equitable access to culturally significant materials. The work will establish methodological precedents for computational archival science, offering transferable strategies for institutions navigating resource limitations while confronting the technical and ethical complexities of 21st-century digital preservation.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to identify, manage, preserve, and make available records with long-term value for documentation, legal, research, and other purposes. Includes instruction in appraisal and collection development, information and records management, archival preservation, access systems, management of electronic records, archival outreach, and legal and ethical issues.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the molecular mechanisms driving antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacterial pathogens and their interactions with host immune responses. A critical challenge in infectious disease management is the rapid evolution of multidrug-resistant pathogens, which undermines therapeutic efficacy and complicates global health interventions. Current gaps in understanding how microbial communities adapt to antimicrobial pressures—and how these adaptations modulate host-pathogen interactions—limit the development of targeted treatments. To address this, we propose a computational study integrating molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and machine learning (ML) to model bacterial protein-ligand interactions under selective drug pressure, alongside agent-based simulations of microbial population dynamics in host environments. MD simulations will focus on key resistance-conferring enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamases, efflux pumps) to map structural and energetic changes associated with resistance mutations. Concurrently, agent-based models will simulate polymicrobial community behaviors under varying immune conditions, incorporating data on phagocyte activity and cytokine signaling. ML algorithms will analyze genomic and transcriptomic datasets from clinical isolates to identify predictive markers of emergent resistance. By utilizing HPC resources, these computationally intensive workflows will enable large-scale, parallelized simulations and high-dimensional data integration. Expected outcomes include mechanistic insights into resistance evolution, immune evasion strategies, and community-level microbial resilience. This work will directly inform the design of next-generation antimicrobials and immunotherapies, while providing a framework to anticipate resistance trends in clinical and environmental settings. The requested computing resources are essential to achieve the resolution and throughput required for these analyses, which are infeasible with standard laboratory infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the biological, social, and behavioral factors contributing to the cause and spread of infectious diseases. Includes instruction in research design and evaluation, infectious disease epidemiology, international health policy and management, microbiology, microbial genetics, molecular virology, disease mechanisms, antimicrobial resistance, immunology, and bioterrorism.

abstract: The proliferation of decentralized, edge-centric computing environments has introduced significant challenges in optimizing real-time decision-making across spatially distributed, resource-constrained devices. This project addresses the problem of dynamically coordinating heterogeneous edge computing nodes—such as IoT sensors, drones, and mobile devices—to execute latency-sensitive tasks in environments with intermittent connectivity and variable energy budgets. Traditional centralized or cloud-dependent approaches fail to meet the strict timing and autonomy requirements of applications like disaster response or precision agriculture, where decisions must adapt to rapidly changing physical conditions. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hybrid computational framework combining decentralized graph neural networks (GNNs) for local pattern recognition with lightweight, physics-informed reinforcement learning (RL) agents that negotiate resource-sharing policies in real time. The framework will be tested through large-scale simulations emulating urban flood monitoring scenarios, where nodes must collaboratively process hydrological sensor data, prioritize emergency alerts, and redistribute computational loads during network fragmentation. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for two components: (1) training GNN-RL models on synthetic datasets representing millions of device configurations and environmental permutations, and (2) deploying parallelized digital twin instances to stress-test coordination protocols under extreme edge network conditions. Expected outcomes include a novel algorithm suite for adaptive edge resource allocation, benchmarked against existing federated learning and swarm intelligence baselines, and a publicly accessible dataset capturing device-level telemetry from simulated emergencies. This work advances the understudied intersection of distributed systems theory and embedded AI, with direct implications for resilient infrastructure in smart cities and environmental monitoring. By focusing on computational strategies that respect both physical constraints and information exchange limits, the project contributes foundational methods for next-generation edge computing architectures.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on computing, computer science, and information science and systems. Such programs are undifferentiated as to title and content and are not to be confused with specific programs in computer science, information science, or related support services.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a dynamic, agent-based simulation model for optimizing decentralized decision-making in tourism ecosystems under climate volatility. The tourism industry faces escalating risks from climate disruptions, yet existing resource allocation frameworks remain centralized and reactive, struggling to adapt to real-time environmental shifts, localized traveler behavior, and multi-stakeholder coordination. Traditional analytical models lack the granularity to simulate hyper-localized interactions between tourists, businesses, and environmental conditions at scale. To address this gap, the project will construct a spatially explicit simulation platform integrating real-time climate data feeds, stochastic tourist preference models, and adaptive business response algorithms. The HPC environment will enable parallelized execution of millions of agent interactions across heterogeneous scenarios, incorporating machine learning-driven climate anomaly predictions and game-theoretic coordination mechanisms for businesses. Key computational challenges include scaling network-based reputation systems for tourism service providers and optimizing GPU-accelerated spatial clustering of risk-mitigation strategies. Outcomes will include a decision-support toolkit for regional tourism boards and small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs), enabling proactive resource reallocation—such as adaptive pricing, route diversifications, and capacity buffers—during climate-induced demand shocks. The project’s interdisciplinary approach bridges computational sustainability, behavioral economics, and distributed systems design, offering a novel framework for resilience in tourism networks. By testing scenarios across synthetic and real-world datasets (e.g., coastal tourism hubs and alpine destinations), the research aims to reduce economic losses from climate disruptions by an estimated 12–18% in simulated models while maintaining service quality benchmarks. This work will contribute methodological advances in decentralized resource optimization for complex service industries facing existential environmental threats.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to manage travel-related enterprises and related convention and/or tour services. Includes instruction in travel agency management, tour arranging and planning, convention and event planning, travel industry operations and procedures, tourism marketing and promotion strategies, travel counseling, travel industry law, international and domestic operations, and travel and tourism policy.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the role of dynamic social network evolution in shaping health disparities among aging populations, leveraging computational social science frameworks to model longitudinal interactions between social connectivity and biological aging. While gerontology traditionally emphasizes biomedical or public health approaches, this work integrates complex systems theory, network science, and computational linguistics to analyze how shifting social ties—mediated by retirement, caregiving demands, and digital communication patterns—influence trajectories of cognitive decline and multimorbidity. The research problem centers on identifying critical transition points where social network fragmentation accelerates health deterioration, particularly in understudied rural aging populations. Using anonymized longitudinal data from health surveys, electronic health records, and natural language processing of community forum interactions (spanning 15 years across 3 regions), we will develop agent-based models simulating network-aging feedback loops. High-performance computing resources are required to handle three computational challenges: 1) Bayesian inference for missing data imputation across heterogeneous sources, 2) multiscale network simulations incorporating individual-level biomarker data and community-level resource maps, and 3) sensitivity analyses quantifying policy intervention impacts through counterfactual scenarios. Expected outcomes include a novel metric of "social frailty" that predicts vulnerability thresholds more accurately than existing clinical tools, along with an open-source simulation platform for testing community support strategies. By computationally modeling the entanglement of social dynamics and biological aging processes, this work aims to advance predictive frameworks for aging equity while establishing methodological bridges between computational social science and lifespan health research.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the human aging process and aged human populations, using the knowledge and methodologies of the biological and health sciences.

abstract: Welding processes involve complex interactions between thermal, mechanical, and metallurgical phenomena that are challenging to model experimentally due to the rapid timescales, extreme temperatures, and safety constraints inherent to the field. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop advanced multiphysics simulations of arc welding and laser-based welding processes, with a focus on optimizing parameters for joining advanced alloys used in aerospace and energy applications. The research problem centers on predicting and mitigating defects such as porosity, residual stress, and microstructural inhomogeneities, which compromise weld integrity. Current experimental methods are costly and time-intensive, limiting the exploration of parameter spaces for novel materials. We propose a computational approach integrating finite element analysis (FEA) for heat transfer and stress evolution, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for weld pool dynamics, and machine learning (ML) models trained on experimental datasets to correlate process variables with defect formation. High-resolution simulations will account for phase transformations, Marangoni convection, and keyhole stability in laser welding, validated against synchrotron X-ray imaging data. The HPC environment is critical for scaling these models to realistic 3D geometries and millisecond-level process times, which require parallelized solvers and large memory allocations. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework for optimizing welding speed, power input, and shielding gas composition to minimize defects in high-strength aluminum and titanium alloys. This work will advance the fundamental understanding of weld pool solidification under non-equilibrium conditions and provide actionable guidelines for industry partners seeking to adopt next-generation materials. By integrating computational tools into welding technology research, the project also aims to bridge gaps in workforce training, equipping students with skills in numerical modeling and data-driven process design. The requested computing resources will enable parameter sweeps and sensitivity analyses impractical on local clusters, directly supporting innovation in welding techniques critical to sustainable manufacturing and infrastructure resilience.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to join or cut metal surfaces. Includes instruction in arc welding, resistance welding, brazing and soldering, cutting, high-energy beam welding and cutting, solid state welding, ferrous and non-ferrous materials, oxidation-reduction reactions, welding metallurgy, welding processes and heat treating, structural design, safety, and applicable codes and standards.

abstract: The increasing complexity of translational research in Laboratory Animal Medicine necessitates advanced computational tools to address challenges in experimental design, data integration, and predictive modeling. Current limitations in analyzing high-dimensional datasets—including multi-omics, histopathology, behavioral monitoring, and longitudinal health records—hinder efforts to optimize animal models, reduce experimental variability, and improve translational relevance to human and veterinary medicine. This project seeks high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and apply computational workflows that integrate heterogeneous data streams from murine and non-human primate models of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The research problem centers on identifying biomarker signatures predictive of disease progression and treatment response while accounting for inter-individual variability in immune and microbiome profiles. A multi-scale computational approach will be implemented, combining genome-scale metabolic modeling, Bayesian network inference, and deep learning architectures to analyze longitudinal metagenomic, transcriptomic, and clinical datasets. Computational pipelines will be optimized for parallel processing of high-resolution imaging data (e.g., intravital microscopy) and real-time sensor outputs from automated husbandry systems. The HPC environment will enable ensemble modeling to quantify uncertainty in therapeutic predictions and facilitate virtual screening of candidate interventions. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated framework for predictive monitoring of complex phenotypes in laboratory animals, (2) optimized protocols for reducing sample sizes through precision experimental design, and (3) open-source tools for reproducible analysis of multi-modal data in veterinary translational research. This work will directly enhance the translational value of animal studies while addressing critical needs in research animal welfare through computational refinements to experimental endpoints and dosing strategies. The requested resources will support iterative model training, large-scale sensitivity analyses, and the development of cloud-compatible interfaces for collaborative use across biomedical research facilities.
cip_definition: Research focused on the principles and practices of applied veterinary research and related techniques, equipment, data systems and research design. May included related research in the management of veterinary and other animal research laboratories and health care facilities.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the role of tumor microenvironmental stressors in driving metabolic plasticity and metastatic progression in epithelial cancers. A critical gap in cancer biology lies in understanding how dynamic interactions between hypoxic gradients, nutrient availability, and mechanical forces collectively reprogram cellular decision-making in heterogeneous tumors. Current experimental models struggle to capture the spatiotemporal complexity of these systems-level physiological interactions. To address this, we will develop a 3D multiscale computational platform integrating discrete cell-scale agent-based models with continuum tissue-scale biophysical simulations. The framework will parameterize cancer cell responses to microenvironmental variables—including oxygen diffusion, extracellular matrix stiffness, and glucose distribution—using empirical data from our lab’s prior organoid studies and in vivo imaging. HPC resources will enable iterative simulations of tumor growth under varying metabolic constraints, with parallelized solving of coupled differential equations governing nutrient transport, cellular energetics, and phenotype switching. Key outcomes will include predictive maps of metastatic propensity based on microenvironmental stressor combinations and identification of nodal points in metabolic decision-making networks that could be targeted to disrupt adaptation. This work will provide the first systems-level computational model of cancer cell functional dynamics that explicitly links subcellular metabolic pathways to tissue-scale physiological forces. By clarifying how tumors exploit physiological plasticity to overcome microenvironmental limitations, the results will advance translational strategies to impair metastatic fitness while avoiding the pitfalls of targeting static molecular vulnerabilities. The computational framework will also serve as a community resource for simulating therapeutic interventions within realistic, evolving tumor ecosystems.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the scientific study of the functional dynamics, morphology, and biochemical and biophysical communications within organisms and between living systems at all levels of complexity and integration. Includes instruction in reproduction, growth, hormonal action, vascular function, respiration, digestion, sensory perception and processing, sensorimotor integration, signal encoding and conveyance, homeostasis, physical function and malfunction, evolutionary physiology, and disease processes.

abstract: This project aims to elucidate the genetic mechanisms driving adaptive divergence in non-model plant species, focusing on the role of structural genomic variation in shaping complex trait evolution. Despite advances in sequencing, the contribution of large-scale genomic rearrangements (e.g., inversions, translocations) to local adaptation remains poorly characterized due to challenges in resolving these regions and modeling their population-level effects. We will analyze whole-genome data from 40 populations of Helianthus anomalus, a hybrid sunflower species thriving in extreme habitats, to identify structural variants associated with environmental gradients. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for processing long-read sequencing data (∼15 TB), performing de novo genome assembly across ecotypes, and conducting landscape genomic analyses integrating climatic, edaphic, and phenotypic variables. Custom population genetics simulations will quantify how structural variants influence recombination suppression and allele frequency dynamics under selection. These computationally intensive simulations require parallelized execution across multiple nodes to test evolutionary scenarios over millennial timescales. Expected outcomes include 1) a pan-genome resource documenting adaptive structural variation in wild sunflowers, 2) quantitative models linking genomic architecture to adaptive trait evolution, and 3) novel methods for detecting selection on non-coding structural elements. Results will advance fundamental understanding of how large-scale genomic reorganization facilitates rapid adaptation, with implications for predicting species responses to climate change and improving crop resilience. The scale of genomic data and complexity of evolutionary models necessitate HPC capabilities beyond typical campus infrastructure, particularly for memory-intensive assembly steps and stochastic simulation replicates. This work bridges critical gaps in evolutionary genetics by revealing the spatial and temporal dynamics of structural variation’s adaptive role, while developing computational frameworks applicable to other non-model systems.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in genetics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project seeks to develop a computational framework to model the dynamic interactions between climate risk, urban infrastructure resilience, and real estate valuation in coastal metropolitan markets. Traditional appraisal methods often fail to account for nonlinear environmental shocks, adaptive policy interventions, or spatial interdependencies in asset pricing—a critical gap as climate volatility intensifies. The study will integrate geospatial climate projections, granular property transaction data, and infrastructure adaptation scenarios to simulate how flood risks, zoning changes, and mitigation investments propagate through real estate markets over 30-year horizons. Leveraging high-performance computing resources, we will implement coupled agent-based models and Monte Carlo simulations at metropolitan-scale resolution (1km² grids), incorporating 10+ million parcel-level data points across three U.S. coastal regions. Computational challenges include solving partial differential equations for floodwater diffusion across urban topography, optimizing reinforcement learning algorithms for developer/purchaser decision trees, and parallel-processing high-dimensional sensitivity analyses across climate-emission pathways. Expected outcomes include a validated open-source modeling toolkit for climate-adjusted property valuation, quantitative benchmarks for resilience ROI in commercial real estate, and policy simulations demonstrating how targeted infrastructure investments could mitigate systemic devaluation risks. This interdisciplinary approach bridges computational urban science with real estate economics, providing stakeholders with decision-support systems to navigate accelerating environmental market disruptions. The scale of spatiotemporal analysis and need for daily model recalibration based on live climate data streams necessitate dedicated GPU-accelerated computing resources beyond institutional cluster capacities.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to develop, buy, sell, appraise, and manage real estate. Includes instruction in land use development policy, real estate law, real estate marketing procedures, agency management, brokerage, property inspection and appraisal, real estate investing, leased and rental properties, commercial real estate, and property management.

abstract: Anatomic pathology is central to diagnosing diseases through the analysis of tissue specimens, yet the increasing complexity and volume of high-throughput histopathological, imaging, and molecular data pose significant challenges to traditional diagnostic workflows. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing computational models to enhance the precision and efficiency of disease diagnosis, with a focus on integrating multimodal datasets, including whole-slide imaging, spatial transcriptomics, and clinical metadata. The primary research problem involves resolving the computational bottlenecks in processing and interpreting large-scale, heterogeneous anatomic pathology data, which current clinical systems are ill-equipped to handle. To overcome this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to deploy scalable machine learning frameworks for automated anomaly detection, tissue morphometry, and predictive modeling of disease progression. Key computational methods include deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for subcellular feature extraction, graph-based algorithms to model spatial relationships in tumor microenvironments, and Bayesian hierarchical models to integrate multi-omics data with clinical outcomes. These approaches require parallelized GPU-accelerated processing, large-scale memory allocation, and high-throughput storage to manage terabyte-scale imaging datasets and complex genomic annotations. The expected outcomes include the development of validated diagnostic tools that improve classification accuracy for rare cancers and pre-malignant lesions, identification of novel biomarkers linked to therapeutic response, and optimized workflows for pathology laboratory quality control. By enabling rapid, reproducible analysis of anatomic data, this project aims to advance precision diagnostics, reduce inter-observer variability, and provide a scalable computational framework for future pathology research. The requested HPC resources are critical to achieving these objectives, as they directly support the data-intensive demands of modern anatomic pathology and facilitate translation of computational insights into clinical practice.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis of disease and anatomic abnormalities. Includes instruction in autopsy pathology, cytology, diagnostic surgical pathology, forensic medicine, laboratory management, and quality control.

abstract: The diagnosis and management of endocrine disorders in pediatric populations are complicated by dynamic hormone interactions, heterogeneous disease presentations, and a paucity of validated biomarkers for treatment optimization. This project seeks to address these challenges by developing computational models to predict individualized therapeutic responses in children with endocrine conditions such as type 1 diabetes, growth hormone deficiency, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Current clinical decision-making relies on population-level guidelines that often fail to account for developmental variability in hormone-receptor dynamics, genetic modifiers, and environmental influences. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating multi-omics data (genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic profiles) with longitudinal clinical data from electronic health records (EHRs) to build patient-specific predictive models. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process and analyze these large-scale datasets, which include time-series hormone measurements, epigenomic markers, and high-resolution EHR entries from over 5,000 patients. Machine learning algorithms, including federated learning frameworks, will be trained to identify subtype-specific treatment pathways, while dynamical systems models will simulate hormone network perturbations under varying therapeutic interventions. The computational workflow will require parallelized processing for genome-wide association studies (GWAS), real-time optimization of differential equation systems, and high-dimensional data integration. Anticipated outcomes include the identification of novel biomarkers for early diagnosis, stratification of patients into mechanistically distinct subgroups, and the generation of adaptive treatment algorithms for clinical validation. This work will advance precision medicine in pediatric endocrinology by bridging gaps between molecular mechanisms and clinical heterogeneity. Successful implementation depends on HPC capabilities to manage memory-intensive simulations, reduce model training timescales, and enable scalable analysis of sensitive health data within secure environments. Findings will directly inform ongoing clinical trials and contribute open-source tools for hormone dynamics modeling in developmental contexts.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis and management of endocrine diseases and the regulation of hormone balance in childhood and adolescence.

abstract: The emergence and spread of zoonotic infectious diseases pose significant threats to animal health, food security, and public health systems. Current challenges in predicting pathogen evolution, understanding interspecies transmission dynamics, and optimizing intervention strategies are hindered by limitations in analyzing large-scale genomic, epidemiological, and host-pathogen interaction datasets. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical gaps in modeling the molecular and ecological drivers of veterinary infectious diseases, with a focus on high-impact pathogens such as avian influenza viruses, antimicrobial-resistant zoonotic bacteria, and emerging vector-borne parasites. We propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating phylogenetic reconstruction, molecular dynamics simulations of host receptor binding, and machine learning-driven epidemiological risk mapping. Genomic datasets from surveillance networks will be analyzed using Bayesian evolutionary models to identify antigenic shift patterns and spatiotemporal spread hotspots. Atomistic simulations will probe mechanisms of cross-species viral fusion protein adaptation, while graph neural networks will predict outbreak risks by synthesizing environmental, livestock movement, and wildlife interface data. The computational workflow requires parallel processing of terabyte-scale genomic repositories, GPU-accelerated molecular simulations exceeding 10^6 core-hours, and distributed training of deep learning models on heterogeneous agricultural landscape data. Expected outcomes include predictive models of pathogen emergence in livestock populations, actionable insights into antibody evasion mechanisms for vaccine design, and precision maps for targeted biosecurity interventions. By elucidating transmission networks at the animal-human interface, this research will directly support evidence-based strategies for disease containment in agricultural systems while advancing computational methodologies for veterinary pathogenomics. The requested HPC allocation will enable transformative scale in analyzing complex, multi-modal datasets that are intractable with current institutional infrastructure.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of zoonotic infectious diseases, disease mechanisms, and prevention and treatment strategies. Includes instruction in disease pathogenesis, vector biology, mycobacterial infection, blood parasites, retroviruses, food-borne diseases, new infectious agents, ecotoxicology, mechanisms of disease transfer, antibody resistance, comparative pathology, communicable diseases, and disease prevention and eradication.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance precision in barbering practices through computational modeling of hair dynamics, ergonomic tool design, and personalized style optimization. While barbering is traditionally a manual craft, emerging challenges—such as the need for hyper-personalized styling in diverse populations, the biomechanical impacts of repetitive tool use on practitioners, and the lack of data-driven frameworks for predicting hair behavior under cutting or chemical treatments—highlight gaps that computational approaches can address. The research problem centers on bridging these gaps by integrating principles from fluid dynamics, material science, and machine learning into barbering workflows. Proposed computational methods include finite element analysis (FEA) to simulate shear forces during hair cutting, agent-based modeling to predict hair follicle responses to styling products, and generative adversarial networks (GANs) trained on 3D-scanned facial geometries to recommend client-specific styles. Additionally, motion-capture datasets of barbering techniques will be analyzed using graph-based algorithms to optimize ergonomic tool handling and reduce occupational strain. The project will utilize GPU-accelerated simulations for real-time rendering of hair-texture interactions and distributed computing for large-scale analysis of demographic hair characteristics. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for virtual hairstyle testing, predictive models for chemical treatment outcomes, and evidence-based guidelines for tool design. By establishing computational barbering as a novel interdisciplinary niche, this work aims to elevate technical training standards, reduce trial-and-error in practice, and foster innovation in a field historically underserved by advanced computational research. The resource request supports scaling these models to accommodate diverse hair types and global stylistic preferences, ensuring equitable applicability across communities.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to shave and trim facial/neck hair and beards, cut and dress hair, fit hairpieces, give facial and scalp massages, apply cosmetic treatments, and to prepare for licensure as professional barbers at various levels.  Includes instruction in facial shaving; beard and mustache shaping and trimming; shampooing; hair cutting; hair styles and styling art; facial treatments and massage; chemical applications; hair and scalp anatomy and physiology; hairpiece and toupee fitting; equipment operation; health and safety; customer service; and shop business practices.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of Jewish philosophical and legal thought across diasporic communities through computational text analysis and network modeling. The research addresses a critical gap in understanding how Jewish intellectual traditions adapted to diverse cultural and geographic contexts, particularly in understudied regions such as pre-modern North Africa, the Caucasus, and South Asia. By integrating digitized manuscripts, responsa literature, and philosophical treatises spanning the 12th to 18th centuries, the project will construct a multilingual corpus (Hebrew, Judeo-Arabic, and Judeo-Persian) to trace conceptual shifts in key themes such as divine law, ethics, and communal authority. Computational methods include natural language processing (NLP) pipelines optimized for rabbinic texts, semantic similarity analysis using transformer-based models, and dynamic network simulations to map intellectual exchanges between scholars. Challenges such as non-standardized orthography in manuscript sources and the need for context-aware entity recognition in legal debates necessitate fine-tuned machine learning models and significant parallel processing. The HPC infrastructure will enable large-scale data integration, reduce runtime for iterative model training, and support the visualization of knowledge networks across temporal and spatial axes. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of annotated texts, quantitative frameworks for assessing ideological continuity or divergence in Jewish thought, and novel insights into how localized cultural practices influenced universal religious principles. This work will provide a methodological foundation for computational humanities in Judaic studies while advancing interdisciplinary dialogue on the role of minority intellectual traditions in shaping global philosophical discourse.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, culture, and religion of the Jewish people. Includes instruction in Jewish religious heritage, sacred texts, and law; Jewish philosophy and intellectual history; Jewish life and culture, both in Israel and the Jewish Diaspora; historical Jewish minority cultures such as the Yiddish, Sephardic, and other; anti-Semitism, gentile relations and Shoa; Zionism; and modern developments within Judaism.

abstract: Wildlife populations in rapidly urbanizing landscapes face unprecedented sensory challenges due to anthropogenic noise and artificial light, yet the systemic impacts of these stressors on cross-species communication networks remain poorly understood. This project seeks to model how multi-sensory pollution disrupts acoustic and visual signaling dynamics among vertebrate communities, with a focus on avian and mammalian species in hybrid urban-wildland interfaces. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we will develop spatially explicit, agent-based simulations integrating real-world data on species distributions, anthropogenic activity patterns, and habitat structures. The computational framework will couple bioacoustic signal propagation models with machine learning-driven analyses of species-specific visual and auditory perception thresholds, informed by empirical field data from camera traps and autonomous recording units. Key innovations include the incorporation of adaptive behavioral plasticity in response to dynamic noise gradients and the simulation of cascade effects across trophic levels. Expected outcomes include predictive maps of communication network fragmentation under varying urban development scenarios, identification of critical thresholds for signal masking, and evidence-based guidelines for preserving wildlife communication corridors in urban planning. By addressing the intersection of sensory ecology, anthropogenic disturbance, and adaptive behavior, this work bridges gaps between traditional wildlife biology and emerging computational approaches to complex system resilience, offering novel insights into conservation strategies for noise- and light-polluted ecosystems.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of biological principles to the study of vertebrate wildlife, wildlife habitats, and related ecosystems in remote and urban areas. Includes instruction in animal ecology; adaptational biology; urban ecosystems; natural and artificial habitat management; limnology; wildlife pathology; and vertebrate zoological specializations such as mammalogy, herpetology, ichthyology, ornithology, and others.

abstract: Clinical educators face significant challenges in analyzing complex, multimodal datasets generated from simulation-based training, competency assessments, and longitudinal evaluations of interprofessional education outcomes. Traditional analytical methods struggle to integrate high-dimensional data from diverse sources—including performance metrics, behavioral logs, and free-text feedback—limiting the ability to optimize training efficacy or personalize learning pathways. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing scalable computational models to identify patterns in educational effectiveness and learner progression across health professions specialties. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process terabytes of anonymized data from institutional learning management systems, virtual patient simulations, and competency assessments spanning medicine, nursing, and allied health disciplines. Machine learning approaches, including natural language processing for qualitative feedback analysis and graph neural networks for modeling skill acquisition trajectories, will be implemented. Parallelized algorithms will enable real-time analysis of simulation log files to correlate clinical decision-making patterns with post-training patient outcomes. A key innovation involves federated learning architectures to preserve data privacy while training models across multiple institutions. Expected outcomes include predictive frameworks for identifying at-risk learners, evidence-based guidelines for adaptive curriculum design, and open-source tools for benchmarking interprofessional competency development. By enabling large-scale, integrative analysis of educational data, this work will advance precision education strategies in health professions training, ultimately improving the scalability and equity of clinical instruction. The requested HPC resources are critical for managing distributed datasets, reducing model training times from weeks to days, and supporting the computational demands of multimodal artificial intelligence pipelines. Findings will directly inform accreditation standards and faculty development initiatives aimed at addressing systemic gaps in healthcare education.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on education and administration leadership skills for clinical educators across health professions and specialties. Includes instruction in academic leadership, assessment, clinical decision making, curriculum development, ethics, primary care education, program evaluation, research methods, and statistics.

abstract: This project seeks to optimize safety and efficacy in patient handling practices by health aides and attendants through advanced biomechanical modeling and machine learning. Despite being critical to patient care, routine tasks such as transfers, repositioning, and mobility assistance lack evidence-based, personalized protocols, contributing to high rates of musculoskeletal injuries among caregivers and suboptimal patient outcomes. Current guidelines rely on static risk assessments that fail to account for dynamic variables such as patient-specific biomechanics, real-time fatigue metrics, or environmental constraints. To address this gap, we propose a computational framework integrating wearable sensor data, 3D motion capture, and patient-specific digital twin simulations to model biomechanical stress during caregiving tasks. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable large-scale simulations of diverse handling scenarios, incorporating variables such as patient body composition, caregiver ergonomic patterns, and adaptive assistive devices. Machine learning algorithms will analyze simulated and empirical datasets to identify risk-minimizing techniques and generate predictive models for injury prevention. The project will also develop a real-time feedback system prototype to guide caregivers via augmented reality interfaces during complex maneuvers. Outcomes include open-access datasets of biomechanical interactions, validated computational models for training program design, and a proof-of-concept adaptive guidance tool. This work bridges gaps between rehabilitation science, occupational biomechanics, and human-computer interaction, offering translational insights to improve safety standards in an understudied yet essential healthcare workforce. By leveraging HPC capabilities to process multimodal sensor data and simulate high-resolution dynamic interactions, the project advances precision approaches to caregiver training and patient handling protocols.
cip_definition: Any other instructional program that prepares individuals to provide routine patient care and assistance.

abstract: Understanding the chemical evolution of silicate melts in planetary interiors remains a fundamental challenge in geochemistry, with critical implications for magma ocean crystallization, mantle differentiation, and ore-forming processes. Current limitations in experimentally constraining the coupled effects of extreme pressures (up to 25 GPa), temperatures (2000–3500 K), and redox states on melt structure and elemental partitioning hinder predictive modeling of planetary-scale geochemical cycles. This project proposes to overcome these barriers by developing a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled multiscale simulation framework to quantify thermodynamic and kinetic properties of multicomponent silicate melts. Atomistic simulations using density functional theory (DFT) and deep potential molecular dynamics (DPMD) will be conducted to parameterize melt viscosity, diffusion coefficients, and metal-silicate partitioning behaviors across PT conditions spanning Earth’s upper mantle to core-mantle boundary. These data will feed into phase equilibrium calculations using the Gibbs free energy minimization software MELTS, augmented with machine learning emulators to accelerate iterative simulations of fractional crystallization sequences. The HPC environment is essential for managing the computational load of 10,000+ core-hour DFT simulations, training neural network potentials on TB-scale trajectory datasets, and conducting ensemble modeling of melt-solid equilibria in heterogeneous systems. Anticipated outcomes include (1) a publicly accessible database of silicate melt properties under ultrahigh PT conditions, (2) improved predictive capacity for chalcophile element distributions in magmatic sulfide systems, and (3) new constraints on the role of reduced melts in early Earth core formation. By bridging atomic-scale geochemical processes with planetary-scale differentiation models, this work will provide transformative insights into silicate-driven geochemical cycles while establishing computational workflows adaptable to extraterrestrial mantle systems. The project requires dedicated HPC allocations to support parallelized quantum mechanical calculations, large-scale reactive flow simulations, and data synthesis across disparate timescales.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the chemical properties and behavior of the silicates and other substances forming, and formed by geomorphological processes of the earth and other planets. Includes instruction in chemical thermodynamics, equilibrium in silicate systems, atomic bonding, isotopic fractionation, geochemical modeling, specimen analysis, and studies of specific organic and inorganic substances.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical challenges in concrete finishing practices by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model and optimize the interplay between material composition, environmental conditions, and structural performance. Despite advances in concrete technology, inconsistencies in curing dynamics, thermal stress distribution, and crack propagation remain persistent issues, often leading to reduced durability and increased maintenance costs. Traditional empirical approaches struggle to account for the complex, multi-variable interactions inherent in concrete mixtures and placement techniques, particularly under extreme environmental conditions. This research proposes a computational framework to simulate these processes at unprecedented resolution, enabling data-driven optimization of concrete formulations and finishing protocols. Using multi-scale modeling techniques, molecular dynamics simulations will analyze hydration kinetics and microstructure formation in cementitious materials, while finite element analysis (FEA) will predict thermal and mechanical stresses during curing and service life. Machine learning models, trained on simulation outputs and experimental datasets, will identify optimal mixture proportions and finishing sequences to minimize defects. The computational workflow requires HPC resources to manage large parametric studies spanning diverse material combinations (e.g., additives, aggregate gradations) and environmental scenarios (temperature, humidity). Expected outcomes include predictive models correlating mixture properties with long-term performance metrics, a decision-support tool for real-time adjustment of finishing operations, and novel guidelines for defect-resistant concrete designs. By reducing trial-and-error waste in construction workflows, this research aims to enhance the sustainability and cost-effectiveness of concrete infrastructure while advancing pedagogical resources for workforce training in concrete finishing technologies. The project’s computational demands—particularly the parallel processing needs for coupled thermo-mechanical simulations and generative AI-driven optimization—necessitate access to scalable HPC infrastructure to achieve industrially relevant turnaround times.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to prepare, construct, and finish buildings, components, and related structures using compound masonry mixtures of stone, gravel, sand, cement, and water.
