Includes instruction in performance balancing; redundancy; local area (LAN) and wide area (WAN) network management; system migration and upgrading; outage control; problem diagnosis and troubleshooting; and system maintenance, budgeting, and management.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a high-resolution, integrated modeling framework to predict the impacts of climate change and anthropogenic stressors on coastal wetland resilience and marine resource sustainability. Coastal and estuarine ecosystems face compounding threats from sea-level rise, nutrient pollution, and habitat degradation, yet current models lack the spatial granularity and computational efficiency to resolve fine-scale hydrodynamic-biogeochemical interactions across dynamic land-water interfaces. To address this gap, we propose coupling a three-dimensional hydrodynamic model (Delft3D Flexible Mesh) with a biogeochemical module (FABM) to simulate sediment transport, nutrient cycling, and vegetation dynamics in critical wetland-marine transition zones. The computational workflow will integrate multi-source data, including LiDAR-derived bathymetry, satellite-based water quality indices, and in situ sensor networks, to parameterize scenarios of storm surge intensification, nutrient loading, and managed retreat interventions. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute ensemble simulations at meter-scale resolution across decadal timescales, leveraging parallel processing for Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification and machine learning-driven parameter optimization. Expected outcomes include predictive maps of wetland accretion rates under varying sea-level rise trajectories, identification of eutrophication thresholds for submerged aquatic vegetation, and cost-benefit analyses of nature-based flood mitigation strategies. By quantifying feedbacks between hydrologic connectivity and ecosystem services, this research will provide actionable insights for adaptive management of wetlands and coastal marine habitats. The resulting open-source tools will enable resource managers to prioritize conservation investments, optimize restoration designs, and balance ecological integrity with human development needs in rapidly changing aquatic environments.
detailed_field: Environmental/ natural resources management and policy
cip_title: Water, Wetlands, and Marine Resources Management
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply the principles of marine/aquatic biology, oceanography, natural resource economics, and natural resources management to the development, conservation, and management of freshwater and saltwater environments. Includes instruction in subjects such as wetlands, riverine, lacustrine, coastal, and oceanic water resources; water conservation and use; flood control; pollution control; water supply logistics; wastewater management; aquatic and marine ecology; aquatic and marine life conservation; and the economic and recreational uses of water resources.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to optimize the design, safety, and longevity of steam boiler systems, addressing critical challenges in boilermaking practices. Traditional methods for boiler fabrication and maintenance rely heavily on empirical testing and standardized codes, which can limit adaptability to novel materials, complex geometries, or extreme operating conditions. To overcome these limitations, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate multiphysics interactions within boiler systems, including thermal stress, fluid dynamics, and material degradation under high-pressure environments. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) will model steam flow and heat distribution, while finite element analysis (FEA) will assess structural integrity under cyclic thermal loading. Machine learning algorithms will be integrated to predict weld joint performance and corrosion rates based on material composition and operational data. These simulations require large-scale parallel processing to resolve fine-scale phenomena, such as microcrack propagation in welded seams or turbulent flow in irregular pipe networks, which are computationally prohibitive on standard systems. The outcomes will generate predictive frameworks to guide material selection, welding protocols, and maintenance schedules, aligning with ASME boiler standards while enabling innovation in component design. By validating these models against experimental pressure-testing data, the project aims to reduce prototyping costs, enhance failure prediction accuracy, and inform updates to industry safety codes. The requested HPC resources will also support the development of interactive training modules for boilermaking students, bridging computational literacy with hands-on technical skills. This work advances the boilermaking field by integrating modern computational tools into traditional practices, fostering safer, more efficient energy systems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to fabricate and repair steam boiler components. Includes instruction in principles of steam power, material selection, welding, riveting, sealing materials, pressure testing, pipefitting, and applicable codes and standards.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational research in Dutch/Flemish philology and literary studies, addressing gaps in large-scale analysis of historical and contemporary language variation. The primary research problem centers on tracing the evolution of Dutch dialects and Creoles across time and geography, particularly in understudied textual corpora spanning the 16th–21st centuries. Traditional methods struggle to process the scale and complexity of these multilingual, multidialectal datasets, which include digitized manuscripts, print archives, and modern social media texts featuring code-switching between Dutch, Flemish variants, and Creoles like Berbice Dutch. The project proposes a hybrid computational approach combining transformer-based language models, dialectometric mapping, and phylogenetic algorithms to model language change. Custom NLP pipelines will be developed to handle orthographic variation in historical texts, while graph-based methods will analyze syntactic shifts in Flemish literature compared to Standard Dutch. A key innovation involves training a diachronic BERT model on a curated corpus of 10+ billion tokens from the Dutch Language Institute archives, requiring GPU-accelerated training across multiple nodes. Expected outcomes include 1) the first quantitative atlas of Dutch dialect convergence/divergence patterns, 2) computational evidence for Creole stabilization timelines in colonial contexts, and 3) open-access tools for automated variant detection in heritage texts. This work will provide humanities researchers with scalable methods to interrogate language contact phenomena while preserving minority linguistic features. The requested HPC resources are critical due to the memory-intensive nature of processing scanned archival materials (15+ TB image-to-text datasets) and the parallel computing demands of comparative syntactic trees across 50+ dialect nodes. By bridging computational linguistics with Dutch philology, this project aims to redefine historical language studies in the digital humanities landscape.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Dutch language and related dialects. Includes instruction in philology; literature; Dutch Creoles; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: The development of advanced fibrous materials with tailored mechanical and functional properties requires a comprehensive understanding of polymer dynamics and hierarchical assembly under processing conditions. However, existing experimental methods struggle to resolve multiscale structural transitions during fiber formation, particularly at the molecular-to-meso scales. This project seeks to employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model the non-equilibrium behavior of semi-crystalline polymer systems during electrospinning and post-drawing processes. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will be conducted using coarse-grained and atomistically informed models to capture chain orientation, crystallization kinetics, and defect propagation in polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polyacrylonitrile (PAN) fibers. Reactive force fields will be implemented to study degradation pathways under thermal and mechanical stress. A multiscale framework will integrate simulation outputs with experimental fiber characterization data to predict tensile strength, modulus, and thermal stability as functions of processing parameters. The computational workflow demands significant parallel processing capabilities due to system sizes exceeding 1 million atoms and simulation timescales spanning microseconds. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for optimizing fiber processing conditions, reducing trial-and-error experimentation, and enabling the design of high-performance fibers for smart textiles and composite applications. The resource allocation will directly support the development of open-source simulation tools tailored for fiber science, fostering collaboration across materials research communities. By elucidating structure-property relationships in synthetic fibers, this work aims to advance sustainable manufacturing strategies and contribute to next-generation materials for biomedical and energy storage applications.
detailed_field: Materials chemistry and materials sciences nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the synthesis, structure and properties of polymers with an emphasis on fibers. Includes instruction in polymer chemistry and synthesis, fiber and polymer physics and physical chemistry, the production, processing and properties of fibrous materials, and chemistry of dyes, finishes, and their processes.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a novel computational framework to optimize the preservation and accessibility of heterogeneous digital collections within modern library systems, addressing critical gaps in scalable digital curation. As libraries increasingly manage complex, multi-format archives—spanning digitized manuscripts, born-digital media, and interactive multimedia—traditional metadata schemas and preservation workflows struggle to adapt to evolving technical demands. The research problem centers on creating adaptive, AI-driven models to automate metadata enrichment, detect format obsolescence risks, and prioritize preservation actions across large-scale repositories. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, the project will employ transformer-based neural architectures to analyze semantic patterns in unstructured text and multimedia collections, paired with graph neural networks to model relationships between digital objects and their preservation dependencies. Computational experiments will focus on training models using distributed deep learning frameworks to process petabytes of library-held data, simulating decay scenarios for format migration benchmarking, and optimizing resource allocation for preservation workflows through reinforcement learning. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for predictive preservation analytics, dynamic risk assessment matrices for digital collections, and scalable metadata harmonization pipelines. By integrating library science principles with advanced computational methods, this work aims to establish new standards for sustainable digital stewardship in cultural heritage institutions, while advancing interdisciplinary methodologies at the intersection of information management, AI ethics, and decentralized archival systems. The requested HPC resources are essential for handling memory-intensive model training, parallelized processing of heterogeneous data types, and large-scale simulations of long-term digital preservation strategies.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in library science, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the impacts of shifting climatic gradients on the population dynamics and adaptive capacity of a keystone species in montane ecosystems, using high-performance computing (HPC) to overcome critical scalability challenges in spatially explicit ecological modeling. The research problem centers on disentangling how temperature-mediated habitat fragmentation and altered biotic interactions (e.g., predator-prey relationships, competition) collectively influence metapopulation persistence under projected climate scenarios. Current models often simplify landscape heterogeneity or assume static species traits, limiting their ability to predict eco-evolutionary feedbacks over decadal timescales. To address this gap, we propose an integrative computational framework combining individual-based models (IBMs) with dynamic landscape layers and quantitative genetics modules. The IBM will simulate 10^5–10^6 individuals across a spatially resolved elevation grid (1 km² resolution), incorporating stochastic demographic processes, dispersal constraints, and trait evolution under selection pressures from both abiotic and biotic factors. HPC resources are essential for parallelizing parameter sweeps across climate projection ensembles (CMIP6), scaling genetic algorithm optimizations for trait-space exploration, and managing petabyte-scale output from 50-year simulations across multiple emission scenarios. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of threshold rates of climate change beyond which adaptive tracking fails for focal species, (2) quantification of emergent metacommunity stability metrics under hybrid disturbance regimes, and (3) open-source modular code for coupled eco-evolutionary forecasting. Results will directly inform regional conservation strategies and provide a template for integrating genomic-ecological data into predictive frameworks for climate-vulnerable taxa. The computational infrastructure will enable unprecedented resolution in capturing genotype-to-ecosystem linkages across realistic spatial and temporal scales.
detailed_field: Ecology, evolutionary biology, and epidemiology nec
cip_title: Ecology, Evolution, Systematics and Population Biology, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in ecology, evolution, and systematics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the historical and sociopolitical dynamics shaping educational policy diffusion across diverse cultural contexts, with a focus on how ideological frameworks embedded in policy documents influence equity outcomes. Using a mixed-methods approach combining computational text analysis, network modeling, and geospatial simulation, we propose to analyze over 1.2 million pages of digitized policy documents, legislative records, and educational literature from 15 nations (1890–2020). The research addresses two core questions: (1) How have transnational networks of philosophical thought circulated through policy mechanisms to perpetuate or challenge educational inequalities? (2) What computational models best capture the interaction between localized cultural values and globalized policy paradigms in education reform? High-performance computing resources are required to process multilingual textual corpora through transformer-based NLP pipelines, reconstruct historical policy networks via temporal graph algorithms, and simulate policy adoption patterns using agent-based modeling at scale. The computational workflow will integrate qualitative hermeneutic coding of key philosophical concepts with quantitative analysis of semantic shifts and network centrality metrics. Expected outcomes include a novel interdisciplinary framework for analyzing education policy as a sociotechnical system, open-access tools for critical policy archaeology, and evidence-based insights into how computational humanities methods can inform equity-oriented educational philosophy. This work advances the field by developing methodological bridges between normative philosophical inquiry and data-driven social science while maintaining critical attention to education’s role in reproducing or transforming power structures. The requested resources will enable processing historically dense texts and simulating complex policy ecosystems beyond the capacity of standard computing infrastructure.
cip_title: Social and Philosophical Foundations of Education
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic study of education as a social and cultural institution, and the educational process as an object of humanistic inquiry. Includes instruction in such subjects as the philosophy of education, history of education, educational literature, educational anthropology, sociology of education, economics and politics of education, educational policy studies, and studies of education in relation to specific populations, issues, social phenomena, and types of work.

abstract: The hydrodynamic performance of high-speed marine vessels is critically influenced by the complex interplay between hull form, structural dynamics, and operational conditions. Current design methodologies often rely on compartmentalized simulations that inadequately capture fluid-structure interactions (FSI) at extreme velocities, leading to suboptimal efficiency and unanticipated structural fatigue. This project proposes an integrated computational framework to resolve multi-physics interactions in high-speed hulls operating in irregular wave environments, with a focus on optimizing energy efficiency while maintaining structural integrity. Leveraging high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) coupled with finite element analysis (FEA), the study will simulate transient wave loads, hull deformation, and localized cavitation effects at Reynolds numbers exceeding 10^7. Machine learning techniques will be embedded to iteratively refine hull geometries based on real-time feedback from coupled simulations, targeting a 15-20% reduction in wave-making resistance compared to conventional designs. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve the spatiotemporal scales of turbulent boundary layers and structural resonance modes, requiring parallelized simulations across 10,000+ cores with adaptive meshing capabilities. Expected outcomes include a validated predictive model for FSI in high-speed regimes, a generative design toolkit for adaptive hull forms, and open-source datasets correlating operational profiles with fatigue hotspots. This research directly addresses the U.S. Navy’s strategic priorities in sustainable maritime mobility by advancing computational methods for next-generation vessel design, with potential applications in commercial fast ferries and unmanned surface vehicles. The proposed framework bridges gaps between traditional naval architecture, materials science, and data-driven optimization, establishing a paradigm for computationally intensive marine engineering challenges.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of self-propelled, stationary, or towed vessels operating on or under the water, including inland, coastal and ocean environments; and the analysis of related engineering problems such as corrosion, power transfer, pressure, hull efficiency, stress factors, safety and life support, environmental hazards and factors, and specific use requirements.

abstract: This research project seeks to optimize dynamic pricing and personalized marketing strategies in hospitality and recreation operations through the integration of real-time customer behavior modeling and large-scale operational data analytics. The hospitality industry faces growing complexity in balancing demand fluctuations, heterogeneous customer preferences, and multi-channel marketing efforts—particularly in sectors like resort operations, recreational equipment rentals, and experiential tourism packages. Traditional revenue management systems often fail to account for real-time behavioral signals from IoT-enabled facilities, mobile engagement patterns, and cross-channel customer journeys. To address this gap, we propose developing an adaptive computational framework combining graph neural networks (GNNs) to model customer decision cascades, reinforcement learning agents for price optimization, and hyper-personalization engines capable of processing multimodal data streams from reservation systems, wearable devices, and service interaction logs. The project requires high-performance computing resources to train GNNs on temporal guest behavior graphs containing up to 10 million nodes representing customer-product-service interactions, while simultaneously running Monte Carlo simulations of pricing scenarios across distributed recreation service portfolios. Expected outcomes include a novel decision-support system that reduces marketing cost inefficiencies by 18-22% in pilot tests with partner resorts, along with predictive models quantifying the lifetime value impact of micro-targeted recreation package recommendations. By advancing computational methods for synthesizing operational telemetry with marketing responsiveness, this work aims to establish new paradigms for data-driven hospitality resource allocation while maintaining compliance with evolving customer privacy regulations in digital leisure markets.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide marketing services in the hospitality and leisure fields. Includes instruction in hospitality operations, customer sales and assistance operations and techniques, telephone operations, basic office management, retail sports, recreation equipment, food and beverage.

abstract: This project seeks to address unresolved questions about turbulence and magnetic field dynamics in molecular clouds, critical drivers of star formation efficiency in galaxies. Despite advances in observational astronomy, the interplay between supersonic turbulence, magnetic pressure, and gravitational collapse remains poorly quantified, limiting predictive models of galactic evolution. We propose a high-resolution numerical study using magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to resolve multiphase gas interactions at scales from 0.1 pc to 100 pc, capturing both cloud-scale dynamics and localized collapse thresholds. The simulations will utilize the FLASH code, augmented with custom modules for radiative transfer and non-equilibrium chemistry, to model turbulence injection by supernova remnants and feedback from young stellar populations. A parameter space of magnetic field strengths (1–50 μG), metallicities, and cloud densities will be explored to assess their roles in regulating star formation rates under varying galactic environments. The computational workload necessitates high-performance computing resources due to the simulations’ scale: adaptive mesh refinement will require up to 10^6 core-hours to achieve the necessary resolution for tracking density fluctuations and magnetic field topology. Data outputs will be analyzed using machine learning-based feature detection to identify statistical correlations between initial conditions and star formation outcomes. This work will directly inform interpretation of JWST and ALMA observations of nearby galaxies while providing open-source turbulence metrics for the astrophysics community. Results will constrain key parameters in next-generation semi-analytic galaxy evolution models, reducing uncertainties in predictions of stellar mass assembly across cosmic time. The derived datasets will be made publicly available through a dedicated portal, enabling cross-disciplinary studies in interstellar medium physics and computational fluid dynamics.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the planetary, galactic, and stellar phenomena occurring in outer space. Includes instruction in celestial mechanics, cosmology, stellar physics, galactic evolution, quasars, stellar distribution and motion, interstellar medium, atomic and molecular constituents of astronomical phenomena, planetary science, solar system evolution, and specific methodologies such as optical astronomy, radioastronomy, and theoretical astronomy.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of cross-border digital misinformation campaigns and their impact on diplomatic trust-building processes, leveraging computational social science methods within the interdisciplinary domain of International Relations and Affairs. While traditional studies focus on state-level policy or institutional responses, this research addresses a gap in understanding how algorithmically amplified misinformation disrupts non-state actors’ roles in Track II diplomacy—a critical yet understudied facet of modern conflict resolution. The core research problem examines how machine learning-driven content recommendation systems interact with grassroots diplomatic networks, potentially eroding the credibility of informal dialogue channels in post-conflict regions. To model these complex interactions, the project will employ large-scale agent-based simulations incorporating neural network architectures to represent adaptive misinformation actors, paired with graph-theoretic analyses of real-world diplomatic communication networks. High-performance computing resources are essential for processing multilingual social media corpora (spanning 10TB of historical data from conflict zones), running Monte Carlo simulations of trust dynamics under varying misinformation regimes, and training transformer-based models to detect emerging narrative manipulation patterns. Expected outcomes include a novel framework for quantifying diplomatic resilience to digital misinformation, predictive metrics for early warning systems in multilateral organizations, and open-source tools for simulating hybrid threats in informal diplomacy contexts. By bridging computational linguistics, network science, and diplomatic theory, this work aims to establish empirical foundations for safeguarding non-traditional peacebuilding mechanisms in an era of weaponized information ecosystems.
detailed_field: International relations and national security studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic study of international politics and institutions, and the conduct of diplomacy and foreign policy. Includes instruction in international relations theory, foreign policy analysis, international law and organization, the comparative study of specific countries and regions, and the theory and practice of diplomacy.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the role of biomechanical forces in tumor progression and therapeutic resistance within physiologically relevant microenvironments. Despite advances in cancer biology, the interplay between mechanical stress, hypoxia, and interstitial fluid pressure in driving metastatic behavior remains poorly understood. Traditional in vitro models fail to capture the dynamic complexity of these interactions, while clinical data alone cannot isolate causative biomechanical factors. To address this gap, we propose a multiscale computational framework integrating agent-based modeling (ABM) of tumor cell populations with finite element analysis (FEA) of tissue-scale mechanical properties. The ABM component will simulate cellular responses to variable stiffness, fluid shear stress, and oxygen gradients, informed by experimental data from 3D-bioprinted tumor models. Concurrently, FEA will map stress distribution patterns in patient-derived tumor geometries obtained via medical imaging. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve spatiotemporal interactions across scales, particularly for parameter optimization, sensitivity analyses, and validation against longitudinal clinical outcomes. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of mechanical biomarkers predictive of invasion risk, (2) quantification of stress-mediated changes in chemoresistance pathways, and (3) a predictive platform for testing mechanotherapeutic interventions. This work will advance integrative pathobiology by bridging tissue-level biomechanics with organ-scale disease manifestations, offering novel strategies to disrupt force-dependent metastatic niches. The requested allocation will support GPU-accelerated simulations of up to 10^6 interacting cells in heterogeneous environments, large-scale fluid-structure interaction computations, and machine learning-driven analysis of multiparametric output data. By elucidating how mechanical cues shape tumor evolution, this research aligns with the program’s mission to decode disease mechanisms across biological scales while directly informing translational approaches in solid tumor management.
detailed_field: Physiology, oncology, and cancer biology nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the mechanisms underlying human disease. Includes instruction in the causes and nature of disease processes in animals and humans at the molecular, cellular, tissue, organ and organ systems level, tissue structure and function, cellular mechanisms of disease and organ systems response to disease.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to quantify and mitigate systemic risks in insurance markets, particularly those arising from interconnected economic, environmental, and demographic factors. Traditional actuarial methods often rely on simplified assumptions that inadequately capture the nonlinear dependencies and tail risks inherent in large-scale systems, such as climate-related catastrophes or pandemic-driven health and economic crises. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework integrating stochastic simulation, agent-based modeling, and machine learning to analyze multi-domain risk interactions. The research will parameterize models using heterogeneous datasets—including insurance claims, climate projections, demographic trends, and real-time economic indicators—to simulate cascading risk scenarios under varying regulatory and environmental conditions. Key computational challenges include scaling Monte Carlo methods for high-dimensional uncertainty propagation, optimizing gradient-based solvers for dynamic risk allocation, and training neural networks to identify latent risk correlations across disparate data streams. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallelized execution of millions of scenario iterations, sensitivity analyses, and real-time calibration against emerging data. Expected outcomes include (1) a publicly accessible library of modular risk simulation tools tailored for actuarial applications, (2) empirically validated metrics for capital adequacy under compound stress scenarios, and (3) policy insights for managing systemic risks in sectors such as catastrophe reinsurance and longevity-based financial products. By leveraging distributed computing architectures, this work will overcome memory and latency constraints that limit conventional actuarial software, providing insurers and regulators with scalable tools to address 21st-century risk landscapes. The resource request supports GPU-accelerated nodes for deep learning tasks and high-memory nodes for large-scale optimization, ensuring robust handling of datasets exceeding 100TB in size.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the mathematical and statistical analysis of risk, and their applications to insurance and other business management problems. Includes instruction in forecasting theory, quantitative and non-quantitative risk measurement methodologies, development of risk tables, secondary data analysis, and computer-assisted research methods.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model the spread of zoonotic pathogens at the interface of domestic animal populations, wildlife, and human communities, with a focus on optimizing early detection and intervention strategies. Despite advances in veterinary epidemiology, predicting outbreak dynamics remains limited by the complexity of interspecies interactions, environmental variables, and gaps in high-resolution host movement data. To address this, we propose integrating spatially explicit agent-based modeling (ABM) with machine learning (ML) to simulate transmission pathways of high-concern pathogens, such as avian influenza and leptospirosis, across heterogeneous landscapes. The ABM will incorporate real-world data on livestock densities, wildlife migration patterns, and anthropogenic factors (e.g., trade networks, land use) sourced from public health databases and satellite imagery. ML algorithms will then analyze simulated and historical outbreak data to identify high-risk spatiotemporal hotspots and evaluate the efficacy of targeted vaccination, biosecurity measures, or surveillance protocols. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to manage the scale of these simulations, which involve millions of agents representing individual animals and humans, as well as stochastic environmental variables. The computational workflow will leverage parallelized simulations across multiple nodes, coupled with GPU-accelerated training of deep neural networks to optimize parameter estimation and scenario testing. Outcomes will include predictive risk maps for veterinary practitioners, policy recommendations for outbreak preparedness, and open-source tools for adaptive resource allocation in animal health systems. By elucidating pathways of zoonotic spillover, this work aims to reduce economic losses in agriculture and mitigate public health threats, aligning with One Health priorities. The project also provides training opportunities for veterinary students in computational methods, bridging a critical skills gap in data-driven veterinary medicine.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of veterinary medicine, involving the diagnosis, treatment, and health care management of animals and animal populations and the prevention and management of zoonosis. Includes instruction in the veterinary basic sciences, infectious and noninfectious disease, diagnostic procedures, veterinary clinical medicine, obstetrics, radiology, anesthesiology, surgery, toxicology, animal health and preventive medicine, clinical nutrition, practice management, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical challenges in mineral extraction efficiency and mine safety through advanced computational modeling and simulation. A key research problem in mining technology is the inability of conventional methods to accurately predict geomechanical instabilities in complex geological formations or optimize mineral processing workflows under dynamic environmental constraints. Current approaches often rely on oversimplified analytical models or limited-scale experimental data, leading to suboptimal resource recovery and elevated risks of structural failures. To overcome these limitations, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating finite element analysis (FE), discrete element method (DEM), and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to model rock fracturing, granular material flow, and slurry transport processes at unprecedented resolution. The HPC environment will enable parallelized simulations of mine-scale geometries with heterogeneous material properties, coupled with machine learning algorithms trained on historical sensor data from operational mines to refine predictive accuracy. Key deliverables include GPU-accelerated simulations of stress redistribution during excavation, real-time predictive models for equipment wear in processing plants, and probabilistic risk assessments for collapse scenarios under varying mineralogical conditions. The computational workflow will utilize open-source platforms like OpenFOAM and LAMMPS, optimized for distributed-memory architectures to handle terabytes of spatially resolved geological data. Expected outcomes include validated protocols for adaptive drilling strategies, improved tailings management systems, and digital twins for mine ventilation networks. By integrating HPC-driven insights with field operations, this research aims to reduce energy consumption in mineral processing by 15–20%, enhance worker safety through early hazard detection systems, and extend the operational lifespan of aging mines. Results will be disseminated as open-access simulation toolkits tailored for mining engineers, fostering broader adoption of data-driven decision-making in resource-intensive industries.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and other professionals engaged in the development and operation of mines and related mineral processing facilities. Includes instruction in principles of mineral extraction and related geology, mineral field mapping and site analysis, testing and sampling methods, instrument calibration, assay analysis, test equipment operation and maintenance, mine environment and safety monitoring procedures, mine inspection procedures, and report preparation.

abstract: The increasing complexity of drug discovery and development necessitates advanced computational approaches to predict pharmacological outcomes accurately. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical challenges in optimizing drug efficacy and safety through multi-scale computational modeling. We aim to integrate molecular dynamics simulations, machine learning-driven predictive analytics, and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models to investigate drug-target interactions, metabolic pathways, and patient-specific response variability. Current limitations in simulating large-scale biomolecular systems and analyzing heterogeneous datasets (e.g., genomic, proteomic, and clinical pharmacokinetic data) restrict the precision of in silico drug design. By employing GPU-accelerated molecular docking and ensemble simulations, we will characterize binding affinities and conformational dynamics of novel compounds targeting kinase enzymes implicated in inflammatory disorders. Concurrently, neural network architectures will be trained on curated chemical libraries to predict off-target effects and toxicity profiles, enabling virtual screening of compound libraries with over 500,000 entries. The HPC environment is essential for parallel processing of stochastic PK/PD models that incorporate population-level variability in metabolic enzymes and transporters, particularly for polypharmacy scenarios common in geriatric therapeutics. Expected outcomes include the identification of three lead compounds with optimized selectivity profiles, predictive algorithms for dose individualization in renal-impaired populations, and open-source tools for rapid assessment of drug-drug interaction risks. This work will advance computational pharmacy methodologies while directly supporting ongoing preclinical studies in collaborative drug development pipelines.
detailed_field: Pharmacy, pharmaceutical sciences, and administration nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent or employed practice of preparing and dispensing drugs and medications in consultation with prescribing physicians and other health care professionals, and for managing pharmacy practices and counseling patients. Includes instruction in mathematics, physics, chemistry, biochemistry, anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmacognosy, pharmacy practice, pharmacy administration, applicable regulations, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to optimize radiation shielding designs for industrial radiologic systems, addressing critical gaps in efficiency and safety for high-intensity applications. Current shielding approaches rely on conservative, empirically derived parameters that often lead to over-engineering, increased material costs, and operational inefficiencies. To overcome these limitations, we propose a multi-scale simulation framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model radiation transport, material interactions, and thermal-mechanical responses under dynamic operational conditions. The computational approach integrates Monte Carlo methods for stochastic particle transport simulations with finite element analysis (FEA) to predict stress distributions and degradation in shielding materials. Machine learning techniques will be applied to iteratively refine material compositions and geometric configurations, targeting minimized radiation leakage while maintaining structural integrity. The project will utilize GPU-accelerated computing to handle the high-resolution, three-dimensional geometries typical of industrial radiologic setups, with parallelized workflows to manage stochastic and deterministic simulations concurrently. Expected outcomes include validated models for predicting shielding performance across diverse neutron and gamma-ray spectra, as well as a generative design toolkit to propose novel material configurations for next-generation shielding systems. This work will directly support the development of safer, cost-effective radiologic technologies for nuclear instrumentation, non-destructive testing, and waste management applications. By coupling HPC-driven insights with experimental validation, the project aims to establish a transformative framework for radiation shielding optimization, with potential impacts on industrial safety standards, regulatory guidelines, and educational training tools for radiologic technology professionals.
cip_title: Nuclear and Industrial Radiologic Technologies, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in nuclear and industrial radiologic technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development and validation of computational models for predicting individualized treatment outcomes in patients with complex psychological disorders. A critical challenge in clinical psychology is the heterogeneity of patient responses to evidence-based interventions, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) or pharmacotherapy. Traditional statistical methods often fail to account for high-dimensional interactions among neurobiological, behavioral, and environmental variables, limiting their utility in personalizing care. To address this, we propose a machine learning framework integrating multimodal data—including neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG), electronic health records (EHRs), and real-time ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data—to identify predictive biomarkers of treatment response. The computational workflow will involve preprocessing large-scale neuroimaging datasets (~10 TB), training ensemble models (e.g., graph neural networks, gradient-boosted decision trees) to capture nonlinear relationships between baseline patient characteristics and longitudinal outcomes, and performing Bayesian optimization to simulate treatment effect heterogeneity. HPC resources are essential due to the computational intensity of feature extraction from high-resolution fMRI data, the need for parallelized hyperparameter tuning across thousands of model iterations, and the deployment of permutation-based significance testing to control for multiple comparisons. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated predictive algorithm for matching patients with optimal interventions, (2) open-source tools for clinical psychologists to replicate the analytic pipeline, and (3) novel insights into transdiagnostic neural circuits associated with resilience to specific therapies. By enabling rapid analysis of complex datasets, this project aims to bridge the gap between computational psychiatry and real-world clinical decision-making, ultimately reducing trial-and-error approaches in mental health care. The requested resources will support GPU-accelerated model training, large-memory nodes for handling dense connectivity matrices, and scalable storage for multi-site collaborative data.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of clinical psychology, involving the analysis, diagnosis, and clinical treatment of psychological disorders and behavioral pathologies. Includes instruction in clinical assessment and diagnosis, personality appraisal, psychopathology, clinical psychopharmacology, behavior modification, therapeutic intervention skills, patient interviewing, personalized and group therapy, child and adolescent therapy, cognitive and behavioral therapy, supervised clinical practice, ethical standards, and applicable regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in professional and technical communication (PTC) through large-scale analysis of digital writing practices and multimodal document design. The research problem centers on the challenges of modeling complex rhetorical decisions in dynamic, data-rich environments, such as user experience (UX) documentation, scientific reports, and algorithmically generated content. Current methods for analyzing writing processes and audience engagement rely on small-scale qualitative studies or manual coding, limiting scalability and generalizability. To address this gap, the project proposes a computational approach combining natural language processing (NLP), network analysis, and machine learning to examine patterns in document revision histories, cross-platform content adaptation, and visual-textual coherence across 10,000+ technical documents. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of heterogeneous datasets—including version control logs, eye-tracking metrics, and A/B testing results—to identify correlations between writing strategies, usability outcomes, and stakeholder feedback. Key methods include training transformer-based models to classify rhetorical moves in technical genres and simulating document interaction pathways using agent-based modeling. Expected outcomes include: (1) a publicly available corpus of annotated technical documents with metadata, (2) predictive models for optimizing content clarity and accessibility in STEM communication, and (3) frameworks for integrating computational analytics into writing pedagogy. By scaling textual analysis to previously unmanageable levels, this work will advance empirical foundations in PTC research while providing actionable insights for organizations managing large documentation ecosystems. The requested resources directly support computationally intensive tasks, including GPU-accelerated model training and distributed processing of 50+ TB of multimedia writing artifacts, which exceed the capacity of local institutional infrastructure.
cip_title: Professional, Technical, Business, and Scientific Writing
cip_definition: A program that focuses on professional, technical, business, and scientific writing; and that prepares individuals for academic positions or for professional careers as writers, editors, researchers, and related careers in business, government, non-profits, and the professions. Includes instruction in theories of rhetoric, writing, and digital literacy; document design, production, and management; visual rhetoric and multimedia composition; documentation development; usability testing; web writing; and publishing in print and electronic media.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a computational framework for simulating and optimizing the ecological and socio-cultural impacts of urban green infrastructure at a metropolitan scale. Landscape architecture faces a critical challenge in addressing climate resilience and equitable access to green spaces while balancing competing demands of urbanization, biodiversity, and cultural heritage. Traditional design methods, reliant on static models and limited datasets, struggle to account for dynamic interactions between ecological processes, human behavior, and long-term environmental stressors. This project proposes an agent-based modeling (ABM) approach integrated with machine learning (ML) to simulate feedback loops between vegetation growth, stormwater dynamics, pedestrian movement patterns, and community engagement metrics across diverse urban typologies. High-resolution geospatial datasets, including LiDAR, hyperspectral imagery, and crowdsourced social preference data, will be processed using parallelized workflows to parameterize multi-scale simulations. The computational framework will enable real-time scenario testing of landscape interventions under varying climate projections, demographic shifts, and maintenance regimes. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for predictive performance metrics of green infrastructure designs, validated against ecological field measurements and participatory planning records from three case study cities. By enabling rapid iteration of complex, data-driven landscape systems analysis, this work aims to advance evidence-based design practices while establishing computational benchmarks for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of urban ecology, spatial analytics, and community-centered design. The requested HPC resources are essential for handling memory-intensive 3D terrain processing, training ML models on heterogeneous urban datasets, and executing ensemble simulations that capture stochastic social-environmental interactions over decadal timescales.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of landscape architecture and research in various aspects of the field. Includes instruction in geology and hydrology; soils, groundcovers, and horticultural elements; project and site planning; landscape design, history, and theory; environmental design; applicable law and regulations; and professional responsibilities and standards.

abstract: Emerging infectious diseases in agricultural livestock pose significant threats to food security, animal welfare, and public health. Current disease transmission models often lack the resolution to integrate multi-scale data—such as host-pathogen interactions, genomic variability in disease resistance, and dynamic environmental factors—limiting their predictive accuracy. This project seeks to develop a high-resolution, multi-agent computational framework to simulate disease spread within heterogeneous animal populations and evaluate targeted intervention strategies. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement spatially explicit agent-based models that incorporate individual animal movement, contact networks, and environmental pathogen persistence. These models will integrate genomic datasets to explore correlations between genetic markers and disease susceptibility in cattle populations, alongside machine learning algorithms trained on historical outbreak data to identify high-risk transmission scenarios. By simulating millions of agent interactions across diverse herd configurations and environmental conditions, the project aims to optimize vaccination protocols, biosecurity measures, and culling strategies while minimizing economic losses. Expected outcomes include a scalable computational toolkit for predicting outbreak trajectories under climate variability, genetic profiles associated with resilience to common pathogens, and data-driven guidelines for regional disease management. The results will directly inform livestock health policies, enhance the precision of veterinary interventions, and reduce reliance on broad-spectrum antimicrobials, advancing sustainable agricultural practices. This work requires HPC capabilities due to the parallel processing demands of large-scale simulations, the need for rapid parameter optimization across complex biological datasets, and the analysis of high-dimensional genomic-environmental interactions.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of biological and chemical principles to the study, prevention, and control of diseases in agricultural animal populations. Includes instruction in environmental science, pharmacology, animal population studies, genetics, animal physiology and diet, disease prevention, treatment methodologies, and laboratory and testing procedures.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in understanding the interplay between neurobiological, genetic, and psychosocial factors contributing to late-life mental disorders, with a focus on treatment-resistant depression and Alzheimer’s disease-related psychosis in geriatric populations. Current clinical models lack the resolution to disentangle multidimensional risk profiles or predict individualized treatment outcomes, partly due to limitations in analyzing large, heterogeneous datasets spanning neuroimaging, genomic, electronic health record (EHR), and longitudinal behavioral data. To overcome these barriers, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop integrative machine learning frameworks capable of modeling complex interactions within and across these data types. The computational approach will involve three phases: (1) preprocessing and harmonizing multimodal neuroimaging data (structural MRI, fMRI, and amyloid-PET) using GPU-accelerated pipelines to extract disease-relevant biomarkers; (2) training interpretable ensemble models to identify genetic-epigenetic signatures (e.g., polygenic risk scores, DNA methylation patterns) associated with treatment response trajectories; and (3) implementing federated learning architectures to analyze distributed EHR data while preserving patient privacy. Computational workflows will utilize containerized environments for reproducibility and scale across HPC nodes to handle datasets exceeding 500 TB. Expected outcomes include the identification of novel predictive biomarkers for psychosis progression in early-stage dementia and actionable stratification tools for antidepressant selection in comorbid depression-cognitive impairment cases. By enabling real-time analysis of aging-related brain networks and genomic interactions at unprecedented resolution, this work will directly inform the development of personalized intervention protocols, reduce trial-and-error prescribing practices, and advance mechanistic insights into geriatric neuropsychiatric disorders. The proposed HPC resources are essential to overcome memory-intensive bottlenecks in whole-brain connectome analyses and reduce model training times for large-scale genomic-EHR integration from months to days.
cip_definition: Research focused on the prevention, evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment of mental and emotional disorders in the elderly, and to improve the psychiatric care of the elderly both in health and in disease.

abstract: The adverse effects of synthetic and naturally occurring chemical substances on animals present complex challenges in veterinary toxicology, particularly in understanding species-specific toxicokinetics, mechanisms of action, and long-term health outcomes. Current experimental models often lack the resolution to predict interspecies variability or elucidate molecular pathways underlying toxicity, limiting clinical interventions. This project seeks to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to develop predictive models of chemical toxicity across diverse animal species. Computational approaches will integrate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, machine learning (ML)-driven quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, and multi-scale pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) simulations. MD simulations will characterize interactions between toxicants and target proteins, such as ion channels and metabolic enzymes, across species-specific structural variants. Ensemble docking workflows will assess binding affinities for a library of 500+ known toxins, including mycotoxins and agrochemicals, against protein structures from companion animals, livestock, and wildlife. Concurrently, ML models trained on heterogeneous datasets—including toxicogenomic databases, clinical case reports, and in vitro assay results—will predict toxicity endpoints and identify biomarkers of exposure. PK/PD models parameterized with species-specific physiological data will simulate toxin distribution and organ-level effects under varying exposure scenarios. These computational workflows require HPC resources to manage large-scale parallel simulations, optimize hyperparameters for ensemble ML architectures, and process high-dimensional omics data. Expected outcomes include mechanistic insights into neurobehavioral and reproductive toxicants, predictive tools for risk assessment in underrepresented species, and actionable frameworks for antidote development. By bridging molecular mechanisms to clinical manifestations, this research aims to advance evidence-based veterinary care, inform regulatory policies, and contribute to One Health initiatives addressing cross-species toxicological threats. The requested computing infrastructure is critical to overcoming current limitations in data integration and computational scalability inherent to toxicological studies.
cip_definition: Research focused on the clinical application of research on the nature and extent of adverse effects of synthetic and naturally occurring chemical substances on animals. May included related research in chemical mechanisms and the specialties of reproductive, developmental, genetic, forensic, inhalation and neurobehavioral toxicology.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize the ethical alignment of automated decision-making systems in business operations, focusing on dynamic resource allocation under conflicting stakeholder priorities. As organizations increasingly deploy AI-driven tools for supply chain management, financial forecasting, and customer engagement, existing systems struggle to transparently balance profitability requirements with emerging ethical imperatives (e.g., environmental impact, data privacy, and equity considerations). The research addresses this gap by creating multi-objective optimization models that computationally formalize both quantitative business metrics and qualitative ethical dimensions through novel constraint hierarchies. Leveraging high-performance computing resources, we will implement parallelized evolutionary algorithms to simulate decision pathways across large-scale, stochastic business environments, incorporating real-world data from partner organizations in healthcare logistics and sustainable manufacturing. Computational experiments will evaluate trade-off surfaces between traditional KPIs and ethical performance indicators under varying market conditions and regulatory scenarios. The project further develops a prototype explainability interface using graph neural networks to map how specific ethical parameters influence system outputs. Expected outcomes include a benchmark dataset of ethical-business trade-off scenarios, optimized decision architectures for reconciling competing priorities, and performance metrics quantifying the computational overhead of ethical alignment mechanisms. This work contributes to the emerging field of computational business ethics by providing practical tools for implementing value-sensitive design in enterprise systems while maintaining operational efficiency. Results will inform both technical standards for ethical AI in business applications and organizational policies for responsible innovation in resource-intensive industries.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply principles of information technology, computer systems management, and business operations to the planning, management, and evaluation of information services in organizations. Includes instruction in telecommunications, systems planning and integration, information policy, information security, contracting and purchasing, budgeting, information technology, operations management, human resources, communications skills, and applicable law and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to analyze the relationship between structured dance movements, physiological responses, and therapeutic outcomes in dance therapy interventions. While dance therapy has demonstrated empirical benefits for mental and physical health, the mechanisms linking specific movement patterns to psychological or neurological changes remain poorly quantified. Current evaluation methods rely heavily on qualitative observation, limiting scalability and reproducibility. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process multimodal datasets—including motion-capture recordings, biometric sensor data (e.g., heart rate variability, galvanic skin response), and longitudinal clinical assessments—from group and individual dance therapy sessions. Machine learning models will be trained to identify movement signatures correlated with stress reduction, emotional regulation, or motor rehabilitation progress. Computational fluid dynamics simulations will model kinetic energy transfer in group dance interactions, testing hypotheses about synchrony and social connectivity. Additionally, agent-based modeling will explore how therapist-guided improvisation scaffolds neuroplastic adaptation in participants with trauma-related motor dysfunction. The scale of data (terabytes of high-resolution movement trajectories and biometric time series) and complexity of simulations (real-time analysis of multi-agent interactions) necessitate parallelized GPU computing and large-memory nodes. Outcomes will include open-source tools for quantifying therapeutic movement efficacy, predictive models to personalize interventions, and evidence-based frameworks for optimizing dance therapy protocols in clinical populations such as PTSD and Parkinson’s disease. By bridging embodied creative practice with computational rigor, this work aims to advance dance therapy as a data-informed discipline within integrative healthcare.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, in consultation with other rehabilitation team members or in private practice, to use the therapeutic application of creative dance movement to assist in promoting client rehabilitation and physical, emotional, and mental health. Includes instruction in neuroanatomy, personality development, movement and motor behavior, psychology, dance, creative expression modalities, improvisation, group psychology and leadership, client evaluation and supervision, dance therapy practice, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: The proposed research aims to investigate the dynamics of pattern formation in spatially extended ecological systems using advanced computational models rooted in reaction-diffusion theory. A critical challenge in mathematical biology lies in understanding how nonlinear interactions between species and environmental factors drive self-organized spatial structures—such as vegetation bands in arid ecosystems or plankton blooms in marine environments—and how these patterns influence ecosystem resilience to perturbations. Traditional analytical approaches struggle to capture the multiscale, stochastic, and heterogeneous nature of these systems, particularly when incorporating empirical data from field studies or genomic influences on species traits. This project will develop high-resolution, spatially explicit simulations integrating partial differential equations with agent-based modeling to study bifurcation thresholds and transient dynamics in pattern stability. The computational framework will employ adaptive mesh refinement to resolve localized phenomena while maintaining tractability across ecosystem-scale domains. Key innovations include coupling these models with machine learning-driven parameter estimation using ecological and metabolomic datasets, enabling the exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces linked to climate change scenarios. By leveraging high-performance computing resources, we will perform ensemble simulations across distributed-memory architectures to quantify uncertainty in tipping points and recovery pathways. Expected outcomes include predictive models for ecosystem response to anthropogenic stressors, open-source computational tools for interdisciplinary collaboration, and theoretical advances in understanding how genomic plasticity modulates spatial self-organization. This work bridges mathematical rigor with biological realism, addressing urgent questions in conservation while advancing methodologies for multiscale modeling in evolutionary ecology. The requested resources are essential to manage memory-intensive simulations, parallelize parameter sweeps, and enable runtime scalability for time-evolving systems spanning months to decades of ecological time.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of mathematics to genomics, molecular modeling, structural biology, ecology, evolutionary biology and systems of analysis of neurobiology, physiology, and metabolism. Includes instruction in computational mathematics, chaos and nonlinear systems, perturbation methods, evolutionary biology, molecular biology, bioinformatics, and neurobiology.

abstract: This project investigates the resilience of decentralized information ecosystems under cascading disruptions caused by climate-driven environmental stressors. As global infrastructural and ecological systems become increasingly interdependent, understanding how localized failures propagate through information networks—particularly those reliant on hybrid human-machine decision-making—is critical. The research integrates computational social science, network theory, and environmental informatics to model multi-layer networks that couple physical sensor arrays, community reporting platforms, and institutional data-sharing protocols. Using agent-based modeling and temporal graph neural networks, we will simulate how distributed information systems adapt (or collapse) when facing compound events such as simultaneous power grid failures, communication outages, and population displacement. The computational approach requires high-performance resources to handle three core challenges: 1) scaling discrete-event simulations across heterogeneous network topologies with >10^6 dynamic nodes, 2) training attention-based models on sparse, multi-modal data streams (satellite imagery, crowdsourced text, IoT sensor logs), and 3) optimizing parameter space exploration for resilience metrics under uncertainty bounds derived from climate projection ensembles. Expected outcomes include a framework for quantifying information criticality thresholds in coupled human-technical systems, novel protocols for dynamic network rerouting in resource-constrained environments, and open-source tools enabling communities to stress-test local information infrastructures against climate scenarios. By bridging gaps between disaster informatics, participatory sensing, and adaptive systems theory, this work advances predictive capabilities for information continuity in crisis contexts while informing policy on equitable resource allocation for climate-resilient communication architectures.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theory, organization, and process of information collection, transmission, and utilization in traditional and electronic forms. Includes instruction in information classification and organization; information storage and processing; transmission, transfer, and signaling; communications and networking; systems planning and design; human interfacing and use analysis; database development; information policy analysis; and related aspects of hardware, software, economics, social factors, and capacity.

abstract: This project seeks to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of real-time multilingual interpretation and specialized translation systems through advanced computational modeling, with a focus on low-resource language pairs involving English and Canadian French. Current challenges in automated interpretation—particularly for morphologically complex languages and domain-specific terminology (e.g., legal, medical, or technical texts)—stem from limited training data and the computational intensity of processing long-context, bidirectional speech or text streams. To address this, we propose developing a hybrid neural architecture integrating transformer-based models with dynamic memory networks, optimized for high-performance computing (HPC) environments. The research will leverage large-scale parallel corpora, including Canadian government multilingual documents and annotated interpreter datasets, to train models capable of context-aware, low-latency translation. Computational workflows will involve distributed training across GPU nodes to manage memory-intensive tasks such as attention mechanism optimization and real-time disambiguation of polysemous terms. Additionally, we will simulate simultaneous interpretation scenarios using time-synchronized speech-text alignment algorithms, requiring parallel processing to minimize latency. Expected outcomes include open-source models with improved robustness for rare language pairs (e.g., Inuktitut-French), a computational framework for evaluating interpretation fidelity under time constraints, and scalable pipelines for domain adaptation in translation systems. This work directly supports Canada’s bilingual policy and global linguistic diversity initiatives by reducing reliance on human intermediaries in critical cross-cultural communication contexts. The requested HPC resources are essential for handling terabyte-scale datasets, iterative hyperparameter tuning, and deploying containerized inference services to benchmark performance against industry standards.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to be professional interpreters and/or translators of documents and data files, either from English or (Canadian) French into another language or languages or vice versa. Includes intensive instruction in one or more foreign languages plus instruction in subjects such as single- and multiple-language interpretation, one- or two-way interpretation, simultaneous interpretation, general and literary translation, business translation, technical translation, and other specific applications of linguistic skills.

abstract: The increasing complexity of human-machine collaborative systems necessitates advanced computational models that bridge cognitive decision-making and embodied motor control. Current approaches in artificial intelligence often decouple high-level reasoning from physical action, limiting their applicability in dynamic, real-world environments such as assistive robotics or responsive neuroprosthetics. This project proposes to develop a unified neuromorphic framework that integrates symbolic task planning with biologically plausible motor control simulations, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to overcome the temporal and spatial scalability challenges inherent in such models. The research focuses on simulating neural circuits responsible for transforming abstract goals into coordinated movement sequences, accounting for variable latency, noise tolerance, and adaptive error correction observed in human sensorimotor systems. Computational methods will combine spiking neural networks—implemented via NEST Simulator—with hybrid architectures that interface symbolic AI planners (using Answer Set Programming) to low-level motor dynamics. Large-scale parameter optimization will be performed using evolutionary algorithms parallelized across GPU clusters, while real-time validation against motion capture datasets of human-object interaction will ensure biological fidelity. Expected outcomes include 1) a novel computational model demonstrating hierarchical control across timescales (strategic planning to millisecond-level actuation), 2) quantitative benchmarks comparing emergent noise resilience to conventional deep reinforcement learning controllers, and 3) open-source tools enabling efficient co-simulation of neuromorphic and symbolic AI components. This work directly addresses critical gaps in developing AI systems capable of seamless human-like interaction with physical environments, with potential applications in adaptive rehabilitation technologies and human-robot collaboration frameworks. The requested HPC allocation will enable unprecedented granularity in modeling cortico-cerebellar communication pathways at population neuron scales, requiring petascale storage for synaptic weight matrices and dedicated GPU nodes for biologically real-time simulation of >10^6 spiking units.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the symbolic inference, representation, and simulation by computers and software of human learning and reasoning processes and capabilities, and the computer modeling of human motor control and motion. Includes instruction in computing theory, cybernetics, human factors, natural language processing, and applicable aspects of engineering, technology, and specific end-use applications.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model the dynamics of small business resilience within hyperlocal digital marketplaces, a nascent domain intersecting computational economics, behavioral analytics, and decentralized platform design. Small businesses increasingly rely on geographically constrained digital platforms (e.g., neighborhood delivery apps, community-based e-commerce) to compete with larger enterprises, yet the systemic interdependencies between platform algorithms, consumer behavior, and micro-enterprise decision-making remain poorly understood. The core research problem centers on identifying computational strategies to simulate and optimize small business survival rates in these environments, where traditional econometric models fail to capture real-time feedback loops and nonlinear scaling effects. Using agent-based modeling (ABM) frameworks, we will simulate multi-stakeholder interactions across 10,000+ agent businesses and consumers, incorporating geospatial data, dynamic pricing algorithms, and stochastic demand shocks. HPC resources will enable parallelized scenario testing of platform governance policies (e.g., fee structures, visibility algorithms) and their impact on small business viability under varying macroeconomic conditions. The computational architecture integrates reinforcement learning to model adaptive business strategies, validated against empirical datasets from regional small business alliances. Anticipated outcomes include a scalable simulation toolkit to predict platform-induced market distortions and evidence-based design principles for equitable digital ecosystems. This work addresses a critical gap in small business policy by quantifying how algorithmic platform features disproportionately affect micro-enterprises, providing actionable insights for policymakers and platform developers. The project’s computational demands—including terabyte-scale scenario libraries and real-time optimization of high-dimensional parameter spaces—necessitate cluster computing infrastructure to achieve practical runtime for iterative, data-driven experimentation. Results will directly inform regulatory frameworks and small business training programs focused on digital transition challenges.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to develop and manage independent small businesses. Includes instruction in business administration; enterprise planning and entrepreneurship; start-up; small business operations and problems; personnel supervision; capitalization and investment; taxation; business law and regulations; e-commerce; home business operations; and applications to specific sectors, products, and services.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a large-scale, cross-cultural analysis of narrative structures and transnational literary influences across digitized archives spanning the 18th to 21st centuries. Current methodologies in cultural studies and comparative literature face limitations in systematically analyzing the vast, multilingual corpora necessary to trace evolving themes such as postcolonial identity, ecological consciousness, and diaspora experiences. Traditional close-reading approaches struggle to identify patterns across temporal, linguistic, and geographic boundaries, while existing computational tools lack the capacity to process non-Latin scripts, low-resource languages, and culturally specific semantic contexts at scale. Our interdisciplinary team proposes a hybrid computational framework integrating transformer-based multilingual language models, graph neural networks, and culturally informed topic modeling to map intertextual networks and ideological shifts across 15 million pages of primary texts in 12 languages. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallel processing of OCR-corrected texts, training of domain-specific embeddings that account for historical semantic change, and dynamic visualization of transnational narrative flows through interactive knowledge graphs. Expected outcomes include 1) a publicly accessible database linking literary works through shared thematic and stylistic features, 2) quantitative models tracing the diffusion of narrative conventions between Global South and Euro-American traditions, and 3) new methodologies for computational humanities research that balance scale with cultural nuance. By enabling the first systematic comparison of Indigenous storytelling frameworks, colonial-era texts, and contemporary world literature at this magnitude, the project aims to redefine theories of cultural hybridity while providing open-source tools for ethically grounded, cross-linguistic digital scholarship.
cip_definition: A program with a general synthesis of cultural studies and comparative literature or a specialization which draws from cultural studies and comparative literature. Includes instruction in anthropology, comparative linguistics, cultural studies, history, literary criticism, literary studies, philosophy, political economy, sociology, and textual studies.

abstract: Emerging challenges in dynamic network environments—such as rapidly shifting bandwidth demands, ephemeral node failures in decentralized systems, and adversarial interference in wireless communications—expose limitations in conventional network control paradigms. These challenges demand adaptive, real-time decision-making frameworks capable of operating under uncertainty, yet existing methods often rely on rigid protocols or centralized architectures ill-suited for scalable, self-organizing systems.
