The computational intensity of processing terabyte-scale interaction logs and running millions of parallel simulations necessitates HPC infrastructure to achieve practical time-to-solution metrics, making this research infeasible with conventional computing resources.
cip_title: Customer Service Support/ Call Center/ Teleservice Operation
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to assist customers with inquiries and problems in frontline call centers, help desks, teleservice centers, and online. Includes instruction in user interfaces and user behavior, principles of hardware and software systems operation, customer interaction skills, telephone and e-mailing skills, data entry, and database and Internet searching and retrieval.

abstract: This research project seeks to address the critical gap in computational modeling of percussion instrument acoustics and performance kinematics, which are essential for advancing pedagogical, compositional, and design practices in percussion arts. Despite the physical and temporal complexity of percussive sound production—spanning transient impacts, nonlinear material responses, and performer-instrument interactions—existing studies lack high-resolution, real-time analyses capable of informing artistic innovation. To bridge this gap, we propose developing a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework integrating finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML) to model the dynamic behavior of percussion instruments across diverse performance contexts. The project will simulate acoustic signatures of membranophones (e.g., snare drums) and idiophones (e.g., marimbas) under varying strike techniques, materials, and environmental conditions, while synchronizing these models with motion-capture datasets of performer kinematics. HPC resources are indispensable for resolving the microsecond-scale transients and multiphysics interactions inherent to percussive events, which exceed the capacity of standard workstations. Expected outcomes include: (1) validated computational models correlating gesture, impact physics, and timbral outcomes; (2) an open-access database of simulated and empirical percussion sound profiles; and (3) ML-driven tools for real-time feedback in pedagogical settings, enabling students to visualize and refine technique. By elucidating the causal relationships between performance parameters and acoustic results, this work will empower composers to exploit extended techniques informed by physics-based synthesis and guide instrument designers in material optimization. The project establishes a novel interdisciplinary nexus between computational science and percussion arts, fostering innovation in both artistic practice and acoustic engineering.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to master percussion instruments and performing art for a variety of musical settings, including orchestral, solo, chamber, commercial, or nontraditional. Includes instruction in playing and personal style development.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of federal-provincial policy coordination in Canada through computational modeling of intergovernmental negotiation processes. The research problem centers on understanding how institutional design, partisan alignment, and regional disparities influence the efficiency and outcomes of multilateral agreements, such as those addressing climate policy or healthcare funding. While qualitative studies dominate existing literature, quantitative gaps persist in systematically analyzing how institutional rules (e.g., formal consultation requirements) interact with political incentives to shape bargaining success. The project will employ agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate negotiation scenarios using parameters derived from historical federal-provincial agreements (1982–present), constitutional frameworks, and electoral data. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to handle the combinatorial complexity of modeling 13 provincial/territorial agents with heterogeneous preferences, dynamic party affiliations, and variable resource dependencies. Simulations will test hypotheses about veto point thresholds, side-payment effectiveness, and the impact of asymmetric decentralization. Complementary NLP methods will process parliamentary debate transcripts and intergovernmental communiqués to refine model inputs. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable computational framework for simulating multilevel governance interactions, (2) empirical insights into institutional bottlenecks affecting contemporary policy coordination, and (3) open-access datasets mapping negotiation trajectories across policy domains. Results will advance scholarly debates about Canadian federalism’s adaptability to collective action challenges while providing actionable evidence for constitutional and intergovernmental affairs practitioners. The requested resources will support parallelized simulation runs, large-text corpus analysis, and validation exercises requiring GPU-accelerated computation for deep learning classifiers applied to political discourse.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic study of Canadian political institutions and behavior. Includes instruction in British and North American political theory, political parties and interest groups, provincial and local governments, Constitutional law, federalism and national institutions, executive and legislative politics, judicial politics, popular attitudes and media influences, political research methods, and applications to the study of specific issues and institutions.

abstract: This project seeks to develop and validate a computational framework to model the effectiveness of STEM instructional strategies that integrate real-world problem-solving with K-12 curricular standards. A persistent challenge in STEM education is the lack of scalable, data-driven methods to design classroom activities that balance foundational knowledge, interdisciplinary connections, and computational thinking skills. Current approaches rely heavily on qualitative assessments, limiting the ability to predict how pedagogical choices influence long-term student engagement or competency development. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze multimodal educational datasets and simulate learning outcomes under varied instructional conditions. The computational workflow will combine machine learning analysis of classroom interaction patterns (e.g., discourse transcripts, problem-solving logs, and formative assessments) with agent-based modeling of student cohort dynamics. By training models on anonymized datasets from 50+ STEM classrooms (grades 6-12) and synthetically generated scenarios, we aim to identify critical thresholds in task complexity, collaborative structures, and technology integration that predict measurable improvements in student outcomes. The HPC environment will enable parallel processing of heterogeneous data streams and large-scale parameter sweeps to optimize instructional design variables. Expected outcomes include (1) a predictive toolkit to guide teachers in sequencing computational thinking activities within standard-aligned STEM units and (2) evidence-based thresholds for equitable implementation across diverse classroom contexts. This work directly supports the program’s focus on STEM education methods by creating transferable computational models to bridge theoretical frameworks with classroom practice, ultimately helping educators design more effective, inclusive STEM learning experiences.
cip_title: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) Educational Methods
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to connect education practices with scientific, engineering, and mathematical principles for PreK-12 students. Includes instruction in critical thinking, curriculum and instruction, history of STEM education, integrating STEM across curricula, learning sciences and technology, STEM education methods, and teacher leadership in STEM education.

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing computational demands of immersive audio production workflows in the Recording Arts Technology field, where high-fidelity spatial sound design and real-time processing are critical for applications in virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and interactive media. Current consumer-grade systems struggle to handle the latency-sensitive, multi-channel audio rendering required for dynamic 3D soundscapes, particularly when integrating machine learning-driven noise reduction, adaptive acoustic modeling, and live input processing. To overcome these limitations, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and optimize a scalable audio processing pipeline. The computational approach will involve parallelized algorithms for real-time convolution reverbs, wave-field synthesis simulations, and GPU-accelerated neural networks for audio enhancement tasks. By deploying containerized audio processing modules on HPC clusters, we aim to achieve sub-20ms latency for 64-channel ambisonic environments while maintaining 192kHz/32-bit audio fidelity—a benchmark unattainable with conventional studio hardware. The project will also investigate distributed computing strategies for collaborative remote production scenarios, where multiple artists interact with shared spatial audio assets simultaneously. Expected outcomes include open-source toolkits for HPC-assisted sound design, performance benchmarks for cloud-based audio workflows, and novel methodologies for integrating physical modeling synthesis with live input streams. This work will directly benefit academic research in adaptive audio systems while providing industry-relevant solutions for next-generation media production challenges, bridging gaps between artistic practice and computational audio engineering. Resource requirements include access to GPU nodes for deep learning tasks, high-memory nodes for large impulse response datasets, and low-latency interconnects to simulate real-world production environments.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to the production of sound recordings as finished products or as components of film/video, broadcast, live, or mixed media productions. Includes instruction in sound equipment operation and maintenance; music, dialogue, and sound effects recording; soundtrack editing; dubbing and mixing; sound engineering; tape, disk, and CD production; digital recording and transmission; amplification and modulation; and working with producers, editors, directors, artists, and production managers.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the dynamics of multigenerational household resilience under socio-environmental stressors, an underexplored area within human development and family studies. While prior work has focused on demographic trends or qualitative assessments of family structures, this study addresses a critical gap by modeling complex, nonlinear interactions between cultural, economic, and environmental factors that influence household adaptability over time. The research problem centers on identifying threshold behaviors and cascading effects within family systems exposed to compounding stressors such as climate-driven migration, intergenerational caregiving demands, and shifting cultural norms. A computational approach combining agent-based modeling (ABM) and machine learning-driven sensitivity analysis will be employed to simulate household decision-making processes across diverse geographic and cultural contexts. The ABM framework will integrate longitudinal demographic data, ethnographic case studies, and environmental exposure datasets to parameterize agents representing family members with heterogeneous values, resource constraints, and risk perceptions. HPC resources are essential for scaling simulations to capture rare but high-impact events (e.g., abrupt family dissolution or relocation cascades) and for conducting global sensitivity analyses across millions of parameter combinations. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible computational toolkit for predicting household vulnerability hotspots, novel metrics for quantifying intergenerational resource equity, and evidence-based insights into policy interventions that strengthen family resilience without compromising cultural autonomy. By bridging computational social science with human development frameworks, this work advances methodological innovation in a field traditionally reliant on small-scale surveys, while providing actionable knowledge for organizations supporting at-risk families in rapidly changing environments.
cip_title: Human Development, Family Studies, and Related Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in human development, family studies, and related services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical gaps in the computational analysis of syntactic and dialectal variation across under-resourced Slavic, Baltic, and Albanian languages. While these languages exhibit rich morphosyntactic structures and significant dialectal diversity, their study has been hindered by fragmented corpora, limited digitized resources, and the computational complexity of parsing highly inflected grammatical systems. Traditional methods struggle to systematically compare syntactic patterns or trace dialectal evolution at scale, particularly for Albanian and Baltic languages, which remain underrepresented in computational linguistics. This project proposes a multi-stage computational approach to analyze syntactic structures and dialectal features across these languages using advanced natural language processing (NLP) techniques. HPC resources will enable the parallel training of transformer-based models on distributed datasets of annotated texts and spoken dialects, including historical and contemporary sources. Custom syntactic parsers will be optimized for morphologically complex languages, requiring iterative fine-tuning on GPU clusters to manage memory-intensive tasks. Dialectometric analysis of phonetic and lexical features will employ acoustic modeling and clustering algorithms to map regional variations, processing terabytes of audio data. Outcomes include the creation of open-access, annotated corpora for Albanian and Baltic languages, computational tools for syntactic comparison, and evidence-based insights into language contact and divergence. The project will advance methodological frameworks for low-resource language analysis while preserving endangered dialectal data. By integrating computational rigor with linguistic theory, this work aims to bridge gaps in cross-linguistic research and empower future studies in Slavic, Baltic, and Albanian linguistics.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: Slavic, Baltic, and Albanian Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, Other
cip_definition: A program that focuses on Slavic languages, literatures, and linguistics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Veterinary clinical pharmacology faces unique challenges in optimizing drug therapies across diverse species, where interspecies variability in drug metabolism, physiological differences, and disease pathophysiology complicate dose prediction. Current pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) models often lack the resolution to account for multi-scale biological interactions or population-level variability in domesticated animals, leading to suboptimal therapeutic outcomes. This project proposes to develop a computational framework integrating species-specific genomic, proteomic, and physiological data with advanced PK/PD modeling to predict individualized dosing regimens. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to overcome the computational demands of multi-omics integration, Bayesian hierarchical modeling, and large-scale simulations of drug behavior across heterogeneous populations. The research will leverage machine learning algorithms to identify biomarkers of drug response variability and simulate drug-disease interactions in silico, using datasets from clinical trials in companion animals and livestock. Key outcomes include validated predictive models for dose optimization in species such as canines, felines, and bovines, with a focus on antimicrobials and chemotherapeutics. The computational workflow will employ parallelized parameter estimation, sensitivity analysis, and uncertainty quantification to ensure robustness. By enabling real-time adaptation of models to patient-specific data, this work aims to reduce adverse drug events and improve therapeutic efficacy in veterinary medicine. The resulting open-source tools and datasets will provide a foundation for comparative pharmacology research, bridging gaps between veterinary and human clinical pharmacology. Access to HPC infrastructure is critical to manage the iterative processing of high-dimensional data and support the development of scalable, species-agnostic modeling pipelines. This project aligns with broader goals of precision veterinary medicine, offering a paradigm shift in how pharmacological data is translated into clinical decision-making for animal patients.
cip_definition: Research on how to apply advanced knowledge of the chemical properties and biological effects of drugs to rational drug therapy in animal patients. Includes instruction in the comparative pharmacology of principal drug groups, pharmacokinetics, basic mechanisms and features of diseases occurring in domesticated animals, the role of drugs in modifying the disease process, and specific skills critical to the practice of clinical pharmacology.

abstract: This project seeks to address the computational challenges in modeling and optimizing next-generation power electronic systems for grid-scale renewable energy integration. The increasing complexity of modern power converters—driven by high switching frequencies, wide-bandgap semiconductor devices, and dynamic grid stability requirements—demands high-fidelity simulations that exceed the capabilities of conventional computing resources. Current models struggle to resolve nanosecond-scale switching transients while simultaneously simulating system-level interactions over millisecond timescales, creating a critical gap in predicting electromagnetic interference, thermal stresses, and control stability. To overcome this, we propose a multi-scale computational framework combining finite-element analysis (FEA) for device physics, circuit-level transient simulations, and data-driven surrogate modeling accelerated through machine learning. The requested high-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable parallel execution of massively parameterized FEA simulations using COMSOL Multiphysics, coupled with real-time co-simulation of network dynamics via MATLAB/Simulink. GPU-accelerated tensor operations will train neural networks to approximate device behavior, reducing simulation times by orders of magnitude while maintaining physical accuracy. Expected outcomes include validated models for 10kV SiC MOSFET-based converters, predictive algorithms for harmonic mitigation in hybrid AC/DC microgrids, and open-source tools for power electronics co-design. This work directly supports national priorities for decarbonization by enabling the development of efficient, resilient power conversion systems critical for integrating offshore wind and solar farms into aging grid infrastructure. The computational methodologies developed will also find broader applications in electric vehicle drivetrains and industrial motor drives, advancing the state of the art in power electronics research.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of electrical and electronic systems and their components, including electrical power generation systems; and the analysis of problems such as superconductor, wave propagation, energy storage and retrieval, and reception and amplification.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance predictive modeling of watershed-scale hydrological responses to climate variability and land-use change, a critical challenge in natural resource management. Current models struggle to integrate high-resolution spatial datasets with dynamic climate projections, limiting their utility for informing adaptive conservation strategies. The research will develop a coupled modeling framework that combines machine learning (ML) with process-based hydrological simulations to improve predictions of water availability, sediment transport, and nutrient cycling under multiple climate scenarios. Key computational tasks include parameterizing distributed hydrological models using LiDAR-derived topography and satellite-based land-cover data at 10m resolution, training ML surrogates to accelerate ensemble simulations, and conducting sensitivity analyses across 50+ years of downscaled climate data (CMIP6). The HPC environment is essential for managing petabytes of input data, parallelizing thousands of model runs, and optimizing ML architectures through hyperparameter tuning. Expected outcomes include (1) a publicly accessible modeling workflow for predicting localized impacts of extreme weather events on freshwater systems, (2) quantitative assessments of conservation practice effectiveness under varying precipitation regimes, and (3) improved uncertainty quantification through ensemble-based projections. These results will directly support state and federal agencies in prioritizing wetland restoration efforts and updating flood resilience guidelines, while the open-source tools developed will enable broader applications in climate adaptation planning. By addressing computational bottlenecks in current environmental modeling approaches, this work advances interdisciplinary research at the nexus of hydrology, climatology, and sustainable resource management.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of biological, chemical, and physical principles to the study of the physical environment and the solution of environmental problems, including subjects such as abating or controlling environmental pollution and degradation; the interaction between human society and the natural environment; and natural resources management. Includes instruction in biology, chemistry, physics, geosciences, climatology, statistics, and mathematical modeling.

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing complexity of resource allocation and interference mitigation in high-density wireless communication systems, which are critical to emerging IoT and 5G/6G networks. Current analytical models struggle to optimize spectral efficiency and power distribution in dynamically congested environments, particularly when balancing real-time latency constraints with energy consumption. To overcome these limitations, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and validate scalable, adaptive algorithms for network parameter optimization. The computational approach combines parallelized Monte Carlo simulations of channel traffic patterns with machine learning-driven reinforcement learning (RL) models trained on multi-objective reward functions. Finite-element electromagnetic simulations will further model antenna array interactions and signal propagation anomalies in heterogeneous urban environments. These methods require HPC capabilities to process terabytes of network telemetry data, execute millions of parameterized scenarios, and train deep neural networks with complex state-action spaces. Expected outcomes include (1) a robust framework for dynamically allocating time-frequency resources while minimizing co-channel interference, (2) validated protocols for energy-efficient beamforming in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted networks, and (3) open-source simulation tools tailored for industrial technicians to prototype adaptive base station configurations. The results will directly support the design of next-generation communication infrastructure, reducing development cycles for edge-computing-integrated networks. By aligning HPC-driven insights with hands-on engineering technology practices, this work bridges theoretical optimization and deployable solutions for communication system technicians.
cip_title: Electrical, Electronic, and Communications Engineering Technology
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of electrical, electronics and communication engineers. Includes instruction in electrical circuitry, prototype development and testing, systems analysis and testing, systems maintenance, instrument calibration, and report preparation.

abstract: The increasing complexity of drug discovery and development necessitates advanced computational tools to address challenges in pharmacokinetics, drug-target interactions, and formulation optimization. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to accelerate the design of novel small-molecule therapeutics with enhanced efficacy and reduced off-target effects. A central focus is the development of multi-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to model drug binding kinetics across diverse biological targets, including membrane-bound receptors and intracellular enzymes. These simulations will integrate structural data from cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography with machine learning-driven pharmacophore models to predict binding affinities and residence times under physiological conditions. Concurrently, we will employ quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations to analyze enzymatic degradation pathways of drug candidates in cytochrome P450 systems, addressing critical stability challenges in oral dosage forms. The computational workflow will utilize GPU-optimized packages (e.g., GROMACS, AMBER) for large-scale parallel simulations, requiring terabytes of memory and thousands of core-hours to achieve microsecond-scale sampling for complex lipid bilayer systems. Expected outcomes include the identification of three lead compounds with improved metabolic stability for experimental validation, alongside predictive models correlating simulation-derived descriptors with in vitro absorption parameters. This work directly supports precision pharmacy initiatives by enabling rational drug design strategies that reduce reliance on iterative trial-and-error approaches. The requested HPC resources are essential to handle the combinatorial complexity of ligand-receptor systems, solvent interactions, and free energy calculations inherent to pharmaceutical sciences, providing foundational insights for optimizing therapeutic regimens and patient-specific dosing protocols.
detailed_field: Pharmacy, pharmaceutical sciences, and administration nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent or employed practice of preparing and dispensing drugs and medications in consultation with prescribing physicians and other health care professionals, and for managing pharmacy practices and counseling patients. Includes instruction in mathematics, physics, chemistry, biochemistry, anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmacognosy, pharmacy practice, pharmacy administration, applicable regulations, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to optimize dynamic in-store customer traffic patterns using high-resolution behavioral simulations to enhance retail operational efficiency and customer experience. Traditional retail space planning relies on static models or historical sales data, which fail to account for real-time variables such as shifting crowd densities, seasonal promotions, or emergent in-store bottlenecks. We propose a computational framework integrating agent-based modeling (ABM) with reinforcement learning (RL) to simulate and predict customer movement, inventory interaction, and staff responsiveness in hyper-realistic retail environments. The research leverages anonymized video analytics data from partner retailers, processed via convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract spatiotemporal movement patterns, which inform the ABM’s decision rules. A parallelized RL pipeline will then iteratively optimize layout configurations, staff allocation, and inventory placement by minimizing simulated congestion and maximizing product engagement metrics. The scale of this analysis—requiring millions of parallel simulations across diverse store formats and customer demographics—necessitates high-performance computing (HPC) resources for GPU-accelerated deep learning, distributed ABM execution, and multi-objective optimization. Expected outcomes include a scalable toolkit for real-time retail space adaptation, validated against empirical data from pilot implementations. This work bridges computational social science and retail operations, offering a novel paradigm for responsive store design while advancing methodologies for large-scale behavioral simulation in constrained physical environments. Successful implementation could reduce operational costs by 12–18% in test cases and inform adaptive retail systems for rapidly changing consumer landscapes.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to perform operations associated with retail sales in a variety of settings. Includes instruction in over-the-counter and other direct sales operations in business settings, basic bookkeeping principles, customer service, team/staff leadership and supervision, floor management, and applicable technical skills.

abstract: The development of advanced materials with tailored properties for extreme environments remains a critical challenge in materials science and engineering. Traditional experimental approaches struggle to capture the complex interplay of atomic-scale defects, microstructural evolution, and thermomechanical responses under high-stress or high-temperature conditions. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable multiscale simulations that bridge quantum mechanical calculations, molecular dynamics, and phase-field modeling. The research focuses on two interconnected thrusts: (1) predicting the formation and mobility of dislocations in refractory alloys under cyclic thermal loading, and (2) modeling phase transformations in ceramic matrix composites during oxidation. Density functional theory (DFT) will parameterize interatomic potentials for alloy systems, while large-scale molecular dynamics simulations will elucidate defect dynamics across microsecond timescales. Concurrent phase-field simulations will track oxide layer growth and stress development at grain boundaries. These computational efforts will be validated against synchrotron X-ray diffraction data and electron microscopy characterization. The requested HPC resources are essential for managing the high computational cost of ab initio calculations, the statistical sampling required for rare event detection in defect evolution, and the memory-intensive 3D phase-field simulations. Expected outcomes include new predictive models for microstructure stability in extreme environments, accelerated design rules for oxidation-resistant coatings, and open-source simulation tools for dislocation network analysis. This work directly addresses fundamental gaps in our understanding of degradation mechanisms in structural materials while providing a computational framework to guide the synthesis of next-generation high-temperature alloys and ceramics. By reducing reliance on empirical trial-and-error approaches, the project aims to significantly shorten development cycles for materials critical to energy systems and advanced manufacturing.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the general application of mathematical, engineering and scientific principles such as internal structure, chemical properties, transport and energy flow properties, thermodynamics of solids, stress and failure factors, chemical transformation states and processes, and compound materials, to the analysis, design, evaluation, industrial applications, and production of materials a in a wide variety of settings.

abstract: This project seeks to advance foundational understanding of computational hardness in approximation algorithms, with a focus on bridging gaps between empirical observations and theoretical complexity classifications. Despite significant progress in complexity theory, practical limitations persist in solving NP-hard optimization problems, particularly those involving high-dimensional combinatorial structures. Current approaches often rely on heuristics or relaxations that lack rigorous guarantees, while exact methods fail to scale. We propose a hybrid computational framework integrating algebraic, spectral, and probabilistic methods to systematically explore the parameterized complexity landscape of constraint satisfaction problems. The core research problem involves identifying phase transition boundaries in approximation thresholds for Max-3-LIN and related Boolean constraint networks under non-uniform distributions. High-performance computing resources will enable large-scale simulations across parameterized problem spaces, including parallelized semidefinite programming hierarchies, Monte Carlo sampling of solution spaces, and distributed constraint graph generation. Computational experiments will test conjectures about the existence of approximation-resistant predicates beyond current theoretical proofs, while novel tensor decomposition methods will analyze low-degree polynomial bounds. Expected outcomes include new hardness amplification techniques applicable to error-correcting codes and cryptographic primitives, as well as refined complexity classifications for dense versus sparse problem instances. The computational demands stem from the need to process exponentially large solution spaces (up to 2^50 variables) while maintaining precision for spectral gap measurements. This work will provide the first empirical characterization of conjectured barriers in the Unique Games Conjecture framework at scales beyond analytical methods, offering insights into the fundamental limits of efficient computation. Results will be disseminated through theoretical computer science venues and open-source algorithm libraries for complexity research.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on computability theory, complexity theory, and the nature of computation.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational legal research by analyzing the structural and semantic evolution of judicial decision-making patterns across transnational jurisdictions. While legal scholarship traditionally relies on qualitative methods, the increasing volume and complexity of case law—coupled with the need to identify latent biases and systemic inconsistencies in judicial reasoning—demand scalable computational approaches. The research focuses on developing a machine learning framework to process multilingual legal texts from supranational courts (e.g., European Court of Human Rights, Inter-American Court of Human Rights) and national high courts, spanning 150 years of jurisprudence. By integrating natural language processing (NLP) techniques with graph-theoretic network analysis, the project aims to model how legal concepts propagate, mutate, and interact within and across jurisdictions. Key computational challenges include handling noisy historical texts, resolving cross-lingual legal terminology discrepancies, and constructing dynamic knowledge graphs to trace precedent influence. The HPC environment is critical for training transformer-based models on terabyte-scale legal corpora and simulating hypothetical legal reasoning scenarios through agent-based modeling. Expected outcomes include (1) a publicly accessible database mapping temporal and jurisdictional shifts in legal argumentation, (2) quantitative metrics for assessing judicial consistency, and (3) prototype tools to visualize precedent cascades in complex litigation contexts. This work bridges computational social science and legal informatics, offering novel methodologies for evaluating legal systems’ responsiveness to societal change while circumventing the constraints of manual doctrinal analysis. Results could inform judicial training programs, treaty design, and reforms addressing algorithmic transparency in automated legal decision-making systems.
cip_definition: An integrated or undifferentiated program in one or more of the legal research or advanced practice fields.

abstract: The increasing complexity of industrial equipment and the critical need for minimizing operational downtime demand advanced predictive maintenance strategies beyond conventional rule-based approaches. This project addresses the challenge of accurately modeling multiphysics interactions in heavy machinery under dynamic operational conditions, where factors such as thermal stress, vibrational fatigue, and material wear collectively influence failure modes. Current maintenance paradigms struggle to integrate real-time sensor data from IoT-enabled equipment with high-fidelity simulations of component degradation, resulting in suboptimal maintenance schedules and costly unplanned outages. To overcome these limitations, we propose developing a hybrid computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to unify three core components: 1) physics-informed neural networks trained on terabyte-scale historical maintenance records and telemetry data, 2) distributed finite element analysis simulating mechanical stress propagation across complex assemblies, and 3) reinforcement learning algorithms optimizing maintenance intervals through continuous adaptation to operational patterns. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallel execution of multiphysics simulations across 10,000+ CPU cores while simultaneously training deep learning models on GPU clusters, achieving temporal resolutions below 1ms for critical component analysis. By implementing a distributed data pipeline architecture, the system will process real-time sensor streams from multiple industrial sites, correlating field observations with simulation outputs to identify emerging failure signatures. Expected outcomes include a 40-60% improvement in early fault detection accuracy compared to existing condition-based maintenance systems and a predictive framework capable of recommending component-specific maintenance actions with 95% confidence intervals. This research will provide technicians with a decision-support tool that synthesizes equipment physics, operational history, and real-world performance data, fundamentally transforming maintenance protocols in energy generation, mining, and heavy manufacturing sectors. The computational scale required for this integration—processing 15TB/day of heterogeneous data while maintaining sub-second latency for critical alerts—necessitates dedicated HPC resources to achieve transformative impacts in industrial equipment reliability.
cip_title: Heavy/ Industrial Equipment Maintenance Technologies/ Technicians, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in heavy or industrial equipment maintenance technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of modeling syntactic and semantic ambiguities in low-resource languages using computationally intensive neural architectures. While transformer-based models have advanced natural language processing (NLP) for high-resource languages, their application to languages with limited annotated data and complex morphosyntactic structures remains underexplored. The research will develop a multi-task learning framework integrating syntactic parsing, semantic role labeling, and cross-lingual transfer to improve model generalization. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for training large-scale multilingual transformers (e.g., XLM-R, mT5) on distributed GPU clusters, enabling efficient fine-tuning across 15+ typologically diverse languages, including Indigenous and endangered languages from the Americas and Asia. The computational pipeline involves parallelized preprocessing of heterogeneous corpora, hyperparameter optimization via Bayesian methods, and iterative evaluation of model outputs against linguist-annotated gold standards. Key innovations include a syntax-aware attention mechanism to prioritize hierarchical structures and a dynamic sampling strategy to balance data scarcity across languages. Anticipated outcomes include open-source tools for low-resource NLP, quantitative metrics for ambiguity resolution in understudied languages, and theoretical insights into cross-linguistic transferability of syntactic features. This work bridges computational efficiency with linguistic typology, directly supporting language preservation efforts and equitable NLP applications. The scale of experiments—requiring 8,000+ GPU hours for training and validation—necessitates HPC infrastructure to manage memory-intensive tasks and ensure reproducibility. Results will be disseminated through computational linguistics conferences and collaborations with language documentation initiatives, advancing both technical methodologies and interdisciplinary dialogue.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the relationship between computer and human language and computational techniques applied to natural language. Includes instruction in computer programming, human languages, linguistic analysis, logic, natural language processing, semantics, machine learning, psycholinguistics, software engineering, and syntax.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the linguistic and cultural interconnectedness of Ural-Altaic and Central Asian communities through large-scale textual and artifact datasets. The research problem centers on tracing the evolution of shared cultural narratives and linguistic features across historically mobile populations in Inner Asia, particularly along the Silk Road corridor, where dynamic interactions between Turkic, Mongolian, and other groups remain understudied due to computational limitations. Current scholarship lacks integrative models that account for both temporal depth and spatial diffusion of cultural practices, a gap this project aims to address. The computational approach combines natural language processing (NLP) for analyzing digitized historical manuscripts in Old Turkic, Classical Mongolian, and Chagatai with network analysis to map semantic and thematic parallels across oral traditions. A custom convolutional neural network (CNN) will be trained to detect visual patterns in archaeological artifacts (textiles, epigraphy) that correlate with linguistic data, requiring parallelized processing of high-resolution imagery. Phylogenetic algorithms will model language divergence timelines, while geospatial clustering techniques will identify cultural contact zones. The HPC infrastructure is critical for handling multi-terabyte datasets spanning 10th–18th century sources, enabling comparative analysis at unprecedented scale. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible knowledge graph visualizing cultural-linguistic exchange networks and their relationship to historical trade routes, climatic shifts, and migration patterns. This work will provide new methodologies for synthesizing material culture and textual evidence in area studies, offering insights into how shared heritage elements persisted despite political fragmentation. Results will directly support endangered language revitalization initiatives and inform contemporary cross-cultural policy frameworks in Central Asia by clarifying historical precedents for intergroup collaboration.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples and countries of Inner/Central Asia, including the Turkic and Mongolian inhabitants of the Caspian, Amur, Tien Shan, Baikal, Gobi, Siberian, and Manchurian areas and the historical Silk Road, in terms of their past and present development.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of sustainable, high-performance textiles through multiscale computational modeling of bio-derived polymer systems. Traditional textile science relies heavily on empirical experimentation to optimize fiber properties, dye interactions, and finishing processes, which is time-intensive and limited in its capacity to predict complex material behaviors at molecular and mesoscopic scales. The research addresses this gap by integrating molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, coarse-grained modeling, and machine learning (ML) to decode the relationships between molecular structures of bio-based polymers (e.g., cellulose derivatives, chitin composites) and their macroscopic performance in textile applications. Key objectives include simulating the self-assembly of novel fiber-forming polymers under varying thermal and mechanical conditions, predicting dye adsorption kinetics on functionalized surfaces, and optimizing enzymatic finishing processes for reduced environmental impact. The computational workflows will involve large-scale parallelized simulations using GROMACS and LAMMPS, coupled with ML-driven surrogate models to accelerate parameter space exploration. Expected outcomes include predictive frameworks for designing biodegradable fibers with tailored mechanical strength, colorfastness, and moisture-wicking capabilities, directly addressing industry demands for eco-conscious textiles. By elucidating fundamental structure-property relationships in bio-polymer systems, this work will establish computational textile science as a critical tool for sustainable material innovation, reducing reliance on trial-and-error methods. The requested HPC resources are essential for handling the high-throughput simulations and datasets required to model heterogeneous polymer-dye interactions at experimentally relevant scales, enabling advancements unattainable with conventional laboratory techniques.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the properties and processing of fibers, yarns, whole fabrics, dyes, and finishes, both natural and synthetic. Includes instruction in the chemical and physical properties of textile materials; end-use analysis; interior furnishing applications; and industrial applications.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a digital humanities study examining the evolution of cultural narratives in Russian society from the late imperial period through the Soviet era. The research problem centers on identifying and analyzing patterns in linguistic and visual representations of collective identity across a corpus of digitized archival materials, including regional newspapers, propaganda posters, and amateur art collections. Traditional qualitative methods struggle to process the scale and heterogeneity of these sources, which span over 70 years and include multilingual, image-text, and handwritten materials. To address this, the project will apply computational methods, including multilingual natural language processing (NLP) for Russian, Ukrainian, and minority languages; computer vision techniques to detect recurring visual motifs; and graph-based network analysis to map thematic connections across time and media types. The HPC infrastructure is critical for training custom transformer models on non-standard historical texts, processing high-resolution image datasets (totaling ~15 TB), and running iterative simulations to test hypotheses about regional vs. centralized identity construction. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible annotated dataset, visualization tools for spatiotemporal analysis of cultural discourse, and a framework for integrating computational methods into Slavic archival studies. By revealing understudied interactions between official and vernacular cultural production, this work aims to reshape scholarly understanding of continuity and rupture in Russian identity formation while demonstrating the value of HPC-driven approaches in area studies. The resource request prioritizes GPU nodes for deep learning workflows and high-memory nodes for large-scale network analysis, with an estimated need for 12,000 core-hours over six months.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples of the Russian Federation and its Soviet, Czarist, and medieval predecessors and related borderlands.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the interplay between environmental variability and morphological evolution in hominin species using advanced computational methods. A central challenge in physical anthropology lies in quantifying how climatic and ecological pressures over the past 5 million years shaped skeletal adaptations, such as bipedalism and craniofacial morphology. Traditional analytical approaches struggle to integrate high-dimensional datasets spanning paleoclimatic reconstructions, genomic evidence, and 3D morphometric data from fossil records. To address this, we propose a multi-scale computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources. First, we will employ Bayesian phylogenetic comparative models to reconstruct ancestral states and identify correlations between environmental shifts and morphological traits. Concurrently, finite element analysis (FEA) simulations will model biomechanical stress patterns in hominin skeletal structures under varying locomotor and dietary scenarios. These simulations require iterative solutions to partial differential equations, necessitating parallelized computing architectures. Second, machine learning algorithms will be applied to classify morphological traits across fragmented fossil specimens, training on a global database of micro-CT scanned hominin remains. The HPC environment is critical for handling the storage and processing of terabyte-scale imaging data and optimizing neural network architectures. Expected outcomes include a refined understanding of selective pressures driving hominin diversification and open-source computational tools for integrating paleoanthropological datasets. By elucidating adaptive responses to past environmental changes, this research will provide insights into human evolutionary resilience, with implications for interpreting anatomical variations in forensic and biomedical contexts.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of the biological sciences and anthropology to the study of the adaptations, variability, and the evolution of human beings and their living and fossil relatives. Includes instructions in anthropology, human and mammalian anatomy, cell biology, paleontology, human culture and behavior, neuroscience, forensic anthropology, anatomical reconstruction, comparative anatomy, and laboratory science and methods.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for optimizing urban flood resilience strategies using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Urban flooding, exacerbated by climate change and aging infrastructure, poses critical risks to transportation systems, water networks, and public safety. Current hydrodynamic models struggle to integrate real-time sensor data with multi-scale hydrological simulations while accounting for uncertainties in rainfall patterns and land-use dynamics. To address this gap, we propose a coupled modeling approach combining finite volume methods for 2D shallow water equations with stochastic optimization algorithms. The computational workflow will parallelize hydraulic simulations across GPU clusters to resolve meter-scale flow dynamics across city-scale domains (>100 km²), incorporating real-time inflow boundary conditions from distributed IoT sensors. Machine learning surrogates will accelerate probabilistic risk assessments of infrastructure failure under extreme precipitation scenarios. The HPC implementation will leverage containerized workflows to manage heterogeneous data streams from municipal databases and environmental monitoring networks. Expected outcomes include a validated open-source platform for adaptive flood mitigation planning, enabling cities to prioritize infrastructure upgrades and emergency response protocols. This work will advance computational civil engineering by establishing scalable methods to quantify interdependencies between transportation networks, drainage systems, and socio-economic vulnerabilities. The requested resources—including multi-node GPU allocations and high-memory nodes for ensemble simulations—are essential to overcome computational bottlenecks in resolving transient, multi-physics processes at relevant spatiotemporal resolutions. Results will directly inform resilience guidelines for municipal agencies and contribute to NSF-funded initiatives on climate-adaptive infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of structural, load-bearing, material moving, transportation, water resource, and material control systems; and environmental safety measures.

abstract: Chronic disease management in primary care requires dynamic treatment strategies tailored to individual patient trajectories. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) presents significant heterogeneity in treatment response, leading to suboptimal glycemic control and increased risk of complications. Current clinical decision-support tools lack the capacity to adaptively model long-term outcomes based on evolving patient data, limiting personalized care. This project proposes the development of a reinforcement learning (RL) framework to optimize adaptive treatment regimens for T2DM using longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). The research will integrate structured EHR data—including medication histories, laboratory results, and comorbidities—with unstructured clinical notes processed via natural language processing (NLP) to capture nuanced patient contexts. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for training deep RL models on large-scale datasets, enabling the simulation of multi-step treatment pathways across diverse patient cohorts. Computational challenges include handling high-dimensional data, managing temporal dependencies, and ensuring model interpretability for clinical translation. The project will validate model predictions against real-world outcomes and assess potential reductions in hemoglobin A1c levels and diabetes-related complications. Successful implementation will yield a scalable tool for generating personalized treatment recommendations, enhancing primary care providers' ability to make data-driven decisions. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this work aims to bridge the gap between machine learning innovation and practical clinical applications in Family Medicine, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing healthcare costs associated with T2DM management.
cip_definition: Research focused on Family Medicine

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of personalized biomechanical models for optimizing assistive rehabilitation devices in patients with neuromuscular impairments. Current device design relies on population-averaged parameters, leading to suboptimal fit, comfort, and functional outcomes. The research problem centers on bridging the gap between individualized neuromuscular dynamics and real-world device actuation through computational modeling. A hybrid approach integrating finite element analysis (FEA), musculoskeletal simulations, and machine learning will be employed to process multimodal patient data—including electromyography (EMG), motion capture kinematics, and tissue elasticity measurements—into adaptive device control algorithms. High-resolution FEA will model tissue-device interaction stresses across anatomically variable regions (e.g., residual limb sockets), while dynamic simulations will predict compensatory movement patterns under different device configurations. Machine learning pipelines will iteratively refine control parameters using simulated and clinical outcome data. The computational workflow demands parallelized processing of terabyte-scale datasets, real-time optimization of multi-physics models, and validation against experimental bench testing. Anticipated outcomes include an open-source framework for patient-specific device tuning, validated against a pilot cohort of 15 individuals with lower-limb amputations. This work addresses a critical niche in rehabilitative engineering, where interdisciplinary convergence of biomechanics, materials science, and computational physiology can transform assistive technology paradigms. Successful implementation will provide foundational tools for reducing device abandonment rates and improving mobility outcomes, with broader implications for adaptive human-machine interfaces in chronic disability care. The scale of data integration and model complexity necessitates HPC capabilities beyond local cluster limits, particularly for GPU-accelerated simulations and distributed training of predictive control networks.
cip_title: Health Services/ Allied Health/ Health Sciences, General
cip_definition: A general, introductory, undifferentiated, or joint program in health services occupations that prepares individuals for either entry into specialized training programs or for a variety of concentrations in the allied health area. Includes instruction in the basic sciences, research and clinical procedures, and aspects of the subject matter related to various health occupations.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to optimize safety and efficiency in deep-water diving operations, with a focus on mitigating decompression sickness (DCS) risks and improving equipment design. Current decompression protocols rely on generalized models that inadequately account for individual physiological variability, environmental factors, or complex dive profiles. Similarly, the hydrodynamic performance of diving gear—such as rebreathers and propulsion systems—is often designed using static simulations that fail to capture dynamic underwater conditions. To address these limitations, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating physiological modeling, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML). High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve time-dependent tissue gas exchange across diverse dive scenarios, simulate turbulent flow around equipment in heterogeneous marine environments, and train predictive ML algorithms on multi-modal datasets (e.g., diver biometrics, environmental sensor data, historical DCS cases). Parallelized CFD simulations will model fluid-structure interactions for gear design, while Monte Carlo methods will assess probabilistic DCS risks under variable dive parameters. The resulting models aim to generate personalized decompression schedules, real-time risk-assessment tools, and equipment optimized for reduced hydrodynamic drag and energy expenditure. Outcomes will directly support safer commercial, scientific, and instructional diving practices, reducing occupational hazards and operational costs. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this work bridges gaps between theoretical diving medicine and practical technology design, offering scalable solutions adaptable to emerging challenges such as deep-sea exploration and climate-related underwater infrastructure maintenance. The computational workflows developed will also be disseminated as open-source tools for the global diving community, enhancing interdisciplinary collaboration in underwater research and education.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to function as professional deep-water or scuba divers, diving instructors, or diving support personnel. Includes instruction in the use of diving equipment and related specialized gear; diving safety procedures; operation and maintenance of underwater life-support systems; underwater communication systems; decompression systems; underwater salvage; exploration, rescue, and photography; and installation and fitting of underwater mechanical systems and their maintenance, repair or demolition.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the design of adaptive human-computer interfaces by investigating how real-time, multimodal user data can dynamically inform interface personalization at scale. Current models for interface adaptation struggle to integrate behavioral, cognitive, and contextual signals (e.g., eye-tracking, biometrics, voice patterns, and environmental sensors) efficiently, particularly in scenarios involving large, heterogeneous user populations. To address this gap, we propose developing a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework that combines machine learning, agent-based modeling, and cognitive simulations to optimize adaptive interfaces for usability, accessibility, and ethical alignment. The computational approach will involve training transformer-based architectures on multimodal interaction datasets to predict user intent and emotional states, coupled with distributed reinforcement learning agents to simulate diverse user behaviors across demographic and cultural contexts. These models will be validated against experimental data from controlled user studies measuring task performance, cognitive load, and user satisfaction. The HPC infrastructure is critical for managing the high dimensionality of multimodal data, enabling parallelized training of context-aware algorithms, and simulating population-scale interactions with low-latency responsiveness. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable computational pipeline for real-time interface adaptation, (2) empirically grounded insights into trade-offs between personalization and privacy in adaptive systems, and (3) open-source tools for simulating sociotechnical impacts of interface designs across diverse populations. This work will directly contribute to the Human-Computer Interaction field by bridging gaps between behavioral theory and computational practice, while providing a resource-efficient framework for equitable technology design. The requested computing resources will support GPU-accelerated model training, large-scale agent-based simulations, and storage for anonymized interaction datasets, which are infeasible to process on local institutional clusters due to memory and throughput constraints.
cip_definition: An interdisciplinary program that focuses on the study of the interaction between people and technology and how that technology impacts society, and combines disciplines within the fields of computing and information science (information systems, software engineering, artificial intelligence and design), engineering, and the behavior sciences (cognitive science, cognitive psychology, sociology, organizational psychology, and social psychology). Includes instruction in information technology, cognitive and behavioral sciences, and systems design.

abstract: The sustainable management of rangelands faces critical challenges due to complex interactions between vegetation dynamics, livestock grazing pressures, and climate variability. Current models often oversimplify these multidimensional feedbacks, particularly in arid and semi-arid ecosystems, limiting their utility for predicting ecosystem thresholds or optimizing management strategies. This project proposes to develop a spatially explicit, process-based model integrating plant-soil-water interactions, livestock foraging behavior, and climate projections to quantify rangeland resilience under alternative management scenarios. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to parameterize and validate the model using multi-scale datasets, including drone-derived vegetation maps, soil moisture sensor networks, and decades-long grazing records. Parallelized simulations will assess how varying stocking densities, drought frequencies, and reseeding interventions affect grassland productivity and soil stability across heterogeneous landscapes. Machine learning approaches will be implemented to identify early warning indicators of degradation from high-resolution temporal data. By coupling agent-based modeling of herd movement with ecohydrological processes, the framework will elucidate tradeoffs between short-term forage availability and long-term carbon sequestration potential. Expected outcomes include predictive tools to guide adaptive grazing systems, drought mitigation protocols, and restoration planning for invaded or eroded rangelands. The computational scalability enabled by HPC will permit landscape-level analyses while preserving mechanistic fidelity at the plant-patch scale—a critical advance for translating ecological theory into management practice. This work directly supports agricultural stakeholders in balancing livestock production with ecosystem health, while advancing fundamental understanding of feedback mechanisms in disturbance-prone rangeland systems.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of rangelands, arid regions, grasslands, and other areas of low productivity, as well as the principles of managing such resources for maximum benefit and environmental balance. Includes instruction in livestock management, wildlife biology, plant sciences, ecology, soil science, and hydrology.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the resilience of plant-pollinator networks under rapid environmental change. The research addresses a critical gap in understanding how anthropogenic stressors—such as habitat fragmentation and phenological mismatches—alter mutualistic interaction dynamics, potentially destabilizing ecosystems. Current models often oversimplify species traits and adaptive responses, limiting their predictive power for conservation planning. To address this, we propose a spatially explicit, individual-based modeling framework that integrates empirical data on pollinator behavior, plant phenology, and coevolutionary feedbacks across heterogeneous landscapes. The model incorporates trait-mediated interactions, stochastic environmental drivers, and adaptive foraging strategies to simulate network rewiring under multiple climate scenarios. HPC resources are essential to parameterize and run simulations at ecologically realistic scales, encompassing 10^4–10^5 individual agents across decadal timescales. Parallelized sensitivity analyses will quantify uncertainty in key parameters, while machine learning workflows will identify tipping points in network robustness. A novel aspect involves coupling these simulations with phylogenetic comparative methods to assess how evolutionary history constrains or facilitates species’ adaptive capacity. Expected outcomes include predictive metrics for at-risk mutualisms, maps of priority areas for habitat restoration, and a publicly accessible database of simulated network trajectories under global change. This work will directly inform regional pollinator conservation strategies while advancing theoretical ecology through mechanistic insights into the interplay between ecological resilience and evolutionary processes. The computational demands of scaling individual-based eco-evolutionary models necessitate dedicated HPC allocation to achieve biologically meaningful spatiotemporal resolution and ensemble sizes.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the relationships and interactions of small-scale biological systems, such as organisms, to each other, to complex and whole systems, and to the physical and other non-biological aspects of their environments. Includes instruction in biogeochemistry; landscape and/or marine/aquatic dynamics; decomposition; global and regional elemental budgets; biotic and abiotic regulation of nutrient cycles; ecophysiology; ecosystem resilience, disturbance, and succession; community and habitat dynamics; organismal interactions (co-evolution, competition, predation); paleoecology; and evolutionary ecology.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to analyze and simulate the dynamic interplay of traditional drawing media (e.g., charcoal, ink, pastel) with diverse surfaces, enabling novel artistic exploration at scale. While traditional drawing emphasizes manual techniques, the complexity of modeling material interactions—such as pigment dispersion, texture response, and layering effects—exceeds the capabilities of conventional software tools. Current digital alternatives lack the fidelity to replicate the nuanced behaviors of physical media, limiting artists’ ability to experiment computationally with traditional methods. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven approach combining physics-based simulation, machine learning, and large-scale parameter optimization. Multi-physics models will simulate media-surface interactions at microscopic resolutions, validated against empirical data from controlled experiments. Neural networks trained on high-resolution scans of hand-drawn artworks will predict aesthetic outcomes of hybrid techniques (e.g., charcoal over ink wash) and suggest adaptive strategies for achieving target textures or gradients. The computational workload necessitates parallelized GPU rendering for real-time visual feedback and distributed CPU clusters for batch analysis of material permutations. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for artists to virtually test unconventional media combinations, generate procedural sketches informed by historical styles, and optimize large-scale compositions through iterative simulation. This resource will empower practitioners to transcend physical material constraints while preserving the tactile logic of traditional drawing, fostering innovation at the intersection of computational design and manual practice. By bridging empirical art methodologies with scalable computational models, the project aims to redefine how drawing is taught, preserved, and evolved in digital contexts, with broader implications for archival practices and cross-disciplinary media research.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals creatively and technically to express emotions, ideas, or inner visions through representation by lines made on a surface. Includes instruction in eye-hand coordination; line, value, shape, and perspective; figure and still life drawing; the use of media such as pen and ink, pencil, charcoal, pastel, and brush; and personal style development.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational tools to model and analyze speech production and language processing impairments in individuals with communication disorders, with a focus on improving diagnostic precision and therapeutic outcomes. Current clinical assessments for disorders such as aphasia, dysarthria, and pediatric speech-sound disorders rely on manual, time-intensive analyses of speech samples, which lack the granularity to capture subtle kinematic, acoustic, and linguistic features predictive of pathology progression or treatment responsiveness. To address this, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating high-resolution biomechanical simulations of vocal tract dynamics, deep learning-based acoustic pattern recognition, and natural language processing (NLP) models to quantify disordered speech and language patterns. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to train neural networks on multimodal datasets (including audio, articulatory kinematics, and fMRI-derived neuroimaging data), simulate fluid-structure interactions during swallowing and phonation, and optimize real-time analysis pipelines for clinical deployment. The project will leverage GPU-accelerated frameworks like PyTorch and FEniCS to parallelize finite element modeling of vocal fold vibrations and transformer-based NLP architectures for parsing syntactically complex language samples. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models linking specific articulatory biomechanics deficits to perceptual speech intelligibility metrics, (2) automated tools for detecting subclinical language deterioration in neurodegenerative populations, and (3) open-source software enabling clinicians to personalize therapy targets using patient-specific computational profiles. By bridging computational linguistics and motor speech physiology, this work aims to establish scalable, data-driven paradigms for speech-language pathology that enhance both research and clinical practice.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to evaluate the speaking, language interpretation, and related physiological and cognitive capabilities of children and/or adults and develop treatment and rehabilitative solutions in consultation with clinicians and educators. Includes instruction in the anatomy and physiology of speech and hearing, biomechanics of swallowing and vocal articulation, communications disorders, psychology of auditory function and cognitive communication, language assessment and diagnostic techniques, and rehabilitative and management therapies.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in the design of microbial consortia for bioremediation and bioproduction by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model complex metabolic interactions within synthetic microbial communities. Current approaches often rely on simplified pairwise interaction models, which fail to capture the emergent dynamics of multispecies systems under fluctuating environmental conditions. To overcome this limitation, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating agent-based modeling (ABM) with genome-scale metabolic reconstructions. The ABM will simulate spatial and temporal microbial behaviors (e.g., growth, metabolite exchange, quorum sensing) while constraint-based metabolic models, solved via flux balance analysis, will predict species-specific metabolic fluxes. The integration of these methods requires iterative, resource-intensive simulations to resolve feedback between community structure and metabolic output. HPC resources will enable parallelized parameter sweeps across environmental variables (pH, substrate gradients, oxygenation) and genetic perturbations (knockouts, overexpression), generating datasets to train machine learning models for predicting community stability and productivity. Additionally, we will employ molecular dynamics simulations to characterize enzyme kinetics in novel biosynthetic pathways engineered for enhanced substrate specificity. Expected outcomes include validated computational workflows for optimizing microbial consortia, identification of keystone species and metabolic bottlenecks in lignocellulosic waste conversion, and predictive design rules for synthetic communities in anaerobic bioreactors. This work will advance the scalability of bioengineered systems for sustainable waste valorization and low-cost biomanufacturing, directly contributing to the program’s focus on biosystem modeling and ecological process engineering. The requested computing resources are critical for handling the ∼10^6 core-hour computational load and managing terabytes of simulation data, which exceed the capacity of local cluster infrastructure.
detailed_field: Biological/ biosystems engineering and biomedical technology
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and management of biological systems; and includes applications to biology, biochemistry, ecology, and microbiology. Includes instruction in organic chemistry; microbiology; biochemistry; chemical, biological, biochemical, and process engineering; thermodynamics; process control; kinetics and reactor design; electric circuits; biosystem modeling; and bioelectronics and instrumentation.

abstract: Aromatherapy’s therapeutic potential is widely recognized, yet its molecular mechanisms and optimization strategies remain empirically underexplored. This project seeks to address this gap by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model the interactions between essential oil compounds and human physiological targets, with a focus on neurochemical pathways and dermal absorption dynamics. The research problem centers on the lack of systematic, data-driven frameworks to predict how specific essential oil blends modulate biological systems, limiting clinical reproducibility and personalized application. Using computational chemistry and machine learning, we aim to map the binding affinities, pharmacokinetics, and synergistic effects of terpenes, phenolics, and other bioactive constituents found in common aromatherapeutic oils. Molecular dynamics simulations will model compound interactions with ion channels, olfactory receptors, and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels linked to pain and inflammation. Concurrently, ensemble machine learning models will integrate chemical descriptors, proteomic data, and clinical outcome datasets to predict optimal oil combinations for targeted physiological effects. HPC resources are critical to manage the combinatorial complexity of multi-oil formulations and the high-dimensional parameter space of protein-ligand interactions. Expected outcomes include predictive algorithms for blend efficacy, safety profiles for dermal and inhalational use, and a publicly accessible database of simulated compound-receptor interactions. This work will establish a foundational computational platform for evidence-based aromatherapy, bridging traditional practices with modern systems biology. By elucidating mechanistic pathways and optimizing formulation design, the project advances a niche interdisciplinary field within health sciences, with implications for integrative care models and non-pharmacological therapeutic innovation.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide therapeutic care through the preparation and application of extracted essential oils from plants, including flowers (botanicals), roots, berries, and bark.
