Includes instruction in gerontology, developmental and adult psychology, age-related development and decline of cognitive processes, age-related psychological and neurological disorders, social and personality development in aging populations and individuals, and applications to the clinical treatment and care of older adults.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the biomechanical and adaptive dynamics of plant root systems in response to heterogeneous soil environments, integrating principles of continuum mechanics, materials science, and plant physiology. While root growth and nutrient uptake are well-studied at molecular and ecological scales, the real-time mechanical behavior of root networks as they navigate spatially variable soil substrates—such as compacted layers, granular interfaces, or moisture gradients—remains poorly characterized. The research problem centers on understanding how roots dynamically redistribute growth-induced stresses at the tissue and organ levels to optimize structural integrity while minimizing energy expenditure under mechanical constraints. To address this, we propose a high-resolution, 3D finite element model simulating root-soil interactions across multiple spatial scales (µm to m). The model will incorporate viscoelastic properties of root tissues derived from experimental micromechanical testing, coupled with soil hydro-mechanical data from field sensors. High-performance computing resources are essential to resolve the nonlinear, transient interactions between deforming root architectures and evolving soil matrices, requiring parallelized solvers for multiphysics simulations (solid mechanics, fluid flow, and growth algorithms). Machine learning techniques will be applied to parameterize stochastic soil variability and predict emergent root branching patterns. Expected outcomes include (1) a first-of-its-kind computational framework linking microscale tissue mechanics to macroscale root architectural plasticity, (2) identification of mechanical "trade-off" thresholds governing root penetration efficiency in compacted soils, and (3) predictive models for optimizing crop root traits in mechanistically challenging environments. This interdisciplinary approach bridges gaps between plant biomechanics and geotechnical engineering, offering novel insights into sustainable agricultural practices and bio-inspired material design. The requested computing resources will enable simulations at biologically relevant scales, currently unfeasible with conventional laboratory computing infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of plant internal dynamics and systems, plant-environment interaction, and plant life cycles and processes. Includes instruction in cell and molecular biology; plant nutrition; plant respiration; plant growth, behavior, and reproduction; photosynthesis; plant systemics; and ecology.

abstract: The study of enzyme-catalyzed organic reactions holds significant potential for advancing sustainable synthesis and pharmaceutical development, yet the mechanistic complexity of these processes often limits rational design. This project seeks to address the challenge of predicting and optimizing enzymatic reaction pathways for hydrocarbon derivatization, focusing on systems where traditional experimental methods struggle to resolve short-lived intermediates or transition states. We propose a computational approach integrating quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) simulations with machine learning (ML)-guided molecular dynamics to model reaction dynamics at atomic resolution. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to handle the scale of these calculations, which involve thousands of parallelized simulations across multidimensional free energy landscapes. The project will utilize software packages such as GAMESS, AMBER, and PyTorch to iteratively train neural networks on QM/MM-derived datasets, enabling the identification of key electronic and steric factors governing catalytic efficiency. Initial work will focus on cytochrome P450-mediated C–H activation in polycyclic substrates, a reaction class critical to drug metabolite synthesis. Subsequent phases will expand to engineered enzymes for asymmetric [4+2] cycloadditions, targeting biocatalysts with improved stereoselectivity. Expected outcomes include predictive models for active-site mutagenesis effects, a database of optimized transition-state geometries, and protocols for rapid in silico screening of substrate scope. These results will directly inform collaborative experimental efforts to develop novel biocatalysts, reducing reliance on rare-metal catalysts in fine chemical production. The requested HPC allocation will support GPU-accelerated simulations, large-scale data storage for trajectory analysis, and ML model training, enabling calculations impractical on local clusters. By bridging gaps between computational organic chemistry and enzymology, this work aims to accelerate the design of environmentally benign synthetic routes with applications in medicinal chemistry and industrial biotechnology.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the properties and behavior of hydrocarbon compounds and their derivatives. Includes instruction in molecular conversion and synthesis, molecular synthesis and design, the molecular structure of living cells and systems, the mutual reactivity of organic and inorganic compounds in combination, the spectroscopic analysis of hydrocarbon compounds, and applications to specific problems in research, industry, and health.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the morphosyntactic variation of under-documented languages in the Austronesian family using advanced computational modeling, a task requiring high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Despite extensive typological research, the interplay between morphological complexity and syntactic flexibility in these languages remains poorly understood, partly due to the scarcity of digitized corpora and the computational demands of analyzing non-linear grammatical patterns. The research will develop and train transformer-based models on a curated dataset of annotated texts from 15 Austronesian languages, focusing on capturing agglutinative morphology and its interaction with clause structure. Key computational challenges include managing sparse, heterogeneous data and scaling dynamic programming algorithms to infer probabilistic grammars across languages. The project will leverage GPU-accelerated nodes for parallelized training of neural models and CPU clusters for large-scale syntactic simulations. Expected outcomes include (1) a computational framework for modeling morphosyntactic diversity in low-resource languages, (2) quantitative evidence supporting or revising current typological classifications of Austronesian languages, and (3) open-access tools for automated morphological segmentation in agglutinative systems. By bridging theoretical linguistics and computational methods, this work will advance the empirical basis of language typology while demonstrating how HPC resources can address longstanding analytical bottlenecks in linguistic fieldwork. The results will directly inform both language preservation initiatives and cross-linguistic studies of grammatical complexity.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: Foreign Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to advance the design and optimization of next-generation electromechanical systems through high-fidelity computational modeling and simulation. Electromechanical technologies increasingly rely on tightly integrated hardware-software interactions, particularly in applications such as smart manufacturing, autonomous robotics, and energy-efficient industrial systems. However, the multiphysics nature of these systems—spanning mechanical, electrical, thermal, and control domains—poses significant challenges in predicting dynamic behaviors, failure modes, and energy efficiency at scale. Traditional experimental approaches are cost-prohibitive and limited in resolving coupled phenomena, while existing computational tools struggle with the required spatiotemporal resolution for system-level optimization. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework combining finite element analysis, circuit simulation, and data-driven control algorithms. The research will focus on three interconnected thrusts: (1) developing multiscale models of electromechanical actuators under variable load and thermal conditions, (2) simulating real-time embedded control systems interfaced with physical component models, and (3) optimizing system performance through machine learning-enhanced parameter space exploration. The computational workload necessitates parallelized simulations across thousands of cores, leveraging GPU acceleration for matrix-intensive operations and adaptive meshing algorithms for dynamic resolution scaling. Expected outcomes include predictive models for wear reduction in servo-mechanical systems, validated control strategies for energy-constrained environments, and open-source tools for coupled electromechanical simulation. These results will directly inform the development of more reliable, efficient industrial automation systems while establishing a computational foundation for future research in adaptive electromechanical architectures. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling the tera-scale datasets and complex solver interactions inherent to this multidisciplinary work.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in electromechanical technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop a real-time adaptive middleware framework for tactile-augmented reality (tAR) platforms, addressing the computational challenges of synchronizing dynamic tactile feedback with heterogeneous sensor arrays in resource-constrained environments. Current tAR systems struggle with latency and cross-platform compatibility due to the variable computational demands of multi-modal tactile inputs (e.g., pressure, temperature, vibration) and the need for deterministic response times under fluctuating workloads. The research will employ a hybrid computational architecture combining edge-based preprocessing clusters with cloud-hosted predictive models to optimize resource allocation. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will be critical for simulating large-scale tAR environments, training physics-informed neural networks to predict tactile interaction patterns, and stress-testing dynamic load-balancing algorithms across GPU-accelerated nodes. Methods include the development of a platform-agnostic API for tactile data normalization, implementation of latency-aware task schedulers using reinforcement learning, and validation through biomechanical user interaction datasets. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework capable of reducing perceptual latency by ≥40% in multi-user tAR scenarios while maintaining <5ms jitter across industrial and consumer-grade hardware. This work directly impacts emerging fields such as tactile teleoperation systems for hazardous environments and adaptive assistive technologies, bridging gaps between real-time systems design, human-computer interaction, and distributed computing paradigms. The requested HPC resources will enable large-scale validation of fault-tolerant tactile data pipelines and energy-efficient scheduling strategies critical for next-generation embodied computing platforms.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to design, develop, and implement software-based solutions for specific business and consumer platforms including industrial, game, mobile, tactile, and web platforms. Includes instruction in computer programming, computer hardware, data structures, database theory, maintenance, operating systems, project management, software development, and systems analysis.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance interdisciplinary research in Korean Studies, focusing on the analysis of large-scale cultural and textual datasets to uncover patterns in the evolution of Korean identity, gender dynamics, and diasporic narratives. Traditional humanities methodologies often struggle to process the volume and complexity of digitized archives, multilingual corpora, and audiovisual materials central to contemporary cultural studies. The research problem centers on developing scalable computational workflows to analyze these diverse sources, enabling systematic comparisons of historical and modern discourses across media, including literature, film, social media, and public records. The computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) for Korean text analysis, computer vision techniques for visual media annotation, and network analysis to map transnational cultural exchanges. Key challenges include handling non-Latin scripts, dialect variations in historical texts, and ethical considerations in processing sensitive cultural materials. HPC resources will be critical for training custom transformer models on curated Korean-language corpora, parallelizing metadata extraction from terabyte-scale multimedia repositories, and simulating diffusion patterns of cultural narratives across temporal and geographic boundaries. Expected outcomes include an open-access computational toolkit optimized for Korean Studies research, a series of visualized network models tracing gendered representations in 20th-century media, and a longitudinal dataset tracking semantic shifts in diasporic identity discourse. By bridging computational methods with area studies frameworks, this project aims to establish new methodologies for analyzing cultural change at scale while preserving contextual nuance. The results will provide scholars with reproducible workflows to interrogate understudied facets of Korean cultural production, fostering collaborations across digital humanities, gender studies, and computational social science. Resource allocation will directly support GPU-accelerated model training, distributed storage for collaborative annotation, and high-throughput processing of legacy media formats.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of the peoples of Korea, including related island groups and borderlands.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the acoustics and cultural transmission of medieval Byzantine chant through computational analysis of its microtonal structures, performance practices, and spatial resonance in sacred contexts. While Byzantine chant has been studied historically and theologically, its complex intervallic systems—preserved through oral tradition and neumatic notation—remain underexplored as a dynamic sonic medium shaped by ritual architecture and collective memory. The research problem centers on how computational modeling can reconstruct latent patterns in pitch variability, vocal timbre, and acoustic environments that contributed to the chant’s perceived spiritual efficacy. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are required to process and cross-reference three datasets: (1) spectral analyses of field recordings from monastic communities across Greece, Turkey, and Syria; (2) 3D simulations of liturgical spaces (e.g., Hagia Sophia) using architectural acoustics software; and (3) machine learning-driven comparisons of contemporary performances with digitized medieval chant manuscripts. The computational approach will employ Python-based signal processing tools for audio decomposition, finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) methods for reverberation modeling, and variational autoencoders to identify latent features in melodic contours. By integrating these methods, the project aims to map how microtonal nuances and site-specific acoustics interacted to produce affective experiences central to Byzantine worship. Expected outcomes include an open-access corpus of annotated chant recordings linked to acoustic metadata, a computational framework for analyzing sacred music’s embodied dimensions, and peer-reviewed studies redefining historiography of liturgical arts through auditory culture. This work bridges ethnomusicology, digital heritage, and sensory studies, offering novel methodologies to preserve endangered traditions while advancing HPC applications in understudied areas of humanistic inquiry.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, theory, composition, and performance of music for religious or sacred purposes, and that prepares individuals for religious musical vocations such as choir directors, cantors, organists, and chanters.

abstract: This research project seeks to develop a scalable computational framework to optimize dynamic resource allocation in large-scale, multi-stakeholder engineering projects under uncertainty. Traditional engineering management approaches often rely on static models that inadequately capture the interdependencies between technical, financial, and human resources in complex systems, particularly when faced with fluctuating supply chains, shifting regulatory constraints, or emergent risks. The proposed work will integrate stochastic optimization, agent-based modeling, and machine learning to simulate resource allocation decisions across distributed engineering enterprises. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable parallelized Monte Carlo simulations to explore decision trees under thousands of scenario permutations, coupled with graph neural networks to model stakeholder interactions and resource flow bottlenecks. Key computational challenges include managing sparse high-dimensional datasets representing project timelines, workforce capabilities, and equipment availability, while maintaining real-time adaptability through reinforcement learning agents. The framework will be validated against historical data from infrastructure development megaprojects, with sensitivity analyses quantifying how computational granularity affects solution robustness. Expected outcomes include an open-source decision support tool capable of identifying Pareto-optimal resource distribution strategies that balance efficiency, risk mitigation, and equity across stakeholders. This work advances engineering management by providing quantitative methods to address "wicked" resource allocation problems in next-generation engineering systems, from decarbonization initiatives to global technology deployment programs. The requested computing resources will specifically support GPU-accelerated optimization workflows and hyperparameter tuning for ensemble models, which are computationally prohibitive on local clusters. Successful implementation could reduce preventable delays in critical engineering projects by 15-30% while improving transparency in cross-organizational resource governance.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the development and application of management and administration principles to engineering systems and applications. Includes instruction in resource allocation theory, control theory, statistical analysis, business management and administration, and applications to specific engineering research problems.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for optimizing quality control protocols and safety assessments in complex industrial systems using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Traditional quality control methodologies often struggle to adapt to dynamic, multi-variable environments, particularly in emerging manufacturing processes and automated safety-critical systems. The proposed research addresses this gap by integrating real-time sensor data, machine learning (ML), and physics-based simulations to predict failure modes, assess risk, and recommend adaptive quality assurance strategies. The computational approach involves three phases: (1) training ensemble ML models on heterogeneous datasets (e.g., material properties, operational telemetry, and environmental conditions) to identify latent defect patterns; (2) deploying finite element analysis and agent-based simulations to model cascading failure scenarios under stochastic conditions; and (3) optimizing decision pathways via multi-objective evolutionary algorithms that balance safety thresholds, production efficiency, and regulatory constraints. The scale of data ingestion (terabyte-level inputs from distributed IoT networks) and the need for low-latency iterative simulations necessitate HPC resources to manage parallelized workloads and GPU-accelerated model training. Expected outcomes include a novel predictive-analytic toolkit capable of reducing false-negative defect detection rates by 30–40% compared to current statistical process control methods, as well as dynamically updated safety risk profiles for industrial systems operating near regulatory boundaries. This work will contribute to the advancement of adaptive quality control standards in high-stakes sectors such as additive manufacturing, pharmaceutical production, and autonomous robotics, where traditional safety certification frameworks face scalability challenges. The resulting open-source software suite will enable broader academic and industry collaboration in computational quality assurance research.
cip_title: Quality Control and Safety Technologies, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in quality control and safety technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development and evaluation of large-scale, personalized interventions for workplace stress reduction, a critical challenge in applied psychology. Current approaches to designing organizational mental health programs often rely on static, population-level analyses, which fail to account for dynamic interactions between individual differences (e.g., personality traits, coping styles) and contextual factors (e.g., team dynamics, workload variability). To address this gap, we propose agent-based modeling (ABM) simulations to replicate complex workplace ecosystems and test intervention efficacy under diverse scenarios. The computational framework will integrate empirical data from longitudinal employee surveys (N ≈ 10,000) with organizational records to parameterize agents representing employees, managers, and workplace conditions. Machine learning techniques will be applied to identify clusters of risk profiles and predict intervention responsiveness. The scale of these simulations—encompassing thousands of agents interacting over simulated months—requires HPC capabilities to manage parallelized runs, optimize parameters via genetic algorithms, and analyze high-dimensional output data. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated predictive model of intervention effectiveness across heterogeneous subgroups, (2) actionable guidelines for tailoring digital mental health tools in corporate settings, and (3) open-source computational tools for simulating psychosocial interventions. By enabling fine-grained analysis of how individual and systemic factors jointly influence program success, this work will provide organizations with evidence-based strategies to implement cost-effective, adaptive mental health supports. The requested resources will directly address computational bottlenecks in handling large parameter spaces and real-time sensitivity analyses, advancing applied psychology’s capacity to bridge theoretical models with scalable workplace solutions.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of psychological theories and methods to real-world settings and problems, such as business and industry, government, education, military, and community settings. Includes instruction in applications of psychology, industrial/organizational psychology, developmental psychology, social psychology, cognitive psychology, counseling, human factors, research methods and statistics, and program evaluation.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the historical evolution of diagnostic frameworks for neurological disorders in 19th-century Europe using advanced computational text analysis and network modeling. While the socio-cultural dimensions of medical history are well-studied, quantitative analyses of how diagnostic criteria shifted in response to emerging technologies (e.g., microscopy, electrical stimulation) remain limited. The research problem centers on identifying patterns in the adoption and rejection of diagnostic paradigms across medical institutions, using digitized archives of clinical case notes, practitioner correspondence, and institutional records from 1830–1900. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process approximately 500,000 pages of multilingual texts, including handwritten materials processed via optical character recognition (OCR) adapted for historical scripts. Natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will be developed to extract entities (e.g., symptom terminologies, treatment protocols) and map conceptual networks across temporal and geographic axes. Graph-based models will analyze how diagnostic consensus formed among practitioners, with attention to the influence of technological innovations versus socio-professional hierarchies. A secondary computational aim involves simulating patient case trajectories through agent-based modeling to assess how diagnostic variability impacted hypothetical therapeutic outcomes under historical constraints. Expected outcomes include (1) a novel corpus of annotated historical medical texts, (2) quantitative visualizations of paradigm shifts in neurological diagnosis, and (3) open-source tools for temporal network analysis in medical historiography. By bridging computational methods with historical inquiry, this work will provide new insights into the co-evolution of medical technologies and diagnostic reasoning, offering a framework for analyzing contemporary challenges in precision medicine through historical analogues. The project requires HPC resources for large-scale OCR correction, distributed NLP tasks, and network simulations, with an estimated need for 200,000 core-hours and 20 TB of storage for intermediate datasets.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the historical evolution and socio-economic context of medical theories, education, practices, and technologies; and on the history of diseases, therapeutics, patients, and healers. Includes instruction in the concepts and methods of the historiography of medicine; the history of science, medicine, and technology; and of research methods in the history of medicine.

abstract: The increasing prevalence and complexity of allergic, asthmatic, and immunologic diseases demand advanced approaches to unravel their molecular mechanisms and optimize therapeutic strategies. Current challenges include understanding patient-specific immune response variability, predicting therapeutic outcomes, and identifying biomarkers for early intervention. This project aims to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multi-omics datasets (genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic) and clinical data from heterogeneous patient cohorts. The primary research problem centers on resolving the computational limitations of integrating large-scale biological data with real-world clinical variables to model disease progression and treatment responses in allergic inflammation and immune dysregulation. We propose a computational pipeline combining network medicine frameworks, machine learning algorithms, and probabilistic graphical models to identify critical immune pathways, predict patient subphenotypes, and simulate therapeutic perturbations. Key methods include dimensionality reduction of high-throughput immune profiling data, Bayesian inference for causal network modeling, and molecular dynamics simulations of allergen-antibody interactions. HPC resources are essential for processing terabytes of single-cell RNA sequencing data, running parallelized simulations of immune receptor-ligand binding events, and training deep neural networks on multimodal electronic health records. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models linking genetic variants to treatment-resistant asthma phenotypes, (2) dynamic maps of mast cell signaling cascades in food allergy exacerbations, and (3) a computational platform for virtual screening of biologics targeting Th2-mediated inflammation. These results will directly inform clinical trial designs for personalized immunotherapy and advance decision-support tools for allergy/immunology practitioners. By bridging computational biology with translational immunology, this work addresses critical bottlenecks in understanding immune system complexity while demonstrating how HPC-enabled analytics can transform the precision medicine paradigm for allergic and immunologic diseases.
cip_definition: Research focused on the delivery of skilled medical care to patients suffering from allergic, asthmatic, and immunologic diseases. Requires completion of a prior residency program in internal medicine or pediatrics.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the transmission and transformation of cultural narratives across Scandinavia from the medieval period to the early modern era, utilizing advanced computational methods. The research addresses a critical gap in understanding how regional identities and collective memory were shaped through shared stories, folklore, and literary exchanges, particularly in understudied peripheral regions such as Greenland and the Sami borderlands. The primary challenge lies in analyzing fragmented and multilingual textual corpora—including manuscripts, sagas, and oral histories—which require large-scale semantic parsing, cross-referential analysis, and spatial-temporal modeling. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process these datasets, which encompass over 50,000 digitized pages in Old Norse, Swedish, Danish, and indigenous languages, alongside geolocated archaeological records. Computational approaches will include natural language processing pipelines optimized for historical linguistics, dynamic network analysis to trace narrative diffusion pathways, and machine learning classifiers to identify thematic shifts across centuries. The integration of geospatial data will enable the visualization of cultural hubs and peripheries through interactive maps correlated with socioeconomic and environmental variables. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible digital atlas of Scandinavian cultural narratives, algorithms tailored for heritage language processing, and new theoretical frameworks for analyzing intercultural contact in premodern Northern Europe. By enabling the synthesis of dispersed and heterogeneous sources, this project will provide unprecedented insights into the mechanisms of cultural resilience and adaptation, offering methodological innovations for digital humanities in area studies while supporting the preservation of endangered Nordic heritage.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples of Scandinavia, defined as Northern Europe including Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, and related island groups (e.g., Greenland) and borderlands.

abstract: Financial crimes, including fraud, money laundering, and terrorist financing, are increasingly sophisticated, leveraging complex networks and vast datasets to evade detection. Traditional forensic accounting methods struggle to analyze the scale and intricacy of modern financial transactions, particularly those involving cross-jurisdictional flows, cryptocurrency, or obfuscated asset trails. This project seeks to address these challenges by developing computational tools to detect, map, and predict illicit financial activities through advanced data analytics and machine learning (ML) models. The research will focus on creating scalable algorithms to process heterogeneous datasets—including banking records, corporate filings, blockchain ledgers, and open-source intelligence—to identify anomalous patterns indicative of fraud or criminal networks. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to train deep learning models on terabyte-scale transaction histories, simulate money laundering scenarios via agent-based modeling, and perform graph network analyses to uncover hidden relationships across entities. Key computational tasks include parallelized feature engineering for temporal financial data, optimization of unsupervised anomaly detection models, and real-time risk scoring using stream processing frameworks. The project will validate results against known case studies of financial malfeasance and collaborate with law enforcement agencies to refine operational relevance. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for forensic accountants and investigators, improved detection accuracy for high-volume transactions, and actionable insights into emerging fraud typologies. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this work aims to enhance the forensic community’s capacity to disrupt financial crimes, support asset recovery efforts, and contribute to policy frameworks for combating illicit financial networks. The resource allocation will directly enable large-scale computational experiments that are infeasible on standard infrastructure, accelerating the development of proactive forensic methodologies in alignment with homeland security priorities.
cip_definition: A program focusing on the principles and techniques of conducting investigations into financial crime, terrorist activity, and the analysis and use of accounting data as evidence. Includes instruction in the principles of accounting, investigative auditing, computer investigations, accounting system documents and software, business corruption, criminal and terrorist financial networks, international money markets and movement, net worth analysis, financial fraud, exposing concealed assets, records seizure, fraud and money laundering statutes, fraud case initiation, case management, and case presentation.

abstract: The research addresses critical gaps in modeling submesoscale oceanic turbulence (1-10 km), which significantly influences energy transfer, nutrient dispersion, and air-sea interactions but remains poorly resolved in current climate models. Traditional approaches struggle to capture the multiscale, stochastic nature of these processes, limiting predictive accuracy for regional climate dynamics and extreme weather events. This project proposes a novel mathematical framework integrating stochastic parameterization and adaptive multiscale numerical methods to bridge microscale turbulence with larger-scale oceanic and atmospheric models. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute high-resolution simulations of submesoscale eddies and fronts using a discontinuous Galerkin finite element method, optimized for GPU-accelerated architectures. These simulations will be coupled with a stochastic uncertainty quantification framework to assess model sensitivity and validate outputs against Lagrangian drifter datasets and satellite-derived turbulence metrics. Expected outcomes include a scalable open-source solver for submesoscale dynamics, reduced-order models to improve energy flux representations in global climate simulations, and probabilistic estimates of turbulence-driven heat transport variability. The results will advance fundamental understanding of scale interactions in ocean-atmosphere systems while providing actionable insights for coastal resilience planning and climate mitigation strategies. By integrating mathematical innovation with geophysical fluid dynamics, this work occupies an emerging niche in climate modeling, where computational mathematics directly addresses unresolved physical complexities.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of mathematics to atmospheric and oceanic problems. Includes instruction in chemistry, physics, atmospheric/ocean dynamics, climatology, weather simulation, climate modeling, mathematics, oceanography, and atmospheric science.

abstract: This research project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize predictive maintenance strategies for complex electrical and electronics systems using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The growing complexity of modern industrial equipment, combined with the need for rapid fault diagnosis and repair, presents a critical challenge in maintenance technologies. Traditional failure prediction models often lack the resolution to account for dynamic operational conditions, material degradation, and interdependent component behaviors, leading to unplanned downtime or excessive maintenance costs. This work proposes a multi-physics simulation approach integrating finite element analysis (FEA), thermal-electrical coupling models, and machine learning to predict failure modes in high-voltage systems, printed circuit boards (PCBs), and industrial automation controllers. The computational pipeline will process sensor-derived operational data, material property datasets, and historical failure records to train time-dependent degradation models. HPC resources are essential to handle the scale of 3D transient simulations, which model electromagnetic interference, thermal stress propagation, and solder joint fatigue under variable load conditions. Additionally, graph neural networks will be implemented to analyze system-level interdependencies in multi-component assemblies. Expected outcomes include a validated digital twin framework for real-time fault prognosis, optimized maintenance scheduling algorithms, and open-source tools for simulating aging effects in heterogeneous electronics. The project will directly contribute to advancing technician training methodologies by generating synthetic fault datasets and interactive visualization modules, bridging the gap between theoretical maintenance principles and data-driven decision-making in industrial settings. By leveraging parallel computing architectures, this work aims to reduce simulation times for complex systems by 40–60% compared to conventional methods, enabling practical deployment in vocational training programs and industry workflows.
cip_title: Electrical/ Electronics Maintenance and Repair Technologies/ Technicians, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in electrical and electronics equipment installation and repair technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The proliferation of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and advanced ordinance systems necessitates innovative computational approaches to enhance explosive hazard mitigation strategies. Current explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) protocols rely heavily on manual risk assessment and static modeling frameworks, which lack the dynamic adaptability required for rapidly evolving threat landscapes. This project proposes the development of a high-fidelity, multi-physics simulation environment to model blast dynamics, fragmentation patterns, and secondary effects (e.g., electromagnetic pulse disruption, structural collapse cascades) under diverse operational conditions. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will implement coupled computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and finite element analysis (FEA) frameworks to simulate explosive interactions with heterogeneous materials (e.g., urban infrastructure, vehicle armor, electronic countermeasure systems). Machine learning algorithms will be integrated to analyze historical IED incident data, identifying latent patterns in device construction and deployment tactics to improve predictive threat modeling. The computational pipeline will additionally incorporate real-time sensor inputs from field-deployed robots and drones, enabling adaptive scenario testing for countermeasure optimization. Expected outcomes include a validated decision-support tool for EOD operators, capable of generating probabilistic risk assessments and containment strategies within tactically relevant timeframes. This work bridges computational engineering, materials science, and defense logistics, addressing a critical gap in modern EOD training and mission planning. By quantifying previously intractable variables—such as the synergistic effects of multiple simultaneous detonations or non-Newtonian fluid-based explosive compounds—the project aims to reduce false-negative identification rates by 40% and improve neutralization pathway success metrics by 25% in complex urban environments. The requested HPC allocation will enable large-scale parameter sweeps across threat scenarios while maintaining the granular resolution required for millimeter-scale fragmentation analysis and microsecond-level detonation sequencing.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the identification, containment, analysis and neutralization of explosive devices. Includes instruction in nuclear science, computer science, ordinance and bomb systems, electronics, computer science, industrial radiography, non-destructive testing, equipment operation, inventory management, investigative techniques, forensics, schematic interpretation, safety procedures, site containment and emergency medicine.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance precision and efficacy in electrology, the specialized practice of permanent hair removal using targeted electrical currents. Despite its established clinical use, electrology lacks robust computational frameworks to model the biophysical interactions between electrical probes, skin tissue, and hair follicles. Current practice relies heavily on empirical protocols, leading to variability in treatment outcomes, client discomfort, and inefficiencies in probe design. This project aims to address these gaps by developing multiscale computational models to simulate the thermal, electrical, and mechanical dynamics of electrolysis, thermolysis, and blend modality treatments. A finite element analysis (FEA) approach will be employed to model tissue-probe interactions across spatial scales, integrating parameters such as current frequency, voltage, probe geometry, and tissue heterogeneity. These simulations will be validated against clinical data, including thermal imaging and histological outcomes, to ensure biological fidelity. Machine learning techniques will then optimize treatment parameters for diverse skin types and hair morphologies, reducing trial-and-error in practice. The HPC environment is critical for handling the high-resolution, three-dimensional simulations and large parameter spaces inherent to this nonlinear, multiphysics problem. Expected outcomes include predictive models for follicle destruction thresholds, optimized probe configurations, and evidence-based protocols to minimize collateral tissue damage. By bridging electrology’s practical expertise with computational biophysics, this work will establish a foundational framework for personalized, data-driven treatments, enhancing both safety and efficacy. The results will directly inform electrology training programs, equipment design, and regulatory standards, positioning computational modeling as a transformative tool in this specialized field.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to permanently remove hair from the human scalp, face, and body using specialized charged solid needle probes, and to function as licensed electrologists and electrolysis technicians.  Includes instruction in direct current electrolysis, alternating current/high frequency thermolysis, blend/dual modality treatments, equipment theory and operation, safety and sanitation, client evaluation and care, laws and regulations, and business practices.

abstract: This research project seeks to develop computational tools to model and simulate the structural and aesthetic behaviors of complex woven and non-woven textile systems, advancing the intersection of fiber arts and computational design. Traditional textile creation relies on iterative physical prototyping, which limits exploration of large-scale, multidimensional, or materially heterogeneous designs due to time, cost, and material constraints. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework combining finite element analysis (FEA), agent-based modeling, and generative adversarial networks (GANs) to predict the physical dynamics (e.g., drape, tension, shear) and visual outcomes of textiles under variable parameters. The computational pipeline will integrate multiscale simulations of fiber interactions, dye diffusion kinetics, and nonlinear weaving geometries, validated against empirical data from sensor-embedded looms and 3D-scanned textile samples. Machine learning models will be trained on cultural and contemporary textile corpora to generate pattern proposals that balance structural integrity with artistic intent. By leveraging GPU-accelerated parallel processing, this approach will enable real-time exploration of design spaces impractical to test physically, such as hypercomplex Jacquard weaves or shape-memory textiles responsive to environmental stimuli. Outcomes will include an open-source simulation toolkit for artists, a database linking material properties to computational parameters, and a series of digitally prototyped artworks exhibited to demonstrate scalability. This work aims to redefine creative workflows in fiber arts by establishing computational methods for sustainable, precision-driven textile innovation while preserving craft-informed aesthetics. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling memory-intensive 3D texture mapping, iterative physical simulations, and large-scale generative model training, which exceed the capacity of local workstations.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals creatively and technically to express emotions, ideas, or inner visions by constructing art works from woven or non-woven fabrics and fibrous materials. Includes instruction in weaving techniques and loom operation; non-woven techniques such as knitting, coiling, netting, and crocheting; quilting; dyeing and pigmentation; printing and other finishing techniques; pattern design; tapestry; and personal style development.

abstract: This project seeks to develop an adaptive machine learning framework to predict acute health deteriorations in homebound individuals receiving care from home health aides (HHAs). Despite advances in remote monitoring, real-time prediction of emergent events (e.g., falls, sepsis, cardiac episodes) in home settings remains limited by heterogeneous data streams, environmental variability, and sparse annotation. The research problem centers on integrating multimodal data—including wearable sensor outputs, HHA-reported activity logs, and ambient smart home device signals—to identify early risk signatures while accounting for the unique constraints of home-based care (e.g., intermittent connectivity, non-clinical observers). High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process high-frequency sensor data (accelerometry, pulse oximetry), train temporal-convolutional neural networks on irregularly sampled time series, and simulate stochastic home-environment scenarios through agent-based modeling. The computational approach includes three phases: (1) federated learning across synthetic patient cohorts to preserve privacy while capturing demographic and comorbidity diversity; (2) reinforcement learning to optimize HHA alert thresholds based on evolving patient states and caregiver capacity; (3) uncertainty quantification to flag low-confidence predictions for human review. Expected outcomes include an open-source pipeline for adaptive risk stratification in resource-constrained home environments, validated against retrospective HHA intervention records. The project addresses a critical gap in decentralized care by enabling proactive, data-driven decision-making for HHAs—a workforce traditionally underserved by predictive technologies. Success could reduce avoidable hospitalizations among homebound populations while establishing a computational toolkit for ethically aligned AI in paraprofessional healthcare settings.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide routine care and support services for homebound disabled, recovering, or elderly people. Includes instruction in basic nutrition, home sanitation, infection control, first aid, taking vital signs, personal hygiene, interpersonal communication skills, supervised home management, emergency recognition and referral, geriatric care, and legal and ethical responsibilities.

abstract: This project seeks to address the critical challenge of optimizing real-time emotional intelligence in AI-driven customer service interactions within call center environments. While existing systems prioritize operational efficiency and script adherence, they often fail to dynamically adapt to nuanced customer emotions, leading to suboptimal satisfaction and retention. The research leverages high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a multimodal machine learning framework that analyzes vocal tone, speech patterns, and semantic content from live customer calls, integrating these inputs to predict emotional states and recommend context-aware agent responses. The computational approach involves training transformer-based models on a proprietary dataset of anonymized call recordings (over 500,000 hours) paired with post-call customer feedback and agent intervention logs. Parallelized processing will enable real-time inference across distributed GPU nodes, while reinforcement learning techniques simulate iterative agent-customer interaction scenarios to refine response strategies. Key challenges include minimizing latency for live voice processing, managing high-dimensional audio-textual data streams, and ensuring algorithmic fairness across diverse linguistic and demographic groups. Expected outcomes include an open-source inference pipeline for emotion-aware dialogue systems, a benchmark dataset for customer service emotion analysis, and quantitative evidence linking adaptive emotional intelligence to reduced escalations and improved net promoter scores. By bridging computational linguistics, affective computing, and service operations, this work aims to establish a new paradigm for AI-augmented customer interactions that balances technical scalability with human-centric communication demands. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling the project’s large-scale distributed training requirements and for deploying containerized microservices that stress-test the system under realistic peak call volume conditions.
cip_title: Customer Service Support/ Call Center/ Teleservice Operation
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to assist customers with inquiries and problems in frontline call centers, help desks, teleservice centers, and online. Includes instruction in user interfaces and user behavior, principles of hardware and software systems operation, customer interaction skills, telephone and e-mailing skills, data entry, and database and Internet searching and retrieval.

abstract: The proposed research seeks to address critical gaps in understanding the functional consequences of structural variations (SVs) across diverse human populations, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze large-scale genomic datasets. Despite their recognized role in evolution, adaptation, and disease, SVs remain understudied compared to single-nucleotide variants due to technical challenges in detection and interpretation. This project will employ long-read sequencing data from global populations to resolve complex SVs with high precision, integrating these findings with transcriptomic datasets to elucidate their regulatory impacts on gene expression. A key computational challenge involves processing multi-terabyte datasets to identify population-specific SV patterns, associate them with regulatory element disruptions, and model their three-dimensional chromatin interactions. Custom pipelines will combine graph-based genome representations, machine learning classifiers for SV impact prediction, and population genetics statistics to quantify selection pressures. HPC resources are essential for parallelizing alignment, variant calling, and association analyses across thousands of genomes while managing memory-intensive tasks such as de novo genome assembly and chromatin conformation reconstruction. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive atlas of functionally consequential SVs, novel algorithms for SV prioritization in clinical genomics, and open-source tools for population-scale SV analysis. This work will directly advance precision medicine by improving the interpretation of non-coding SVs in underrepresented populations and provide foundational insights into how genomic architecture shapes phenotypic diversity. The requested computing infrastructure will enable scalable, reproducible workflows critical for handling the growing volume of global genomic data while adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of whole genome sequences and patterns of gene expression. Includes instruction in molecular and cellular biology, genetics, protein technologies, genomic sciences and techniques, bioinformatics, and scientific and research ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to integrate advanced computational modeling and machine learning techniques into the study of material behaviors and design processes within traditional craft practices. A core challenge in craft research lies in quantitatively predicting the dynamic interactions between natural materials (e.g., ceramics, textiles, wood) and artisan techniques, particularly when scaling designs or adapting heritage methods to modern sustainable materials. Current manual experimentation is time-intensive and limited in capturing multivariate factors such as thermal stress, tensile strain, or organic material degradation. To address this, we propose a computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate material responses, optimize fabrication parameters, and model culturally significant design patterns. Finite element analysis will be applied to predict structural integrity in complex ceramic glazes and woven textiles under variable environmental conditions, while generative adversarial networks (GANs) will analyze historical craft corpora to identify and extrapolate region-specific aesthetic motifs. The scale of 3D voxel-based material simulations and high-resolution pattern training datasets necessitates parallelized GPU computing to achieve practical iteration times. Expected outcomes include a predictive model library correlating traditional techniques with measurable material performance, an open-access repository of simulated craft workflows, and algorithmic tools to assist artisans in prototyping hybrid (traditional-digital) designs. By bridging computational analytics with tacit craft knowledge, this research aims to expand the methodological scope of craft preservation and innovation, offering empirically grounded insights into sustainable material reuse and culturally informed generative design. The project directly supports interdisciplinary partnerships between craft practitioners and computational researchers, fostering new frameworks for heritage adaptation in contemporary visual culture.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_title: Crafts/ Craft Design, Folk Art and Artisanry
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the aesthetics, techniques, and creative processes for designing and fashioning objects in one or more of the handcraft or folk art traditions, and that prepares individuals to create in any of these media.

abstract: This project seeks to optimize dynamic resource allocation in enterprise-scale IT support systems through computational modeling of user interaction patterns and infrastructure resilience. Current help desk frameworks struggle to adapt to fluctuating demand, heterogeneous device ecosystems, and cascading failure scenarios in modern distributed networks. We propose developing a multi-agent simulation environment that models concurrent technical support requests across realistic organizational hierarchies, integrating variables such as ticket complexity, technician skill matching, and infrastructure interdependencies. High-performance computing resources will enable large-scale parameter space exploration using modified discrete-event simulation techniques, with neural network surrogates trained on historical support ticket data to accelerate scenario evaluation. The computational framework will incorporate real-time network telemetry feeds and failure propagation models derived from graph-based dependency analysis. Expected outcomes include predictive allocation algorithms that preemptively position support resources based on topological risk factors and usage pattern forecasting. This work bridges operational research methodologies with information systems management, offering novel metrics for quantifying organizational "support capacity" under constrained resources. Successful validation could transform how institutions provision technical assistance staff, prioritize critical incidents, and maintain service continuity during infrastructure stress events. The resulting models will be made available as open-source plugins for major IT service management platforms, potentially impacting over 10,000 organizations currently using legacy resource scheduling systems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide technical assistance, support, and advice to computer users to help troubleshoot software and hardware problems. Includes instruction in computer concepts, information systems, networking, operating systems, computer hardware, the Internet, software applications, help desk concepts and problem solving, and principles of customer service.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a high-fidelity computational framework to optimize traffic control strategies in dynamic work zones, addressing critical safety and efficiency challenges faced by flagging personnel and drivers. Current traffic management models often rely on static assumptions about driver behavior, environmental conditions, and crew placement, leading to suboptimal resource allocation and increased risks in real-world scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we propose a multi-scale simulation approach leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model interactions between autonomous vehicles, human drivers, pedestrians, and flagging crews under diverse conditions (e.g., night operations, emergency response scenarios). Agent-based modeling will simulate decision-making processes of individual actors, while machine learning techniques will predict emergent traffic patterns using real-time sensor data streams. The computational pipeline will integrate geospatial data, weather simulations, and historical incident reports to evaluate the effectiveness of pavement marker configurations, signal timing, and crew positioning strategies. By scaling these simulations across thousands of parallelized scenarios on HPC clusters, we aim to identify robust traffic control policies that minimize congestion and accident risks while adapting to variable traffic densities and unexpected disruptions. Expected outcomes include a validated decision-support tool for training programs and a dynamic risk assessment matrix for field deployment. This work will directly enhance curriculum development in flagging certification programs and provide transportation agencies with data-driven protocols for work zone configuration. The project’s computational demands stem from the need to process terabyte-scale datasets from LiDAR-equipped flagging vehicles and statewide traffic monitoring networks, requiring distributed memory architectures for real-time parameter optimization. Successful implementation will advance both pedagogical frameworks and operational standards in traffic control technology.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to control the movement of traffic through construction and maintenance zones and to protect the safety of work crews, drivers, and pedestrians. Includes instruction in flagging duties and responsibilities, the traffic control zone, flagging signals, pavement markers, freeway flagging, utility flagging, emergency response flagging, and night traffic control.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a high-fidelity computational framework to model and optimize human-machine teaming dynamics within next-generation combat systems. Modern military platforms increasingly integrate artificial intelligence (AI) with human operators, yet the emergent behavioral patterns, trust calibration, and decision-making latencies in high-stress combat environments remain poorly quantified. Traditional systems engineering approaches often treat human operators as static components, leading to suboptimal system designs that fail to account for cognitive load fluctuations, adaptive adversary tactics, or real-time reconfiguration needs. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate multi-agent combat scenarios involving AI-driven subsystems, human operators, and adversarial agents within a synthetic battlespace. The framework will combine agent-based modeling, neurosymbolic AI architectures, and physiologically informed cognitive models to capture bidirectional human-system interactions at scale. Key computational challenges include parallelizing discrete-event simulations of tactical decision cycles, integrating real-time biometric data streams for stress response modeling, and applying reinforcement learning to optimize system reconfiguration policies under resource constraints. Expected outcomes include predictive metrics for human-system performance degradation under cyber-physical attacks, validated protocols for dynamic task allocation between human and AI agents, and a risk-aware optimization toolkit for combat system designers. By quantifying previously intractable human-factors variables within mission-critical timelines, this work aims to reduce operational vulnerabilities in networked combat systems while ensuring compliance with ethical human-in-the-loop requirements. The HPC environment is essential to manage the stochasticity of multi-domain combat scenarios, which involve 10^4–10^5 concurrent agents and require petascale processing for sensitivity analyses across diverse threat landscapes.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of systems engineering and system architecture to the design and construction of modern combat systems and their integration with each other, with host platforms and with other forces into network-centric warfighting systems. Includes instruction in systems engineering, computer programming, chemical systems, biological systems, material systems, human factors, combat environments, sensor systems, threat and system risk assessment, conventional and unconventional weapons, combat simulation, reliability and maintenance, testing, engineering project management, strategic planning and applications to aerospace, ground, and naval combat systems.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a scalable computational framework to analyze the efficacy of digital resource curation strategies in K-12 school library settings, with a focus on optimizing equitable access to age-appropriate, curriculum-aligned media. School librarians face increasing challenges in evaluating and selecting digital resources—including e-books, databases, and multimedia tools—amid rapidly expanding content volumes, diverse learner needs, and limited time for manual assessment. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process large-scale datasets encompassing student engagement metrics, resource metadata, and text complexity indices across multiple school districts. Machine learning models, including NLP-based classifiers and collaborative filtering algorithms, will be trained to identify patterns in resource utilization, predict alignment with state educational standards, and flag potential accessibility gaps for neurodiverse or multilingual learners. The computational workload involves processing terabyte-scale datasets of anonymized student interaction logs (e.g., search queries, clickstreams, and time-on-resource metrics) alongside semantic analysis of digital resource content. HPC resources are critical for parallelizing feature extraction across heterogeneous data types and enabling rapid iterative testing of recommendation models. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit that assists school librarians in prioritizing resource acquisitions, tailoring collection development to demographic needs, and generating evidence-based reports for stakeholders. This work directly supports the pedagogical role of school library media specialists by augmenting their ability to make data-informed decisions while maintaining human judgment at the core of curation processes. Results will be validated through partnerships with three school districts piloting the toolkit during the 2025-2026 academic year.
cip_title: School Librarian/ School Library Media Specialist
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to serve as librarians and media specialists in elementary and secondary schools as well as special instructional centers.

abstract: This research project seeks to employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the doctrinal synthesis and evolution of theological concepts across geographically dispersed religious communities from the 12th to 16th centuries. While historical theology traditionally relies on qualitative textual analysis, this study addresses the computational challenge of mapping large-scale doctrinal interactions within and between faith traditions—particularly those documented in understudied manuscripts, conciliar records, and polemical treatises. The research problem centers on identifying patterns of theological adaptation and resistance in response to cross-cultural encounters, such as those between Eastern Christian, Islamic, and Jewish scholastic traditions, which remain poorly understood due to the volume and linguistic complexity of primary sources. The computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) models fine-tuned for theological Latin, Classical Arabic, and Judeo-Arabic, combined with network analysis algorithms to trace conceptual linkages across multilingual corpora. Key technical challenges include optimizing transformer-based architectures for low-resource ancient languages and scaling graph-based analyses to handle approximately 50,000 digitized texts. The project will leverage GPU-accelerated computing for parallelized text embedding and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling, enabling systematic comparison of doctrinal formulations across temporal and cultural boundaries. Expected outcomes include a geotemporal knowledge graph visualizing theological concept diffusion and a quantitative framework for assessing doctrinal innovation in premodern religious discourse. This work aims to establish computational methods as critical tools for theological studies, offering empirically grounded insights into how doctrinal systems adapt to intercultural exchange—a contribution with implications for both academic theology and contemporary interfaith dialogue. By bridging digital humanities and theological inquiry, the project demonstrates how HPC can advance intramural theological research while maintaining methodological rigor consistent with confessional perspectives.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the beliefs and doctrine of a particular religious faith from the intramural point of view of that faith. Includes instruction in systematic theology, historical theology, moral theology, doctrinal studies, dogmatics, apologetics, and applications to specific questions of ecclesiastical polity and religious life.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing horticultural production systems for specialty crops through advanced computational modeling, with a focus on improving yield predictability, resource efficiency, and economic viability for small-to-medium horticultural enterprises. Current decision-making tools in horticultural business services often lack the resolution to account for dynamic interactions between plant physiology, environmental variables, and market constraints. To bridge this gap, we propose developing a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework integrating hyperspectral imaging data, real-time climate sensor inputs, and machine learning models. The computational workflow will simulate crop growth under varying resource allocation scenarios (e.g., irrigation schedules, nutrient regimens, lighting configurations) while incorporating stochastic market demand forecasts. Parallelized agent-based modeling will be employed to evaluate how localized microclimate variations and supply chain disruptions propagate through multi-site production networks. By leveraging GPU-accelerated tensor operations, we aim to process terabyte-scale datasets from distributed greenhouse monitoring systems, enabling near-real-time optimization of horticultural operations. Expected outcomes include a decision-support system capable of recommending resource allocation strategies that balance profitability with sustainability metrics such as water-use efficiency and carbon footprint. This work will advance precision horticulture by providing business operators with scalable computational tools to navigate complex trade-offs between production targets, operational costs, and environmental impacts. The proposed models will be validated against empirical data from partner nurseries, with results disseminated through an open-access API tailored for agricultural extension services. By demonstrating the value of HPC in horticultural business analytics, this project aims to establish a template for data-driven resource management in understudied specialty crop sectors.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
detailed_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences nec
cip_title: Applied Horticulture/ Horticultural Business Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in horticultural service operations, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Neuroimaging plays a pivotal role in diagnosing and managing neurological disorders, yet current clinical workflows face challenges in analyzing the growing complexity and volume of multi-modal imaging data (e.g., MRI, CT, DTI, fMRI) and correlating it with clinical, genetic, and molecular biomarkers. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing a scalable computational framework for advanced neuroimaging analytics, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable high-throughput processing, multi-parametric modeling, and machine learning-driven classification of structural and functional brain abnormalities. The research will focus on three aims: (1) creating automated pipelines for artifact correction, segmentation, and registration of multi-sequence neuroimaging data across heterogeneous patient cohorts; (2) training deep neural networks to detect subtle patterns in imaging biomarkers associated with gliomas, demyelinating diseases, and neurodegenerative disorders; and (3) integrating imaging features with clinical data to predict treatment responses and disease trajectories. HPC resources will be critical for managing petabyte-scale datasets, optimizing computationally intensive tasks (e.g., 3D convolutional networks, diffusion tensor tractography), and conducting large-scale simulations to validate model generalizability across diverse populations. Expected outcomes include novel open-source tools for quantitative neuroradiology, improved diagnostic accuracy in differentiating lesion subtypes, and predictive models to guide personalized therapeutic strategies. By enabling rapid analysis of complex imaging phenotypes and their clinical correlates, this work aims to bridge the gap between computational neuroscience and routine clinical practice, directly advancing the diagnostic capabilities of neuroradiologists while fostering data-driven paradigms in neuro-oncology, neuroinflammatory disease management, and precision medicine.
cip_definition: Research focused on that prepares diagnostic radiologists in the diagnosis and treatment of disorders of the brain, spine, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, and head and neck in adults and children.

abstract: The increasing availability of large-scale clinical datasets, including longitudinal therapy transcripts, dream reports, and patient outcome records, presents an unprecedented opportunity to investigate psychodynamic processes underlying psychoanalytic practice. However, the complexity and volume of these data—encompassing unstructured narrative content, temporal dynamics, and multivariate interactions—exceed the analytical capabilities of traditional qualitative methods. This project seeks high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable advanced computational analysis of such datasets, integrating natural language processing (NLP) for semantic and affective feature extraction from therapy transcripts, graph-theoretical network modeling to map relationships among psychological constructs (e.g., defense mechanisms, transference patterns), and machine learning frameworks to predict therapeutic outcomes based on developmental and clinical variables. Additionally, agent-based simulations will be developed to model dyadic therapist-patient interactions under varying psychodynamic conditions, informed by principles from Freudian, Adlerian, and Jungian theory. These computational approaches will be applied to a curated repository of over 10,000 anonymized clinical hours and corresponding outcome metrics, stored in a HIPAA-compliant environment. The anticipated outcomes include: (1) identification of latent linguistic markers associated with therapeutic alliance rupture and repair processes, (2) empirically derived network models of personality reorganization during analysis, and (3) validated predictive algorithms for treatment responsiveness in anxiety and depression spectra. By bridging psychodynamic theory with computational rigor, this research aims to establish scalable frameworks for hypothesis testing in psychoanalysis, enhance training through data-driven case simulations, and inform ethically grounded, personalized intervention strategies. The requested HPC resources are critical for managing memory-intensive NLP pipelines, parallelized model training across multimodal datasets, and real-time simulation of complex interpersonal dynamics central to psychotherapeutic change.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to practice the provision of psychoanalytic counseling to individuals and groups based on the psychodynamic principles evolved from authorities such as Freud, Adler, and Jung. Includes instruction in self-analysis, personality theory, dream analysis, free association and transference theory and techniques, psychodynamic theory, developmental processes, applications to specific clinical conditions, practice management, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the structural and thematic patterns within orally transmitted ritual narratives of Indigenous Pacific Islander spiritual traditions, a critically understudied area in theological studies. While significant work has focused on textual analysis of major religious canons, non-literate traditions remain marginalized due to methodological challenges in analyzing ephemeral, performance-based practices. The research employs high-performance computing (HPC) to process and analyze a corpus of over 10,000 audio-visual recordings of chants, ceremonies, and oral histories collected across Micronesian, Melanesian, and Polynesian communities. Computational linguistics methods, including transformer-based language models adapted for low-resource languages, will identify recurring theological motifs and narrative frameworks, while graph-based algorithms will map the diffusion of ritual elements across regions. Concurrently, agent-based simulations will model the hypothetical evolution of these traditions under varying sociocultural pressures. The scale and complexity of the multimodal dataset—requiring parallel processing of audio, video, and textual annotations—necessitates GPU-accelerated computing and large-memory nodes. Expected outcomes include the first systematic taxonomy of Pacific Islander theological structures, a publicly accessible annotated archive for Indigenous communities, and novel computational frameworks for analyzing oral religious practices. This work bridges theological scholarship, cultural preservation, and computational anthropology, offering methodological innovations for studying non-textual traditions while supporting Indigenous-led efforts to revitalize endangered spiritual knowledge systems.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in theological and ministerial studies not elsewhere classified, including preparation for religious vocations in faiths other than Christianity and Judaism.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of adaptive, data-driven tools for educators working with K–12 students with speech or language impairments (SLI). A critical challenge in this field is the heterogeneity of SLI profiles, which complicates the design of individualized interventions. Traditional methods for analyzing speech patterns, monitoring progress, and predicting intervention outcomes rely on manual, time-intensive processes ill-suited to dynamic classroom environments. To address this, we propose a computational framework integrating machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) to model speech-language development trajectories, identify impairment subtypes, and recommend personalized instructional strategies. Large-scale datasets—including longitudinal audio recordings of student-teacher interactions, standardized assessment scores, and demographic variables—will be processed using parallelized pipelines to extract acoustic, linguistic, and paralinguistic features.
