This work will contribute methodological advances in scalable logistics simulation and empirically inform best practices for adaptive supply chain design. The requested HPC resources are essential for handling memory-intensive simulations, training large-scale reinforcement learning models, and achieving computational feasibility for real-world case studies involving multinational supply networks. Results will be disseminated through open-source toolsets and partnerships with industry stakeholders to bridge academic research and operational logistics management.
cip_title: Logistics, Materials, and Supply Chain Management
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to manage and coordinate all logistical functions in an enterprise, ranging from acquisitions to receiving and handling, through internal allocation of resources to operations units, to the handling and delivery of output. Includes instruction in acquisitions and purchasing, inventory control, storage and handling, just-in-time manufacturing, logistics planning, shipping and delivery management, transportation, quality control, resource estimation and allocation, and budgeting.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of legal norm diffusion across international jurisdictions using computational methods to analyze large-scale multilingual legal corpora. The research problem centers on understanding how legal principles, particularly in human rights law, are adopted, adapted, or resisted in different national contexts. Traditional legal scholarship often relies on manual comparative analysis, limiting scalability and obscuring macro-level patterns. This study proposes a computational approach to map doctrinal transfers and semantic shifts in legal texts from treaties, domestic legislation, and judicial decisions across 50+ jurisdictions from 1945 to the present. The project will employ transformer-based natural language processing (NLP) models fine-tuned for legal language to perform cross-lingual semantic similarity analysis, temporal trend detection, and network modeling of citation patterns. High-performance computing resources are critical for training domain-specific embeddings on a 10-terabyte corpus of legal documents, running parallelized comparative analyses across jurisdictions, and simulating norm diffusion pathways through agent-based modeling. Expected outcomes include 1) identification of latent convergence points in international human rights frameworks, 2) quantification of cultural and institutional factors influencing legal transplantation, and 3) predictive models of norm adoption trajectories under varying geopolitical scenarios. The computational infrastructure will enable processing of non-Latin script legal texts and low-resource language documents often excluded from comparative law studies. Results aim to provide empirical foundations for improving legal harmonization efforts while preserving contextual sensitivity, with implications for international policymaking and transitional justice mechanisms. By bridging computational linguistics and comparative legal theory, this work establishes a methodological framework for data-driven analysis of global legal systems at unprecedented scale.
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on law and legal issues from the perspective of the social sciences and humanities.

abstract: This project seeks to develop an advanced natural language processing (NLP) framework to analyze patterns of error and proficiency progression in learners of English and French as additional languages, with the goal of refining pedagogical strategies for language instructors. While existing research has identified common learner errors, the dynamic interplay of linguistic, cognitive, and sociocultural factors in real-world language acquisition remains under-modeled, particularly across diverse learner populations. To address this gap, we propose training a suite of transformer-based models on a multilingual corpus of learner-generated texts and transcribed spoken responses, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process large-scale, heterogeneous datasets. The computational workflow will include (1) preprocessing and annotating learner language samples using GPU-accelerated spaCy pipelines, (2) training contrastive models to detect developmental trajectories across proficiency levels, and (3) simulating error propagation patterns through Monte Carlo methods. The scale of data—anticipated to exceed 10 million tokens across four languages (L1s: Mandarin, Arabic, Spanish; L2s: English/French)—necessitates distributed training across multiple nodes, with planned use of PyTorch’s distributed data parallelism for transformer fine-tuning. Expected outcomes include a novel diagnostic toolkit that identifies probabilistic error hotspots in learner language, enabling instructors to prioritize high-impact pedagogical interventions. Additionally, the project will produce open-source code for efficient gradient-based attribution analysis in educational NLP tasks. By combining psycholinguistic theory with computational modeling at scale, this work aims to advance evidence-based practices in language teacher education while contributing methodological innovations for processing pedagogically relevant linguistic data. The requested HPC allocation is critical given the memory-intensive nature of transformer architectures and the need for rapid iteration across multiple experimental conditions in hyperparameter space.
cip_title: Teaching English or French as a Second or Foreign Language, Other
cip_definition: Any program in teaching English or French as a second or foreign language, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model the efficacy of personalized learning strategies in elementary classrooms, with the goal of informing teacher preparation programs. A central challenge in elementary education is designing instruction that adapts to diverse student needs while maintaining alignment with curricular standards. Current approaches to individualized lesson planning rely heavily on teacher intuition and small-scale assessments, limiting scalability and evidence-based refinement. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate classroom dynamics under varying instructional conditions. Agent-based models will represent student cohorts with heterogeneous learning profiles, incorporating empirical data on cognitive development, engagement metrics, and socioemotional factors. These simulations will test hypotheses about how different pedagogical interventions—such as differentiated scaffolding or real-time formative feedback—affect learning trajectories across virtual classroom environments. Machine learning techniques will then identify patterns in the simulated outcomes to generate predictive tools for optimizing lesson plans. The computational pipeline will integrate anonymized datasets from partner school districts, including standardized assessment results, attendance records, and teacher-reported instructional strategies. By scaling to thousands of parallel simulations, this approach will enable systematic analysis of how variables like class size, resource availability, and skill heterogeneity interact with teaching methods. Expected outcomes include (1) evidence-based guidelines for integrating adaptive pedagogies into teacher training curricula and (2) open-source simulation tools to help educators pre-test instructional designs. The project directly supports the Elementary Education program’s mission by bridging computational research with practical strategies for classroom differentiation, ultimately aiming to equip pre-service teachers with data-informed approaches to address student diversity.
detailed_field: Teacher education, specific levels and methods
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach students in the elementary grades, which may include kindergarten through grade eight, depending on the school system or state regulations. Includes preparation to teach all elementary education subject matter.

abstract: This project seeks to address the computational challenges inherent in simulating large-scale economic systems with embedded strategic decision-making, a problem critical to understanding market dynamics in increasingly digital and data-driven environments. Traditional economic models often simplify agent behavior or system scale to remain computationally tractable, limiting their ability to capture real-world complexities such as high-dimensional strategic interactions, dynamic pricing mechanisms, and network effects. We propose developing an agent-based modeling framework that integrates game-theoretic principles, econometric estimation, and machine learning to simulate heterogeneous agents—consumers, firms, and policymakers—operating within dynamic, interconnected markets. The computational approach will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to parallelize simulations across thousands of agents, optimize equilibrium-finding algorithms using distributed computing techniques, and train deep reinforcement learning models to approximate adaptive agent strategies. Key challenges include scaling Monte Carlo methods for uncertainty quantification in econometric parameter estimation, managing memory-efficient data structures for real-time interaction logs, and ensuring numerical stability in high-dimensional optimization tasks. The project will validate the framework using real-world datasets from digital marketplaces and public policy evaluations. Expected outcomes include novel insights into the resilience of algorithmic pricing systems under regulatory constraints, scalable methods for simulating decentralized financial networks, and open-source tools for interdisciplinary researchers working at the computer science-economics interface. By combining economic theory with advanced computational techniques, this work aims to advance predictive modeling of complex socio-economic systems while demonstrating how HPC resources can bridge gaps between theoretical abstraction and empirically grounded policy analysis.
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the theoretical and practical connections between computer science and economics. Includes instruction in data analysis, database design, data mining, computer algorithms, economics, econometrics, computer programing, mathematics, and statistics.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the dynamic structural and functional relationships of metalloenzymes involved in redox signaling and oxidative stress regulation. Metalloenzymes such as superoxide dismutases and catalases play critical roles in maintaining cellular redox homeostasis, yet the atomistic mechanisms underlying their catalytic efficiency, metal cofactor integration, and redox-state-dependent conformational changes remain poorly resolved. Traditional experimental techniques struggle to capture transient intermediate states and precise electronic interactions at catalytic sites due to temporal and spatial resolution limitations. To address this, we propose a multi-scale computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM), and free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations. All-atom MD simulations will model enzyme dynamics across microsecond timescales to identify conformational ensembles linked to catalytic activity. QM/MM will elucidate electronic structures and reaction pathways for oxygen radical dismutation, while FEP calculations will quantify binding affinities of metal cofactors (e.g., Cu/Zn, Fe) and their contributions to enzymatic stability. These simulations require significant HPC resources due to the size of enzyme complexes (>200,000 atoms), the need for explicit solvent models, and the computational intensity of QM/MM iterations. Outcomes will reveal how metalloenzyme plasticity and metal coordination chemistry fine-tune catalytic scavenging of reactive oxygen species, providing mechanistic insights into pathologies linked to oxidative stress. The project will also establish predictive frameworks for engineering metalloenzyme variants with enhanced therapeutic potential. By integrating computational biochemistry with biophysical validations, this work advances fundamental understanding of redox biochemistry while demonstrating the critical role of HPC in bridging molecular-scale phenomena to cellular function.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the chemistry of living systems, their fundamental chemical substances and reactions, and their chemical pathways and information transfer systems, with particular reference to carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. Includes instruction in bio-organic chemistry, protein chemistry, bioanalytical chemistry, bioseparations, regulatory biochemistry, enzymology, hormonal chemistry, calorimetry, and research methods and equipment operation.

abstract: The proposed research aims to investigate the dynamic interplay between tumor-induced physiological adaptations and systemic host responses in cancer progression, with a focus on mechanisms underlying vascular dysfunction, metabolic reprogramming, and interorgan communication. While cancer physiology is increasingly recognized as a determinant of therapeutic outcomes, computational models capable of integrating multiscale physiological parameters with tumor behavior remain underdeveloped. This project will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to construct spatially resolved, multiscale models simulating bidirectional interactions between evolving tumors and critical physiological systems, including cardiovascular networks, hepatic metabolism, and neuroendocrine signaling. A hybrid agent-based modeling framework will be implemented to capture cellular-scale tumor heterogeneity while coupling to continuum-based representations of tissue oxygenation, hemodynamic forces, and nutrient distribution. Physiological data from murine cancer models—including intravital microscopy, pressure-volume loop analyses, and metabolomic profiles—will parameterize model components. Computational experiments will test hypotheses regarding how tumor-derived factors induce systemic physiological imbalances that subsequently feed back to promote treatment resistance. Memory-intensive simulations will analyze emergent patterns across 10⁶–10⁷ simulated cells interacting with dynamically evolving vascular networks. The HPC environment is essential for optimizing Monte Carlo sampling of parameter spaces related to host physiological variability and for executing ensemble simulations to identify critical transition points in tumor-host system stability. Expected outcomes include predictive models of how baseline physiological states influence therapeutic response thresholds and mechanistic insights into organ-specific vulnerabilities during cancer-associated cachexia. This work will establish a computational framework to bridge tissue-level pathophysiology with systems-level host responses, directly informing translational efforts to personalize cancer therapies based on physiological profiling.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the scientific study of the functional dynamics, morphology, and biochemical and biophysical communications within organisms and between living systems at all levels of complexity and integration. Includes instruction in reproduction, growth, hormonal action, vascular function, respiration, digestion, sensory perception and processing, sensorimotor integration, signal encoding and conveyance, homeostasis, physical function and malfunction, evolutionary physiology, and disease processes.

abstract: Urban transportation systems face complex challenges in balancing economic efficiency, social equity, environmental sustainability, and spatial accessibility. Traditional planning methods often struggle to integrate these multidimensional factors at scale, particularly in rapidly growing metropolitan regions where dynamic population shifts, climate risks, and infrastructure interdependencies compound decision-making complexity. This project seeks to develop an integrated computational framework for evaluating equitable and sustainable transportation policies using high-performance computing (HPC). The research will employ agent-based modeling to simulate travel demand patterns across diverse socioeconomic groups, coupled with geospatial optimization algorithms to assess infrastructure investment scenarios under environmental constraints. Large-scale datasets—including anonymized mobile device GPS traces, transit ridership records, emissions inventories, and climate projection data—will be processed using distributed computing techniques to parameterize models and quantify system-wide tradeoffs. Machine learning methods will enhance scenario forecasting by identifying nonlinear relationships between land-use policies, transportation behaviors, and equity outcomes. By leveraging parallelized computations, the project will enable real-time sensitivity analyses of policy interventions across multiple sustainability metrics, such as greenhouse gas reductions, accessibility disparities, and fiscal feasibility. The computational outputs will inform a decision-support tool for planners to visualize tradeoffs between competing priorities under uncertainty. Expected outcomes include novel methodologies for embedding equity considerations into infrastructure resilience planning and evidence-based recommendations for prioritizing transit investments in underserved communities. This work addresses critical gaps in public administration by advancing scalable, data-driven approaches to multicriteria transportation planning, with direct applications to regional climate action plans and federal infrastructure funding guidelines. The requested HPC resources are essential for managing memory-intensive simulations, training predictive models on heterogeneous datasets, and optimizing runtime for iterative scenario testing across hypothetical population growth and climate risk pathways.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the economic, social, spatial, and environmental aspects of transportation and infrastructure planning. Includes instruction in economics, environmental analysis, geographic information systems (GIS), logistics, risk analysis, transportation economics, transportation evaluation, transportation planning, transportation policy, and urban transportation planning.

abstract: Wildland fire management faces escalating challenges due to climate change, urbanization encroaching on fire-prone ecosystems, and the increasing complexity of fire investigations. Current predictive models for fire behavior and post-event forensic analysis often lack the resolution to account for micro-terrain variability, dynamic fuel moisture interactions, or the stochastic nature of human-caused ignition patterns. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a multi-scale simulation framework that integrates fire spread dynamics, forensic data assimilation, and probabilistic risk assessment. The computational approach combines physics-based fire modeling using coupled atmospheric-fire interactions (WRF-Fire) with machine learning algorithms trained on historical fire incident data, satellite-derived vegetation maps, and forensic evidence from arson cases. By parallelizing stochastic simulations of ignition scenarios and fire progression across diverse landscapes, the framework will quantify uncertainty in fire origin determination and evaluate the efficacy of mitigation strategies such as adaptive firebreak placement or prescribed burn scheduling. Additionally, real-time data assimilation workflows will be prototyped to ingest streaming inputs from IoT sensors, drones, and airborne infrared imagery during active fire events, enabling dynamic resource allocation. Outcomes include open-source tools for fire investigators to reconstruct ignition sequences with higher confidence and operational dashboards for incident commanders to optimize suppression tactics. The project’s interdisciplinary integration of computational fluid dynamics, forensic statistics, and environmental sensing addresses a critical gap in non-engineering wildfire research, directly supporting agencies in mitigating ecological losses, protecting communities, and improving evidentiary rigor in fire cause determination.
cip_definition: A program focusing on the application of fire science, firefighting and investigation to the prevention, control and mitigation of wildland fires and the analysis of causes. Includes instruction in fire science and behavior, wildland environments, meteorology, wildland fire hydraulics and dynamics, water and chemical supply systems, wildland firefighting operations, airborne firefighting, firebreak engineering, communications systems, wildland arson, forensic procedures, wildland fire prevention, investigation techniques, case management and preparation.

abstract: Adult literacy programs face persistent challenges in addressing the diverse cognitive, linguistic, and socioemotional needs of learners, compounded by limited tools to dynamically adapt instructional strategies. This project seeks to develop a computational framework for modeling adult literacy acquisition processes, with the goal of optimizing real-time tutor interventions. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we propose to analyze multimodal datasets—including eye-tracking during reading tasks, vocal pitch dynamics during verbal exercises, and longitudinal assessment performance—to identify patterns predictive of learning bottlenecks or engagement drops. Machine learning models will be trained on these datasets to simulate learner trajectories under varying instructional conditions, while agent-based modeling will test the efficacy of tutor feedback protocols in silico. A key innovation lies in integrating cognitive load theory with natural language processing (NLP) techniques to quantify the readability of customized literacy materials and their alignment with individual learner profiles. The computational pipeline will also incorporate sociolinguistic variables (e.g., dialectal features, L1 interference) often overlooked in standardized curricula. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for generating adaptive lesson plans, a predictive dashboard for tutor decision support, and novel metrics for measuring latent skill integration in adult learners. By bridging psycholinguistics, adaptive systems design, and educational data science, this work aims to advance precision pedagogy in non-traditional learning environments while maintaining strict ethical safeguards for learner data. The requested HPC resources are critical for scaling neural architecture search in our NLP models and enabling parallelized simulation of population-level learning outcomes across diverse demographic cohorts.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to serve as instructors and mentors for adults in basic or functional literacy programs in school, institutional, community, and private settings.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the dynamic interplay between cultural narratives, psychological resilience, and biological markers in end-of-life decision-making processes. Thanatology, as an interdisciplinary field, lacks integrative computational models capable of synthesizing large-scale qualitative, quantitative, and biomolecular datasets to predict how individuals and communities navigate terminal illness and grief. The research problem centers on the absence of predictive frameworks that reconcile ethical, emotional, and epigenetic factors influencing palliative care choices, particularly in underrepresented populations. To address this gap, we propose a mixed-methods computational approach combining natural language processing (NLP) of longitudinal patient narratives, agent-based modeling of social support networks, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling of stress-related biomarkers (e.g., cortisol, inflammatory cytokines). The NLP pipeline will process ethnographic interviews and digital diaries to identify linguistic patterns associated with adaptive vs. maladaptive grieving, while agent-based simulations will explore how community-level interventions alter collective bereavement outcomes. Concurrently, biomarker data from hospice patients will be integrated to quantify biological correlates of psychological states. HPC resources are critical for managing the heterogeneous data streams, enabling parallel processing of text corpora (>10^6 documents), stochastic simulation ensembles (>10^4 parameter variations), and computationally intensive Bayesian inference across high-dimensional datasets. Expected outcomes include: (1) a novel computational framework for personalized thanatological risk stratification, (2) evidence-based guidelines for culturally responsive grief interventions, and (3) open-source tools bridging computational social science and palliative biomedicine. By elucidating the multiscale drivers of end-of-life experiences, this work aims to transform interdisciplinary thanatology into a predictive science, directly informing clinical practice and policy while preserving the humanistic core of death studies.
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the biological, philosophical, psychological, sociological, and theological aspects of death, dying, and bereavement. Includes instruction in counseling, ethics, grief, palliative and hospice care, philosophy, thanatology, and theology.

abstract: Heavy equipment maintenance is critical for industries reliant on construction, mining, and agricultural machinery, yet unscheduled downtime due to component failures remains a persistent challenge. This project seeks to address this problem by developing predictive maintenance models through high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled simulations and machine learning. The research will focus on analyzing failure patterns in key systems—such as hydraulic components, engine performance degradation, and structural wear in tracks and joints—using multi-physics simulations and large-scale sensor datasets. Current approaches rely on static maintenance schedules or basic diagnostic tools, which often fail to account for dynamic operational stresses, material fatigue, and environmental variables. To overcome these limitations, the project will employ HPC resources to train ensemble machine learning models on heterogeneous data streams (vibration, thermal, and pressure sensor logs, maintenance records) and simulate equipment behavior under complex load scenarios. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) will model hydraulic system inefficiencies, while finite element analysis (FEA) will assess stress distribution in critical welded joints. These simulations will inform real-time anomaly detection algorithms and optimize maintenance thresholds. The expected outcomes include (1) a predictive framework for identifying failure-prone components with ≥90% accuracy 100–300 operating hours pre-failure, (2) validated computational models of wear mechanisms in high-stress environments, and (3) a digital twin prototype for scenario-based maintenance training. By reducing unplanned downtime by an estimated 15–25%, this work will directly benefit equipment operators and manufacturers. The HPC infrastructure is essential due to the scale of sensor data (10+ TB/month per machine fleet) and the computational intensity of coupled mechanical-thermal-fluid simulations, which require parallelized processing across thousands of cores. Results will be disseminated through industry partnerships and integrated into technician training modules, enhancing both maintenance practices and workforce preparedness.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills in the field maintenance and repair of heavy equipment, and in the general maintenance and overhaul of such equipment. Includes instruction in inspection, maintenance, and repair of tracks, wheels, brakes, operating controls, pneumatic and hydraulic systems, electrical circuitry, engines and in techniques of welding and brazing.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model and analyze the impact of evidence-based instructional strategies on student engagement and learning outcomes in diverse K–12 classrooms. Current approaches in teacher education often rely on qualitative or small-scale observational studies, limiting the ability to predict how variables such as classroom composition, technology integration, or culturally responsive pedagogy interact at scale. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate dynamic classroom environments using agent-based modeling (ABM) and machine learning (ML). The ABM framework will parameterize student demographics (e.g., race, gender, socioeconomic status), teacher behaviors, and curricular interventions, while reinforcement learning algorithms will iteratively optimize pedagogical strategies under varying conditions. Simulations will draw on anonymized datasets from partner school districts, including longitudinal academic performance, attendance, and behavioral records. The computational workload requires parallel processing to manage thousands of concurrent simulations, each testing hypotheses about the efficacy of specific teaching practices. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models identifying instructional approaches that maximize equitable participation and content mastery in heterogeneous classrooms and (2) a generative AI tool that synthesizes simulation results into actionable training modules for pre-service teachers. By quantifying relationships between pedagogical choices and student outcomes, this work aims to advance data-driven teacher education, directly supporting programs focused on school reform, technology integration, and reducing disparities in educational access. The scalability of this approach—enabled by HPC—offers a transformative lens for designing adaptable, evidence-based training frameworks that address the complex realities of 21st-century classrooms.
detailed_field: Teacher education, specific levels and methods
cip_definition: Any instructional program in teacher education that prepares individuals to be effective educators or trainers. Includes instruction in school reform and design; arts and technology in the classroom; theories of teaching and learning; adult and adolescent development; race, class, and gender dynamics; and the history and future of education in America.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research on the dynamic interplay between psychosocial interventions and athletic performance optimization. A critical gap exists in understanding how multimodal interventions—integrating biofeedback, cognitive-behavioral strategies, and team dynamics modeling—interact to influence sport outcomes at scale. Current approaches often rely on small-sample studies or linear statistical models, limiting the ability to capture complex, non-linear relationships between psychological factors (e.g., resilience, attentional focus) and performance metrics (e.g., reaction time, endurance). To address this, we propose developing computational models using machine learning (ML) and network analysis to process heterogeneous datasets, including psychometric surveys, biometric wearables data, and video-based behavioral coding from 5,000+ collegiate and professional athletes. The HPC infrastructure will enable large-scale parallel processing of time-series data to identify latent patterns in stress-recovery cycles, team communication efficacy, and skill acquisition trajectories. Agent-based modeling will simulate how individualized mental skills training propagates through team ecosystems, while deep learning architectures will predict optimal intervention timing based on neurophysiological baselines. The computational pipeline will integrate Python-based ML libraries (TensorFlow, PyTorch) with R for multilevel statistical analysis, requiring GPU-accelerated nodes for real-time optimization. Expected outcomes include: (1) a validated framework for personalizing performance psychology protocols using predictive analytics, (2) evidence-based guidelines for balancing group cohesion and individual athlete mental health, and (3) open-source tools enabling coaches and practitioners to model intervention impacts. By scaling data-driven insights beyond traditional laboratory paradigms, this work will enhance the precision and accessibility of sport psychology practices while maintaining rigorous ethical standards for performance enhancement. The requested HPC resources are essential to manage the computational intensity of analyzing high-dimensional, longitudinal datasets central to advancing counseling-oriented approaches in applied sport psychology.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the motor, physiological, and psychosocial aspects of sport behavior. Includes instruction in applied sport psychology, clinical mental health counseling, coaching, exercise physiology, ethical performance enhancement; human development, leadership and team building, mind-body practices, neuroscience, and personality and health.

abstract: This project seeks to enhance biology teacher preparation by modeling the impact of instructional strategies on student conceptual understanding of complex biological systems. A key challenge in biology teacher education is identifying pedagogical approaches that effectively address persistent student misconceptions (e.g., ecosystem dynamics, cellular respiration) across diverse classroom contexts. While qualitative studies have explored this issue, scalable computational methods are needed to generalize patterns from large multimodal datasets, including lesson videos, student assessments, and teacher reflections. We propose developing machine learning models to analyze 5,000+ annotated classroom interactions from a national teacher observation database, alongside longitudinal learning outcomes from 15,000 high school biology students. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable the parallel training of transformer-based NLP models to detect pedagogical strategies in teacher discourse and correlate these with conceptual growth metrics derived from pre/post assessments. Agent-based simulations will further model how variations in teaching tactics propagate through student knowledge networks during inquiry-based lessons. By integrating empirical data with computational simulations, this work aims to 1) identify instructional sequences that optimally reduce misconceptions in core biology topics and 2) generate synthetic training modules that dynamically adapt to novice teachers’ coaching needs. The resulting frameworks will inform the design of adaptive professional development tools, enabling teacher educators to personalize feedback using evidence-based interaction patterns. This project directly supports the program’s mission to bridge disciplinary pedagogy with computational literacy, equipping future biology teachers with data-driven insights to address heterogeneous learning needs in STEM classrooms.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach biology programs at various educational levels.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolving legal and regulatory frameworks governing precision agriculture technologies, with a focus on algorithmic decision-making systems in farming operations. As advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), sensor networks, and automated machinery reshape agricultural practices, legal doctrines addressing liability, data ownership, and environmental compliance face unprecedented challenges. The project aims to systematically model interactions between heterogeneous legal domains—including intellectual property, tort law, and environmental regulations—and computationally intensive agricultural systems. By developing agent-based simulations of farm operations under varying regulatory regimes, the research will quantify how legal uncertainty impacts the adoption rates of precision agriculture technologies. Natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will be deployed to analyze case law, policy documents, and contractual agreements across jurisdictions, identifying emergent patterns in liability disputes and regulatory enforcement. Graph neural networks will map the interdependencies between multi-scale legal constraints (local, national, international) and technology diffusion pathways. The computational framework will integrate stochastic optimization models to propose adaptive policy mechanisms capable of balancing innovation incentives with environmental and equity concerns. Expected outcomes include an open-access repository of annotated legal corpora specific to agricultural technology, predictive models of litigation risk for AI-driven farming systems, and scenario analyses informing the design of interoperable regulatory standards. By bridging computational social science methodologies with legal informatics, this project addresses a critical gap in governance strategies for 21st-century agricultural systems while demonstrating the transformative potential of HPC resources in non-traditional, policy-relevant research domains.
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the law, policies, and regulations for lawyers and non-legal professionals in food and agriculture.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the interplay between cultural dynamics, environmental change, and societal decision-making across historical and contemporary contexts through an integrative computational framework. The research problem centers on understanding how complex, nonlinear interactions among cultural narratives, ecological pressures, and institutional structures shape human behavior and collective outcomes—a challenge requiring analysis of heterogeneous datasets spanning archaeology, environmental science, political philosophy, and digital humanities. Current methodologies struggle to reconcile the scale and diversity of relevant data or model emergent phenomena arising from cross-domain feedback loops. To address this, we propose deploying high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop agent-based models simulating decision-making processes in resource-constrained environments, coupled with natural language processing (NLP) pipelines for analyzing historical texts and oral histories. These computational methods will be integrated with geospatial analysis of environmental data and network-based approaches to trace the evolution of cultural ideas. The agent-based models will parameterize agents using behavioral patterns extracted from ethnographic records and sociological surveys, enabling large-scale simulations of societal responses to environmental stressors. The HPC infrastructure is critical for managing the scale of these simulations, which involve thousands of agents interacting across multi-layered networks, and for processing terabyte-scale corpora of digitized historical documents. Expected outcomes include novel insights into resilience strategies adopted by past and present societies, identification of cultural-institutional configurations that promote sustainable resource use, and open-access tools for interdisciplinary data integration. This work will advance methodological innovation in digital humanities by demonstrating how computational modeling can bridge qualitative and quantitative approaches, while contributing actionable knowledge for addressing contemporary challenges at the intersection of cultural preservation and environmental stewardship.
cip_title: Liberal Arts and Sciences/ Liberal Studies
cip_definition: A program that is a structured combination of the arts, biological and physical sciences, social sciences, and humanities, emphasizing breadth of study. Includes instruction in independently designed, individualized, or regular programs.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a predictive maintenance framework for complex electromechanical systems using high-performance computing (HPC) to address inefficiencies in traditional diagnostic and repair methodologies. Current approaches to failure prediction in multi-component systems, such as industrial machinery or advanced automotive systems, often rely on heuristic models or oversimplified simulations, leading to suboptimal maintenance schedules, unplanned downtime, and resource waste. To overcome these limitations, this research will employ large-scale computational modeling to simulate system degradation under operational stresses, integrating finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML) to predict failure modes with higher accuracy. The HPC resources will enable parallelized simulations of heterogeneous mechanical components—such as bearings, actuators, and thermal management systems—across diverse operating conditions, capturing interactions between wear, thermal cycling, and material fatigue. Sensor-derived operational data from field deployments will train ML models to correlate simulation outputs with real-world failure signatures, creating adaptive prognostic tools. Key deliverables include an open-source computational workflow for failure mode identification and a decision-support system to prioritize repair interventions based on risk-criticality metrics. The anticipated outcomes are a 20-30% improvement in failure prediction accuracy compared to existing methods, validated through case studies on commercial HVAC systems and electric vehicle drivetrains. By optimizing repair timelines and resource allocation, this framework aims to reduce maintenance costs by up to 15% and extend equipment service life, contributing to sustainable practices in industrial and transportation sectors. The scalability of the HPC-driven approach will also support future research in emerging repair technologies, such as additive manufacturing-based component restoration and autonomous robotic repair systems.
cip_title: Mechanic and Repair Technologies/ Technicians, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in mechanic and repair technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance understanding of neurodevelopmental mechanisms underlying pediatric anxiety disorders, with a focus on identifying biomarkers and optimizing early intervention strategies. Current limitations in clinical child psychology stem from the complexity of integrating multimodal data—including neuroimaging (fMRI), genetic susceptibility markers, and longitudinal behavioral assessments—while accounting for dynamic developmental trajectories. Traditional analytical approaches struggle to model the nonlinear interactions between biological, cognitive, and environmental risk factors that drive disorder onset and progression. The proposed research will employ machine learning frameworks to analyze high-dimensional datasets from a cohort of 800 children (ages 6–12) with anxiety symptoms, incorporating resting-state fMRI connectivity, polygenic risk scores, and caregiver-reported psychosocial stressors. Computational workflows will include federated learning to preserve participant confidentiality across collaborating clinical sites, graph neural networks to model evolving brain-behavior relationships, and Bayesian hierarchical models to quantify uncertainty in developmental predictions. HPC resources are critical for training these models efficiently, given the scale of imaging data (~10 TB) and the need for real-time parameter optimization in iterative simulations. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of neural circuitry patterns predictive of treatment resistance, (2) risk stratification algorithms to guide personalized therapeutic interventions, and (3) open-source tools for developmental psychopathology research that integrate ethical AI practices. By clarifying how neurocognitive vulnerabilities interact with environmental contexts during critical developmental windows, this work aims to transform clinical decision-making in pediatric mental health while adhering to FAIR data principles. The computational infrastructure will enable scalable replication of findings across diverse populations, directly addressing gaps in equitable access to precision child psychology frameworks.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the developmental processes of children and associated disorders and that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of clinical child psychology. Includes instruction in developmental neuropsychology, child psychopathology, testing of children and adolescents, pediatric psychology, psychosocial variables in child development, clinical skills, family therapy, behavioral assessment and intervention, clinical skills, consultation, professional standards and ethics, and applications to topics such as infancy, childhood, and adolescence.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a scalable computational framework for optimizing real-time resource allocation in distributed, heterogeneous computing environments, with a focus on dynamic workflows common in edge computing and IoT applications. The research addresses the challenge of efficiently managing computational tasks across devices with varying capabilities, network latencies, and energy constraints—a problem exacerbated by the growing complexity of distributed systems that blend traditional cloud infrastructure with edge nodes and embedded sensors. Current scheduling algorithms often fail to account for the multi-objective nature of these environments, where priorities such as energy efficiency, data locality, and latency minimization must be balanced dynamically. The proposed methodology combines evolutionary computation techniques with lightweight reinforcement learning agents to create adaptive allocation strategies that operate without centralized coordination. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will be employed to simulate large-scale networks (>100,000 nodes) with realistic volatility patterns, enabling the training and validation of models under diverse topological configurations. The computational approach includes developing parallelized evaluation pipelines for population-based optimization algorithms and implementing distributed neural architecture search mechanisms to evolve context-aware scheduling policies. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for benchmarking decentralized resource allocation strategies and novel protocols that reduce energy consumption by 15-30% in simulated edge environments compared to state-of-the-art methods. This work bridges gaps between distributed systems theory and practical implementation challenges, offering insights into programming paradigms for emergent computing ecosystems while avoiding direct overlap with traditional computer science subfields. The requested resources will enable parameter space exploration at scales infeasible with conventional computing infrastructure, particularly for stress-testing allocation policies under bursty workloads and partial network failure scenarios.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the general writing and implementation of generic and customized programs to drive operating systems and that generally prepares individuals to apply the methods and procedures of software design and programming to software installation and maintenance. Includes instruction in software design, low- and high-level languages and program writing; program customization and linking; prototype testing; troubleshooting; and related aspects of operating systems and networks.

abstract: The integration of high-performance computing (HPC) into oncology pharmacy research is critical to advancing precision medicine strategies for cancer treatment. Current challenges in optimizing chemotherapy regimens, predicting drug resistance, and personalizing dosing protocols are constrained by the complexity of pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) models, multi-omics data analysis, and the need for real-time simulations of drug interactions. This project seeks to leverage HPC resources to develop and validate computational frameworks that address these gaps. Specifically, we aim to (1) construct large-scale, patient-specific PK/PD models integrating genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic datasets to predict tumor response to chemotherapy; (2) apply machine learning algorithms to identify patterns in electronic health records (EHRs) associated with adverse drug reactions and therapeutic failure; and (3) simulate molecular dynamics of drug-target interactions under varying tumor microenvironment conditions to elucidate resistance mechanisms. The computational workflows will utilize parallelized processing for Bayesian hierarchical modeling, deep neural networks for EHR analysis, and GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics simulations (e.g., GROMACS). These methods demand significant memory allocation, multi-node processing, and rapid I/O capabilities due to the scale of genomic datasets (>10 TB), iterative model training, and nanosecond-scale simulation sampling. Expected outcomes include predictive algorithms for individualized dosing, biomarkers for early detection of resistance, and dynamic visualization tools for drug-target binding affinities. By enabling real-time analysis of heterogeneous data streams, this research will directly inform clinical trial design and therapeutic decision-making, reducing trial-and-error prescribing. The requested HPC resources are essential to overcome current limitations in single-node computational power, ensuring clinically actionable results within pharmacologically relevant timeframes. This work bridges computational oncology and clinical pharmacy, offering a scalable platform to improve treatment efficacy and safety in diverse cancer populations.
cip_definition: Research focused on oncology pharmacy.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model and optimize decentralized decision-making frameworks in multi-agent business ecosystems, with a focus on emergent coordination dynamics in fragmented markets. Traditional business research often assumes centralized control or homogeneous stakeholder behavior, yet modern digital economies increasingly operate through distributed, self-organizing systems—e.g., cross-platform supply chains, decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, and AI-driven pricing agents. The computational challenge lies in simulating hyper-scale, heterogeneous agent interactions under real-world constraints (resource scarcity, regulatory boundaries, asymmetric information) to identify stable equilibria and systemic vulnerabilities. Using agent-based modeling (ABM) enhanced by graph neural networks (GNNs), we will simulate 10^6+ autonomous agents representing firms, consumers, and regulatory entities across dynamically evolving networks. The HPC environment will enable parallelized scenario testing of incentive alignment mechanisms, shock propagation in multi-tiered value chains, and emergent collusion risks in algorithmic markets. Data will integrate real-world transaction logs, API-fed market signals, and synthetic agents trained via reinforcement learning to mimic strategic adaptation. Expected outcomes include: (1) a scalable computational framework to predict tipping points in decentralized business systems, (2) quantitative metrics for resilience in fragmented markets, and (3) policy-relevant insights into mitigating cascading failures in algorithmically mediated economies. This work bridges complexity science, computational economics, and operational research, offering novel tools to analyze business ecosystems where centralized governance is impractical or undesirable. Results will inform both corporate strategy in platform-driven markets and regulatory approaches to emergent decentralized organizational forms.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the general study of business, including the processes of interchanging goods and services (buying, selling and producing), business organization, and accounting as used in profit-making and nonprofit public and private institutions and agencies. The programs may prepare individuals to apply business principles and techniques in various occupational settings.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the ecological and evolutionary drivers of zoonotic disease spillover and spread using integrative computational modeling. Emerging infectious diseases often arise from complex interactions between host ecology, pathogen evolution, and environmental change, yet current predictive frameworks lack resolution to disentangle these dynamics at scale. We propose developing spatially explicit, agent-based models to simulate host-pathogen interactions across heterogeneous landscapes, informed by longitudinal field data on reservoir species distributions, pathogen genomic diversity, and environmental variables (e.g., land-use change, climate gradients). High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to parameterize models with high-resolution remote sensing data (~1 km² grids), conduct phylogenetically informed simulations of viral evolution under ecological constraints, and run ensemble projections under multiple climate and land-management scenarios. A key innovation involves coupling Bayesian phylodynamic inference with ecological niche models to identify hotspots of adaptive evolution and cross-species transmission risk. Initial case studies will focus on Lassa virus dynamics in West African rodent reservoirs and Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) spread in North American tick-host communities. Expected outcomes include predictive risk maps of spillover potential, mechanistic insights into how habitat fragmentation accelerates pathogen dispersal, and evolutionary models quantifying selection pressures at wildlife-human interfaces. By integrating ecological, epidemiological, and evolutionary processes into a unified computational framework, this work will advance theoretical understanding of emergence risks while providing actionable tools for surveillance prioritization. The scale of genomic, spatial, and climate datasets (~50 TB) and the need for computationally intensive parameter sensitivity analyses (10,000+ core-hours) necessitate access to HPC infrastructure. Results will directly inform One Health strategies aimed at mitigating zoonotic threats in rapidly changing environments.
cip_definition: A program with a general synthesis of epidemiology and biostatistics or a specialization which draws from epidemiology and biostatistics. Includes instruction in biostatistics, disease and injury determinants, epidemiology, health services research, pathology, spatial analysis, and statistics.

abstract: Rheumatologic diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), are characterized by complex, heterogeneous molecular mechanisms that drive inflammation, autoimmunity, and tissue damage. Despite advances in targeted therapies, many patients exhibit incomplete treatment responses due to poorly understood genetic, epigenetic, and microenvironmental factors. This project seeks to address this gap by integrating multi-omics data—including single-cell RNA sequencing, chromatin accessibility profiles, and plasma proteomics—from longitudinal clinical cohorts to map disease-specific cellular states and signaling networks. A central computational challenge lies in resolving patient-specific molecular signatures from high-dimensional datasets while accounting for technical variability, sparse longitudinal sampling, and diverse clinical trajectories. To overcome this, we propose a machine learning framework leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) to model cell-cell communication dynamics and prioritize pathogenic interactions. Bayesian hierarchical models will quantify uncertainty in cross-modal data integration, and agent-based simulations will explore how microenvironmental perturbations alter immune-stromal cell interactions. These analyses require high-performance computing (HPC) resources due to the scale of single-cell datasets (>500,000 cells across 200 patients), iterative optimization of GNN architectures, and computationally intensive simulations of signaling network rewiring. The project will utilize GPU-accelerated nodes for deep learning workflows and high-memory nodes for large matrix operations. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of conserved and patient-specific biomarkers predictive of treatment response, (2) mechanistic insights into how synovial fibroblast subsets drive therapy-resistant inflammation in RA, and (3) open-source tools for scalable analysis of rheumatologic multi-omics data. By linking computational findings to clinical metadata, this work aims to advance personalized therapeutic strategies while establishing a framework for dynamic modeling of immune-mediated diseases. The requested HPC allocation is critical to achieving these goals within biologically relevant timescales, as local computational infrastructure cannot support the simultaneous processing of terabyte-scale datasets or complex in silico perturbation experiments.
cip_definition: Research focused on Rheumatology

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize modular construction workflows, addressing inefficiencies in resource allocation, scheduling, and material utilization within rapidly evolving construction trades. Modular construction—a process where building components are prefabricated off-site—requires precise coordination of labor, equipment, and supply chains to meet project timelines and cost targets. However, current industry practices rely on heuristic decision-making, leading to delays, material waste, and suboptimal energy use in prefabrication facilities. To overcome these challenges, we propose a multi-scale simulation approach leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model dynamic interactions between workforce availability, equipment throughput, material delivery logistics, and energy consumption patterns. Agent-based modeling will simulate worker-task assignments under varying site conditions, while discrete-event simulations will optimize fabrication sequencing across parallel production lines. Machine learning algorithms will be integrated to predict material stress behavior in modular units under transport and assembly conditions, informed by finite element analysis datasets. The computational workload necessitates parallel processing for stochastic scenario testing across thousands of parameter combinations, including variable weather impacts, supply chain disruptions, and design alterations. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for (1) real-time adjustment of fabrication schedules based on material lead times and labor capacity, (2) energy-efficient facility layouts minimizing robotic arm motion paths, and (3) machine learning-derived material specifications reducing waste by 15-20% in modular component production. By deploying these HPC-enabled models through a cloud-based interface, the research aims to provide trade professionals with actionable insights to improve project feasibility in off-site construction—a critical need as urbanization pressures demand faster, greener building solutions. The proposed resource allocation will support GPU-accelerated simulations of up to 10,000 concurrent agent interactions and terabyte-scale analysis of LiDAR-scanned construction site data.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in construction trades, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project seeks to optimize dynamic pricing and resource allocation strategies for independent boutique hotels using high-performance computing (HPC) to model complex, real-time interactions between guest behavior, sustainability incentives, and operational constraints. The hospitality industry faces mounting pressure to balance profitability with eco-conscious practices, particularly for small-scale operators lacking the infrastructure of large chains. Current pricing models often fail to account for hyperlocal demand signals, energy consumption patterns, and the growing consumer preference for sustainability-certified accommodations. We propose developing an adaptive decision-support system that integrates stochastic demand forecasting, energy usage simulations, and game-theoretic pricing algorithms. The computational approach will leverage agent-based modeling to simulate guest decision-making processes influenced by real-time pricing, carbon footprint disclosures, and seasonal amenities. Parallelized Monte Carlo methods will assess risk profiles under varying climate scenarios and regulatory conditions, while graph neural networks will map cross-property competitive dynamics within regional markets. By processing multi-source data streams—including IoT sensor feeds from building management systems, social media sentiment, and granular energy pricing—the HPC framework will enable micro-optimizations across room inventory, staffing, and energy grids at 15-minute intervals. Expected outcomes include a scalable toolkit for independent operators to dynamically adjust rates and resource commitments while maintaining profit margins and achieving sustainability certifications. The models will be validated against historical data from a network of 12 boutique hotels across three climate zones, with success metrics measuring improvements in revenue per available room (RevPAR), energy cost reductions, and guest satisfaction scores. This interdisciplinary approach bridges hospitality operations, behavioral economics, and environmental systems engineering, offering a novel computational paradigm for small businesses navigating the decarbonization transition.
cip_definition: An instructional program that prepares individuals to manage operations and facilities that provide food and/or lodging services to the traveling public. Includes instruction in hospitality industry principles; supplies purchasing, storage, and control; hotel and restaurant facilities design and planning; hospitality industry law; personnel management and labor relations; financial management; facilities management; marketing and sale promotion strategies; convention and event management; front desk operations; and applications to specific types of hotel, motel, and/or restaurant operations. Note: this program was re-instated after being deleted from CIP 2000; previously, it was coded as 52.0902.

abstract: The adaptive immune system’s ability to distinguish self from non-self relies on the dynamic diversity of T cell receptors (TCRs), yet dysregulation of this process underpins autoimmune pathologies and failed responses to pathogens. A critical gap persists in understanding how TCR structural variability influences cross-reactivity with self-antigens and pathogen-derived epitopes, particularly in diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. This project seeks to elucidate the molecular determinants of TCR specificity by integrating large-scale structural modeling of TCR-antigen complexes with longitudinal immune repertoire sequencing data from patient cohorts. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to perform all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of TCR-pMHC (peptide-major histocompatibility complex) interactions, which will model conformational changes and binding energetics across diverse TCR clonotypes. Parallelized docking workflows will assess cross-reactivity landscapes between viral epitopes and human autoantigens implicated in molecular mimicry. Concurrently, machine learning algorithms will analyze paired TCRα/β sequencing data from autoimmune patients to identify clonal signatures predictive of disease progression or remission. These computational approaches will be validated against in vitro binding assays and single-cell transcriptomic profiles of autoreactive T cells. The integration of structural predictions with repertoire dynamics aims to uncover mechanistic links between TCR diversity, host-pathogen conflict, and loss of self-tolerance. Expected outcomes include predictive models of TCR autoreactivity, novel biomarkers for early autoimmune diagnosis, and structure-guided targets for immunotherapeutic intervention. This work directly addresses the NIH priority area of advancing precision immunology through computational innovation, with potential to transform the management of immune-mediated diseases. Access to HPC infrastructure is required to manage the terabyte-scale simulation outputs and optimize deep learning architectures for high-dimensional immune repertoire analysis.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on scientific study of the biological mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of disease, host-pathogen interactions, and host response to disease. Includes instruction in antigen and antibody structure and function, effector mechanisms, receptors, histocompatibility, host-pathogen recognition, disease modeling, autoimmune systems, antibody formation, cytotoxic responses, regulation of immune response, virulence determinants, intercellular signaling, immunosuppression, immunotherapy, immunogenetics, disease markers, transplantation, antibody humanization, and microbial pathogenesis.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the complex interplay between human movement, choreographic structures, and computational modeling in contemporary dance practice. While traditional dance research relies on qualitative analysis and manual notation systems, the scale and dimensionality of movement data in ensemble choreography present challenges that exceed conventional methods. The research problem centers on developing a framework to analyze and simulate emergent patterns in group choreography, with a focus on how individual dancers’ kinematic decisions propagate through ensembles to create collective aesthetic outcomes. The computational approach integrates motion capture data from live performances with agent-based modeling to simulate choreographic dynamics under varying parameters. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for processing terabytes of high-frequency motion capture data, training recurrent neural networks to identify movement motifs, and running large-scale simulations of dancer interactions in virtual environments. Machine learning pipelines will classify movement signatures across cultural dance traditions, while parallelized physics simulations will model the biomechanical constraints of multi-dancer systems. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of annotated dance movement sequences, tools for generative choreography assisted by AI, and quantitative metrics for assessing collective coordination in performance. This work bridges computational science and artistic practice, offering new methods to preserve intangible cultural heritage in dance and enabling choreographers to explore complex spatial-temporal relationships at scales impractical for human-led experimentation. The requested resources will directly support the first systematic study of self-organization principles in dance ensembles, with implications for both performing arts pedagogy and interdisciplinary research in complex systems.
detailed_field: Dance, drama, theatre arts, and stagecraft
cip_definition: Any instructional program in dance, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of quantum turbulence in superfluid systems through large-scale numerical simulations. Quantum turbulence, characterized by chaotic tangles of quantized vortices in ultra-cold superfluids, presents unresolved questions about energy transfer mechanisms, decay pathways, and connections to classical turbulence. Current experimental and analytical approaches face limitations in resolving the full spatiotemporal complexity of these systems, necessitating advanced computational methods. We propose to employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to solve the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, a nonlinear Schrödinger equation governing superfluid dynamics, across three-dimensional domains. Our simulations will model vortex interactions, reconnections, and collective behavior under varying initial conditions and external perturbations. A hybrid pseudo-spectral and finite-difference approach will be implemented to balance accuracy and computational efficiency, with adaptive mesh refinement applied to resolve fine vortex structures. The simulations will track energy spectra, vortex line density, and topological invariants to characterize turbulence evolution. By scaling to system sizes exceeding current state-of-the-art simulations, we aim to identify universal statistical properties and test theoretical predictions about energy cascade processes. Outcomes will directly inform ongoing experimental efforts in superfluid helium systems and contribute to foundational models of quantum turbulence. This work will establish a computational framework for probing non-equilibrium quantum hydrodynamics, with potential implications for understanding analogous phenomena in neutron star interiors and quantum-enhanced fluid systems. The requested HPC resources are critical for achieving the necessary resolution and statistical sampling to advance this emerging frontier in quantum fluid dynamics.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in physical sciences, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for optimizing the design and safety of electrical power transmission systems, with a focus on integrating renewable energy sources into aging grid infrastructures. The increasing complexity of modern power systems—driven by distributed generation, variable renewable inputs, and evolving load demands—requires advanced simulations to evaluate stability, fault tolerance, and compliance with safety standards. Traditional analytical methods lack the scalability to model large-scale, heterogeneous grids in dynamic operating conditions, creating gaps in risk assessment and installation planning. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled approach combining electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations, machine learning (ML)-based fault prediction, and multi-objective optimization algorithms. The computational workflow will simulate grid behavior under diverse scenarios, including extreme weather events, equipment failures, and intermittent renewable generation, using parallelized power system solvers such as OpenDSS and GridLAB-D. ML models will be trained on synthetic and real-world grid data to predict arc flash hazards, insulation breakdowns, and line sagging risks, informing adaptive protection schemes. Additionally, genetic algorithms will optimize conductor placement, transformer sizing, and grounding system configurations to minimize material costs while meeting NEC and IEEE standards. The HPC resources are critical for managing the high-dimensional parameter space and real-time constraints of these simulations, which involve millions of nodes and sub-millisecond time steps. Expected outcomes include validated design protocols for resilient hybrid AC/DC grids, open-source tools for risk-aware installation planning, and data-driven recommendations for updating industry training curricula. By bridging computational engineering with hands-on electrical installation practices, this work aims to enhance the safety, efficiency, and scalability of power transmission systems in transitioning energy landscapes.
cip_title: Electrical and Power Transmission Installation/ Installer, General
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to install indoor and outdoor residential, commercial, and industrial electrical systems, and associated power transmission lines. Includes instruction in electricity, safety procedures, wiring, insulation and grounding, schematic blueprint interpretation, equipment operation and maintenance, and applicable codes and standards.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamic interplay between collective decision-making and environmental stressors in human populations using a novel computational framework integrating cognitive modeling, ecological data assimilation, and network science. While existing research has examined cognitive processes or environmental systems in isolation, critical gaps remain in understanding how distributed cognitive systems adapt to rapidly changing ecological conditions—particularly in scenarios where traditional behavioral heuristics may become maladaptive. The proposed work will develop agent-based models of cognitive-environmental interaction, incorporating real-world climate datasets, neurocognitive constraints on decision-making, and multi-scale social network structures. High-performance computing resources are essential to simulate population-level emergent behaviors across diverse ecological scenarios (e.g., drought patterns, extreme weather events) while maintaining granular individual cognitive representations. The computational architecture will combine parallelized Monte Carlo methods for parameter space exploration with graph neural networks to model the co-evolution of social ties and belief systems under stress. Expected outcomes include 1) identification of critical thresholds in environmental change rates that disrupt collective problem-solving capacities, 2) predictive models of cognitive adaptation lag times in climate-vulnerable communities, and 3) an open-source toolkit for simulating coupled cognitive-ecological systems. By bridging cognitive science methodologies with complex systems approaches, this work aims to establish new theoretical foundations for understanding resilience in human-environment interactions while providing actionable insights for policymakers addressing climate adaptation challenges. The scale of required simulations—involving >10^5 agents with heterogeneous cognitive architectures interacting across temporally evolving networks—necessitates dedicated HPC resources beyond typical institutional computing capacities.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in cognitive science, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational legal research, focusing on the dynamic interplay between emerging technologies and the evolution of legal frameworks. The research problem centers on the inadequacy of traditional legal analysis methods to process and interpret the vast, unstructured datasets generated by decentralized technologies (e.g., blockchain-based smart contracts, AI-driven regulatory compliance tools) and their real-world legal implications. Current approaches struggle to model the nonlinear, adaptive interactions between technological systems and legal norms, particularly in cross-jurisdictional contexts. To address this gap, the project proposes a hybrid computational methodology combining natural language processing (NLP), graph-based network analysis, and agent-based modeling. Legal texts (statutes, case law, treaties) and technology governance artifacts (smart contract code, algorithmic audit trails) will be processed using transformer models fine-tuned on legal corpora to extract semantically rich representations of rule structures and obligations. These outputs will inform the construction of multilayer networks mapping relationships between technical systems, legal entities, and regulatory requirements across jurisdictions. Agent-based simulations will then model how perturbations in technological ecosystems—such as protocol upgrades or adversarial exploits—cascade through legal and institutional frameworks. The computational workflow demands HPC resources to handle terabyte-scale datasets, parallelize graph traversals for cross-jurisdictional analysis, and execute high-fidelity simulations at scale. Expected outcomes include 1) a novel framework for quantifying legal adaptability to technological change, 2) predictive models identifying systemic vulnerabilities in tech-law interfaces, and 3) an open-access repository of annotated legal-technical corpora. By enabling granular, data-driven analysis of legal systems as complex adaptive systems, this work aims to inform the design of more resilient governance mechanisms for emergent technologies while establishing computational methods as critical tools in advanced legal studies.
cip_definition: An integrated or undifferentiated program in one or more of the legal research or advanced practice fields.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the study of dance as a dynamic, embodied cultural practice through computational analysis of large-scale movement datasets. The research addresses a critical gap in dance studies: the lack of scalable methods to systematically analyze and compare movement patterns across diverse dance traditions, populations, and contexts. While qualitative methods remain central to dance scholarship, the increasing availability of motion capture data—drawn from archival recordings, ethnographic fieldwork, and laboratory-based experiments—presents an opportunity to quantitatively model dance movement at unprecedented resolution. However, processing and analyzing these complex, multidimensional datasets requires computational resources beyond typical workstation capacities. This project will develop and implement machine learning pipelines to classify movement signatures, simulate biomechanical constraints in choreographic sequences, and identify latent patterns in cross-cultural dance repertoires. Key computational tasks include training 3D convolutional neural networks on annotated motion capture data, running iterative optimization algorithms for generative choreography models, and conducting high-dimensional statistical analyses of movement variability. These methods will be applied to two case studies: 1) tracing the evolution of rhythmic footwork patterns in Afro-diasporic dance forms, and 2) quantifying the relationship between improvisational structures and physiological load in contemporary dance practice. By integrating HPC-enabled computational techniques with dance ethnography and performance studies, this work aims to produce new frameworks for preserving intangible cultural heritage, inform inclusive dance pedagogy through evidence-based movement analysis, and establish benchmarks for computational dance research. Anticipated outcomes include open-source tools for dance data visualization, a public repository of processed movement datasets, and novel theoretical insights into the relationship between embodied knowledge and computational modeling in the performing arts.
detailed_field: Dance, drama, theatre arts, and stagecraft
