The proposed simulations will resolve microsecond-scale fluid-structure interactions across kilometer-scale dam and turbine geometries, enabled by parallelized solvers and adaptive mesh refinement. Key objectives include (1) quantifying the relationship between turbulent flow features and sediment erosion patterns on turbine blades, (2) identifying operational thresholds to minimize cavitation and fatigue damage under peak load scenarios, and (3) validating predictive models against experimental data from partner hydropower facilities. The HPC scale required—estimated at 250,000 core-hours—will support ensemble runs to assess uncertainty in climate-driven flow variability and sediment load projections. Anticipated outcomes include a publicly accessible database of optimized blade geometries and operational protocols to extend turbine lifespan by 15–20%, reduce maintenance costs by 30%, and improve annual energy output by 8–12% in aging hydroelectric plants. By advancing predictive capabilities for sediment management and component durability, this work directly aligns with national priorities to modernize hydroelectric infrastructure while addressing interdisciplinary challenges in renewable energy systems engineering. Results will be disseminated through open-source simulation tools and workshops for industry stakeholders, bridging computational innovation with practical technology deployment.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and other professionals engaged in developing hydroelectric energy systems. Includes instruction in hydroelectric energy principles, energy storage and transfer technologies, testing and inspection procedures, system maintenance procedures, and report preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing complexity of optimizing energy-efficient communication protocols for next-generation IoT-enabled embedded systems, which face stringent constraints in latency, power consumption, and scalability. Current simulation tools struggle to model large-scale networks with the fidelity required to account for dynamic interference patterns, heterogeneous device behaviors, and multi-physics interactions between analog circuitry and digital signal processing components. To overcome these limitations, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a parallelized simulation framework integrating finite-element electromagnetic analysis, discrete-event network modeling, and machine learning-driven optimization. The computational workflow will employ MPI and GPU-accelerated solvers to simulate millimeter-wave signal propagation in densely packed electronic environments while concurrently evaluating packet routing strategies across thousands of networked nodes. By coupling these typically siloed analyses, the platform will enable co-optimization of physical-layer circuit designs and network-layer protocols under real-world operating conditions. Expected outcomes include validated models for predicting interference mitigation in reconfigurable RF front-ends, adaptive power allocation algorithms for edge computing architectures, and benchmark datasets for energy-delay tradeoffs in industrial IoT deployments. This resource-intensive approach directly supports the program’s focus on applied engineering technology by providing students and researchers with a scalable testbed for prototyping hybrid hardware-software solutions, while contributing methodologies that bridge the gap between theoretical communication models and practical electronic system constraints. The requested computing resources will be critical for handling the memory-intensive electromagnetic simulations and combinatorial optimization runs that exceed the capacity of local laboratory infrastructure.
cip_title: Electrical, Electronic, and Communications Engineering Technology
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of electrical, electronics and communication engineers. Includes instruction in electrical circuitry, prototype development and testing, systems analysis and testing, systems maintenance, instrument calibration, and report preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a large-scale computational analysis of stylistic and thematic evolution in 20th-century Anglophone speculative fiction. While traditional literary scholarship has produced foundational close readings of individual texts, the research problem lies in systematically mapping macro-level patterns across a corpus of over 50,000 novels, short stories, and serialized works—a scale unmanageable through manual methods. The study aims to identify underrecognized trends in narrative structure, lexical innovation, and thematic preoccupations correlated with historical events, technological shifts, and sociopolitical movements. Computational methods will include natural language processing (NLP) pipelines for syntactic parsing and semantic role labeling, transformer-based models for context-aware sentiment analysis, and graph-based algorithms to trace intertextual networks of influence. Custom tools will be developed to quantify stylistic markers (e.g., sentence complexity shifts by decade) and cross-reference them against metadata on author demographics, publication contexts, and critical reception. The HPC environment is critical for training domain-adapted language models on genre-specific text, running distributed feature extraction across multi-terabyte archives, and performing high-dimensional clustering to detect latent thematic clusters. Expected outcomes include 1) a publicly accessible interactive visualization platform mapping the genre’s evolution, 2) quantitative evidence challenging periodization assumptions in existing literary histories, and 3) methodological frameworks for hybrid computational-philological analysis applicable to other understudied corpora. By integrating distant reading with hermeneutic traditions, this work will provide new pathways for understanding how speculative fiction both reflects and shapes cultural anxieties about modernity, while demonstrating the transformative potential of HPC-enabled humanities research.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in English language literature, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing large-scale, dynamic manufacturing systems under stochastic demand and resource constraints, a critical problem in industrial engineering and operations research. Traditional analytical models often fail to capture the complexity of real-world production environments, where factors such as machine downtime, fluctuating order volumes, and multi-objective scheduling requirements create computationally intractable optimization landscapes. We propose developing a hybrid computational framework integrating parallelized discrete-event simulation, deep reinforcement learning (DRL), and distributed mixed-integer programming to enable real-time decision support for complex manufacturing operations. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement massively parallel simulations of digital twin environments, training DRL agents through distributed asynchronous gradient descent while simultaneously solving equipment allocation subproblems via decomposition algorithms. Key computational challenges include managing memory-intensive production system state representations across nodes, optimizing communication overhead in distributed optimization routines, and scaling hyperparameter searches for neural network architectures. Expected outcomes include novel algorithms for adaptive production scheduling, quantitative benchmarks comparing centralized versus decentralized learning approaches in manufacturing contexts, and open-source software tools for scalable production system optimization. By enabling near-optimal solutions for problems involving 10^4+ decision variables—an order-of-magnitude improvement over current industrial practice—this work will directly contribute to advancements in sustainable manufacturing through reduced energy consumption, minimized material waste, and improved equipment utilization rates. The requested HPC resources are essential for overcoming memory and processing limitations that currently restrict the complexity of manufacturable system models in both academic research and industrial applications.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply scientific and mathematical principles to the design, development, and implementation of manufacturing systems. Includes instruction in materials science and engineering, manufacturing processes, process engineering, assembly and product engineering, manufacturing systems design, and manufacturing competitiveness.

abstract: This research project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize dynamic, adaptive scheduling for large-scale construction projects under uncertainty, integrating real-time data streams from IoT sensors, supply chain logistics, and environmental monitoring systems. Traditional construction scheduling methods rely on static critical path models that fail to account for cascading delays from material shortages, labor variability, weather disruptions, or equipment failures. The proposed system will employ agent-based modeling (ABM) coupled with hybrid simulation (discrete-event and system dynamics) to create a decision-support tool capable of predictive scenario analysis and autonomous schedule reconfiguration. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process multi-source data at scale, including geospatial inputs, equipment telemetry, and supplier dashboards, while running parallel simulations to evaluate thousands of contingency plans in near-real time. Machine learning components will be embedded to identify latent patterns in delay propagation and refine risk probability estimates through iterative project benchmarking. The computational architecture will leverage graph neural networks to model complex interdependencies between tasks, resources, and external constraints, with validation against historical datasets from 12 completed infrastructure projects. Expected outcomes include a 15-20% reduction in schedule overruns for test cases involving renewable energy plant construction, along with an open-source toolkit for adaptive resource allocation under volatile conditions. This interdisciplinary approach bridges construction operations research with computational sustainability science, offering novel methodologies for resilient project management in climate-sensitive environments. The work will directly inform revised industry standards for dynamic scheduling in the ASCE Construction Institute’s digital transformation guidelines while advancing HPC applications in construction-specific combinatorial optimization problems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to manage, coordinate, and supervise the construction process. Includes instruction in commercial, residential, mechanical, highway/heavy civil, electrical, environmental, industrial, and specialty construction; facilities management; budgeting and cost control; logistics and materials management; organization and scheduling; personnel management and labor relations; site safety; construction contracting; construction processes and techniques; and applicable codes and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamic interplay between glacial retreat, bedrock erosion, and landscape evolution in high-latitude alpine environments under accelerating climate warming. Recent observations indicate that rapid glacier thinning alters subglacial hydrology and basal sliding regimes, which in turn modulate erosional efficiency and sediment transport. However, existing models lack the spatiotemporal resolution to capture transient feedbacks between ice dynamics, bedrock stress fields, and erosional processes at scales relevant to geomorphic change. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled coupled modeling framework integrating 3D ice-flow simulations, particle-based bedrock fracture models, and stochastic sediment transport algorithms. The ice-flow component will solve Stokes equations using finite-element methods with adaptive meshing to resolve high-stress zones near glacier beds. Bedrock erosion will be modeled via a discrete element approach, simulating fatigue fracturing under cyclic ice loading and quantifying debris production. Sediment transport will be treated as a coupled advection-diffusion process, informed by subglacial hydrology outputs. Simulations will be validated against field data from instrumented glaciers in the Alaska Range, including lidar-derived erosion rates and ice-penetrating radar observations of basal conditions. The computational scale requires HPC resources due to the high-resolution domains (10-100 m grid cells across 100 km² glacial systems), multi-year model timeframes, and iterative coupling between model components. Expected outcomes include (1) quantitative constraints on how shifting thermal regimes and hydrologic pathways govern spatial patterns of glacial erosion, (2) probabilistic projections of post-glacial landscape morphology under different warming scenarios, and (3) open-source release of optimized code for community use. Results will advance predictive understanding of climate-driven landscape change in glaciated regions while providing a computational framework to assess feedbacks between cryospheric processes and topographic evolution.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the origin and evolution of topographic features created by physical, chemical or biological processes operating at or near the Earth's surface, including glaciers.

abstract: Adult and Continuing Education (ACE) programs face persistent challenges in optimizing resource allocation, program accessibility, and learner retention across diverse populations. Current administrative decision-making often relies on fragmented data and manual processes, limiting the ability to model complex interactions between program design, demographic variables, and institutional constraints. This project proposes to develop computational models that simulate ACE program operations at scale, enabling evidence-based strategies for improving equitable access and operational efficiency. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze multi-source datasets (enrollment records, community needs assessments, and regional economic indicators) and execute agent-based simulations of adult learner pathways under varying administrative policies. Machine learning techniques will be applied to identify predictive patterns in program completion rates, while optimization algorithms will test hypothetical resource distribution scenarios across virtual campuses serving urban, rural, and hybrid populations. Computational experiments will focus on three administrative priorities: 1) dynamic staffing models that align instructor expertise with emerging learner needs, 2) predictive scheduling systems responsive to adult learners’ temporal constraints, and 3) cost-benefit analyses of technology investments for underserved communities. By simulating ten years of operational data across synthetic populations exceeding 500,000 agents, the HPC environment enables stress-testing of administrative strategies beyond the scope of traditional case studies or institutional data warehouses. Expected outcomes include open-source simulation frameworks for ACE program planning, validated decision support tools for continuing education administrators, and scalable models for adapting adult learning ecosystems to demographic shifts. This work advances computational social science methodologies in education leadership while addressing critical gaps in data-driven administration practices for non-traditional learner populations.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the principles and techniques of administering programs and facilities designed to serve the basic education needs of undereducated adults, or the continuing education needs of adults seeking further or specialized instruction, and that prepares individuals to serve as administrators of such programs. Includes instruction in adult education principles, program and facilities planning, personnel management, community and client relations, budgeting and administration, professional standards, and applicable laws and policies.

abstract: The spatial organization and dynamic behavior of cells within complex anatomical systems are fundamental to understanding tissue morphogenesis, homeostasis, and repair. Traditional experimental approaches in cell biology and anatomy often lack the resolution to capture multicellular interactions across 3D anatomical scales, limiting insights into how cellular dynamics translate into emergent tissue-level structures. This project seeks to bridge this gap by developing a multiscale computational model of cell-matrix interactions within vertebrate limb bud development—a classical system for studying anatomical patterning. The research will integrate high-resolution imaging data from confocal microscopy and histological sections with agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate how localized cellular behaviors (e.g., adhesion, migration, and differentiation) drive the formation of spatially organized tissues. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to handle the iterative simulation of millions of interacting cellular agents within a 3D extracellular matrix environment, incorporating biophysical parameters such as tensile forces and matrix stiffness. Computational outputs will be validated against time-lapse imaging of ex vivo embryonic mouse limb cultures and compared to anatomical landmarks in developing human embryos. Expected outcomes include (1) a predictive framework linking subcellular signaling to regional anatomical patterning, (2) identification of critical mechanical and biochemical thresholds required for robust tissue organization, and (3) mechanistic insights into developmental defects such as syndactyly or limb hypoplasia. By leveraging HPC to resolve multiscale dynamics, this work will advance the field of developmental anatomy by providing a quantitative, systems-level understanding of how cellular heterogeneity gives rise to anatomical complexity. The computational tools developed will be adaptable to studying tissue regeneration and degenerative diseases, offering broader applications for translational research in congenital anomalies and musculoskeletal disorders.
detailed_field: Cell/ cellular biology and anatomy nec
cip_definition: An integrated, combined program that focuses on the scientific study of cell structure, function, and dynamics within the context of organismic, regional, and gross anatomical systems. Includes instruction in molecular biology, cell biology and histology, structural biology, anatomy, embryology, endocrinology, and applications to specific systems, diseases, defects, and processes.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model the complex interplay between dietary patterns, gut microbiota dynamics, and host metabolic responses, with the goal of advancing precision nutrition strategies. While human nutrition research traditionally relies on clinical trials and in vitro studies, the nonlinear interactions between thousands of dietary compounds, microbial species, and host signaling pathways remain poorly quantified. Current limitations in computational power restrict the resolution of mechanistic models that integrate multi-omics data (metagenomic, metabolomic, proteomic) with individualized dietary intake records and physiological parameters. To address this gap, we propose developing a scalable agent-based modeling framework to simulate gut ecosystem dynamics under diverse nutritional conditions. The model will incorporate strain-level microbial metabolism, host epithelial cell signaling, and systemic immune responses, parameterized using existing datasets from longitudinal dietary interventions. HPC resources will enable parallelized simulations across thousands of virtual patient profiles, varying in baseline microbiota composition, genetic polymorphisms, and dietary adherence patterns. Machine learning techniques will be applied to simulation outputs to identify critical leverage points for microbiome-targeted nutritional interventions. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive algorithms linking specific dietary components to microbial metabolic shifts, (2) quantification of interindividual variability in nutrient processing efficiency, and (3) a publicly accessible simulation toolkit for testing personalized nutrition hypotheses. By bridging computational systems biology and nutritional epidemiology, this work will provide novel insights into the mechanisms underlying diet-microbiome-host interactions while establishing infrastructure for data-driven dietary recommendations. The scale of microbial community modeling and multi-omics integration required necessitates dedicated HPC allocation beyond standard institutional resources.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the relationships between food consumption and human development and health. Includes instruction in the cellular and molecular processes of food processing in the human body, related metabolic processes, the relationship of food and nutrition to disease, and nutritional needs across the life span.

abstract: The development of advanced materials with tailored mechanical and thermal properties requires understanding complex multiscale interactions spanning atomic to macroscopic regimes. Traditional experimental approaches are costly and time-intensive, while existing computational models often lack the fidelity to capture cross-scale phenomena critical for predicting material performance. This project seeks to address these limitations by implementing a scalable, high-fidelity multiscale modeling framework to simulate the behavior of high-strength alloys and composite systems under extreme operational conditions. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will integrate density functional theory (DFT) calculations for electronic structure analysis, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to model mesoscale defect dynamics, and finite element methods (FEM) to predict macroscopic stress-strain responses. Key challenges include establishing robust data transfer protocols between scales and optimizing parallelization for heterogeneous computational workloads. The proposed simulations will focus on two material systems: next-generation titanium-aluminum composites for aerospace applications and rare-earth-doped ceramics for high-temperature energy storage. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for fracture toughness and thermal degradation thresholds, as well as open-source tools for automated cross-scale parameterization. By elucidating the interplay between microstructural features and bulk material properties, this work aims to accelerate the design of materials capable of withstanding multidomain stressors while reducing reliance on iterative physical prototyping. The allocation of HPC resources is critical to achieving the necessary computational throughput for statistically significant sampling across parameter spaces spanning multiple orders of magnitude in temporal and spatial resolution.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the general application of mathematical and scientific principles to the analysis and evaluation of the characteristics and behavior of solids, including internal structure, chemical properties, transport and energy flow properties, thermodynamics of solids, stress and failure factors, chemical transformation states and processes, compound materials, and research on industrial applications of specific materials.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the computational analysis of large-scale architectural heritage datasets, addressing critical gaps in the preservation and interpretation of culturally significant structures. The core challenge lies in the integration of fragmented archival records, 3D laser scan data, and environmental simulation models to reconstruct and predict the degradation trajectories of historic buildings. Current methods in architectural conservation lack the capacity to process spatially and temporally heterogeneous datasets at the resolution required for actionable insights, particularly in contexts where climate change accelerates material decay. This project proposes a novel computational workflow combining graph neural networks (GNNs) to map historical building modifications, finite element analysis (FEA) to model structural stress under environmental variables, and generative adversarial networks (GANs) to fill gaps in archival imagery. By parallelizing these processes across GPU nodes, the workflow will enable dynamic, multi-scale simulations of architectural evolution over centennial timescales—a task currently infeasible with conventional tools. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework for predictive conservation planning, validated against case studies of UNESCO World Heritage sites in tropical and arid zones. The research will also generate synthetic datasets to train models on rare decay patterns, addressing data scarcity in heritage informatics. By bridging computational engineering methods with humanistic inquiry, this project aims to establish new standards for evidence-based conservation policy while demonstrating how HPC resources can catalyze interdisciplinary innovation in architectural history. The results will directly inform risk mitigation strategies for vulnerable sites and provide a replicable model for integrating machine learning with cultural heritage stewardship.
cip_title: Architectural History, Criticism, and Conservation, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in architectural history, criticism, and conservation, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the evolutionary origins of social learning strategies in non-human primates through large-scale computational modeling of behavioral and neurophysiological data. A core challenge in comparative psychology is identifying how species-specific cognitive architectures arise from interactions between genetic predispositions, environmental pressures, and neural constraints. While behavioral experiments have cataloged interspecies differences in social learning, the computational mechanisms driving these differences remain poorly characterized. We propose to develop agent-based models simulating decision-making processes under varying ecological conditions, parameterized by empirical data from macaques, capuchins, and chimpanzees. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute evolutionary simulations across multidimensional parameter spaces (e.g., neural network complexity, reward sensitivity thresholds, memory decay rates) while incorporating neuroanatomical constraints derived from comparative diffusion tensor imaging datasets. Parallelized Monte Carlo methods will test adaptive hypotheses about the emergence of imitation versus emulation strategies, with fitness landscapes evaluated through dynamic programming optimization. The models will integrate reinforcement learning frameworks with phylogenetic comparative analyses to disentangle conserved versus derived cognitive traits. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable computational framework linking neurophysiological adaptations to observable learning behaviors, (2) quantitative evidence for selective pressures shaping primate social cognition, and (3) open-source tools for simulating cross-species neurobehavioral evolution. By leveraging HPC capabilities to bridge neural mechanisms and evolutionary dynamics, this work aims to advance comparative psychology's capacity to generate testable predictions about the origins of complex cognitive phenotypes.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the behavior of members of particular species or groups and the relationship of the behaviors of the species or group to their evolutionary origins. Includes instruction in differential psychology, experimental and physiological psychology, psychopharmacology, psychology of individual differences, reinforcement theory, and neurophysiology.

abstract: The proposed research seeks to address a critical gap in predictive modeling of biomechanical systems under extreme environmental conditions, integrating principles from soft matter physics, nonlinear dynamics, and computational physiology. Current models fail to capture the multiscale interactions between tissue deformation, cellular damage cascades, and fluid-structure coupling in high-strain-rate scenarios, limiting progress in applications ranging from protective equipment design to space medicine. This project will develop a novel computational framework combining finite element analysis, discrete element methods, and machine learning-driven parameter optimization to simulate emergent behaviors in hierarchically structured biological materials. The core innovation lies in coupling continuum-scale mechanical responses with subcellular damage initiation thresholds through adaptive mesh refinement and agent-based modeling techniques. High-performance computing resources are essential to resolve the 10^7-10^9 degree-of-freedom systems arising from simultaneous tracking of macroscale tissue dynamics and microscale cytoskeletal remodeling events across relevant biological timescales. Validation will leverage experimental datasets from collaborative synchrotron-based X-ray microscopy studies of dynamically loaded engineered tissues. Expected outcomes include 1) a validated open-source simulation platform for multiphysics biomechanics, 2) predictive models of injury thresholds in anisotropic soft tissues under combined thermal-mechanical loading, and 3) machine learning-derived design principles for bioinspired impact-absorbing metamaterials. This work bridges critical gaps between materials science, systems biology, and computational mechanics while directly informing next-generation biomedical and aerospace engineering solutions. The required computational resources will enable unprecedented resolution of cross-scale feedback mechanisms in viscoelastic biological systems, addressing a fundamental challenge in computational science: the integration of discrete biological responses within continuum-scale engineering frameworks.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of computing and its application for solving challenges in science and engineering fields, with a focus on principles from mathematics, science, engineering and computing.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a digital humanities inquiry into the evolving representation of cultural identity in 20th-century American media. The research focuses on analyzing large-scale corpora of digitized newspapers, film archives, and literary works to trace how narratives of race, gender, and immigration were constructed and contested across different regions and time periods. A central challenge lies in processing unstructured text and multimedia data spanning over 100 million words and 50,000 visual artifacts, which demands advanced computational capabilities for pattern recognition, semantic analysis, and cross-modal correlation. The computational approach combines natural language processing (NLP) techniques—including transformer-based models fine-tuned on historical American English—with computer vision methods to examine linguistic trends, visual motifs, and their intersections in underrepresented communities. Network analysis will map the diffusion of cultural narratives through media ecosystems, while GPU-accelerated clustering algorithms will identify regional variations in discursive frameworks. Expected outcomes include: (1) a publicly accessible dataset of annotated primary sources highlighting marginalized voices, (2) quantitative models of narrative shift correlated with sociohistorical events such as the Great Migration and post-1965 immigration reforms, and (3) methodological innovations in computational cultural studies through hybrid humanistic/ML workflows. By enabling analysis at previously impractical scales, the requested resources will facilitate new insights into how mediated representations have shaped collective understandings of American identity, particularly at the intersections of ethnicity, gender, and regionalism. This work directly aligns with the program’s mission to investigate the United States’ cultural complexity while demonstrating how advanced computing can expand the scope of humanistic inquiry.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of the United States and its Pre-Columbian and colonial predecessors, and including the flow of immigrants from other societies.

abstract: The integration of data-driven methodologies into physical education (PE) pedagogy and sports coaching remains underexplored, particularly in optimizing individualized training regimens and injury prevention strategies. This project seeks to address the challenge of personalizing physical education instruction and athletic coaching by developing computational models that analyze biomechanical, physiological, and behavioral datasets. Current approaches often rely on generalized frameworks, which fail to account for the heterogeneity of student-athlete capabilities, environmental factors, and real-time performance feedback. To bridge this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process multimodal data streams—including motion capture, wearable sensor outputs, and video analytics—at scale. Machine learning algorithms will be employed to identify patterns in movement efficiency, fatigue thresholds, and skill acquisition rates, while agent-based simulations will model adaptive coaching strategies under varying constraints (e.g., class sizes, equipment availability). The computational pipeline will require parallel processing of high-dimensional datasets (10+ TB) and real-time rendering of 3D kinematic visualizations for pedagogical applications. Anticipated outcomes include a validated framework for generating personalized PE lesson plans and dynamic coaching protocols, grounded in predictive analytics. This work will advance the evidence base for technology-enhanced physical education by quantifying relationships between instructional interventions and motor skill development outcomes. The resulting tools will be disseminated as open-source resources for educators, enabling scalable implementation of data-informed teaching practices. By harnessing HPC capabilities, this project aims to transform traditional PE paradigms into adaptive, inclusive systems that cater to diverse learner needs while reducing sport-related injury risks through preemptive biomechanical corrections.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach physical education programs and/or to coach sports at various educational levels.

abstract: Geothermal energy systems are increasingly critical to sustainable energy infrastructure, yet their installation and maintenance face persistent challenges due to the complex interplay of geological, thermal, and mechanical factors. Current approaches to system design and fault diagnosis often rely on simplified models or empirical data, which inadequately capture dynamic subsurface interactions or long-term material stresses. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing high-fidelity computational models to optimize geothermal system performance and reliability. The research will focus on two interconnected objectives: (1) simulating multiphysics interactions within geothermal reservoirs and engineered components under variable operational conditions, and (2) creating machine learning frameworks to predict equipment degradation and maintenance needs. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve the spatiotemporal complexity of coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical processes at scales relevant to real-world installations. Finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) will model heat exchange efficiency and stress distribution in boreholes, piping networks, and heat pumps, while molecular dynamics simulations will investigate material corrosion in high-temperature brine environments. Concurrently, time-series sensor data from field deployments will train neural networks to correlate operational parameters with failure modes. The computational workflows will leverage parallelized solvers and GPU acceleration to manage datasets spanning terabytes of multiphysics outputs and decades of simulated operational timelines. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for geothermal system optimization, risk-reduction strategies for component failures, and open-access simulation tools tailored for technician training programs. By bridging high-resolution simulations with practical maintenance applications, this work aims to advance both the technical foundations of geothermal energy systems and the decision-support resources available to installation professionals. The requested HPC allocation will enable the parameter space exploration and validation required to transform theoretical insights into actionable guidelines for the geothermal workforce.
cip_title: Geothermal Energy System Installation and Repair Technology/ Technician
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to assemble, install, operate, maintain, and repair geothermal energy systems. Includes instruction in installing, maintaining and testing various types of equipment.

abstract: The proposed research seeks to address a critical gap in modeling the failure mechanisms of conductive materials subjected to concurrent mechanical stress and dynamic electromagnetic fields—a scenario prevalent in next-generation energy systems, fusion reactor components, and high-power electromechanical devices. Traditional fracture mechanics frameworks often neglect the bidirectional coupling between electromagnetic forces and material deformation, leading to unreliable predictions in environments where these interactions dominate. This project aims to develop a scalable, multi-physics computational framework to simulate crack initiation and propagation under coupled electromechanical loading. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, the approach integrates nonlinear finite element analysis (FEA) for mechanical response with a time-domain solver for Maxwell’s equations, enabling explicit resolution of Lorentz forces, Joule heating, and their feedback effects on material damage. Adaptive mesh refinement and parallelized iterative solvers will be employed to manage the computational complexity of resolving micron-scale crack features within macroscale geometries. Validation will utilize experimental data from in-situ electromechanical testing of copper and graphene composites. The outcomes will yield a validated open-source simulation toolset, enabling predictive design of materials and components for extreme electromechanical environments. This work bridges classical mechanics and electromagnetism within an engineering mechanics paradigm, offering foundational insights into multi-physics failure modes while advancing computational methods for coupled-field problems. The resulting framework is anticipated to impact the reliability and safety of emerging technologies such as compact fusion devices and high-field magnetic confinement systems, where current empirical approaches lack the resolution to address these interdependent failure mechanisms.
cip_definition: A program with a general focus on the application of the mathematical and scientific principles of classical mechanics to the analysis and evaluation of the behavior of structures, forces and materials in engineering problems. Includes instruction in statics, kinetics, dynamics, kinematics, celestial mechanics, stress and failure, and electromagnetism.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamic interactions between neural systems and behavior by developing large-scale computational models of brain networks involved in decision-making under stress. A core challenge in psychobiological research is capturing the nonlinear, multiscale relationships between molecular, cellular, and circuit-level processes that collectively influence behavioral outcomes. Current models often oversimplify these interactions due to computational constraints, limiting their predictive power. To address this gap, we propose a hybrid approach combining biologically plausible neural network simulations with machine learning-driven analysis of multimodal neuroimaging (fMRI) and psychophysiological (ECG, cortisol) datasets. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for three components: (1) simulating spiking neuron networks across distributed brain regions at subsecond resolution, (2) implementing Bayesian hierarchical models to integrate temporal and spatial neurobehavioral data, and (3) training deep reinforcement learning architectures that map neural activation patterns to behavioral metrics. The computational framework will be validated against empirical data from rodent models of stress-induced decision-making deficits, followed by human subject experiments. Expected outcomes include a mechanistic understanding of how noradrenergic signaling modulates prefrontal-amygdala interactions during cognitive-emotional conflict, as well as open-source tools for multilevel psychobiological modeling. This work will advance computational psychobiology by establishing scalable methods to bridge neurobiological mechanisms with complex behavioral phenotypes, while providing critical infrastructure for future studies of neuropsychiatric vulnerability factors. The requested resources will enable simulations of >10^5 neurons with realistic synaptic dynamics and parallel processing of multimodal datasets exceeding 50TB, which are computationally intractable on standard laboratory systems.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of the biological bases of behavior.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address the growing complexity of integrating generative design algorithms with real-time environmental and structural simulations in architectural practice. Current computational workflows in architecture often operate in silos, limiting the ability to dynamically optimize designs for competing criteria such as material efficiency, energy performance, and spatial quality. The project focuses on developing a unified computational framework that bridges parametric modeling tools, finite element analysis, and climate-responsive machine learning models to enable iterative, multi-objective design exploration at unprecedented scales. Key challenges include the parallel processing of high-resolution 3D geometry datasets, the coupling of fluid dynamics simulations for natural ventilation analysis with structural load calculations, and the training of neural networks to predict embodied carbon impacts across variable material systems. The proposed HPC infrastructure will support GPU-accelerated topology optimization, distributed computing for parametric design space exploration, and in-memory data handling for real-time feedback between simulation modules. Expected outcomes include an open-source computational pipeline for holistic building performance evaluation, validated through case studies of mid-rise mixed-use structures in diverse climatic zones. By enabling simultaneous optimization of architectural form, structural resilience, and operational sustainability, this research aims to advance the integration of performance-driven design methodologies into mainstream architectural practice while reducing computational bottlenecks that currently favor simplified or compartmentalized analyses. The project contributes to emerging discourses on computational eco-urbanism by providing scalable tools to reconcile aesthetic, technical, and environmental priorities in complex urban contexts.
cip_definition: An advanced program of study for architects and related professionals that focuses on theoretical and practical issues in architecture and integrates digital technologies into architectural design, fabrication, and construction. Includes instruction in architectural history and urban theory, 3-D digital technologies, construction, design and fabrication methods, and sustainable practices in architecture.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework to optimize urban soundscape design, addressing the growing public health and ecological impacts of noise pollution in rapidly urbanizing regions. While traditional acoustical engineering focuses on isolated noise reduction, this research integrates real-world urban dynamics—such as traffic patterns, human mobility, and green infrastructure interactions—into a predictive, systems-level model. The computational challenge lies in resolving multiscale phenomena: wave propagation at micrometer resolutions, building-surface interactions at meter scales, and city-wide sound diffusion over kilometer domains. A hybrid approach combining finite element modeling, agent-based simulations, and machine learning will be implemented, leveraging GPU-accelerated solvers for real-time auralization of urban environments. The workflow will incorporate geospatial data, demographic information, and psychoacoustic metrics to quantify human perceptual responses. By parallelizing Monte Carlo simulations across heterogeneous computing architectures, the team will statistically optimize soundscape configurations against competing objectives: noise mitigation, cost efficiency, and community well-being. Expected outcomes include an open-source computational toolkit for urban planners, validated against field measurements from partner cities, and novel insights into how engineered soundscapes affect pedestrian behavior and ecosystem health. This interdisciplinary synthesis of acoustics, data science, and public health fills a critical gap in urban engineering methodologies, providing scalable solutions for noise governance in the era of smart cities. The requested HPC resources are essential for managing the exascale datasets generated by coupled physics-machine learning workflows and enabling parameter sweeps across thousands of urban design scenarios.
cip_definition: A program with a general focus on the general application of various combinations of mathematical and scientific principles to the analysis and evaluation of engineering problems, including applied research in human behavior, statistics, biology, chemistry, the earth and planetary sciences, atmospherics and meteorology, and computer applications.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the spatial and temporal diffusion of social movements across the United States from the early 19th to the mid-20th century. Traditional historical methods struggle to systematically trace connections between localized movements—such as labor organizing, suffrage campaigns, and civil rights activism—and broader national trends due to the scale and fragmentation of archival sources. By integrating digitized newspapers, census records, organizational correspondence, and geospatial data, this research will employ computational text mining, network analysis, and machine learning to map ideological transmission, coalition-building patterns, and demographic influences on movement participation. Key computational challenges include processing terabytes of unstructured text with natural language processing (NLP) models to identify rhetorical shifts, applying graph-based algorithms to reconstruct inter-movement networks from sparse archival metadata, and simulating demographic-environmental interactions using agent-based modeling. The HPC infrastructure is critical for running parallelized workflows to handle heterogeneous data formats, train custom classifiers for historical language, and iteratively test hypotheses about regional vs. national movement dynamics. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database linking localized activism to national organizations, visualizations of movement spread correlated with socioeconomic variables, and statistical models identifying understudied inflection points in cross-movement collaboration. This work aims to advance methodologies in digital history by demonstrating how computational scale can address longstanding gaps in understanding decentralized social change, while providing empirical frameworks to reinterpret the interplay between grassroots activism and institutional power in American democracy. Results will directly inform a monograph and interactive teaching tools, bridging quantitative analysis with qualitative historical narratives.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the development of American society, culture, and institutions from the Pre-Columbian period to the present. Includes instruction in American historiography, American history sources and materials, historical research methods, and applications to the study of specific themes, issues, periods, and institutions.

abstract: Gynecologic cancers exhibit significant molecular heterogeneity, contributing to variable treatment responses and the development of therapy resistance. Current clinical strategies often rely on generalized protocols, which may not account for tumor evolution or patient-specific biomarkers. This project seeks to address these limitations by integrating multi-omics data (genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics) with clinical outcomes to identify predictive signatures of therapeutic resistance and metastasis. The primary computational challenge lies in analyzing high-dimensional datasets spanning tumor sequencing, longitudinal imaging, and electronic health records from a cohort of 1,200 patients with ovarian, endometrial, and cervical cancers. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process these data at scale, employing machine learning frameworks to model tumor dynamics and simulate treatment responses. Key computational steps include unsupervised clustering of molecular subtypes, Bayesian network inference of signaling pathways associated with resistance, and reinforcement learning to optimize personalized treatment sequences. The analysis will leverage containerized workflows for reproducibility, with GPU-accelerated nodes enabling rapid training of deep neural networks on whole-slide histopathology images. Expected outcomes include (1) a predictive model stratifying patients by risk of platinum-resistant recurrence in ovarian cancer, (2) dynamic biomarkers for early detection of endometrial cancer metastasis, and (3) an open-source computational pipeline for adaptive therapy design. By elucidating mechanisms of treatment failure, this work aims to shift clinical practice toward precision interventions, potentially improving progression-free survival rates. The requested HPC allocation will directly support data harmonization across 45 TB of multi-modal inputs, reduce model training times from weeks to days, and facilitate large-scale validation through synthetic cohort generation. This project bridges computational innovation with translational needs in gynecologic oncology, offering a template for resource-efficient, data-driven cancer care.
cip_definition: Research focused on that prepares physicians for consultation and comprehensive management of patients with gynecologic cancer, including those diagnostic and therapeutic procedures necessary for the total care of the patient with gynecologic cancer and resulting complications.

abstract: Turfgrass systems are critical for recreational, aesthetic, and environmental health, yet their sustainability is challenged by climate variability, biotic stressors, and resource limitations. Traditional turfgrass breeding and management strategies are often constrained by the slow pace of phenotypic evaluation and the complexity of genotype-environment interactions. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance predictive modeling of turfgrass performance under diverse environmental and management scenarios. Specifically, we aim to integrate genomic, phenotypic, and environmental datasets to optimize the selection of turfgrass cultivars with enhanced drought tolerance, disease resistance, and nutrient-use efficiency. The research will employ machine learning algorithms to analyze high-throughput genotyping data (e.g., SNP arrays) and multi-year field trial data, including hyperspectral imaging and soil sensor outputs. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models will simulate microclimate conditions affecting turfgrass health, such as heat stress and water distribution patterns, while agent-based models will explore pest and pathogen spread dynamics. These parallelized workflows require significant computational capacity due to the scale of genomic datasets (>10^6 markers per population) and the iterative nature of parameter optimization in predictive models. The HPC infrastructure will enable rapid calibration of models against experimental data, reducing the time needed to identify candidate genes and optimal management practices. Expected outcomes include the development of open-source tools for turfgrass genomics and precision management, as well as publicly accessible datasets linking genetic markers to stress-resilience traits. By accelerating the discovery of climate-adapted turfgrasses, this work will directly support sustainable landscaping, sports field maintenance, and urban green space preservation, aligning with broader agricultural priorities to mitigate resource use while maintaining ecosystem services.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
detailed_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on turfgrasses and related groundcover plants and prepares individuals to develop ornamental or recreational grasses and related products; plant, transplant, and manage grassed areas; and to produce and store turf used for transplantation. Includes instruction in applicable plant sciences, genetics of grasses, turf science, use analysis, turf management, and related economics.

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing complexity of optimizing high-performance automotive and diesel engines by leveraging advanced computational modeling and simulation techniques. Traditional methods for enhancing engine performance—such as physical prototyping, dyno testing, and trial-and-error modifications—are time-intensive, costly, and limited in their ability to explore multidimensional design variables. This research will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop high-fidelity simulations of engine systems, focusing on combustion dynamics, thermal management, and mechanical stress distribution. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) will model airflow, fuel injection, and exhaust gas recirculation in custom engines, while finite element analysis (FEA) will assess structural integrity under extreme operating conditions. Machine learning algorithms will be integrated to identify optimal tuning parameters for engine control units (ECUs), enabling adaptive calibration of fuel-air ratios, ignition timing, and turbocharger boost levels. The computational workflows will be validated against empirical data from dynamometer tests and sensor arrays installed in prototype vehicles. By simulating thousands of design permutations in parallel, this approach aims to reduce reliance on physical prototyping, accelerate development cycles, and improve the precision of performance modifications. Anticipated outcomes include predictive models for engine behavior under high-stress scenarios, data-driven guidelines for aftermarket component integration, and open-source tools to assist technicians in diagnosing inefficiencies. The project aligns with industry demands for sustainable performance enhancements, emphasizing fuel efficiency and emission reduction alongside power gains. Access to HPC resources is critical to handle the computational load of multiphysics simulations and iterative machine learning training, which exceed the capabilities of local workstations. This work will bridge gaps between automotive engineering theory and hands-on technical practice, equipping future technicians with cutting-edge computational skills.
cip_title: High Performance and Custom Engine Technician/ Mechanic
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to increase the power of diesel and automotive engines; enhance the performance of automobiles; and repair, service, and maintain high performance vehicles. Includes instruction in adding performance accessories; modifying powertrains; tuning custom engines, suspension, and exhaust systems; and using dynamometers and other diagnostic equipment.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in urban ground transportation systems through the development of high-fidelity computational models to optimize traffic flow, energy consumption, and infrastructure resilience. Current traffic management strategies often rely on static models that fail to account for real-time variables such as dynamic routing demands, heterogeneous vehicle types (e.g., electric, autonomous, and legacy vehicles), and evolving environmental conditions. To overcome these limitations, we propose a multi-scale simulation framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to integrate real-time sensor data, vehicle-to-infrastructure communication patterns, and stochastic traffic behavior. The computational approach will employ agent-based modeling to simulate individual vehicle dynamics and machine learning algorithms to predict congestion hotspots under varying scenarios, including extreme weather events and infrastructure failures. Key simulations will focus on optimizing traffic signal timings, emergency vehicle routing, and energy-efficient freight corridor planning. The HPC environment is critical for processing large-scale datasets (e.g., city-wide traffic feeds, vehicle telemetry) and executing parallelized simulations with millions of interacting agents at sub-second resolution. Expected outcomes include validated protocols for adaptive traffic control systems, predictive tools for infrastructure maintenance prioritization, and open-source simulation templates for municipal planners. By enabling granular, city-scale analysis, this work aims to reduce average commute times by 15–20% in modeled regions, lower transportation-related carbon emissions, and improve emergency response reliability. The requested computing resources will directly support the iterative training of neural networks for traffic prediction and the storage of petabyte-scale simulation outputs, which are infeasible on local institutional clusters. This research aligns with national priorities for sustainable urban development and intelligent transportation systems, offering transferable methodologies for improving operational safety and efficiency in mixed-use transportation networks.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in vehicle and equipment operation, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Cancer treatment efficacy remains limited by interpatient heterogeneity and dynamic tumor evolution, which drive variable therapeutic responses and acquired resistance. Current approaches to personalize therapy lack robust computational frameworks capable of integrating multi-scale clinical, molecular, and imaging data to predict tumor behavior in real time. This project seeks to address these challenges by developing high-performance computing (HPC)-driven models to optimize therapeutic decision-making in medical oncology. We propose a multi-omics integration platform combining genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and radiomic data from 2,000+ solid tumor patients to identify predictive signatures of treatment response. Machine learning algorithms, including ensemble neural networks and graph-based models, will be trained on this dataset to simulate tumor-immune-drug interactions and predict resistance pathways. Molecular dynamics simulations will model protein-ligand binding affinities for targeted therapies, while Bayesian networks will quantify the probabilistic impact of tumor microenvironment factors on drug delivery. Concurrently, deep learning architectures will analyze histopathology slides and longitudinal imaging to detect subvisual patterns associated with early treatment failure. These computational workflows require HPC resources due to the scale of data (estimated 450 TB), complexity of iterative model training, and need for real-time parallel processing in clinical deployment scenarios. Expected outcomes include validated predictive algorithms for first-line therapy selection, dynamic biomarkers of emergent resistance, and combinatorial treatment strategies to circumvent adaptive tumor survival mechanisms. The project will generate open-source tools for adaptive therapy design, enabling clinicians to simulate treatment outcomes using patient-specific data. By bridging computational oncology with clinical workflows, this work aims to reduce trial-and-error chemotherapy regimens, improve progression-free survival in refractory cancers, and establish a scalable infrastructure for precision oncology research.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis and treatment of all types of cancer and other benign and malignant tumors; this includes deciding on and administering therapy for these malignancies, as well as consulting with surgeons and radiotherapists on other treatments for cancer.

abstract: Reproductive cancers, including ovarian and prostate malignancies, present complex challenges due to their dependence on dynamic hormonal regulation and microenvironmental interactions. Current models inadequately capture the spatiotemporal coordination of endocrine signaling, cellular metabolism, and tumor progression, limiting therapeutic development. This project seeks to address this gap by developing a multi-scale computational framework to simulate hormonal regulation of reproductive cancer pathophysiology. The research will integrate physiological data from in vivo models with clinical parameters to construct agent-based models (ABMs) of tumor-stroma-endocrine interactions, coupled with pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) simulations of hormone-targeted therapies. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve the high-dimensional parameter space of these systems, including stochastic hormone receptor dynamics, metabolic gradients, and heterogeneous cell populations across biologically relevant timescales. Computational workflows will leverage parallelized Monte Carlo sampling for parameter optimization and sensitivity analysis, while finite element modeling will simulate nutrient and drug diffusion in anatomically informed tissue geometries. Expected outcomes include the identification of microenvironmental biomarkers predictive of therapeutic resistance and the optimization of dosing protocols for endocrine-disrupting agents. By bridging computational physiology and oncology, this work aims to advance mechanistic understanding of reproductive cancer adaptation mechanisms and inform personalized treatment strategies. The requested HPC allocation will enable large-scale simulations that are computationally prohibitive on local clusters, particularly for parameter sweeps across diverse hormonal states and tissue architectures. Successful implementation will establish an open-source modeling platform for the reproductive biology community, fostering cross-disciplinary innovation in cancer research.
detailed_field: Physiology, oncology, and cancer biology nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of reproductive processes and biogenesis in animals and human beings. Includes instruction in reproductive ecology and behavior, reproductive system physiology, endocrinology, developmental biology, neuroendocrinology, evolution and types of reproductive systems, reproductive genetics, physiopathology of reproductive processes, and applications of molecular biology and biophysics to the study of reproductive physiology.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of adaptive, data-driven tools for French language teacher training. The core research problem centers on the limited availability of scalable, personalized feedback mechanisms for pre-service teachers practicing pedagogical strategies in immersive or simulated classroom environments. While existing studies emphasize the value of reflective teaching practices, computational approaches to modeling learner-teacher interactions—particularly in multilingual contexts—remain underexplored. To address this gap, the proposed work will employ natural language processing (NLP) and agent-based modeling to simulate dynamic French language classrooms. Large-scale datasets, including annotated transcripts of classroom discourse from francophone regions and learner corpora tracking grammatical and pragmatic development, will be processed to train context-aware language models. These models will underpin virtual student agents capable of generating linguistically diverse, level-appropriate responses during teacher training simulations. Computational experiments will evaluate how variations in input (e.g., corrective feedback strategies, task complexity) affect agent performance across proficiency levels (CEFR A1–B2). HPC resources are critical for parallelizing the training of multilingual transformer models, running Monte Carlo simulations to assess pedagogical scenario outcomes, and processing high-dimensional interaction data from simulated classrooms. Anticipated outcomes include an open-source framework for generating culturally and linguistically nuanced training scenarios, as well as evidence-based guidelines for integrating computational feedback into teacher education curricula. By quantifying relationships between instructional choices and learner responses at scale, this work aims to equip French language educators with empirically validated tools to address heterogeneous classroom needs. The project aligns with broader efforts to modernize language teacher preparation through computational innovation while preserving pedagogical rigor.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach French language programs at various educational levels.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the sociocultural and logistical dynamics of transnational missionary networks from the 19th century to the present using computational modeling and large-scale historical data analysis. While missionary studies traditionally rely on qualitative archival methods, this research addresses the challenge of mapping and analyzing complex, multigenerational networks of missionaries, local communities, and institutional stakeholders across shifting geopolitical contexts. The core research problem lies in quantifying how missionary activities—ranging from educational initiatives to crisis response—have adapted to global conflicts, colonial legacies, and technological changes, while maintaining continuity in doctrinal objectives. To achieve this, the project will employ natural language processing (NLP) on digitized missionary correspondence, field reports, and institutional records (totaling ~250,000 documents across 15 archives), combined with geospatial network analysis of personnel movements and resource flows. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for training transformer-based models to identify patterns in multilingual texts, while parallelized simulations will model decision-making processes under constraints such as political instability or resource scarcity. Expected outcomes include a dynamic, open-access database of missionary networks correlated with socioeconomic indicators, and agent-based models that test hypotheses about the resilience of belief transmission systems. This computational approach offers novel insights into how missionary organizations have navigated cross-cultural mediation at scale—a phenomenon central to understanding modern global humanitarian frameworks. The project’s integration of HPC-driven methods with humanities scholarship aims to establish new analytical paradigms for studying decentralized religious movements and their long-term societal impacts.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theory and practice of religious outreach, social service and proselytization, and that prepares individuals for mission vocations. Includes instruction in theology, evangelism, preaching, medical and social mission work, missionary education, missionary aviation, emergency services, legal and political aspects of working in other countries, and preparation for ordination as missionaries.

abstract: Livestock production systems face increasing pressure to enhance efficiency and sustainability while minimizing environmental impact. A critical challenge lies in optimizing feed utilization and metabolic efficiency across diverse animal populations, as individual variations in genetics, gut microbiota, and environmental interactions lead to heterogeneous growth and emission outcomes. This project seeks to develop a multi-scale computational framework integrating animal physiology, microbial dynamics, and production logistics to predict optimal management strategies. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for executing agent-based models simulating nutrient metabolism in livestock cohorts, coupled with machine learning approaches trained on multi-omics datasets (metagenomic, metabolomic, and transcriptomic profiles from longitudinal studies). The computational workflow will parameterize individual variation in digestive efficiency, methane production, and growth rates using existing experimental data from cattle and poultry trials, then extrapolate to system-level scenarios through Monte Carlo simulations. Key objectives include identifying microbiome signatures associated with feed efficiency, modeling the impact of alternative diet formulations on greenhouse gas emissions, and optimizing facility-scale management protocols under varying climatic conditions. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for precision feeding strategies that reduce enteric methane emissions by 15-20% while maintaining productivity, and decision-support systems for adaptive housing designs that mitigate heat stress. These computational advances will directly inform experimental validations and industry partnerships aimed at scalable solutions for climate-resilient livestock production. The requested HPC allocation will enable processing of petabyte-scale genomic datasets, parallelized simulation of 10^5+ agent-based models, and real-time optimization of management variables—workflows intractable on local computing infrastructure. By bridging biological complexity with operational decision-making, this research aims to establish a new paradigm for data-driven sustainable animal agriculture.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
detailed_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to select, breed, care for, process, and market livestock and small farm animals. Includes instruction in basic animal science, animal nutrition, and animal health as applied to various species and breeds; design and operation of housing, feeding, and processing facilities; and related issues of safety, applicable regulations, logistics, and supply.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the evolution of cultural and gender identities in Latin America through computational analysis of historical texts and visual artifacts. Focusing on understudied indigenous, colonial, and post-colonial sources, the research addresses how marginalized communities navigated cultural assimilation and resistance. The computational approach employs natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision techniques to analyze multilingual texts (including Spanish, Nahuatl, and Quechua) and iconographic materials from Pre-Columbian codices to 19th-century publications. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for processing terabytes of digitized archives, training transformer models on non-standardized historical languages, and conducting large-scale semantic network analyses to trace the diffusion of cultural narratives. The project will leverage parallel computing to optimize OCR correction for degraded manuscripts and GPU clusters to accelerate pattern recognition in visual motifs tied to gender roles and ethnic identity. Expected outcomes include a public corpus of annotated texts, geotemporal visualizations of cultural exchange, and statistical models quantifying shifts in identity discourse across regions and eras. By integrating computational rigor with humanistic inquiry, this work aims to challenge homogenizing narratives of Latin American history while advancing methodologies for analyzing underrepresented languages and ephemeral cultural artifacts. The requested resources will reduce processing times for complex NLP tasks by 12–18x compared to local infrastructure, enabling iterative model refinement crucial for low-resource indigenous languages. This research will provide scholars with novel tools to interrogate the interplay of gender, power, and cultural survival in Latin America’s contested historical landscape.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the Hispanic peoples of the North and South American Continents outside Canada and the United States, including the study of the Pre-Columbian period and the flow of immigrants from other societies.

abstract: The proposed research seeks to investigate the dynamic mechanisms underlying neural circuit plasticity in response to multisensory integration, a process critical for adaptive behavior but poorly understood at the network level. Current limitations in modeling large-scale, biologically realistic neural networks hinder the exploration of how synaptic and circuit-level interactions drive reorganization during sensory processing. To address this gap, we will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate spiking neural network models incorporating anatomically constrained connectivity derived from mammalian sensory cortices. These models will integrate biophysical parameters governing short-term plasticity, dendritic computation, and neuromodulatory effects, enabling the study of emergent network states under varying sensory input conditions. Simulations will leverage parallelized NEURON and Nest simulations across GPU-accelerated nodes to achieve the scale required for whole-circuit analysis (>100,000 neurons with 10^8 adaptive synapses). Computational experiments will systematically perturb cross-modal input timing and intensity while tracking spike-timing-dependent plasticity rules and population coding fidelity. Expected outcomes include 1) identification of critical windows for circuit reorganization during multisensory conflict resolution, 2) predictive models of plasticity thresholds that prevent maladaptive rewiring, and 3) data-driven hypotheses about cortical layer-specific contributions to dynamic integration. The HPC implementation will enable parameter space exploration at scales unachievable with standard computing infrastructure, directly advancing our understanding of neural adaptability. Resulting datasets and optimized simulation workflows will be shared via community platforms to accelerate research in computational neuroscience. This work bridges systems-level neurobiology with computational theory, with potential implications for developing targeted interventions in sensory processing disorders.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in neurobiology and neurosciences, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Orthodontic treatment outcomes are influenced by complex biomechanical interactions between applied forces, craniofacial anatomy, and biological responses, yet current clinical methods for predicting tooth movement remain largely empirical. This project seeks to address the critical gap in personalized, biomechanically driven treatment planning by developing a high-resolution computational framework to simulate and optimize force systems in diverse patient anatomies. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to construct finite element models (FEMs) integrating patient-specific cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) data, periodontal ligament viscoelastic properties, and orthodontic appliance mechanics. Multiscale simulations will quantify stress-strain distributions in the dentoalveolar complex during alignment, root translation, and occlusal correction, while machine learning algorithms trained on retrospective clinical datasets will identify patterns linking force parameters to biological remodeling rates. A key innovation involves coupling biomechanical simulations with probabilistic sensitivity analyses to account for interpatient variability in bone density, collagen turnover, and mechanotransduction pathways. The computational workflow will be validated against longitudinal clinical records of tooth movement accuracy and root resorption outcomes. By enabling real-time optimization of force magnitude, direction, and timing in silico, this research aims to establish predictive protocols for minimizing treatment duration and iatrogenic risks. The HPC environment is essential for managing the nonlinear, transient analyses required for high-fidelity tissue modeling and for processing multi-terabyte imaging datasets across 500+ simulated treatment scenarios. Expected outcomes include an open-source computational platform for virtual treatment testing and clinically actionable guidelines for force system personalization. This work directly addresses the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research priorities on precision orthodontics, with potential to transform evidence-based care for malocclusion correction.
cip_definition: Research focused on the principles and techniques involved in the prevention and correction of dental malocclusions and oral cavity anomalies.
