This project will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model and simulate nanostructured drug carriers, including lipid nanoparticles and polymeric micelles, at atomic and mesoscopic scales. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using GROMACS and coarse-grained models will elucidate molecular interactions governing drug encapsulation, stability, and release kinetics under physiological conditions. Machine learning algorithms will be integrated to predict carrier performance across diverse chemical spaces, reducing experimental trial-and-error. The computational workflow will involve large-scale parameter sweeps to evaluate carrier designs under varied pH, temperature, and concentration gradients, generating multi-terabyte datasets. HPC resources are essential to achieve sufficient sampling timescales (microsecond-range simulations) and to process high-dimensional data from 10,000+ simulated formulation variants. Expected outcomes include the identification of optimal carrier compositions for three model therapeutics with documented solubility challenges, as well as predictive frameworks linking molecular descriptors to release profiles. This work will advance rational design principles for nanomedicine platforms while providing open-access simulation protocols to the pharmaceutical sciences community. Successful implementation could shorten preclinical development timelines by 30-50% for insoluble drugs, with direct applications in oncology and infectious disease treatment. The requested computing allocation will support GPU-accelerated simulations, parallelized data analysis, and storage of reference datasets for reproducibility.
cip_title: Pharmacy, Pharmaceutical Sciences, and Administration, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in pharmacy, pharmaceutical sciences, and administration, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance nursing science through the analysis of complex, multidimensional healthcare datasets. The research problem centers on optimizing clinical decision-making and patient outcomes in high-acuity care settings, where heterogeneous data—including electronic health records (EHRs), real-time physiological monitoring streams, genomic profiles, and patient-reported outcomes—create computational challenges for predictive modeling and intervention design. Current methods struggle to integrate these data types at scale, limiting the ability to identify patterns in patient deterioration, treatment responsiveness, and care-delivery inefficiencies. To address this, the project proposes a computational workflow combining machine learning (ML) and simulation-based approaches. EHR data will be preprocessed using natural language processing (NLP) to extract latent clinical features from unstructured notes, while time-series physiological data will undergo feature engineering for integration with genomic and demographic variables. Federated learning frameworks will be employed to train predictive models for sepsis onset and pressure injury risk across distributed datasets, preserving patient privacy. Agent-based modeling will simulate nurse-patient interactions and workflow scenarios to evaluate the impact of staffing ratios and intervention protocols on care quality. These computationally intensive tasks require HPC resources for parallelized model training, large-scale hyperparameter optimization, and real-time simulation ensembles. Expected outcomes include (1) validated predictive tools for early clinical deterioration, (2) a scalable framework for multimodal data integration in nursing research, and (3) evidence-based recommendations for staffing and workflow redesign. By enabling rapid analysis of terabyte-scale datasets, HPC access will directly support the development of precision nursing interventions, reduce computational bottlenecks in hypothesis testing, and accelerate the translation of findings into clinical practice. This work aligns with national priorities to reduce healthcare disparities through data-driven innovation, positioning nursing science at the forefront of computational health research.
cip_definition: A research program that focuses on the study of advanced clinical practices, research methodologies, the administration of complex nursing services, and that prepares nurses to further the progress of nursing research through experimentation and clinical applications.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance adult literacy education through the development of adaptive, AI-driven language processing tools tailored to the unique needs of adult learners. Adult literacy programs face significant challenges due to the heterogeneity of learners’ backgrounds, varying proficiency levels, and the cognitive and sociolinguistic complexities of acquiring functional literacy later in life. Traditional methods often rely on static curricula or one-size-fits-all approaches, which fail to address individual learning trajectories or the dynamic interplay between linguistic comprehension and real-world application. To bridge this gap, the proposed research will employ computational linguistics and machine learning techniques to analyze large-scale datasets of adult learner interactions, including written responses, verbal dialogues, and behavioral patterns during literacy tasks. Using neural network architectures optimized for natural language processing (NLP), the project will model linguistic development stages and predict optimal intervention strategies. Key computational tasks include real-time sentiment analysis to gauge learner engagement, transformer-based error detection to identify persistent literacy gaps, and generative AI to synthesize personalized practice materials that align with learners’ cultural and vocational contexts. By simulating diverse pedagogical scenarios through agent-based modeling, the research will also evaluate the scalability of adaptive tutoring systems in low-resource settings. The outcomes aim to produce an open-source framework for dynamically generating literacy content, enabling instructors to tailor interventions with unprecedented precision. This work will contribute to emerging interdisciplinary fields at the intersection of adult education, cognitive science, and computational pedagogy, while addressing a critical gap in equitable access to lifelong learning tools. The requested HPC resources are essential for training large language models, processing multimodal educational data, and iteratively refining algorithms to ensure robustness across diverse learner demographics.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to serve as instructors and mentors for adults in basic or functional literacy programs in school, institutional, community, and private settings.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of household resource allocation under socioeconomic stressors using high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate decision-making processes across diverse family structures. While traditional studies in Family and Consumer Sciences rely on survey data or qualitative methods, this research addresses the gap in modeling complex, nonlinear interactions between financial constraints, cultural norms, and policy impacts at scale. The computational approach integrates agent-based modeling (ABM) with machine learning techniques to simulate thousands of virtual households, each programmed with decision-making algorithms reflecting real-world behavioral data on budgeting, childcare, healthcare access, and debt management. By leveraging HPC resources, the simulations will incorporate high-dimensional datasets—including regional economic indicators, demographic trends, and policy scenarios—to explore emergent patterns in resource allocation under varying conditions, such as inflation spikes or unemployment shocks. The scalability of HPC will enable sensitivity analyses across heterogeneous populations, testing hypotheses about resilience strategies and intergenerational equity. Expected outcomes include predictive models identifying tipping points in household financial stability and visualizations of policy interventions’ cascading effects on family well-being. This work bridges computational social science with human ecology, offering a novel framework to assess how macro-level stressors micro-level decisions in understudied populations. The results will inform stakeholders in community programming and policy design, while the open-source simulation toolkit developed through this project will provide a foundation for future interdisciplinary research at the intersection of data science and family systems.
cip_title: Family and Consumer Sciences/ Human Sciences, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in family and consumer sciences/human sciences, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The safe and efficient operation of nuclear reactors relies on accurate modeling of complex, multi-physics phenomena, including neutron transport, thermal-hydraulic behavior, and material degradation under extreme conditions. Current simulation tools often rely on simplified models or decoupled physics due to computational limitations, introducing uncertainties that impact reactor design, fuel cycle optimization, and safety protocols. This project seeks to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and validate high-fidelity, coupled simulations of advanced nuclear reactor systems. The research will focus on a sodium-cooled fast reactor (SFR) design, integrating neutronics, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and thermomechanical strain models to predict reactor behavior under steady-state and transient scenarios. A hybrid computational approach will be employed, combining Monte Carlo methods for precise neutron transport modeling, finite volume techniques for resolving turbulent coolant flow, and machine learning algorithms to accelerate convergence and optimize coupling between physics modules. The simulations will utilize open-source frameworks such as OpenMC and MOOSE, adapted for massively parallel execution on GPU-accelerated architectures. Key deliverables include validated multi-physics workflows for SFR analysis, sensitivity studies on fuel-cladding interaction under thermal stress, and predictive models for coolant voiding effects. By enabling previously intractable resolution of coupled phenomena at reactor scale, this work aims to reduce conservatism in safety margins, improve fuel utilization efficiency, and inform waste reduction strategies through enhanced burnup calculations. The resulting computational toolkit will be shared with the broader nuclear research community, providing a foundation for next-generation reactor simulations while advancing workforce training in HPC-enabled nuclear engineering. Successful completion of this project will directly support national priorities in clean energy innovation and nuclear infrastructure modernization.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply scientific principles and technical skills in support of research scientists and operating engineers engaged in the running of nuclear reactors, and in nuclear materials processing and disposal. Includes instruction in basic nuclear physics and nuclear engineering, monitoring and safety procedures, radioactive materials handling and disposal, equipment maintenance and operation, and record keeping.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamic impacts of trade policy uncertainty on global value chain (GVC) integration using large-scale computational modeling. Recent geopolitical shifts and trade conflicts have amplified uncertainty in international commercial relations, yet existing trade models inadequately capture the heterogeneous responses of multinational firms to stochastic policy environments. The research addresses this gap by developing a high-dimensional structural model that integrates firm-level production network data, tariff schedules, and real exchange rate volatility. The computational approach employs a parallelized dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) framework augmented with agent-based modeling techniques to simulate cross-border input-output linkages under varying policy scenarios. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to handle the model’s scale, which requires solving systems of non-linear equations across 10,000+ firm agents interacting in 45 countries and 30 industrial sectors. Key tasks include Bayesian estimation of shock propagation parameters using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and Monte Carlo simulations to quantify welfare effects under alternative trade agreement designs. Expected outcomes include: (1) granular insights into how tariff uncertainty thresholds influence multinational firms’ reshoring decisions, (2) policy-relevant metrics on the resilience of GVCs to non-tariff trade barriers, and (3) open-source computational tools for trade elasticity estimation. Results will inform multilateral trade negotiations and supply chain risk management strategies. The requested computing resources will enable processing of terabyte-scale datasets from the World Input-Output Database, BEA, and customs transaction records, which are computationally prohibitive on standard workstations. This work advances methodological capabilities in trade policy analysis while addressing urgent questions about economic globalization in an era of increasing protectionism.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic study and analysis of international commercial behavior and trade policy. Includes instruction in international trade theory, tariffs and quotas, commercial policy, trade factor flows, international finance and investment, currency regulation and trade exchange rates and markets, international trade negotiation, and international payments and accounting policy.

abstract: The increasing complexity of modern vehicles, including electrified powertrains, advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS), and autonomous functionalities, presents significant challenges for maintenance and repair protocols. Traditional diagnostic methods, often reliant on static error codes and manual inspections, struggle to address dynamic, interconnected failures in these systems. This project seeks to develop a computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable high-fidelity simulations of vehicle subsystems under diverse operational and failure scenarios. By integrating multi-physics modeling—encompassing thermal, mechanical, and electrical dynamics—with machine learning algorithms trained on real-world diagnostic datasets, the research aims to create predictive maintenance models capable of identifying emerging faults before critical failures occur. The HPC infrastructure will facilitate large-scale parameter sweeps to optimize diagnostic thresholds and validate models against synthetic and empirical data, including sensor streams from connected vehicles. Key outcomes include the generation of adaptive fault-detection algorithms tailored to hybrid/electric architectures, reduced downtime through preemptive repair scheduling, and a publicly accessible simulation toolkit for technician training programs. The computational demands of this work—particularly the need for parallelized finite element analysis, neural network training on terabyte-scale datasets, and real-time co-simulation of vehicle networks—necessitate access to clustered GPU nodes and high-memory nodes. Successful implementation will advance the scalability of data-driven maintenance strategies in the automotive sector while providing educational institutions with cutting-edge resources to train technicians in next-generation repair methodologies.
cip_title: Vehicle Maintenance and Repair Technologies/ Technicians, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in vehicle maintenance and repair technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the understanding of exercise-induced physiological adaptations in cancer survivors, with a focus on mitigating treatment-related morbidity. Cancer therapies, including chemotherapy and radiation, often induce systemic physiological dysfunction—such as cardiorespiratory impairment, metabolic dysregulation, and muscle atrophy—that limits physical function and quality of life. While exercise interventions are promising, the heterogeneity of patient responses and the complexity of multisystem interactions pose challenges in optimizing personalized regimens. This study will develop multiscale computational models integrating clinical, biomechanical, and physiological data to predict how exercise parameters (intensity, modality, duration) influence molecular, cellular, and systemic outcomes in cancer survivors. Computational workflows will include finite element modeling of musculoskeletal dynamics during exercise, agent-based simulations of muscle metabolism and repair processes, and machine learning analyses of longitudinal clinical datasets (e.g., oxygen uptake kinetics, electromyography, circulating biomarkers). HPC resources are essential to manage the high dimensionality of these datasets, execute parallelized simulations of tissue-specific responses, and train predictive algorithms that account for interindividual variability in treatment history, genetic predispositions, and baseline fitness. Expected outcomes include a computational framework to identify exercise protocols that maximize functional recovery while minimizing fatigue and injury risk in vulnerable populations. This work will provide novel insights into the mechanistic links between exercise dosing and physiological resilience in oncology contexts, informing precision rehabilitation strategies. By bridging exercise physiology, oncology, and computational modeling, this project aligns with the program’s mission to address the physiological consequences of disease through innovative, interdisciplinary approaches.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the physiological processes involved in physical or motor activity, including sensorimotor interactions, response mechanisms, and the effects of injury, disease, and disability. Includes instruction in muscular and skeletal anatomy; molecular and cellular basis of muscle contraction; fuel utilization; neurophysiology of motor mechanics; systemic physiological responses (respiration, blood flow, endocrine secretions, and others); fatigue and exhaustion; muscle and body training; physiology of specific exercises and activities; physiology of injury; and the effects of disabilities and disease.

abstract: This research project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing real-time decision-making in decentralized business ecosystems through the development of a novel computational framework for dynamic network resource allocation. As organizations increasingly rely on distributed, multi-stakeholder digital platforms—such as supply chain networks, decentralized finance systems, and collaborative innovation hubs—traditional centralized optimization methods struggle to adapt to rapidly changing conditions, heterogeneous data formats, and conflicting stakeholder incentives. The project will combine game-theoretic modeling, federated machine learning, and evolutionary optimization algorithms to create a self-adapting resource allocation system that preserves data sovereignty while maximizing network-wide efficiency. The computational approach requires high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate large-scale networks (10,000+ nodes) with asynchronous decision cycles, process encrypted multi-modal data streams, and train ensemble models that reconcile competing optimization objectives across financial, operational, and sustainability metrics. Key innovations include a quantum-inspired annealing process for constraint satisfaction problems and a privacy-preserving mechanism for cross-organizational learning. Expected outcomes include 1) an open-source toolkit for decentralized business process optimization, 2) benchmarks comparing computational efficiency and solution quality against existing allocation methods, and 3) novel metrics for assessing network resilience in hyperconnected business environments. This work bridges gaps between distributed systems engineering, computational economics, and operational research, offering practical solutions for organizations navigating complex interdependencies in digital transformation initiatives. The requested HPC resources will enable experimentation at realistic scales while maintaining the security requirements inherent to business-sensitive data, ultimately advancing capabilities for autonomous coordination in next-generation business ecosystems.
cip_title: Management Information Systems and Services, Other
cip_definition: Any program in business information and data processing services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to advance veterinary radiology by developing high-fidelity computational models to optimize image-guided therapies and improve diagnostic accuracy for complex animal diseases. Current limitations in conventional radiologic imaging, such as low resolution in large-animal scans, motion artifacts in uncooperative patients, and inconsistent radiation dose calibration across species, hinder effective treatment planning. To address these challenges, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to train species-specific deep learning models for automated anomaly detection in veterinary CT and MRI datasets. The computational workflow will integrate three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (3D CNNs) with biomechanical simulations of tissue-radiation interactions, accounting for anatomical variability across companion animals, livestock, and exotic species. A multi-institutional dataset comprising over 50,000 annotated veterinary scans will be processed to establish standardized imaging biomarkers for neoplasms, orthopedic disorders, and soft tissue pathologies. Parallelized Monte Carlo simulations will model radiation transport in heterogeneous animal anatomies, enabling precision dose calculations for novel therapies like stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) in canine and feline oncology cases. The HPC infrastructure is critical for managing memory-intensive operations during volumetric image reconstruction and for accelerating the training of ensemble models that combine radiographic data with genomic and clinical metadata. Expected outcomes include an open-source veterinary radiomics platform, validated dose prediction algorithms for 15+ species, and quantitative frameworks for reducing diagnostic false positives in overlapping anatomical structures. By establishing computational pipelines tailored to veterinary medicine, this work aims to bridge the translational gap between human and animal radiology research while addressing unique species-specific challenges in image acquisition and interpretation.
cip_definition: Research focused on the use of radiologic imaging and therapies to diagnose and treat animal diseases and health problems. May included related research in the use and handling of equipment for radionuclides detection and application.

abstract: Plant diseases pose significant threats to global food security, yet predicting pathogen adaptation to climate-driven environmental shifts remains a critical challenge. This project seeks to develop a high-resolution, agent-based modeling framework to simulate the co-evolution of plant-pathogen systems under dynamic climatic conditions, with a focus on soil-borne fungal pathogens in cereal crops. The research integrates heterogenous data streams—including multi-omics datasets of pathogen virulence factors, host root exudate profiles, and microclimate sensor data—to parameterize interactions between biotic and abiotic variables at the rhizosphere scale. Computational challenges arise from simulating stochastic molecular signaling events (e.g., quorum sensing in fungal colonies) alongside macro-scale environmental gradients across geographically diverse agricultural landscapes. High-performance computing resources are essential to execute parallelized simulations spanning parameter spaces that capture genetic variability in pathogen populations, host resistance traits, and projected climate scenarios (RCP 4.5/8.5). Machine learning techniques will be employed to reduce dimensionality in output data and identify tipping points in disease emergence trajectories. Expected outcomes include predictive models quantifying climate-pathogen adaptation rates, spatially explicit risk maps for disease outbreaks, and actionable insights for developing preemptive breeding strategies targeting root-microbe communication pathways. By bridging molecular-scale pathogen behavior with ecosystem-level dynamics, this work advances precision phytopathology tools while addressing a critical gap in climate-resilient crop protection frameworks.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of plant diseases and plant health, and the development of disease control mechanisms. Includes instruction in plant anatomy and physiology, pathogenesis, molecular plant virology, molecular genetics, bacterial epidemiology, causal agent identification, host/agent interactions, disease resistance and response mechanisms, developing plant disease treatments, disease prevention, and disease physiology and control.

abstract: Diagnostic radiologic physics faces persistent challenges in optimizing imaging protocols to balance diagnostic accuracy, patient safety, and operational efficiency. Current approaches to minimizing radiation dose in X-ray and gamma-ray imaging, reducing artifacts in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and enhancing ultrasonic resolution rely on iterative experimental adjustments, which are time-intensive and lack generalizability across diverse patient populations. This project proposes a computational framework to model and optimize imaging parameters using advanced simulations, machine learning, and high-performance computing (HPC). The primary research problem centers on developing patient-specific protocols that reduce radiation exposure and improve image quality while maintaining diagnostic utility. A key limitation in existing methods is the computational expense of modeling complex, time-dependent interactions between radiation, tissue heterogeneity, and imaging hardware, necessitating scalable HPC resources. The project will employ Monte Carlo simulations to map radiation transport in anatomically realistic digital phantoms, coupled with deep learning architectures to predict optimal imaging parameters under dose constraints. For MRI, finite element models will simulate magnetic field inhomogeneities and acoustic noise propagation in ultrasound, enabling artifact correction algorithms. These simulations will be validated against clinical data from collaborating institutions. The computational workflow demands parallel processing capabilities to handle large-scale datasets (10+ TB), iterative optimization loops, and 3D image reconstructions. Expected outcomes include validated, open-source computational tools for protocol optimization, quantitative guidelines for dose reduction in pediatric and high-risk populations, and artifact mitigation strategies for low-field MRI systems. By leveraging HPC, this work aims to advance personalized diagnostic imaging, reduce ionizing radiation risks, and improve the precision of quantitative biomarkers in oncologic and neurologic applications. The resulting frameworks will be disseminated to the clinical radiophysics community, fostering safer and more efficient imaging practices.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnostic applications of x-rays, gamma rays from sealed sources, ultrasonic radiation, and magnetic resonance; and in the use of equipment associated with their production and use, including radiation safety. One of the three subspecialties available to residents in radiologic physics who must select one or more subspecialty areas.

abstract: This project seeks to advance understanding of the integrative physiological responses to prolonged microgravity and radiation exposure during spaceflight, with a focus on systemic cardiovascular deconditioning, musculoskeletal atrophy, and cancer risk modulation. Astronauts experience multi-organ functional decline during extended missions, yet the mechanisms linking fluid redistribution, cellular hypoxia, and tissue remodeling remain poorly characterized. Additionally, while cosmic radiation is a known oncogenic hazard, its interaction with microgravity-induced immune dysregulation and DNA repair pathways in carcinogenesis is underexplored. To address these gaps, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating hemodynamic models, musculoskeletal force dynamics, and radiation-driven genomic instability simulations. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable 3D lattice-Boltzmann simulations of cerebral and peripheral blood flow redistribution under variable gravitational loads, coupled with finite element analysis of trabecular bone loss patterns. Agent-based modeling will simulate radiation-induced double-strand break repair efficiency in hematopoietic stem cells under simulated microgravity cytokine profiles. These outputs will inform a machine learning classifier trained on multi-omics datasets (transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic) from prior bedrest and International Space Station studies to predict individual susceptibility to orthostatic intolerance, muscle wasting, and premalignant clonal expansion. The computational pipeline will be validated against longitudinal astronaut health data, including vascular ultrasound, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, and liquid biopsy findings. Expected outcomes include predictive algorithms for mission-specific countermeasure optimization, mechanistic insights into gravity-dependent carcinogenesis pathways, and a scalable digital twin platform for simulating extraterrestrial physiological adaptations. This work directly supports NASA’s Human Research Program goals by elucidating emergent risks in Artemis-era deep space exploration and providing translational frameworks for mitigating spaceflight-associated morbidity.
detailed_field: Physiology, oncology, and cancer biology nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the physiological processes involved in low and high-altitude flight and living in space and related low-pressure and low-gravity environments, including sensorimotor interactions, response mechanisms, and the effects of injury, disease, and disability. Includes instruction in anatomy, molecular and cellular basis of muscle contraction, fuel utilization, neurophysiology of motor mechanics, systemic physiological responses (respiration, blood flow, endocrine secretions, and others), fatigue and exhaustion, systemic environmental pathologies, muscle and body training, physiology of specific exercises and activities, physiology of injury, and the effects of disabilities and disease.

abstract: The development of advanced chemical processes for sustainable energy and materials production requires high-fidelity computational models to address multi-scale, dynamic interactions inherent in catalytic systems, multiphase reactors, and membrane-based separations. Current challenges include accurately resolving atomic-level reaction mechanisms, predicting fluid dynamics in turbulent reactor environments, and optimizing process parameters under transient conditions—tasks that demand significant computational resources. This project seeks high-performance computing (HPC) allocations to enable large-scale simulations integrating molecular dynamics (MD), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML) frameworks. The research focuses on two interconnected thrusts: (1) modeling catalytic surface reactions in novel metal-organic framework (MOF) materials for carbon capture and conversion, and (2) optimizing multiphase flow and heat transfer in intensified reactor designs for electrochemical ammonia synthesis. MD simulations will elucidate reaction pathways and adsorption energetics at the quantum-mechanical level, while GPU-accelerated CFD simulations will resolve micron-scale bubble dynamics and species transport in three-dimensional reactor geometries. A surrogate ML model, trained on simulation data, will accelerate parameter optimization and uncertainty quantification. The computational workflow leverages hybrid MPI/OpenMP parallelization in LAMMPS and OpenFOAM, coupled with PyTorch-based neural networks. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for MOF-catalyzed CO₂ hydrogenation kinetics, design guidelines for scalable electrochemical reactors, and open-source tools for reactive flow simulation. These advances will directly inform experimental efforts to develop energy-efficient chemical processes, with potential applications in decarbonized fuel production and distributed chemical manufacturing. The requested resources are critical for handling simulations exceeding 10⁶ CPU-core hours, including 500,000-atom MD systems and reactor meshes with >100 million cells, which are computationally intractable on local clusters.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of systems employing chemical processes, such as chemical reactors, kinetic systems, electrochemical systems, energy conservation processes, heat and mass transfer systems, and separation processes; and the applied analysis of chemical problems such as corrosion, particle abrasion, energy loss, pollution, and fluid mechanics.

abstract: This project seeks to integrate computational modeling and high-performance computing (HPC) resources into the study of ceramic materials and processes to advance artistic innovation and technical precision in ceramic arts. Traditional approaches to developing ceramic bodies, glazes, and firing protocols rely heavily on iterative physical experimentation, which is time-intensive, resource-heavy, and constrained by material variability. The research problem centers on overcoming these limitations by simulating the physicochemical behaviors of clay bodies and glazes under diverse compositional and thermal conditions, enabling data-driven predictions of aesthetic and structural outcomes. Proposed computational methods include molecular dynamics simulations to model clay-water interactions during forming stages, finite element analysis (FEA) to predict stress distributions in complex ceramic geometries during drying and firing, and machine learning (ML) algorithms trained on empirical datasets to correlate glaze chemistry with visual effects like color variation, texture, and surface reflectance. High-resolution thermal modeling of kiln environments will also be conducted to optimize energy efficiency and reduce firing anomalies. By leveraging HPC resources, these simulations will operate at scales necessary to capture microstructural evolution in clay matrices and glaze layers, which directly influence macroscale artistic properties. Expected outcomes include a computational framework for designing ceramic materials with tailored aesthetic features, reduced material waste, and reproducible firing protocols. This interdisciplinary approach bridges ceramic arts with materials science and computational engineering, offering novel tools for artists to expand creative possibilities while addressing sustainability challenges inherent in traditional practices. The project will also generate open-access datasets and models to support pedagogical innovation in ceramic arts education, fostering a new paradigm of computationally informed studio practice.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals creatively and technically to express emotions, ideas, or inner visions by producing art works out of clay and similar materials. Includes instruction in handbuilt and wheel thrown techniques; molding; slips and glazes; trimming and decorating; firing and kiln operation; oxidation; mixed media; ceramic murals; and personal style development.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the social dynamics of non-literate, pre-industrial communities through the computational modeling of material culture patterns, integrating large-scale archaeological datasets with environmental and ethnographic data. Traditional approaches to reconstructing past social behaviors—such as kinship systems, resource-sharing practices, or collective decision-making—often rely on qualitative analogies or small-scale artifact analyses, limiting their capacity to address complex, systemic interactions. To overcome these constraints, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework combining agent-based modeling (ABM), geospatial analysis, and machine learning to simulate how social norms and environmental pressures co-evolve over time. The research will leverage existing archaeological datasets from Neolithic Anatolian settlements, including artifact distributions, settlement layouts, and paleoenvironmental reconstructions, to parameterize and validate models. HPC resources will enable the parallel execution of thousands of simulations, systematically varying parameters related to resource availability, mobility patterns, and social exchange rules to identify configurations that best align with observed material patterns. Deep learning algorithms will further analyze simulation outputs alongside artifact typologies and spatial data to detect non-linear relationships between social behaviors and material outcomes. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable computational platform for testing hypotheses about emergent social structures in non-literate societies, (2) novel insights into how collective identities and resource management strategies may have developed in early sedentary communities, and (3) methodological advancements in linking archaeological "big data" to social theory. By bridging computational archaeology and social science inquiry, this work will establish new pathways for studying human sociality in contexts where textual evidence is absent, with broader implications for understanding resilience and inequality in past and present societies.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic study of extinct societies, and the past of living societies, via the excavation, analysis and interpretation of their artifactual, human, and associated remains. Includes instruction in archeological theory, field methods, dating methods, conservation and museum studies, cultural and physical evolution, and the study of specific selected past cultures with a focus on the humanistic aspects of archaeology.

abstract: This project seeks to develop an AI-driven predictive framework to optimize personalized care plans for homebound individuals by integrating multimodal data from wearable sensors, environmental monitors, and caregiver observations. The central challenge lies in processing heterogeneous, high-frequency data streams (including motion patterns, vital sign fluctuations, and home environment variables) to detect subtle precursors of adverse health events such as falls, medication errors, or acute episodes in chronically ill patients. Current clinical decision support systems lack the temporal resolution and contextual awareness required for dynamic home care environments, where limited supervision and diverse living conditions create unique risks. We propose a hybrid computational architecture combining graph neural networks to model patient-environment interactions, transformer-based time series analysis for longitudinal biomarker tracking, and physics-informed reinforcement learning to simulate intervention outcomes. The framework will be trained on a novel dataset aggregating anonymized sensor data from 450 home care recipients, augmented with synthetic cohorts representing understudied populations. High-performance computing resources are critical for three components: 1) Parallel processing of terabyte-scale sensor datasets with subsecond temporal alignment, 2) Multi-agent simulations of caregiver-client-environment dynamics across 10^5 potential scenario permutations, and 3) Federated learning protocols preserving privacy across distributed care provider networks. Anticipated outcomes include a real-time risk stratification system that alerts home health aides to emerging threats with quantified uncertainty estimates, plus adaptive recommendation engines for tailored intervention timing. This computational infrastructure could reduce preventable hospitalizations by 18-22% in pilot populations while establishing methodological foundations for AI-assisted home care—a critical need as aging populations drive demand for scalable, precision-focused support systems outside institutional settings.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide routine care and support services for homebound disabled, recovering, or elderly people. Includes instruction in basic nutrition, home sanitation, infection control, first aid, taking vital signs, personal hygiene, interpersonal communication skills, supervised home management, emergency recognition and referral, geriatric care, and legal and ethical responsibilities.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model the dynamic interplay between psychosocial resilience, environmental stressors, and cognitive aging trajectories in older adults. While prior research has identified static risk factors for age-related cognitive decline, the nonlinear interactions between time-varying elements—such as fluctuating social support, episodic stressors, and neurobiological adaptation—remain poorly understood. Traditional statistical methods struggle to capture these multidimensional, temporally nested relationships, necessitating computational approaches capable of simulating complex systems. Using agent-based modeling (ABM) integrated with empirical longitudinal datasets (e.g., health records, ecological momentary assessments), we will simulate how individual differences in resilience mechanisms modulate the impact of cumulative life stressors on cognitive health across a simulated aging continuum. The HPC environment will enable parallelized simulations across diverse demographic and socioeconomic parameter spaces, including rare but high-impact events (e.g., pandemic-related isolation, economic disruptions). Machine learning techniques will then identify critical inflection points where targeted interventions—such as community resource allocation or personalized cognitive training—could maximally delay decline. Validation will occur via comparison to existing cohort studies (e.g., HRS, ADNI) and prospective data from a partnered adult day center. Expected outcomes include a scalable computational framework to test hypothetical aging policies, optimize timing for community-based support programs, and predict vulnerability windows in at-risk populations. By bridging computational neuroscience, gerontology, and complexity science, this work advances a systems-level understanding of aging that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries, offering actionable insights for promoting cognitive longevity in an aging global population.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the characteristics of aging populations and the needs of older individuals in family and institutional settings. Includes instruction in the biological and psychological stages of aging; the provision of dependent care; serving the social, economic, and psychological needs of aging adults; related public policy issues; and adult community resources.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to resolve complex geoarchaeological questions surrounding the interplay of early human settlement patterns and rapid paleoenvironmental shifts in the Holocene-era Sahul continent (present-day Australia and New Guinea). Traditional methods struggle to integrate heterogeneous datasets—including high-resolution sedimentological records, paleoclimatic proxies, and spatially discontinuous archaeological site data—into a unified analytical framework. The research aims to develop a scalable computational model that simulates landscape evolution, resource availability, and human mobility at sub-centennial resolution across a 10,000-year timeframe. The model will synthesize lidar-derived topographic data, sediment core stratigraphy, and archaeological radiocarbon chronologies using a hybrid approach combining agent-based modeling (ABM), Bayesian chronological analysis, and geostatistical interpolation. HPC resources are critical for parallelizing Monte Carlo simulations to address chronological uncertainties in site occupation phases and for processing high-dimensional datasets (e.g., 3D sedimentological matrices) to reconstruct paleohydrological systems. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of previously undetectable correlations between abrupt climatic events (e.g., 8.2 ka cooling) and shifts in settlement density, (2) predictive maps of high-probability archaeological site locations based on simulated paleoenvironmental parameters, and (3) open-source tools for integrating disparate geospatial and stratigraphic datasets in understudied regions. By bridging computational earth science methods with archaeological inquiry, this work will establish a replicable framework for analyzing human-environment interactions in data-sparse contexts, with implications for both heritage preservation and understanding adaptive responses to environmental change.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of analytical techniques, concepts, and field methods from the earth sciences to solve archaeological questions related to human settlement, artifacts, site taphonomy, and paleoenvironments. Includes instruction in anthropology, ancient civilizations, archeology, geology, paleoclimatic reconstruction, sedimentology, and site taphonomic research.

abstract: Child abuse pediatrics faces critical challenges in accurately diagnosing abuse, particularly in differentiating intentional injuries from accidental trauma or medical conditions. Current diagnostic approaches rely heavily on subjective clinical judgment and fragmented data, leading to inconsistencies that may compromise child safety, legal outcomes, and prevention efforts. This project proposes the development of a computational decision-support framework integrating multimodal data—including electronic health records, radiologic imaging, demographic factors, and forensic interviews—to improve diagnostic accuracy and risk stratification. The research will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to train machine learning models on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets spanning clinical, social, and legal domains. Key computational tasks include natural language processing of unstructured clinical narratives, convolutional neural networks for fracture pattern analysis in radiographic images, and graph-based algorithms to model interactions among caregivers, social services, and medical providers. Validation will leverage retrospective cases with known outcomes from national child abuse registries. The scalable infrastructure will enable real-time simulation of injury mechanisms via finite element modeling to assess biomechanical plausibility of caregiver-reported histories. By unifying disparate data sources and automating complex pattern recognition, this framework aims to reduce diagnostic uncertainty, support multidisciplinary case reviews, and identify high-risk populations for targeted prevention. Successful implementation will provide clinicians, child welfare agencies, and legal systems with evidence-based tools to optimize child safety interventions while preserving familial integrity when appropriate. The project’s computational demands—including terabyte-scale data integration, parallelized model training, and population-level simulations—necessitate dedicated HPC allocation to achieve clinically actionable timelines.
cip_definition: Research on how to accurately diagnose abuse, consult with community agencies on child safety, provide expertise in courts of law, treat consequences of abuse and neglect, direct child abuse and neglect prevention programs and participate on multidisciplinary investigative teams, and manage child abuse cases.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in institutional foodservice systems by developing a computational framework to optimize meal production, distribution, and waste reduction in real time. Institutional food operations—such as those in hospitals, universities, and corporate campuses—face unique challenges, including dynamic demand fluctuations, nutritional compliance, supply chain volatility, and sustainability mandates. Traditional management approaches often rely on static models or heuristic decision-making, which fail to adapt to rapidly changing conditions, leading to resource overuse, food waste, and operational bottlenecks. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes an integrated high-performance computing (HPC) approach combining agent-based modeling, machine learning, and real-time data assimilation. Agent-based simulations will model interactions between stakeholders (e.g., suppliers, kitchen staff, diners) and environmental variables (e.g., seasonal ingredient availability, equipment downtime), while machine learning algorithms will predict demand patterns and optimize procurement schedules. A key innovation involves coupling IoT-derived data streams (e.g., kitchen equipment sensors, diner traffic tracking) with simulation outputs to enable adaptive decision-support tools. The computational intensity of simultaneously running thousands of scenario iterations, training predictive models on heterogeneous datasets, and maintaining low-latency responsiveness necessitates access to HPC resources for parallel processing and large-scale data integration. Expected outcomes include a scalable digital twin platform capable of reducing food waste by 15–25%, improving cost efficiency through dynamic inventory management, and enhancing meal quality via nutrient-preservation analytics. This work bridges gaps between operations research, behavioral analytics, and sustainability science, offering a novel methodology for foodservice systems management. By aligning computational innovation with practical institutional needs, the project aims to establish a benchmark for data-driven decision-making in non-commercial food operations, with potential applications in disaster relief logistics, eldercare nutrition management, and other specialized contexts where traditional supply chain models are insufficient.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the principles and practices relating to the administration of food service systems in institutional settings, and that prepares individuals to manage such operations in public and private facilities. Includes instruction in human nutrition, food safety, the design and organization of food service systems, purchasing, personnel management, and related business practices.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the dynamics of audience engagement and content virality in hybrid digital broadcast environments. As media consumption shifts toward nonlinear, platform-agnostic models, content creators and distributors face challenges in predicting how multimodal narratives—integrating audio, video, and interactive elements—propagate across social media, streaming services, and legacy broadcast channels. The research addresses a critical gap in understanding how algorithmic recommendation systems, user-generated metadata, and real-time audience interactions collectively shape the lifespan and cultural impact of digital content. A computational framework will be developed to simulate large-scale media ecosystems, combining agent-based modeling of user behavior, natural language processing of comment/engagement data, and network analysis of cross-platform content diffusion. The models will train on heterogeneous datasets, including anonymized viewer analytics from partner broadcasters, social media APIs, and synthetic data representing edge-case scenarios. HPC resources are essential to handle the parallel processing demands of simulating millions of agent interactions, processing terabyte-scale multimedia datasets, and running iterative deep learning models to identify latent patterns in cross-platform resonance. Expected outcomes include a predictive toolkit for optimizing content release strategies in multiplatform environments and evidence-based recommendations for mitigating algorithmic bias in culturally sensitive narratives. This work will provide novel methodologies for computational media studies while offering practical insights to communication professionals navigating increasingly fragmented digital audiences.
cip_title: Radio, Television, and Digital Communication, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in radio, television, and digital communications, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance mechanistic modeling of drug-induced organ toxicity, a critical challenge in pharmacological and toxicological research. Traditional in vitro and animal models often fail to predict human-specific toxicities, leading to costly late-stage drug failures and safety-related withdrawals. Our research focuses on developing multiscale computational models to simulate drug interactions with hepatic cellular systems, integrating pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD) parameters, metabolic pathway dynamics, and tissue-level response networks. The core computational challenge lies in simulating nonlinear interactions between xenobiotics, metabolic enzymes (e.g., CYP450 isoforms), and cellular stress pathways at physiologically relevant timescales. We propose to implement hybrid modeling approaches combining ordinary differential equation systems for metabolic flux analysis with agent-based models of hepatocyte population responses. These simulations will incorporate human toxicogenomic datasets from primary hepatocytes and post-market surveillance reports to parameterize species-specific toxicity thresholds. The HPC environment is essential for parallel processing of stochastic model iterations across diverse drug candidates and genetic subpopulations, requiring terabytes of memory allocation and GPU-accelerated computation for molecular docking simulations. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework for identifying hepatotoxic liabilities in drug candidates prior to clinical trials, validated against historical toxicity data from withdrawn pharmaceuticals. This resource will enable rational prioritization of safer lead compounds and guide structure-activity relationship refinements to mitigate toxicity risks. By bridging gaps between cellular-scale mechanisms and organ-level toxicity phenotypes, this work addresses a fundamental need in pharmacological safety assessment while reducing reliance on animal testing.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in pharmacology and toxicology, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project investigates the spatial dynamics of informal knowledge networks in urban environments, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model how transient social interactions shape localized innovation ecosystems. While prior studies focus on formal institutions or economic frameworks, this work addresses a gap in understanding self-organizing, non-hierarchical networks that emerge through ephemeral human contacts in public spaces, transit hubs, and community events. The research combines geolocated social media data, anonymized mobility traces, and ethnographic field observations to construct a multilayer network model capturing temporal, spatial, and social dimensions of knowledge exchange. Agent-based modeling (ABM) simulations will be implemented using parallelized computing architectures to test hypotheses about threshold effects in network formation, scaling relationships between urban morphology and innovation diffusion, and resilience to spatial disruptions. Computational challenges include processing petabyte-scale streaming datasets, optimizing graph neural networks for dynamic spatial networks, and running ensemble simulations across parameter spaces characterizing diverse urban configurations. Expected outcomes include a novel framework for quantifying "serendipity potential" in urban design, predictive models of grassroots innovation spread under different zoning policies, and open-source tools for simulating socio-spatial networks at metropolitan scales. Results will contribute to interdisciplinary scholarship at the intersection of human geography, computational social science, and urban informatics, offering evidence-based insights for planners seeking to foster inclusive innovation ecosystems without centralized coordination. The project's computational demands necessitate dedicated HPC resources due to memory-intensive network analyses, real-time data integration requirements, and the need for comparative scenario testing across multiple city typologies.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in geography, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamic interplay between historical sociopolitical shifts and the evolution of linguistic structures, literary forms, and cultural narratives across multilingual archives from 18th- to 20th-century Eurasia. By integrating computational methods with interdisciplinary frameworks from history, philology, and literary studies, the research will analyze how transformative events—such as imperial collapses, revolutions, and cross-regional migrations—reshaped language use, textual production, and collective memory. The core challenge lies in systematically processing and interpreting vast, heterogeneous corpora spanning manuscripts, periodicals, and official records in seven languages, requiring advanced computational resources to manage morphological complexity, semantic change, and multilingual code-switching patterns. The proposed approach combines natural language processing (NLP) techniques—including transformer-based models for low-resource languages, dynamic topic modeling, and semantic role labeling—with network analysis to trace discursive connections across temporal and geographic boundaries. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for training custom language models on historical texts, running large-scale comparative analyses of syntactic and lexical shifts, and simulating the diffusion of literary motifs through agent-based modeling. Expected outcomes include 1) a scalable computational pipeline for diachronic multilingual text analysis, 2) an open-access repository of annotated historical corpora with cross-referenced metadata, and 3) new interdisciplinary insights into how communities negotiated identity through language during periods of upheaval. By enabling the processing of over 15 million pages of digitized materials at unprecedented resolution, this project will advance methodologies for humanistic HPC applications while contributing to transnational understandings of cultural resilience and adaptation.
cip_definition: A program with a general synthesis of history and the language and literature of one or more countries or regions or a specialization which draws from history and the language and literature of one or more countries or regions. Includes instruction in historiography; historical research methods; linguistics; literature, philology; and studies of specific periods, issues and cultures.

abstract: Forest ecosystems are critical for biodiversity, carbon sequestration, and sustainable resource management, yet their resilience to climate change and anthropogenic stressors remains poorly quantified at landscape scales. This project seeks to develop high-resolution computational models to simulate forest dynamics under varying climate scenarios, disturbance regimes, and management strategies. The research addresses a critical gap in predicting long-term forest health and productivity, particularly in regions experiencing rapid environmental change. Current models lack the spatial granularity and integration of multi-source data—such as LiDAR-derived canopy structure, soil moisture sensors, and satellite phenology—required to capture fine-scale ecological processes. To overcome these limitations, we propose a parallelized modeling framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to integrate terabytes of remote sensing data, species distribution maps, and climate projections at 10-meter resolution. The framework will employ machine learning algorithms to parameterize species-specific growth responses and agent-based simulations to model biotic interactions (e.g., pest outbreaks, wildfire spread) and management interventions. Computational challenges include handling irregularly structured spatial data, optimizing memory usage for large graph-based ecosystem networks, and scaling Monte Carlo simulations to assess uncertainty across ensemble climate models. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive maps of forest composition and carbon stocks under 2050 climate scenarios, (2) quantitative thresholds for disturbance resilience in key timber species, and (3) open-source tools for adaptive forest management planning. By enabling near-real-time simulation of complex ecological trade-offs, this work will directly inform conservation policies, sustainable harvest schedules, and habitat restoration efforts. The requested HPC allocation is essential to achieve the necessary processing speed and data storage capacity, as preliminary tests indicate that a single 50-year simulation for a 10,000-km² domain requires 72 hours on 256 cores. This project bridges computational innovation and applied forest science, advancing both ecological theory and land-use decision-making in natural resource management.
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to manage and develop forest areas for economic, recreational, and ecological purposes. Includes instruction in forest-related sciences, mapping, statistics, harvesting and production technology, natural resources management and economics, wildlife sciences, administration, and public relations.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of legal reasoning in complex, precedent-driven judicial systems through large-scale computational modeling. The research addresses a critical gap in legal scholarship: the lack of empirically grounded, dynamic frameworks to quantify how legal principles transform over time in response to societal, technological, and institutional pressures. By focusing on appellate court decisions in data privacy law—a rapidly evolving domain intersecting technology, ethics, and jurisprudence—the study aims to map the nonlinear interactions between case outcomes, judicial language, and external socio-technical factors. The computational approach combines natural language processing (NLP) techniques optimized for legal texts, network analysis of citation patterns, and agent-based modeling to simulate decision-making dynamics across multi-layered judicial hierarchies. Custom algorithms will process terabyte-scale corpora of case law, dissenting opinions, and legislative histories to identify latent doctrinal shifts and feedback loops. Graph neural networks will model the propagation of legal concepts through jurisdictional boundaries, while probabilistic classifiers will assess the impact of non-legal variables (e.g., public sentiment metrics, technological adoption rates) on judicial outcomes. The HPC infrastructure is essential for training transformer-based models on legal language, running Monte Carlo simulations of alternative legal histories, and handling the sparse, high-dimensional data inherent in longitudinal legal systems. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible computational toolkit for legal impact forecasting, novel metrics for quantifying legal uncertainty in emerging technology domains, and evidence-based insights into systemic bottlenecks in judicial adaptation processes. This work bridges computational social science and legal informatics, offering a paradigm to study law as a complex adaptive system while maintaining rigorous alignment with jurisprudential theory.
cip_title: Legal Research and Advanced Professional Studies, Other
cip_definition: Any program in legal research and advanced professional studies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of Black cultural production across the 20th-century United States and Caribbean, with a focus on interdisciplinary connections between literature, visual art, and music. While existing scholarship has documented key movements like the Harlem Renaissance or Negritude, significant gaps remain in mapping large-scale patterns of creative exchange, thematic recurrence, and diasporic influence due to the scale and complexity of archival materials. Our research will employ computational text analysis, image recognition, and network modeling to process digitized collections of novels, paintings, oral histories, and musical recordings from 1900–1999. Using natural language processing (NLP) tools fine-tuned for African-American Vernacular English and Creole languages, we will identify linguistic motifs in literary works alongside parallel visual patterns in contemporaneous artworks. Audio analysis algorithms will cross-reference musical structures with textual/visual datasets to trace transmedia cultural signatures. Graph neural networks will then model spatial and temporal diffusion of creative themes across geographic nodes (e.g., New York, New Orleans, Port-au-Prince). This approach requires HPC capabilities to manage heterogeneous data (10TB+ of text, images, audio) and run multi-modal machine learning pipelines. Expected outcomes include 1) identification of previously understudied connections between regional artistic movements, 2) visualization of how specific aesthetic strategies persisted or transformed through migration and political change, and 3) an open-access computational framework for analyzing diasporic cultural production. By enabling systematic study of cross-disciplinary creative practices at scale, this project aims to reshape understandings of Black cultural innovation while developing methodologies that center African-American Studies’ unique archival challenges and opportunities.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, sociology, politics, culture, and economics of the North American peoples descended from the African diaspora; focusing on the United States, Canada, and the Caribbean, but also including reference to Latin American elements of the diaspora.

abstract: This project seeks to optimize strategic decision-making in sport organization management through advanced computational modeling of dynamic, multi-variable systems inherent to athletic program operations. The research problem centers on the lack of scalable frameworks for simulating complex interactions between operational factors—including facility utilization patterns, staff scheduling constraints, financial variables, and participant engagement metrics—in sport and fitness environments. Current industry tools rely on simplified linear models that fail to capture the nonlinear relationships and emergent behaviors critical to organizational efficiency. We propose developing a high-fidelity agent-based model leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate facility ecosystems at unprecedented scale, incorporating real-world data streams from partner organizations spanning collegiate athletics, municipal recreation departments, and commercial fitness operators. The computational approach integrates discrete-event simulation for resource allocation patterns with machine learning components trained on historical operational data to predict stress points in scheduling systems and equipment utilization. Parallelized Monte Carlo methods will assess thousands of scenario permutations to identify robust management strategies under variable conditions, including fluctuating membership demand and facility maintenance disruptions. Expected outcomes include a novel decision-support framework capable of forecasting operational bottlenecks 6-18 months in advance with quantified confidence intervals, paired with prescriptive optimization algorithms for staff deployment and capital investment prioritization. The computational toolkit developed through this research will provide sport administrators with evidence-based strategies to balance service quality, financial sustainability, and infrastructure longevity—a critical advancement as organizations face increasing pressure to deliver data-driven management solutions in complex, resource-constrained environments.
detailed_field: Parks, recreation, leisure, fitness, and sport studies and management
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply business, coaching and physical education principles to the organization, administration and management of athletic programs and teams, fitness/rehabilitation facilities and health clubs, sport recreation services, and related services. Includes instruction in program planning and development; business and financial management principles; sales, marketing and recruitment; event promotion, scheduling and management; facilities management; public relations; legal aspects of sports; and applicable health and safety standards.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational legal studies through the analysis of large-scale, unstructured legal text datasets. The research focuses on modeling the evolution of legal doctrines and judicial decision-making patterns across federal courts in the United States, with particular emphasis on identifying latent biases and systemic inconsistencies in the application of precedent. While traditional legal scholarship relies on manual case review, this work employs natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) techniques to process over 1.5 million federal court opinions, spanning 1945–2023, alongside associated briefs, statutes, and legislative histories. The computational approach combines transformer-based language models (e.g., BERT variants fine-tuned for legal reasoning) with graph neural networks to map citation networks, temporal doctrinal shifts, and semantic relationships between legal concepts. Key challenges requiring HPC resources include training domain-specific embeddings on terabyte-scale text corpora, running parallelized network analysis across multi-decade judicial interaction graphs, and conducting sensitivity analyses through agent-based modeling of hypothetical judicial behaviors. Expected outcomes include 1) an open-source framework for quantifying temporal legal concept drift, 2) empirical evidence addressing debates about ideological consistency in statutory interpretation, and 3) predictive models identifying under-examined correlations between rhetorical patterns and case outcomes. By developing computationally intensive methods tailored to legal reasoning’s unique features—including precedent hierarchies, analogical argument structures, and multi-modal evidence integration—this work aims to establish new standards for data-driven legal analysis while maintaining rigorous humanities-based engagement with interpretive traditions. The requested resources will enable processing timelines impractical on standard infrastructure, particularly for graph-based simulations of alternative precedent evolution scenarios and attention mechanism analyses in judicial writing.
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on law and legal issues from the perspective of the social sciences and humanities.

abstract: The detection and characterization of early-stage pathologies in the maxillofacial region remain challenging due to the complex anatomy and subtle radiographic manifestations inherent to structures such as the jaws, temporomandibular joint (TMJ), and associated soft tissues. Current clinical imaging techniques, while advanced, often lack the computational power required for high-resolution 3D analysis and automated pattern recognition at scale. This project proposes to address these limitations by developing deep learning models and computational workflows optimized for multi-modal imaging data, including cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and intraoral radiographs. The research will focus on three core objectives: (1) creating AI-driven segmentation pipelines to delineate intricate anatomical structures and pathologies in 3D, (2) training ensemble neural networks to detect microstructural changes indicative of osteoradionecrosis, osteoarthritis, and occult fractures, and (3) simulating biomechanical bone remodeling processes under pathological conditions using finite element analysis. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to process terabyte-scale datasets, accelerate model training through parallelized GPU workflows, and run computationally intensive simulations of tissue stress distributions. The integration of distributed computing frameworks will enable rapid iteration of hybrid architectures combining convolutional neural networks with transformer-based attention mechanisms for improved anomaly detection. Expected outcomes include validated computational tools for quantitative radiographic analysis, predictive models of disease progression, and open-source software packages tailored for clinical maxillofacial imaging research. By enhancing the precision of image interpretation and enabling large-scale longitudinal studies, this work aims to establish new standards for data-driven diagnosis and personalized treatment planning in oral and maxillofacial radiology.
cip_definition: Research focused on producing and interpreting images of the jaws, teeth, bone, and other structures of the head and neck region; and to diagnose and manage diseases, disorders, and conditions that affect this area of the body.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of bioinspired, programmable materials for next-generation medical devices, a niche domain integrating synthetic biology, materials science, and computational design. Current limitations in implantable biomedical devices—such as mechanical mismatch with native tissues, poor biocompatibility, and static material properties—underscore the need for dynamic, adaptive systems that emulate biological responsiveness. We propose a computational framework to model and optimize hybrid materials incorporating engineered microbial consortia and stimuli-responsive polymers. These materials are designed to sense physiological changes (e.g., pH, temperature, or inflammation biomarkers) and autonomously adjust their stiffness, porosity, or drug-release profiles. The research problem centers on simulating the multi-scale interactions between synthetic genetic circuits in microbial communities and polymer networks, which are experimentally intractable due to nonlinear feedback loops and time-dependent material behaviors. Using agent-based modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and finite element analysis, we will predict system stability, signal propagation delays, and emergent material properties under diverse physiological conditions. Machine learning models will iteratively refine design parameters to maximize performance metrics (e.g., response specificity, durability) while minimizing off-target effects. HPC resources are critical for handling the combinatorial complexity of genetic circuit designs, polymer compositions, and environmental variables, requiring petabytes of parameter space exploration. Expected outcomes include a validated computational pipeline for rapid prototyping of biohybrid materials and proof-of-concept designs for self-regulating wound dressings that dynamically modulate antibiotic release. This work bridges biotechnology and advanced materials engineering, offering transformative potential for personalized medical devices while addressing ethical and safety considerations unique to living-material interfaces. The computational tools developed will be shared via open-source platforms to accelerate innovation in this emerging field.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of the biological sciences, biochemistry, and genetics to the preparation of new and enhanced agricultural, environmental, clinical, and industrial products, including the commercial exploitation of microbes, plants, and animals. Includes instruction in bioinformatics, gene identification, phylogenetics and comparative genomics, bioinorganic chemistry, immunoassaying, DNA sequencing, xenotransplantation, genetic engineering, industrial microbiology, drug and biologic development, enzyme-based production processes, patent law, biotechnology management and marketing, applicable regulations, and biotechnology ethics.

abstract: This research project seeks to develop a computational framework for optimizing dynamic security resource allocation in complex, high-risk environments, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to address inefficiencies in traditional static security models. Current approaches in private security services often rely on fixed deployment strategies for personnel and technologies, which struggle to adapt to real-time threats, fluctuating client needs, and variable operational constraints. The project focuses on integrating heterogeneous data streams—including IoT sensor outputs, historical incident reports, environmental data, and workforce availability—to generate adaptive security protocols. Using agent-based modeling and reinforcement learning, the computational framework will simulate threat scenarios across diverse client contexts (e.g., corporate campuses, event venues, critical infrastructure) to identify optimal resource configurations under uncertainty. HPC resources are essential for scaling these simulations to account for millions of interacting variables, including spatial dynamics, human behavior patterns, and equipment interoperability. Additionally, machine learning models will be trained on synthetic and anonymized real-world datasets to predict emerging risks and recommend preemptive interventions.
